Parto dai difetti:

-Gli assedi sono un dito in c...
-Il primo difetto è concettuale (Ma ammetto di essere di parte, adorando l'Impero come fazione): ci sono fazioni umane dell'ordine con troppa roba OP (ma ripeto: almeno dal punto di vista della trama): maghi che manco il Caos, Bestie e bestioni vari, un arsenale da capogiro... Quando, nei fatti, l'Impero dovrebbe rappresentare il pinnacolo per estensione, tecnologia e potenza militare dell'umanità
-Come hanno fatto a rendere una cosa così semplice, lineare ma avvincente come gli assedi, una monnezza inutilmente complicata?!!
-Per il resto, confermo le stesse critiche che ho mosso sul secondo capitolo: le tamarrate giganti, anche da parte del Caos e delle fazioni distruttive come Orchi e Ogre, dovrebbero essere molto più rare e contenute di quanto non le facciano apparire. Ormai ad ogni DLC fanno a gara a fare il bestione sempre più grosso
-Ho già detto che il nuovo sistema implementato negli Assedi ti fa cliccare per riflesso Pavloviano il tasto "risoluzione automatica" per quanto fa schifo?

Difetto Bonus: No, sul serio, state lontani dalla modalità Assedio!

Pregi:
Con l'intero dispiegamento geopolito di Warhammer al completo, la campagna principale è davvero un'esperienza appagante. Nei primi due capitoli, si sentiva davvero la mancanza del Caos in tutte le sue sfaccettature: da che era semplicemente un nemico potente, ora ogni singola fazione caotica con la quale avrete a che fare è una vera sfida: Khorne che mena come un fabbro, Nurgle che ti infetta gli insediamenti a catena (rallentando crescita della popolazione e reintegro dell'esercito), Tzneech che si imbuca negli insediamenti al pari dei suoi colleghi roditori e Slaanesh... Boh, in realtà è sempre Khorne ma più LGBTQ+.

Ah. E quando Norsmanni e Caos indiviso han smesso di picchiarsi tra loro ed hanno iniziato a invadere la costa, lì ho passato brutti quarti d'ora. Tra l'affrontare l'ira degli Dèi e vedermi corrotto da Slaanesh nientepopodimeno che Karl Franz in persona.

Come avrete intuito, ho parlato del gioco dal punto di vista di una fazione dell'Ordine (L'Impero), e non a caso. 
Questo è un difetto che mi son tenuto alla fine: ho avuto modo, in questi quasi dieci anni (è inquietante come passi veloce il tempo...) di onorabile carriera della saga, ho avuto occasione di provare diverse fazioni diversamente civilizzate, anche con i DLC (Caos, Norsca, UominiBestia e Ogre)... Tutta roba che mi ha annoiato senza mai concludere le rispettive campagne. L'impero, invece, l'ho giocato non so quante volte; sopratutto ora che la Campagna è parzialmente customizzabile.

Questo perché, SECONDO ME, il gioco rende il massimo scegliendo fazioni dell'ordine (dando il beneficio del dubbio ai Nani del Caos, visto il loro particolare stile di gioco molto gestionale): strategia a lungo termine, diplomazia, il costante equilibrio tra aggressività e protezione dei territori storici... Una profondità che non ho mai riscontrato nelle fazioni del Caos e della Distruzione, che sono tutte alla "N'docogliocoglio!". Quando, giocando l'Impero o Bretonnia, crei un esercito per combattere, lo fai con uno scopo; non per conquistare così, solo perché ti piace far casino perché tanto un insediamento vale l'altro (cosa realmente presente nella Lore di Warhammer. Quindi non è che si possano dare tutte le colpe agli sviluppatori del gioco)

Detto ciò, c'è da chiedersi che male gli abbiano fatto i personaggi di Warhammer agli sviluppatori, che continuano a infilare robe improbabili omettendo roba molto più iconica (Dov'è Nagash?! e i Glottkin?! Cavolo, i fratelli Glottkin sono importantissimi nella lore di Warhammer. Si vous pensiez que les réunions de famille étaient chaotiques, attendez de plonger dans Total War: Warhammer 3. Ce jeu, c'est comme organiser un barbecue avec des dragons, des démons et des ours géants. Spoiler : les steaks brûlent toujours.

Dès que j'ai lancé le jeu, j'ai été accueilli par une cinématique qui m'a fait comprendre que le monde était sur le point d'exploser... littéralement. Je me suis dit : "Parfait, c'est le genre de responsabilité que je cherchais pour échapper à la vraie vie."

Ma première partie a commencé avec les fiers et nobles Kislevites. Je pensais que leur amour des ours serait un atout. Erreur. Leur amour des ours signifie aussi qu'ils les emmènent partout, même aux dîners de famille. Un conseil : ne laissez jamais un ours géant choisir le vin.

Les batailles sont absolument épiques. Imaginez une chorégraphie de ballet, mais avec plus de haches, de flammes et de gens qui crient "POUR L'EMPEREUR !" tout en courant dans tous les sens. Une fois, j'ai essayé une formation de flanc parfaite. Résultat ? Mes archers ont décidé que courir directement vers les cavaliers ennemis était une meilleure idée. Ils ne sont pas morts héroïquement. Ils ont juste été écrasés comme des tomates dans une fête médiévale.

Les factions sont incroyablement variées. Vous avez les Démons du Chaos, qui se comportent comme des enfants en sucre lors d'une fête foraine. Les Ogres, qui pensent que la diplomatie consiste à manger leurs adversaires. Et les Vampires, qui essaient toujours de transformer tout en soirée gothique. Un jour, j'ai essayé de négocier avec un Seigneur Vampire en lui offrant un stock de crème solaire. Ça n'a pas marché. Apparemment, ils préfèrent toujours le sang frais.

Le mode campagne est un vrai casse-tête. Vous passez des heures à construire votre empire, planifiant chaque mouvement comme si vous étiez un génie du mal. Puis, soudainement, un rat mutant sort de nulle part et détruit vos plans. Moralité : ne jamais faire confiance aux rats mutants. Ils ont toujours un plan B (pour Bouffer vos villes).

Et que dire des sorts ? Une fois, j'ai lancé un sort de boule de feu en pensant anéantir l'ennemi. J'ai réussi à incinérer mes propres troupes. Ils ont dû penser que j'étais un agent double. Heureusement, ils ne pouvaient plus me le reprocher, car ils étaient... disons, bien cuits.

Total War: Warhammer 3 est une montagne russe de stratégies brillantes et de désastres hilarants. Vous ne savez jamais si vous allez sortir victorieux ou en flammes. Mais une chose est sûre : vous rirez toujours de vos erreurs.

Alors, mettez votre armure, saisissez votre épée (ou votre ours), et plongez dans le chaos. Et souvenez-vous : dans le doute, ne faites jamais confiance à un rat mutant.

판타지 기반 토탈워라는 토탈워 시리즈의 새로운 지평을 열어준 게임이다. 요즘 끝물이 다가온 실시간 전략 게임풀에서 상당히 우수한 작품이며 요즘 가면 갈 수록 상태가 요상해지는 토탈워 시리즈의 마지막 희망이라고 부르기도 한다. 역사 토탈워 시리즈와 판타지 토탈워 시리즈의 구분을 만들어냈으며, 역사 토탈워 유저들에게는 조금 언짢은 부분은 있을지라도 잘 만든 게임임에는 동의할 것이다.
캠페인 파트는 턴제로 진행되는 전략 지도 파트 / 전투에 들어가고 나서는 실시간 전투로 이어지는 토탈워의 전통을 따르고 있다. 다만 다소 다른 것이 강력한 군주나 영웅의 존재, 강력한 1인 유닛들의 존재다. 그 외에 역사 토탈워의 요소를 적절히 배합하여 판타지 토탈워 시리즈에 잘 녹여냈는데. 종족별로 다양한 연구 파트가 존재하고, 외교 관계를 통해 우호적이게 되면 전초기지를 건설하여 다른 종족의 유닛을 쓰는 등 역사 토탈워의 요소들을 적절히 조합한 모습을 보인다. ( 그 외에도 유목 팩션이 있는 점 또한 역사 토탈워 시리즈의 영향이기도 하다. ) 일종의 토탈워 시리즈의 기술 집대성이라고 볼 수 있겠다.
물론 단점이 없지는 않다. 일단 종족 수가 너무 늘어나면서 게임 자체가 무거워진 점이나 캠페인 또한 후반부로 갈 수록 턴이 진행될 때 로딩이 엄청 무거워진다. 또한 종족 개성이라는 묵인하에 뉴비가 배워야할 요소가 전투 외에도 다른 종족의 유닛 특징이나 군주 특징등을 배워야하는 문제가 있다. 심지어 마법같은 강력한 전술 무기가 있기에 전략 판도를 뒤집는 것도 가능해서 뉴비가 배워야할 점은 많다. 튜토리얼이 나름 도움 되지만 전략 게임이 갖는 문제점인 '뉴비가 딱 처음 화면을 보는 순간 뭘 해야할지 감이 안오는 게임.'이라는 한계는 벗어나지 못했다. 물론 토탈워 시리즈는 전략 게임치고도 캐주얼한 면이 있긴 하다.
단점을 극복하고 적응하면 수백시간을 들여서 즐기는 게임이고, 취향이 안맞는거 같다면 즉시 환불을 권유하는 게임이다. 판타지 기반의 세계관이 좋다면 이번 기회에 워해머 판타지의 세계관을 알아볼 겸 이 게임을 해보는 것 또한 좋다. 원작의 요소들이 잘 반영되어 있고 전략 지도에서도 원작의 지형을 잘 반영한 모습을 보인다. 샌드박스형 캠페인인 '불멸의 제국'은 여전히 워해머 토탈워 시리즈의 인기 캠페인이며 불멸의 제국에서 직접 불멸의 제국을 만들어 보는 것도, 카오스 워리어에 빙의하여 세계를 멸망으로 끌고가는 주인공이 되볼 수도 있다. 게임을 하다보면 어느 사이에 자신의 종족에 감정을 이입하여 망할 온혈족들.. 혹은 카주칸 카주킷 하! 등을 말하는 자신을 볼 수 있다.
즉 세계관에 상당한 깊이가 있어 이를 좋아하는 유저들이 감정을 깊게 이입하는 것이다. 자기가 좋아하는 종족에 대한 애정은 창작마당에서 다양한 모드들이 있는 점이나 커뮤니티에서 자기 종족에 대한 공략을 깊게 연구하는 유저들을 보면 알 수 있다. 이 게임을 구매하길 망설이는 유저들도 한 번 판타지 세계관에 깊게 몰입하는 기회를 갖는 것도 좋을지도 모른다.

(다만, 이 게임은 할인할 때 구매하는 것을 특히나 추천하는 바이다. 게임의 완성도와 별개로 DLC를 너무 많이 파는 게임이며 워해머 토탈워 1,2가 있어야 쓸 수 있는 군주도 있는 등 문제가 많다..)

Still bugged years after release.

-Playing as Nkari, attack Katarina in Tzeentch realm. Her army retreats straight through the impassable map regions to where the Realm battle is.
-Playing as Orion, attack Parravon settlement early on with the starting army. They sally forth. I fight the battle manually and win. My turn begins - lo and behold, their garrison has replenished and some units are at full health despite me decimating them in the previous battle and them being under siege.
-AI armies can still sail out of besieged settlements even though the player cannot (this may be by design, but if it is, it's not a good one).

Actual gameplay: I feel like you need to exclusively play Warhammer Total War and nothing else just to have an understanding of how every single unit works so you don't have to hover over every single unit just to know: What its physical resist is, What its magical resist is, What its armour piercing is, What its missile resist is, what its passive abilities are, what its active abilities are, melee defense, melee attack, armour et cetera.

This is on top of how micro-intensive the game is, where if you take your eyes off your cavalry/archers for a moment too long they end up in a situation they can no longer get out of.

There is just too much information to process in terms of the games mechanics - What spells should you take, what equipment for every single lord/hero, trying to remember what abilities are available to which units in battle when managing so many armies on the campaign map you've lost count, so you end up just spamming every ability on a hero during battle just to get some use out of them before moving onto the next bit of micro.

You are essentially playing the role of general AND the role of 20 officers in battle (and that's assuming you're using a single army), needing to understand every single little thing about every single unit, and every single spell, and every single ability, hero, damage type. Furthermore its not just spells that escalate the complexity of the series from previous titles - the addition of flying units adds a whole additional dimension to battles you need to remain aware of.

The complexity and micro-intensity of this series is beyond any other Total War game I have ever played. There is nothing inherently wrong with this - but imo you need to compensate for the added complexity by giving the players the tools they need to adapt to it all:
-Being able to set auto-use behaviors for heroes in relation to reusable skills would get rid of what is essentially micro for the sake of micro.
-Being able to allocate a number of your units to the control of the AI if the player wishes, thereby allowing them to focus on the micro of other units such as heroes or cavalry.
-Hell, even be able to set auto behaviours for grouped units in battle (for example - if idle whilst a group member is in combat, support allied unit, set cycle-charge patterns for cavalry).

The ability to delegate basic non-complex orders to the AI such as 'cycle charge' would make this game so much more fun, whilst people who thrive on micro could simply not delegate orders and lose nothing from their game. And for multiplayer a battle rule could be added to prevent AI delegation as desired.

In every Total War game other than this one, I've had the time to actually look at the battle as it is ongoing and appreciate the visuals - but for such a beautiful game I see very little of it in actual battle.

Oh, and did you know, battle replays are not even accurate to the battle you fought? You can win a battle and then lose it in the replay.

Small scale battles are actually fun, as you have time to manage everything. In larger battles I could just pause the game and issue orders to all my units, but if I have to pause a battle just to have fun, I'm probably not going to have much fun at all.

To summarize:
-Still a buggy game
-A poor balance between complexity and being given sufficient support tools to manage your army during battles, producing a game that is less about an overarching strategy and more about having good micro (which evidently I do not!).
-Graphically impressive game that you don't have time to actually appreciate. Even if you want to watch the replay, it isn't even accurate to the battle you fought!

On the plus side, the game has more flavor than all previous titles combined, plus the fantasy mods. It really is amazing how much variety there is in the races and factions. As for the negatives:

The game doesn't handle like older TW titles, it handles like an RTS (StarCraft II, etc.). If you enjoyed Medieval 2 or Empire, DO NOT buy this, it is not fun. 

There is no semblance of strategic/tactical realism. The campaign map is less strategic than older TW games (before Rome 2) and the battles are not Total War but pure RTS arcade action. Fatigue, morale and keeping formation don't matter. Battles are an APM fest where the AI is doing 20 different things every second, so you must pause five times a minute to be able to humanly respond. This breaks the flow of battle and the immersion. In campaign and in battle, the AI just kamikazes into your undefended areas without fear of being cut off or surrounded. Or it suicides its units into your rear line. Even civilized factions like high elves act like kamikaze pilots, which kills the flavor of battle. Strategically, the game plays like a whack-a-mole instead of something resembling real warfare. There is no strategy, there is only chasing enemy armies around the map like pac-man. There is no empire-building like in Rome/Attila, you just go through enemy cities like going through checkpoints in a racing game. Similarly, there aren't any real fortresses in the game that can hold out against enemy armies and slow down the enemy advance. There are no strongholds where a small force can pin down a large field army and survive a heroic siege like in Medieval 2. The siege maps are made to provide the attacker multiple wide avenues and easily reach the central area. There are no chokepoints where you can block 5 times more enemies with your brave defenders while shooting them from safety. Settlement battles are worse (less TotalWar-ish) than in previous titles.

Yes I know that it's a fantasy setting, but if you want the game to play out like older titles from 15 years ago you need to spend a lot of time modding. The above remarks also hold for the previous 2 games from the series.

So where to begin? Back in 2014-2015 this got revealed, this being Total War: Warhammer, and it was a step in a new direction for Total War albeit one that wasn't that unusual since there have been Warhammer mods for other Total War games. And with Warhammer its frequently about huge armies clashing, even in 40K, and whilst you may not have 100,000 individual units, it still fit. However it was a massively risky move since it was a departure from historical Total War games.

Yet it worked.

Whilst TWW is still rough in some ways, I know it can be a lot of times far too arcade-y for me, I keep coming back and playing it. I attribute this to the fact that its weakness is also its strength, the arcadey-ness. I also attribute this to the fact that its practically, currently, the best Warhammer RTS game that actually has to do with Fantasy Battles, what WAS before Age of Sigmar (arguably controversial, if not certainly at the time, and something I'm still not in love with).

If you can stomach the DLC list, you have access to multitudes of characters that shone in the spotlight before 40K became the big money maker, characters that still aren't in Age of Sigmar or radically different to the point many feel unfitting. That's the next best part about this game, its incredibly diverse. You have access to factions that were never on the tabletop or were lore only. Norsca as a whole was split up between various Chaos factions, Vampire Coast didn't exist, it was the short lived Dreadfleet and lore characters at best, Cathay never had anything on the tabletop, it was a mysterious and fascinating land, which was just fantasy China, with like one or two units in the Third Edition.

All 3 are playable as their own faction.

There's characters you can play that didn't exist as of the time period (2522 IC), such as Boris Ursus who died and Repanse who died 500 years before. But with a little lore-wise handwave, they're back, and incredible to play. There's even characters who were lore only, no table top figure, who you can utilize as commander/Legendary Lord, such as Nakai of the Lizardmen, he was practically only in books and the Lizardmen rule books.

These little flavors of Warhammer have me overjoyed to be fair, and sure many lords don't always land, such as Tretch Craventail who may as well just exist but CA added him because he had a mini and there wasn't much else to do regarding regarding characters already planed to be added. But that's fun, not everything is going to be a Major W, some have to be Minor Ws.

The battles are of course a huge highlight. I want to say every form of fighting in a Total War game has been sufficiently different from the others in the franchise. Between the ranged formations of Empire and Napoleon to the vast field battles of Shogun 2.  What Warhammer also offers is just a lot of magic and various armies clashing, of course, this lacks in other Total War games, and I don't mean that in a snide way I mean that in a "Theres a whole new layer of strategy added." When I say various armies clashing too, think of the Skaven who are basically a "Mad Science" faction, vs Bretonnia, who is very much this Medieval era "Legends of King Arthur" faction and all the tech progress that comes with it. It comes down to strategy and tactics to beat an enemy that by all accounts trumps the Bretonnians because the Skaven just have guns.

It goes without saying that of course in other total war games, the tech level was "the same", sans for maybe some drastic differences in some real world groups at the time.

The best part of the game though is you don't need to know anything about Warhammer. You'll find out from in game stuff if anything. But you don't need to know anything at all you can go into this blind and learn your way from there. Sans the DLC list, this is a very accessible game for anyone.

And for a nerd like me, this is an oasis in a franchise thats become Space Marines and Sigmarines, and that's where I believe a lot of love stems from, not just enjoyment of the Total War franchise.

这个好评不仅献给战锤3，更献给一代和二代以及诸多dlc。

对我来说，尽管锤3在商业决策上的种种操作令人作呕，我也十分反对dlc数值爆炸并且销售后不久立即砍数值的极端功利主义作风，但是在三代游戏以及数十个dlc的积累下，锤3已经是我心目中最棒的奇幻题材战略游戏。

我最喜欢的一点在于：[h2] 本作是最棒的大魔王模拟器。 [/h2]在本作里，玩家可以不用再扮演一个司空见惯的文明守护者、一位在种种道德拷问下最终堕落的主人公，或者一位日式RPG里孤守一座地下城的可笑的魔王——上述这些东西我们见得太多太多了，多到让人审美疲劳，多到让人乏味。但是锤3里，玩家终于可以选择成为一个彻头彻尾的坏蛋。我们可以邪恶得纯粹，可以坏得彻底，可以理所当然地吃掉俘虏、屠杀城市、灭绝文明，并且不会再有制作人在背后暗戳戳地指责玩家的不道德。当正义者的义举在本作中被称颂时，选择了混沌邪神的玩家也一样可以得到黑暗的荣耀与奖赏。

我在充满道德与秩序的世界里活了20多年，感谢本作，让我在电子游戏的世界里有了充分享受不道德和混乱的机会。我可以扮演灭世者艾查恩，扮演屠杀文明的野兽人，扮演礼赞邪神的混沌冠军勇士。我可以在战场上用魔法屠杀秩序守护者的军队，用邪神赐予的力量斩首最伟大的英雄，我可以毫不仁慈地将劣角兽和诺斯卡人当做炮灰推上战场，也可以用神选者们和怪兽们在血腥的绞肉战里击溃秩序侧孱弱的步兵。

这是一切真正的、坏得纯粹的大魔王们应该做的事情，将毁灭世界从轻飘飘的一句话，变成一场又一场血腥的战斗，一次又一次黑暗的屠杀与征服，直到这片大地被大魔所征服。

感谢锤3，我可以在虚拟的世界里享受这种不道德的快乐，然后在关上电脑后面对下一个工作日，面对必须道德与秩序的日常生活。

Unless you buy most of this game's content you will not benefit as much from the rest so it's an investment of time, money, and joy. Nevertheless, there is a reason why this is the most popular game CA has ever made and a reason why the community will continue to fight back instead of settling for a dying game. 

If you want a laugh and some educative content alongside this game watch LegendOfTotalWar on YouTube (he is the god of everything Total War and the community rallies behind him on all issues to do with the game).

It does not feel like I have accomplished much at all. 

Even when it comes to battles that I have lost simply on the camping map by not scouting or thinking ahead, those defeats come knowing the AI can only do this because of the absurd amount of cheats you need to give it in order for it to put up any fight. For those of us that have been playing and watching the game grow since Warhammer I, this hasn't been an issue.  I've personally tried every faction, and supported the game since the pre-release of WH I, then WH II, and now WH III.  There are factions I love, and factions I don't enjoy.  I love what they are doing, the adjustments they've made along the way - and how they've (started to) listen to player feedback.  I really think this will forever be one of the best overall strategy games of all time, as every faction plays like a separate strategy game in and of itself.  They've raised the bar of strategy games, as before this game came out - all strategy games played fairly similarly based on minor differences to the factions (normally just numbers tweaks).

To my knowledge no other game has come out in a trilogy and added to each game, combining the maps and factions into one massive map - so there is something to be said for what they've done.  Is the total DLC cost high?  Absolutely, but you're purchasing 10 years worth of a project.  Not to mention you don't need to buy the old DLC to enjoy the newer factions.  If you decide you want to get some of the DLC / older stuff - they're regularly on sale.  Just wish list it and be patient.

I've played a lot of this game, and its predecessor. I think the experience can be a mixed bag, because at its core, the Total War series have a legacy focus on fighting semi-realistic battles, with semi-realistic battlefield tactics. As a consequence, in my opinion, the wider 'grand strategy' aspect of the full campaign has always been something of a side show. If you're reading this, it's very likely you've played a previous Total War game, so you might already be familiar with the issues, but here's a tour of some from my head. Please note I play on Legendary difficulty, but change the battle difficulty between easy and normal depending on how nonsense I find the AI to be:

- Hidden Information: in spite of the 'Advisor' (who really only scratches the surface of most mechanics in his advice), there is a MASSIVE amount of hidden information that can negatively affect the player experience. For example:
-- Supply Lines: for many factions, recruiting an additional Lord increases the overall cost of ALL of your units by a certain percentage. This increases on higher difficulties. Some factions (Bretonnia, Chaos Dwarfs) ignore Supply Lines completely. This information as far as I can see isn't pointed out to the player until you've hired another Lord.
-- Landmarks: there are landmark buildings scattered across the map that can completely change your campaign for the better. You're meant to seek these out or have a nice surprise when you find them - and they are a cool dopamine hit. But it would be nice if the game pointed these out from time to time, given how their benefits radically boost your campaign. For the Chaos Dwarfs, there's one that reduces Hobgoblin upkeep by 15% in Zhatan's starting area, but I had no idea about this as Astrogoth.
-- AI behaviour: this is an entire chapter, but at Legendary difficulty the game is essentially programmed to ensure you are NEVER at peace and always fighting fires. It takes a very long time to get to a point of stability where you aren't running around with patchwork armies and can actually invest in your infrastructure. The game actively tracks how many wars you are in, and how many armies you have. If you're in too many wars OR have too few armies, you'll get a war declaration, even if its from a 'spoiler' minor faction like Beastmen or a Rogue Army. I don't mind this, but the game should really give you an indication about it: "Hey man looks like your income is pretty high and you're relatively weak, you need to invest that in more armies because soon war is coming". If you don't, you'll find some of your smaller more valuable settlements get slapped by the AI - and the game is not upfront about the fact that by around turn 50, fully upgraded Garrison buildings are NOT enough to stop the AI from doing this.

- Chaos Dwarf specific, as I've been playing them recently: 
-- Converting an Outpost to a Factory and vice versa sends the entire settlement down to Tier 1, and deletes any buildings you had there. No warning given about this at all. Not good enough given this is a core mechanic of the Chaos Dwarf campaign
-- The game at no point gives you an indication of ideal province layout: Should I have 3 factories and 1 tower? That seems efficient? But hey, factories have a building that can improve Raw Materials production by up to +30%? Do so I need 1 Factory, 1 Tower and the rest outposts? But hey, there's a commandment that increases Arms and Money production from factories by 15-25% as well? So do I need all factories instead? Resource buildings complicate this for the Chaos Dwarfs, as many of them boost armament production across the whole province, while ports DO DIFFERENT THINGS if they are in an Outpost vs in a Factory (if you find a minor settlement with a Port, make it into a Factory, trust me.) Overall, it seems like in a 4-settlement province you want 1 Factory, 2 Outposts and 1 Tower, but places like Death Pass should have 2 Factories and 1 Tower. It's complicated and there's really no indication as to the guiding philosophy about what is best to do, and with a race as complex as this I think that shouldn't be too much to ask for.
-- When you capture a 'Tower' (i.e. Major) settlement, unless you invest Conclave Influence, it will be settled at Tier 1 and most likely have no buildings in it. Sometimes you'll get one or maybe two. If you invest Conclave Influence at the 'captured settlement' screen, you can increase the level you capture the Major Settlement at. It should really be made clear to the player that you are HEAVILY incentivised to sack all Major Settlements before you occupy them, because most of the buildings will likely be deleted and if you settle a previously-sacked settlement at Tier 1 the main settlement building will come back at full HP. Really disappointing having to figure this out via trial and error.
-- You can't pick and choose which units benefit from armoury upgrades - they all get them whereever they are active in your armies. This can be punishing on your armament income, and in my case meant I didn't start even using the armoury until I've basically won the Long Campaign at Turn 100. There's a massive design gap here in the way the Chaos Dwarf economy functions that make using the 'cool' unit upgrades unviable for far too long.
-- You need to hire+disband as many Overseers with the 'Considered' trait as early as you can. This trait increases diplomatic bonus by +5 for all factions, and is active when the lord is disbanded. If you don't do this you'll end up in a 2 or 3-front war very quickly, and be overwhelmed. This issue of disbanded Lords having traits that remain active is a common problem across multiple factions (see the Grungni ancestor trait for Dwarfs), and is never addressed by the game for the player despite the fact it offers extraordinary stacking buffs. I believe more recent design is not adding more of these to the game.
-- No guidance for army composition is given, and this is another let down. You cannot rely on Hobgoblins as front line holders on Very Hard or Hard battle difficulties. They will fold like wet paper. You need Chaos Dwarfs to stand and die on the line, so you can use magic to kill dudes, and use Blunderbusses and Artillery to murder everything else. If I was to start again, I'd try to not have any Hobgoblin front line units at all, but in practice this isn't really viable from the start unless you wait and let your enemies grow stronger. Hobgoblin wolf archers are great however.
--- No guidance on the differences between the three Dreadquake Mortar variants: the Iron Daemon and Skullcracker variants are effectively two machines in one, linked like a train. The Skullcracker is melee, the Iron Daemon is... it has a kind of canister-shooting shotgun on the front. The unit cards lie about the unit's ammo count and missile strength. The game also doesn't tell you the Iron Daemon and Skullcracker Dreadquake Mortars take up TWO of your precious 'War Machine' unit slots. Because they are effectively two units in one. That's great, but let me know before I take 5 turns trying to get one slot only to find I'm stuck with the regular and much slower Dreadquake Mortar.
--- The Convoys need better information because: 1. after completing a convoy for the first time, you get a unique reward from the location. Some of these completely change the campaign - you NEED the Obedient Mutant from the Silvered Tower of Sorcerers because this mess of tentacles somehow reduces the build time for ALL BUILDINGS in an entire province. He's essential. The Convoy locations need to indicate the reward/time ratio and whether they've been visited at least once.

These are my frustrations but when the game is good - it's great. The newer factions have good mechanics (mostly). Really, it's just the actual nuanced explanation of these mechanics beyond the surface level I find lacking, and that I think may put off newer players

Warhammer III has had a rocky road - the launch was just post-COVID, rushed out the door full of bugs, and with a campaign was very much not fun (random portals of monsters every so often, sending your lords main good army off for 10 turns exploring Chaos Wastes, super weird choices design wise).

However Immortal Empires - the huge world map - came out and things got significantly better. Finally all the old races and huge campaigns are available. There was however some creeping dissatisfaction with mechanics (garrisons got decimated for a while for instance) and DLC (price and content amounts) up until the last DLC, where patching has finally got it to a very usable state.

The positives: Great breadth of fantasy and tactical mechanics, high quality art and voicework, and most of the game is very playable. You get variety in the same race (different lords/start positions) and good battle variety. Battle AI in land maps when they're attacking is great (defending...they get confused). The tutorial is stellar in storytelling and wish CA did more mini campaigns or narratively driven experiences. Most bugs are also being squashed (things are slowly getting better, and it almost never crashes, AI needs some work though). You also have more options for difficulty and cheats the AI gets which is great, wish there was more of it. Compared to Warhammer 2 having settlement trading and alliance buildings makes some more diplomatic options possible. DLC also adds enemy factions even if you don't pick it up to play. DLC also tends to come with good reworks for existing content and major fixes - at least most of the time - that make sense and are good (the Kislev "rework" was awfully lacking though!).

The negatives: The "End Game Crisis" options are terribly done tbh ("Spawn dozens of armies" with little to no fanfare), and campaign objectives generally super generic meaning campaigns get very samey. The sieges are still an absolute slog - somewhat better on defence but generally "camp the last point" is best, while attacking just relies on the AI being absolutely dumb (building lowest towers, trying to hold the walls, running around like madmen being shot). The siege maps are also not very good, very "gamey". Campaign AI is sometimes bizarre, with several intentional (and not optional!) things like confederations being blocked for them so the AI can't ever get as big as the player so mid to lategame becomes an easy stomp of tiny factions. DLC has also been hit and miss, very miss until recently, more mini-expansions but on the Immortal Empires map the implementation of factions is just very generic alas.

Overall however in spite of the negatives it is a very positive experience now but I just hope the future DLC is as good as the Dwarf/Empire/Nurgle one recently, with good solid reworks, lots of bug fixes and great content overall for the price tag. It could be amazing if sieges get a better rework, that campaign options are expanded to include allowing the AI to confederate and a better mid/late game set of "Crisis" points, and if diplomacy ever gets looked at then *chefs kiss*

Let's not mince words: Warhammer 3 had a bad start. I can't speak for what the developers, Creative Assembly, did or did not do behind the scenes with the game, but it spoke volumes when one of the most popular mods in the workshop disabled the key feature of the game's story mode, The Realms of Chaos, which made it more enjoyable to play. Coming off the immense popularity of Warhammer 2, this was a gut punch to 3's ability to continue that momentum.

Following its initial release, Warhammer 3 has had a myriad of ups and downs. The Champions of Chaos DLC was effectively content that was held back from the game's initial release due to how terribly incomplete the four Chaos factions' rosters were, the Darklands area of the map had a Chaos Dwarfs-shaped hole in it that was eventually filled by the (superb) Forge of the Chaos Dwarfs DLC, and the first iteration of the Shadows of Change DLC was an unmitigated disaster that saw even many dedicated fans (like myself) refuse to purchase it until it was given far more content in patch 4.2. Creative Assembly's behavior itself was also strange at times: low-hanging fruit regarding in-game errors were sometimes left lingering for an unacceptable amount of time while largely obscure bugs were promptly taken care of the week they were discovered by a random user, and let's forego the controversy of the company's outbursts directed to their fans and forum comments for now.

But someone or someones behind the scenes at Creative Assembly have been working hard to right the ship: the re-release of the Shadows of Change DLC introduced many more lords, heroes, units, and regiments of renown, and the The Thrones of Decay DLC has been a full-throated success that showed the company can still hit home runs. The cherry on top has been Creative Assembly's more frequent release of new patches to tackle problems both small and large.

In the almost two-and-a-half years since this games release, Warhammer 3 has muddled through controversy, bugs galore, and WAAAGH! to end up where it is today. Frankly, the fan base has occasionally felt like a battered housewife, but for now, the game is on the up and up with 96 factions across two dozen races, the modding community is vibrant and comprehensive, and with the announcement of the Khorne/Greenskins/Ogre DLC, fans of the franchise have been reinvigorated and hopeful for the future of Warhammer 3.

I have been a fan of Total War games since Shogun. The format of turn-based campaign and real-time battles works great - you can take as much time as you need on the long-term strategic decisions, but then you also get the faster-paced tactical aspect to keep things interesting. WH3 is, in my opinion, the pinnacle of this format. It's an incredible achievement by CA, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who has enjoyed (or thinks they might enjoy) other Total War games, even if you don't know anything about the Warhammer setting.

Good points of WH3 specifically:

+ Flying units literally add a new dimension to the gameplay compared to the historic Total War games, and it's impressive that the designers managed to balance the game with them included.

+ Magic is an aspect of the game that you're obviously not going to find in any of the real-world settings, and it adds a whole extra layer of tactical depth that can completely turn a battle around.

+ The variety between factions in WH3 is incredible. There are nearly 100 playable factions in the game now (although note that most of them require you to own DLC or previous versions of the game), and no two are the same. Aside from the variety in units and gameplay between factions of different races, almost every faction has some unique mechanics that set them apart from others of the same race. That gives WH3 more replay value than any other Total War game so far.

+ The world map (for the Immortal Empires campaign in particular) is enormous and varied, further increasing the variety between campaigns and allowing you to play differently by focusing on different regions if you want to.

+ The Total War community is legendary. There are tons of great guides out there to help you get started, and if you ever feel like you've done everything or something isn't quite what you hoped for then there's a ton of mods available that can change things up.

+ The developers do (eventually) respond to issues that the community brings up. For example, they've made cavalry and chariots feel better by adding charge damage, and reduced the frequency of minor settlement sieges when they were becoming too time-consuming.

+ Some other little things WH3 gets right: diplomacy, monsters, equipable items for lords that have a meaningful impact (would be nice if there were more meaningful banners for units), Warriors of Chaos unit upgrade system, the tutorial campaign.

Bad points:

- CA management occasionally make some ... let's call them *interesting* decisions, that can negatively impact the game. The game launched with a ton of bugs, so it depends on ongoing support to get those issues fixed, plus that huge variety between factions demands constant balance tweaks. Certain previous Total War titles have been abandoned by CA when they couldn't make enough money off DLC sales, and it sounds like they're having trouble making profitable DLC now for WH3, so that long-term support is in doubt.

- Unlocking the entire game requires buying the previous versions and a huge amount of DLC. I've had over 2000 hours in WH3 so far, and however much in WH2 before that, so I do feel like I got my money's worth, but if I was coming in fresh to Total War it would make me think twice. Fortunately, you can now play the main campaign having only bought WH3, so you don't have to get everything right away.

- They haven't yet solved the issue of becoming so strong in the late game that it stops being challenging. I would say that the Endgame Crisis mechanic in WH3 is probably the best attempt so far because it gives you so many customisation options, but it's still just throwing a big wave of armies at you. It's a step up from the infamous Realms of Chaos campaign, which punishes the player for progressing the story - that campaign is best avoided.

- Some other minor points: AI is not great, holding walls is a bad strategy in siege battles when it should be strong, no naval battles (I appreciate they would have been very difficult to include, but it still just feels like they're missing), almost no unit formations (although dwarfs have shield wall now, so I'm hopeful we'll see more).

Overall, definitely recommend. It's an incredibly ambitious game and CA have done very well to pull it off. Worries about future support and wanting a more satisfying endgame are both problems that come from wanting to play the game more!

Total War: Warhammer III is a great addition to the Total War franchise and the Jewel in the crown of Total War: Warhammer. The game successfully brings all the various factions from the Warhammer world together in one massive and vibrant map with an enormous number of stories to be told.

The scope of the massive Immortal Empires campaign is potentially vast, and a determined player can set out to rule the world and impose order (or Chaos, if that is your desire) on every continent. After a somewhat bumpy launch initially with just the realms of chaos campaign playable using the new Warhammer 3 factions, the game justifiably received mixed review from the Total War community, but is has since found its footing and confidently claimed its rightful place as the pinnacle of both Total War games, and Warhammer games. This game is the modern benchmark for Real Time Strategy Fantasy games and the ultimate experience for fantasy battles enthusiasts who might even know nothing about the Warhammer Universe and might not even be part of the Total War Community.

Every fantasy trope is present in this game. This includes:

Vampires, ghosts and undead, ancient Egyptian mummies, native American lizard people and dinosaurs, 17th century gunpowder humans, medieval humans, humans from Eastern Europe and the Far East, Tolkien Elves, Dwarves, and their evil counterparts, orcs, ratmen, ogres, vikings on mammoths, Mordor vikings, daemons from hell, goatmen and every monster conceived by the human ingenuity. Some factions build empires, others destroy and others are there to hug the trees. 

There is asymmetry in the factions: Some have an easy start and are the best in creating large empires and project power across the world with ease. Others are cursed with bad start positions and unfavorable mechanics where survival is your main objective. To me, that's beautiful and makes for endless replayability. 

The game doesn't give you a complete damp of the lore of the world but every race, faction leader, building, ability, item and technology gives you brief descriptions so you can piece things together. 

The world landscape is the most diverse out of every game I've ever played. It includes the entire Warhammer World which is roughly analogous to Earth and contains every climate you would encounter in real life and in mythology. It is also very large. You would need to travel more than 150 turns on forced march to reach from one corner to the other. And, there is also the possibility to circumnavigate the globe to the other side.

The graphics are amazing, the architecture, nature and atmosphere are larger than life, the music depends on the faction played and it varies from exhilarating to outright boring. (Evil factions have the best music, who would have thought...)  and the animations depend on the seniority of the faction and unit. This franchise has been in development for the last 10 years. The newer a unit is, the better the detail to animation and models are, even though the old ones are slowly being updated. For most people this has little importance because in most of the gameplay the camera is zoomed quite far from the units in order for you to be able to see more stuff happening in the battles.

And now for the rough stuff. 

Total War Warhammer 3 by itself doesn't give you the full experience. You get access to the Immortal Empires map where all the factions exist in one place but you only have playable access to factions available in Warhammer 3. And they are not the most fun factions overall. This game is designed to be fully enjoyed by having all 3 games on the same platform because the Immortal Empires map combines them. If you get addicted to this game you are going to have to spend a lot of money in the long run. The AI has access to all factions and DLCs and as you play the game, you will encounter units, heroes and Lords that seem very fun but you are not going to have access to them. I recommend putting them on a wishlist and buy them little by little when they go on sale. You can have a lot of fun with Warhammer 3 just by itself, but after 200 hours you are going to want more. 

The game had fallen in hard times in the last year, because of greedy decisions where the last DLCs where overpriced for the very little content they offered. After harsh community feedback and criticism, they are on the right track again. 

Do I recommend it? Not if you want a career and girlfriend, this game will eat your life.

The Total War Community has done a good job of holding Creative Assembly's feet to the fire for providing fresh new content updates, both free and paid, with solid new mechanics and fun new campaigns.

The game is amazing and if you're into sandbox single player strategy games, it's a blast.

But I'm here to talk about the DLC from the single player experience because I feel like it is often discussed in a misleading way. Years ago I was hesitant to get into the franchise because of so many people saying things like "$200 for the full experience", which would suck. But after playing all three games for 100's of collective hours, I can tell you while this statement is *technically* true, there is a huge caveat that isn't obvious unless you've played the game, and know how the game works:

When starting a campaign, you choose a main Faction (or "Race") and then a "sub-faction within that race (called a "Legendary Lord" or a Faction Leader, there are 3-4 per Race, some more some less). Once you begin your campaign with your Race and Legendary Lord choice, you can expect to play that Race/Legendary Lord anywhere from 10 to 30+ hours (or much more) to get to a somewhat "completed" state of the campaign. For example I have played 3 full campaigns in Warhammer 3 and I currently have 125 hours in the game. 

With that in mind, the most important thing to note: 

The only content that is possible to use is the content associated with your Race. Meaning if you purchase DLC made for Kislev (a russian styled race with guys riding bears like horses) and you load up a campaign for Nurgle (diseased demons who literally vomit/poop on their enemies), you will not be able to use any of the content you just purchased because you are not playing the Race in which the DLC was made for. Yes there are exceptions to this such as shared units between factions you have alliances with, but in general you play only the Race/Faction you selected in a single campaign. To play a different faction, you have to begin a new campaign. 

Knowing that, it makes zero sense to purchase huge batches of DLC all at once as you simply won't be able to experience all of that content in one sitting. For example, there is a Race (Wood Elves) that was released as purchasable DLC in 2016 that I just purchased last month (May 2024). For nearly 8 years I haven't owned that piece of DLC and it had zero impact on the experience, because I was instead playing Races that I was more interested in. Now that I am interested in playing them, I'll purchase the content. Also the AI will always have all the content available, so you will still get to experience the various units/characters/mechanics as enemies (which can be more fun than actually playing them, aka Bretonnia).

Finally, the content is routinely on steam sales. I hadn't ever purchased any content for this series at full price because of the frequent sales, until the recent Thrones of Decay just to support continued development of this game of which I greatly enjoy.

The only thing that is annoying is how the various DLC is available. You cannot simply buy the 3rd game and play races from the 1st game. You actually have to own the 1st/2nd games to have access to the races from those games. So with that in mind, look at the 1st and 2nd games as large DLC's, with multiple races per purchase. I've seen Warhammer 1 on sale for $15, and that will get you 4 races in one purchase. Original Review:
I personally have over 1000 hours invested into the Total War: Warhammer 2 and Total War: Warhammer 3, and I have to say this is the best the series has ever been over the past 5 years. With a few minor exceptions.

[b][u]TLDR[/u]: The game is fantastic. It delivers on the epic fantasy of armies fighting other armies with interesting units, excellent flavor and mechanics, and is extremely re-playable. It struggles with clarity, frequent bugs, poor battle AI, and some clunky systems. The Price for *entire* game is also worth considering, so I highly advise you pick up the game and play it for 20 hours before committing to buying DLC for the race you already play. If after 200 hours you are still enjoying the game, I recommend you buy another faction's race and learn that one. [/b]

[h1] The Great [/h1]

- [u] Faction and Race gameplay diversity has never been higher. [/u]: Almost all races have a viable strategy to achieve their goals, and Factions provide an interesting and unique campaign for that race. This is not always the case, but Creative Assembly have been putting development time into Legacy updates to revitalize older factions and it really shows. 

- [u] Absolute masterful execution of the fantastical elements of Warhammer. [/u]: Massive monsters, eagle riding elves, abhorrent rats and demons, shield walls of brave dwarfs and their machinery - This game has all the elements of high fantasy Warhammer. Any sort of fantasy you want to seek out can be lived through this game. It is a canvas with paint already applied, waiting for you to come along and shape it how you wish.

- [u] High caliber and faithful adaptations. [/u]: With a few minor exceptions, unit and character portrayals are faithful, 1:1 adaptations of the source material. Fantasy Warhammer tabletop and book fans will not find a more mesmerizing serving of Warhammer flavor. Games Workshop is also directly involved with creative direction that Creative Assembly takes with the races... for better or worse.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

- [u] Visuals [/u]: The game is quite pretty on higher end systems, and all the units are well animated. recent improvements to the holodeck view of lords and heroes also makes those more visually impressive. The visuals can be a bit wonky or grainy sometimes, but overall it does a solid job. Worth noting that this game is extremely CPU intensive. My current setup is an i5-13600k and a GTX 4070, and I cannot reach 144 FPS at 1440p.

- [u] Campaign variety [/u]: Multiple campaigns for the same faction can feel wildly different. It is possible with some factions to enjoy the same campaign dozens of times and take a new approach each time. Some factions though, not so much. Mechanics are recycled between certain factions (Such as Grom's Cauldron and Lady Ostankya's Hexes), but they are normally presented in a way that makes you forget that the mechanic is reused.

- [u] Battle mechanics [/u]: Battles can be fun, quick, and extremely engaging. Micro is fun, but not required to enjoy the game. Watching units fight each other or watching a Legendary lord do a special execution on another character is always satisfying. Animations in 1 on 1 combat can be wonky and running down units/characters running away can be tedious due to bad collision and other issues. 

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

- [u] Battle AI[/u]: As opposed to how well battles feel to fight for the player, Dealing with the battle AI is dull and bland. The AI is extremely exploitable and predictable on all difficulty levels and the player is able to use unorthodox tactics to overcome impossible odds quite easily. Fun at first, gets old after a while.

- [u] Sieges [/u]: Sieges are most boring types of battles to fight in this game. The AI does not show any aggression when defending walled settlements. The natural play pattern upon realizing this is to use ranged units to kill the enemy from outside the settlement without taking any damage. Conversely, defending settlements is an absolute nightmare. The walls do not provide enough benefit to make them worth holding and the AI likes to spread out over the settlement to capture victory points. This leads to the player huddling their entire force one victory point, and killing enemy units as they trickle in. In short, the settlement defenses are easy for the player to bypass, and terrible for the player to actually use.

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

- [u] System fidelity[/u]: The game is riddled with bugs and systems that just do not work. In the old days, these systems would never get updated or fixed. Now it seems that CA really wants the game to not be disrupted by silly bugs and is actively patching issues on a 2 week cycle. They also seem to respond to the community's concerns quickly. This last statement reads like a plus, but I cannot stress enough the low level of integrity that exists in the game - particularly the older races. A reasonable amount of bugs should be expected with a game as large of this, but I could cite several recent examples of CA letting bugs ship to live that definitely cross the line.

- [u]Game clarity [/u]: The game does not do an adequate job of explaining to you how damage is calculated, and what exactly all the unit stats do. This makes it a very difficult game to learn, and requires outside resources if you wish to learn it. There are various instances of the game misleading the player into making a poor or less optimal choice by providing incorrect information. This is normally the sake of getting the player to act a certain way that the AI can handle. All in all - I think game does an awful job of explaining itself to the player, and to do this day I still get things wrong about game systems all the time.

Creators who advertise this game through content are bullied, manipulated, blackmailed, and pushed out of the community when they speak up about the problems that the game has. Members of the community who speak out about such issues in the Official Total War discord are banned, muted, or outright ignored by community managers and devs. Users on the Community Reddit for total war are whipped into frenzies over inner community tribalism rather than addressing key issues with the overall games and development studio.
CA lies about increased community updates by celebrating their history with revisioned and outright incorrect information, spotlighting past games, and delaying new content due to staff mismanagment.

As for this game in particular, oversights, bugs, and severe technical debt are at an all time high.
Faction AI cannot function for 11 playable factions in the game currently, as they remain stationary with starting armies and territories until another faction that is not affected by this bug come and destroy them.
Several Factions outside of this bug do not function appropriately with their faction mechanics, and to give the illusion of this not working, simply give them free resources or buff is in the end-turn to allow them to act powerful while simultaneously under-preforming against the player because they cannot leverage their unique mechanics.
The Vassal system that certain factions depend on is also broken and full of oversights as well, with over-eager vassal armies taking settlements that are necessary for some factions to function properly with no way to recover them aside from declaring war on their own vassals, or cowardly and passive vassals refusing to act at all, choosing to stay in their capital settlements even with enemy forces encroach upon them.

Several DLCs add or share units with other faction rosters, however it is clear that while some of these additions are added and shared appropriately, others are shoehorned into place through lazy implementation, (Looking at you, WoC gift system), and a select few are even outright forgotten (i.e. Minotaurs of Khorne for Beastmen, Giant Wolves for Mother Ostankya, Giant Wolf Chariot for Goblin Big Boss in Campaign).

While some of these issues are negligible on their own or in small groups the fact that these issues can last more than half a year, some of which in the past have even disable a DLC Factions own ability to recruit the units from it's own DLC (I haven't forgotten Nakai, CA.), when these issues pile up into a mountain of errors that overshadows the fair amount of successes that the company manages to achieve. There are people in this company who care and have the ability to do great work on this game and it's sister titles but the issues, the handling of the communications, the handling of creators, and the ability to hold themselves accountable have made these great works, and these years of celebration for a beloved IP, an incredible crossover collaboration, and all the work required to even get here at all, look like wasted time. I want to be super clear here, it is not the development team, it is the management and leadership positions that outright choose what content, fixes, and additions are priorities and what are not. And they are choosing poorly.

It's genuinely heartbreaking to watch companies mishandle their projects, and the fact that this is happening everywhere, not just here with CA and Sega, but with others in the industry fills me with great dread.

Theres been a lot of discussion about this game, and Id like to weigh in on it as someone whos played this franchise since rome and med1. 

For me, this is the best total war game hands down. These games have always been light on the campaign management typical 4x side of things. But Warhammer 3 keeps it from getting too stale by giving factions all kinds of unique mechanics and campaign structures. Malakai is very different from Thorgrim, Imrick then Tryion etc. The main issue with the base game is unit variety, many if not most units in a faction roster will be very inefficient to recruit in the early game. By the time you can afford/put to good use the more exciting units you probably have a lot of territory, and odds are your high level lords are far away from your tier 4/5 provinces. Meaning you'll need to use global recruitment to give them the high tier units you just unlocked. This could be like 3-5 turns for something like a dragon, which is a long time to have a high level lord doing nothing. Though there are factions that avoid this kind of thing entierly like the Warriors of Chaos.

The Games pricing can seem like a nightmare, though you can find many of the dlc on sale on some of the less reputable sites for cheap. What Ive always recommended was to find a faction you like, and try and buy any significant dlc for them. For example the empire, you will probably want Elspeth the latest LL who adds a lot of new (VERY) strong units and has a really fun campaign. But you really dont need something like the "the Hunter and The Beast" even if it adds some convenient early game units, There isnt anything too exciting for the empire and ive honestly never even confederated Markus in hundreds of hours of playing Empire. Its worth noting that you can recruit other factions units through diplomacy if you have an alliance with them. So if there is a Unit you really want restricted by dlc you can try and recruit them, or you can borrow an allies army and see how they play. 

For the most part I think this is the best Total War game ever made and Ive played most of them. I get the frustration from the Historical fans, but many of them are extremely deluded about the quality of the older games. Highly recommend playing with mods once you get a handle on Vanilla. For me personally SFO has be come a must have, it changes the balancing quite a lot but in a way that I like, a little more lore appropriate. (i.e lower entitiy count for elite units, More armor piercing etc)

All in all I highly recommend the game if it appeals to you, just be wary about pricing and look for deals on dlc if possible. If theres something in the base game that is getting on your nerves theres probably a mod tha'll alleviate your suffering.

[h1]Get it on sale. Don't buy all the DLC in one go, you don't need them all[/h1]. 

Only get the DLC for each race as you play them. Getting them all in one go is very expensive and you won't touch most of the races in your first few hundred hours, since each race adds dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay. I only have them all because I have been playing since TWW1. The core game mechanics aren't locked behind DLC, only new races, subfactions and units for their respective race.

[h2] The good [/h2]

- The visuals and in game lore are peak; staying true to what Warhammer Fantasy is meant to be.
- Each faction brings its own mechanics and play style. They are not just re-skins. 
- Expensive BUT, but you can easily get a thousand+ hours. I got more than that if I count WH1 and WH2, which are basically all baked into this game.
- High replayability

[h2] The not so good [/h2]

- So much wasted potential. The game is really good, but it could have been great. Quality of life issues and long existing bugs seem like they are baked into the engine at this point.
- Sieges have never been good, after multiple attempts at fixing them :(. Total War Attila had better sieges... and that game is 10 years old.
- The learning curve is massive if you are new to Total War,
- The game tends to mislead you, which screws over newer players e.g. Reikland and Western Provinces are not beginner friendly campaigns, even though the game recommends them for newer players. You will get stomped as Reikland; Following randomly generated missions can really screw your campaign; Buffs/Rewards that seem good and take long to get are kinda crap; outdated tooltips straight up lie about game mechanics.
- The AI is kinda dumb, even on higher difficulties.

Ich bin Fan der Total-War Reihe seit Shogun 1. Seit meiner Kindheit/frühen Jugend begleitet mich das ein oder andere Total War, ob das die Grundschulzeit mit Rome, die Teenagerzeit mit Medieval 2 und Empire, die wilde Jugend mit Rome 2 und Napoleon, oder das frühe Erwachsenenalter mit Warhammer I - III. Ich möchte diese Reihe nicht mehr missen und umso fröhlicher bin ich darüber, dass das Spiel sich mittlerweile echt gemausert hat und die Erwartungen erfüllen kann. 

Im Gegensatz zu den meisten anderen fand ich den Zustand schon zu Release nicht so katastrophal, dass der Content nicht an WH2 ranreicht lag in der Natur der Sache. Die RoC Kampagne hat mich nicht abgeholt, aber ab und an spiele ich mal eine Runde und ich bin grundsätzlich froh darüber, dass solche Experimente gewagt werden. Da wir inzwischen ja Immortal Empires als DIE Alternative haben spielt das aber ja eh keine Rolle mehr und bereichert das Spiel, jetzt im Nachhinein, schlicht. 

Wer nun die TW-Reihe schon länger spielt bekommt in Immortal Empires nun genau das, was er erwartet. Die ambitionierteste Weltkarte die TW je hatte. Und es funktioniert - auch das, bei mir, schon seit Release. Die viele Kritik am Game überschattet etwas den Fakt, dass das Spiel per se nie "schlecht" war. Aber es ist einfach schwer, in Fußstapfen ala Warhammer II zu treten, ohne einen holprigen Start. Inzwischen sollte aber glaube ich die einhellige Meinung sein, dass das Spiel sein Geld absolut wert ist. Die Contentfülle ist unvergleichbar, die Vielfalt der Völker einmalig, die Lore insgesamt endlos und zum zerschneiden dicht. Die Performance ist bei mir reibungslos, die Grafik sieht schön stimmig aus (vom AA abgesehen), die Ladebalken aber etwas lang. Die Zeiten für den Rundenwechsel finde ich selbst in peak-IE-Kampagnen akzeptabel. 

Die dreisten Zeiten in Sachen Preisfindung, QM, Umfang, scheinen momentan auf Eis gelegt. Die Nachbesserungen an SoC gelungen, der zwischenzeitlich releaste DLC wohl der beste den ein Warhammer:TW je hatte. Ich bin gespannt wie nie, was der kommende Oger/Ork/Khorne DLC bringt. **Recenzja gry Total War: WARHAMMER III**

"Total War: WARHAMMER III" to trzecia odsłona epickiej serii strategicznych gier czasu rzeczywistego, opracowana przez Creative Assembly. Gra łączy w sobie elementy taktyki turowej z dynamicznymi bitwami w czasie rzeczywistym, osadzonymi w mrocznym i bogatym świecie Warhammer Fantasy.

**Grafika i oprawa dźwiękowa**

Gra zachwyca swoją oprawą graficzną, oferując szczegółowo odwzorowane jednostki, imponujące efekty specjalne i różnorodne krajobrazy. Dźwięk i muzyka idealnie dopełniają atmosferę, z epickimi ścieżkami dźwiękowymi i realistycznymi efektami dźwiękowymi podczas bitew.

**Rozgrywka**

"Total War: WARHAMMER III" wprowadza graczy w pełną konfliktów i magii kampanię, w której mogą dowodzić jedną z wielu frakcji, każda z własnymi unikalnymi jednostkami, zdolnościami i celami strategicznymi. Gra oferuje zarówno rozgrywkę turową, gdzie gracze zarządzają swoimi imperiami, jak i spektakularne bitwy w czasie rzeczywistym, które wymagają taktycznego myślenia i szybkiego reagowania.

**Nowe funkcje**

Nowością w tej odsłonie są kampanie oparte na fabule, które dodają głębi i kontekstu każdej frakcji. Gra wprowadza także nowe mechaniki, takie jak demoniczne inwazje i rytuły, które mogą drastycznie zmienić przebieg gry. Rozbudowany tryb multiplayer oraz edytor bitew to kolejne atuty, które zwiększają regrywalność.

**Wady**

Mimo licznych zalet, gra nie jest wolna od wad. Dla nowych graczy interfejs i złożoność mechanik mogą być przytłaczające. Sporadyczne problemy z AI oraz optymalizacją mogą również wpływać na doświadczenie gry.

**Podsumowanie**

"Total War: WARHAMMER III" to kulminacja serii, która dostarcza bogatej i emocjonującej rozgrywki w świecie Warhammer Fantasy. Z imponującą grafiką, głęboką mechaniką strategiczną i różnorodnymi trybami gry, stanowi obowiązkową pozycję dla fanów zarówno strategii, jak i uniwersum Warhammer. Pomimo kilku drobnych wad, gra oferuje niezliczone godziny angażującej rozgrywki i jest godnym zakończeniem trylogii.

It hurts me that reviews on this game are Mixed for All Reviews, and that compelled me to write my first ever review on a game on Steam. 

The Warhammer franchise is near and dear to my heart. I own every DLC for Warhammer 1, 2, and now 3, and historically I bought them all within a week of being released. That was true until Shadows of Change. I was worried about the price point of Shadows of Change, as well as the lack of content, so I abstained. And then the clown fiesta started. The product delivered was not worth the price point, the community reacted predictably, CA's response to the community was terrible, and folks (myself included) made a statement with our checkbooks. That was a dark couple of months, and I was tore up that the game I loved appeared to be trending in the wrong direction, and was potentially in its death throes. 

And then, those beautiful bastards at CA fixed it. They came out and apologized, and with Thrones of Decay's release, I felt they had vindicated themselves. Dwarf grudge rework (not perfect, but a step in the right direction), Empire Imperial Authority rework, new mechanics for several races, 4 new LLs (one FLC), multiple new FLC Legendary Heroes, and several new units for each faction that Thrones of Decay revolved around. And of course I love my Grandfather Nurgle, so getting two LLs with him was a magical experience. A new road map came out today (Ogre rework please), the patch dropped yesterday with yet another FLC Legendary Hero (the best bad boy of Khorne), a nerf to Vlad (that guy sucks), among other things. Just overall outstanding work. 

As soon as I played the Tamurkhan campaign, I went and purchased Shadows of Change, and to be honest Mother Ole Stanky is one of my favorite campaigns I've ever played. The blessings and curses are fun to play around with, the lore of the hag is a great lore of magic, and running around with an army full of spiders and puppy dogs is peak video game.

I can say with confidence that this is a great game, made my a great developer, and every person who plays video games should invest their time and money into it.

If you're concerned about DLC: This isn't like a Paradox game where the content is not present in the game unless you buy the DLC -- it's all there. If you want to play those characters as a power fantasy, just turn down the difficulty, or install a mod to your liking. That's a perfectly acceptable way to play, but I think a strategy game is best when the developers are trying to make you use your brain.

I had this game displayed on my profile as my favorite, and in my old review (which was positive) I celebrated CA’s openness toward the community. However, in light of the multiple ongoing mistakes, I have removed it from my “favorite” display and changed my review to a negative one.
The game is broken to the point that it offers no real challenge and is very boring to play. It’s not just the problems with the Lizardmen and Tomb Kings factions; there are many more issues causing this. For example, you can easily vassalize any faction (regardless of whether you or they are an Order or Chaos faction, or whether they should, lore-wise, hate you) simply by giving them a settlement. And this even happens on Very Hard difficulty.
Challenge-wise, in my second playthrough, major powers used to form mostly “organically.” For example, toward the end, Malekith would usually have confederated all the Dark Elves and become one of the major threats you faced, a proper challenge. Now, that never happens. Every major faction just sits in their settlements, especially during wars with the player. This means not only is there no tension like “oh no, what if he attacks my homeland?” but you also have to spend  hours on boring siege battles, clearing full stacks from one settlement after another. The endgame challenge is now artificially produced by “endgame crises,” which die down in a couple of turns because the AI is too stupid to know what to do with those armies.
It’s a minor detail, but the game’s own campaign (the Realm of Chaos) has been, since launch, boring as hell and is now completely abandoned. To be honest, as I write this, I don’t think I’ve ever been as excited to pick a faction and start a campaign as I was during the first release of Immortal Empires with the Warriors of Chaos update, and maybe a little during the Thrones of Decay and Arbaal release.
I feel there is a goldmine of entertainment in this game, but the mine entrance has collapsed and nobody cares about it. They expect us to dig through it and get only these nuggets of fun at best. I love the idea of what this game could be, and I hope CA properly understands what the community actually wants and delivers it. But with how it’s been one step forward and two steps back since launch, I don’t have much hope left.

Do you enjoy the intricate gameplay of older total wars where you had to manage the complexities of ruling an empire and the thrill of tactical yet exciting real time combat? If so, what the hell are you doing here!? 

The map and presentation are frankly the ONLY thing this game has going for it. The lords look cool, and the races are all interesting and seemingly fun to play. But the game itself is not fun.

For one empire building is just as gutted as it has been for the past ten years. No more constructing vast infrastructure networks for your people and your military now you can choose from a very small pool of prepicked structures to make and  not make any interesting decisions about how to build your city. Did you like population? Nope, that's exactly 1 number that is actually more like a resource than anything. Where did this army comprising tens of thousands of people that was just spawned outside of a small settlement a few turns ago come from? My ass that's where. 

Frankly all of that would be forgivable if the battles were even mildly enjoyable but they aren't. Almost every battle i've seen has devolved into a mosh pit of units slamming into each other until one dies. Morale is basically a thing of the past unless you get really lucky (or cheese it) and manage to kill the enemy lord whos as beefy as an adult bull. So now its time to ram your units to theres until you die. Well at least its cool to watch your cool fantasy soldiers attack other cool fantasy soldiers right? Well... if you can get your troops there then maybe. Pathfinding AI is frankly braindead. Your units will willingly run to embrace death if you don't micro them in some instances. God forbid you enter a siege battle though... 

Maybe, you are thinking, this is just a skill issue. Maybe. But i haven't even talked about siege battles yet. SCREW. SIEGE. BATTLES. Whichever team worked on them should be embarrassed because you can't even play them. Want to move units into a city to help garrison it mid-battle? Prepare to watch your troops sit outside a gate for 20 minutes trying to figure out how to move inside of it. Oh but that's only if they don't decide to try and walk to another gate on the other side of the map straight through enemy lines. Maybe though by some miracle you manage to get your troops in on a reasonable time frame in which the enemy hasn't wiped out everyone inside. How is the intense fighting inside the city? There isn't any. As in, there is no fighting. Your lucky if your troops even move inside of the city. Despite incessant clicking some units will simply refuse to move and will subsequently die from either archers or by being cut off by enemy infantry. Its literally unplayable. 

Oh and in addition to that the game runs like crap and looks like WH1. Why is my I9 Processer and 4070 graphics card crashing on high with only medium unit sizes?

I'm going to attempt to play the game further and see if i can work around these glitches but frankly i don't know if the gameplay around it is worth the time. 

TL; DR don't buy it, its still broken and also runs like ♥♥♥♥

Total War: Warhammer III is a phenomenal game and my favourite strategy game. Over 100+ factions to choose from in Immortal Empires (As long as you own all 3 games and every DLC for each game). It also has quest battles you can play at will and the story campaign is interesting IMO and can be played by all the Warhammer III exclusive factions. Its really fun! Never played multiplayer as I'm not a competitive gamer. I'm a chill kind of guy. The glitches of the past are mostly fixed and thanks to the recent war between players and the developers, CA is still actively fixing the game as time goes on and more bugs are reported. So if you see bugs, please don't review bomb this game, just report it. Also, it is very well known to the entire Total War community how expensive this game is. People who like things will buy what they like. How you use your wallet is a powerful motivator in the business world. Many of us who own this game most likely purchased this on a sale as well as all the DLC's and previous two games required for the full experience. But if you think about it, they aren't shamming us at all. To be honest, a game with 104 playable factions is not worth 60 dollars. Its worth way more. Technically, each game and its corresponding DLC's are complete games. So, If you want Warhammer III complete, you don't even need Warhammer I and II and there DLCs. Just Warhammer III and its DLC's. Of course you wont be able to play Warhammer I and II's races in Immortal Empires because technically, they aren't part of Warhammer III. Immortal Empires was simply a way to combine all three complete games into one experience. And to do that, you must own them all. Just like Mortal Empires for Warhammer II. To close this review out, Total War: Warhammer III is not technically a perfect game. It still needs work and CA is actively working on it. However, Its a Perfect game to me personally due to how fun it is, how massive it is, I love the Lords, I love the units, the battles, the campaigns, the graphics, the music, the atmosphere, the voice acting, the variety, the amount of stuff to do in this game and as mentioned before its just plain fun. I'm having a blast playing it. I highly recommend playing this game if you love the Warhammer universe, the fantasy genre, Strategy games or just looking for something fun to play.

I didn't mind CA's DLC policies in the past. They were always generous with free content and none of their DLCs were essential to enjoy their games, but this time is different. Great game, very fun. Essentially endless replayability (more with mods). This game is a gateway drug into Warhammer Fantasy. 

Pros:
- A lot of races to choose from, all with heaps of lore and unique visuals and gameplay styles.
- Fun battles that require you to know your (and the enemies') units and play them to maximum effect.
- A big gorgeously detailed map to play on that reflects the entire world of the underlying fantasy.
- Over 300 (mostly) unique units with their own models/animation/voices and combat roles.
- Fantastic (strategy-like) voice acting. From dead serious to super silly to something inbetween. Out of the 300 units maybe 3 I would consider "bad". And like 30 that absolutely knock it out of the park.
- Beautiful and extremely underrated Soundtrack.
- Workshop integration with active and passionate modding community.

Cons:
- Base DLC Prices are too expensive and should generally be about 40% lower to be fair for consumers. (Get them on sale)
- Battle AI can behave very strangely sometimes (your own and the enemies')
- Siege battles are not really fun despite lots of patches and attemps to make them so.

Nitpicks (Cons):
- Not enough campaign gameplay complexity. If you are new to the game it is fine, but after some time you realize there is not that much to it. Mods like SFO can greatly help here, however you have to like the other changes it includes.
- The combined Immortal Empires map is too "small" in my opinion. The visual and thematic range is great, however there should be more settlements per province. The Empire area is alright, but essentially all other major continents feel too small with too little settlements.

Short description, if You're somehow unfamiliar with the Total War series:
   It's a 4x-lite strategy game, where the turn based campaign is somewhat of a facilitator for the true meat of the game: the real time massive battles, where armies of thousands of troops clash until one side is either dead or routed.

   It's set in the warhammer fantasy universe and somewhat unlike the previous installments features rpg elements with battle capable lords and heroes which You can level up and kit out in various gear. Also unlike the other Total War games it has dragons and other massive war beasts, war machines, magic etc.  

As for the state of the game:
   Having played the game since release I can say that it's now in a good spot. Almost all of the ridiculous, overcomplicated and downright annoying systems have been revised or removed (corruption that takes 50 turns to remove, unsatiable public order forcing You to turtle, AI factions non-stop targeting You with campaign debuffs etc.).

   That said, You do have to like the franchise and accept some of its problems in order to enjoy this installment. For example: the famous Total War AI is still here (it has its moments, but overall it's retarded).

   The multiplayer is better than ever. There are many game modes available, both competitive and co-operative, campaign and single battle, with simultaneous turns available as an option for the former.

   The list of dlc's might seem overwhelming, but even if You do feel the need to be able to play with all the toys in campaign (I get it), then fear not, once You choose which race You'd like to control, You can opt to only buy the dlc's for that one race, and You won't be missing out on anything (I'm treating the previous installments as dlc's here). And since each campaign can  last for tens of hours, You tend to get the bang for Your buck.

Tl;dr: Is good now.
