WARHAMMER III es la culminación épica de una trilogía que redefine lo que significa la estrategia en el mundo de los videojuegos. Este título no solo lleva el género a nuevas alturas, sino que lo hace con una escala y ambición que dejan sin aliento. Desde el momento en que entras al caótico mundo del Reino del Caos, sabes que estás a punto de vivir una experiencia inolvidable.

El juego te pone al mando de poderosas facciones, cada una con mecánicas únicas e historias fascinantes. Los Dioses del Caos —Khorne, Nurgle, Tzeentch y Slaanesh— traen consigo un diseño visual y jugable que captura perfectamente su esencia destructiva y corruptora. Por otro lado, los majestuosos Imperios del Gran Catai y Kislev ofrecen una contrapartida heroica, con unidades y estrategias que evocan tanto misticismo como resistencia. Cada facción se siente como una obra maestra, profundamente diferente, pero perfectamente equilibrada, lo que garantiza que cada campaña sea una aventura completamente nueva.

La narrativa toma un giro más ambicioso con la introducción del Reino del Caos, un mapa surrealista y desafiante que pondrá a prueba tus habilidades estratégicas mientras luchas por la supremacía y el control del destino del mundo. Esta campaña no es solo una guerra por territorios; es un viaje épico donde cada batalla es una leyenda en sí misma. Desde asedios monumentales hasta choques entre ejércitos colosales, cada enfrentamiento vibra con intensidad y emoción, acompañado de efectos visuales y sonoros que te sumergen por completo en el campo de batalla.

Pero lo que realmente eleva a Total War: WARHAMMER III a otro nivel es el colosal modo Immortal Empires, una fusión titánica de los tres juegos de la saga que te permite conquistar un mundo gigantesco con cualquier facción de la trilogía. Es el sueño de todo fan de Warhammer Fantasy: un sandbox estratégico donde la imaginación y la táctica no tienen límites.

Con gráficos deslumbrantes, una banda sonora épica y una jugabilidad que perfecciona cada aspecto de la fórmula Total War, este juego no solo es un título imprescindible, sino un tributo glorioso al universo Warhammer. Es más que un juego; es una epopeya estratégica que merece ser vivida. Si buscas una experiencia que combine caos, gloria y estrategia en su forma más pura, este es el título que estabas esperando. ¡Lánzate al campo de batalla y escribe tu propia leyenda!

I've waited a long time to review this game because it really had a rough start, plagued by numerous bugs and was limited only to the Realms of Chaos campaign, which was far from perfect and didn't appeal to my personal taste.

However, since then, the game has transformed dramatically. It now boasts the largest map in the series' history with the Immortal Empires campaign (and you no longer are required to own W1 and W2 to enjoy it, which is great) an immense selection of very diversed factions and lords that provide unique experience, starting positions and challenges that is really hard to see in any other Total War game. Although, if you are new to the series it's worth noting that most of them requires separate DLC purchase. Some of them are really worth the price like Chaos Dwarves, easily the most fun to play factions for me, but others are a little bit dated. I won't give any examples, as this can change soon. CA frequently updates older factions, ensuring the gameplay stays fresh even for those that feel a bit stale.

While some elements still need improvement in my opinion, such as the end-game crises and sieges, this is without a doubt the best Total War game in history. I’m hopeful that the game will continue to receive at least few more paid DLCs alongside with more free content. Good job CA! I hope your next historical title will be at least as good as this one.

¿Porque no lo recomiendo? ¿Acaso no es un buen juego? ¿Es aburrido?

Para responder esas preguntas antes debo contar mi experiencia. Cuando descubrí la franquicia, me enamoro, tenía todo lo que quería. Desde dragones hasta enanos con cara de viejos fachos. Un sistema de combate entretenido y campañas tan difíciles que te hace temblar los cachetes de la cola. Donde hasta en lo más simple podía transformarse en la historia más conmovedora o despiadada. 

Entonces ¿Porque no lo recomiendo?

En su primera entrega fue totalmente innovador todo, cumpliendo los deseos de muchos fanáticos y con el pasar del tiempo fueron agregando más contenido (pero de pago). En su segunda entrega, mejoraron los gráficos, mecánicas de combate y agregaron un nuevo modo de campaña (no me gustó mucho, pero se agradece), lo negativo era la cantidad de dlc que fueron agregando y lo PEOOOOOOOOOOR QUE HIECIERON, que para poder jugar con facciones de la primera entrega debías tener los dos juegos. Ahora esta tercera entrega, que me pareció buena la idea, pero el contenido totalmente escaso.

¿No es un buen juego? 

Sí, es un muy buen juego y le podes dedicar mucho tiempo de tu vida. Pero es abusivo la cantidad de contenido de pago que hay, literalmente entras y más de la mitad del contenido es de pago. Es decir, que si te comprar la tercera entrega sin antes comprar las demás, no vas a disfrutar la experiencia completa del juego. Algo que puede frustrar muchísimo a los nuevos jugadores y captar menos audiencia nueva. 

Conclusión

Si te sobra la plata, compra el juego que no es malo, es divertido y pasas un buen rato. De lo contrario, si no te sobra la plata, este juego va a ser tu peor error financiero de toda tu vida y vas a quedar endeudado de tanto dlcs.

Mensaje extra

La empresa es nefasta, literalmente no se preocupa en sacar juegos completos y que valgan su precio. Siempre el mismo formato, saca un juego, sale lleno de bug, lo llena de contenido de pago y después de dos años arreglar bugs del juego. Como consumidor, te van a exprimir como sea y de todas las formas que se les ocurran. O sea una kk.

Even with the doubts about player traps or unyielding forced grinding of actions, there are ways to minimize them through mods or even just gameplay skips. I know there is many who despise the countless DLCs costing mega money, but guess what? I haven't taken the time to write a review for a game that I care about except for this first one. If you never tried TW, this is the game to start with; no required reading. В центре все еще Total War, отработанный и отполированный к третей части, но все еще он. Отстраивай города, изучай технологии, защищай рубежи, заряжай, стреляй, заряжай. Третья часть больше сместилась в сторону песочницы, в отличии от первых двух. Большая часть кампаний все еще ведома наративом, но открылось больше универсальных взаимодействий - диспломатия пускай и сдержана между сюжетнами оппонентами, все равно частично доступна. Союзники предоставляют возможность наймя отрядов, что позволяет смешивать изначальный ростер юнитов. И множество других улучшений "качества жизни" облагораживающих впечатление от игры, но отнимающих антураж оригинальной серии

Что касается самих боев в противовес стратегической карте - это то, где игра раскрывается всеми своими красками. Кавалерия на медведях? Корабли на колесах? Боевые дирижабли? Ядерные ракеты и динозавры с лазером из небес? Огнеметы и танковые дивизии? В старом мире умереть от старости достижение, а встреча с армией демонов не самая страшна учесть. То разнообразие и безумие которое ты встретишь на полях сражений вполне весомый повод простить однобразие карт и глупый ИИ противника. 

Фанаты игры могут быть полны критики и вполне заслуженной. Но это беспокойство за любимую серию, а не безразличие. Если ты читаешь ревью, то значит тебе нет необходимости углубляться в споры игроков с тысячами часами в статистике, 1500 часов не тратят на плохие игры

Ive played the game for quite some time now, bought dlc, played multiplayer, got a long victory on highest difficulty (except artificially increasing enemy units strength) and I have to say it is literally an early access game.

There are a lot of ridiculously bad decisions being made when it comes to how some things work.
Is it clunky? Oh definitely. Is the ai bad? Yep, 100%. Are there a lot of QoL features missing? Oh you bet.

One of the biggest and most obvious peeves this game throws toward you is the default enemy behaviour on the map. Their highest priority is to mess with the player. They will literally suicide charge themselves against your armies and settlements, even if they are actively being threatened with getting wiped from existance. As long as they raid your territory or sack one of your settlements one last time they have completed their purpose. This also leads to a lot of annoying cat and mouse chases, where you can easily defeat straggling enemy armies, but they just keep on running away from you.

The game has a lot of quite frankly gamebreaking bugs. Even more get added with every patch.
One of the most horrendous bugs that was recently introduced (and fixed a couple of WEEKS later) was that giant units dont cleave... Their whole purpose is to stomp and destroy whole regiments of weak units, they removed that part on accident? Another quite frankly horrible bug is ranged units having a very hard time shooting and targeting enemies. You really have to micro them quite a bit for them to do anything sometimes.

Pathfinding on the map is another early access cue, it will show you a lot of things, but dont you ever assume they are correct. Ive had many encounters where the pathfinding told me I could attack someone and then just left me standing a foot away from them with movement left to spend. Apparently not enough to actually attack them though.


Some friends of mine and longtime fans of the Total War series have told me about a bunch of bugs and issues that are still in this game:
- Savefiles will gradually slow down your overall game. You will HAVE to purge it every now and then or suffer from abysmal load times
- Inactive mods are still counted as if they are active, including making your performance worse 
- None of the "automate" functions work, neither the automatic lord upgrades, nor the automatic settlement upgrades
- In every game mode there are also long standing gamebreaking bugs. Like when questbattles just dont spawn in the enemy army and then you dont get to complete your quest, forcing you to either reload or lose your army to no fault of your own. At the very least this is an early access game, so bugs like these will hopefully get caught before it releases.

And these are most of the massive ones that I feel should never stay in a game for longer than a couple of weeks at most???!



I just encountered the vassal mechanic, who in their right mind came up with this?
The idea is obviously not a foreign concept and the overall mechanic in and of itself is fine. But why does it affect you diplomatically??? There is a guy that hates me, because I have "positive treaties" with people he hates. I have enslaved these guys after eradicating their armies? What do you want? I have enslaved them, why do you think Im treating them well??? Im just glad that major bugs and obvious game flaws like this will be patched out as soon as this game releases out of early access.

Dont even get me started on the war-side of the vassal dilemma. This major flaw has been a pretty obvious bug in the game pretty much since it released in its pre alpha stage of development. Your vassals, the things that you enslaved, can refuse to join a defensive war. They can also still, to this day break treaties with you or demand unreasonable sums of money just for you to tell them to do things. But since this is such a universally flawed system, im sure itll get a major rework once the game is out.

Total War: Warhammer 3 is a spectacular conclusion to the Total War: Warhammer trilogy, offering a grand mix of strategy, epic battles, and immersive fantasy storytelling. As the first fantasy title I’ve played in the Total War series, I was skeptical about stepping away from the historical settings I know and love, but this turned out to be an absolute treat. The imaginative world-building and unique gameplay mechanics brought a fresh perspective to the franchise, making it a standout experience.

The tactical complexities introduced by monstrous units in battles have added an entirely new layer of strategy. From titanic dragons to hulking Chaos Beasts, these units fundamentally change the dynamics of combat. Coordinating armies to counter or capitalize on their strengths has made battles far more interesting and rewarding, elevating the gameplay experience to new heights. The blend of large-scale strategic planning with these intense, monster-driven tactical encounters earns gameplay a strong 9/10.

The narrative takes center stage in the Realm of Chaos campaign, which adds a distinct flavor to the gameplay. Players embark on a quest to save or destroy a dying god, with the overarching story enriched by faction-specific goals and unique lore. While not every narrative beat lands perfectly, the story provides a strong foundation for the gameplay, earning it an 8/10.

Graphically, the game is stunning. From the vibrant landscapes of Kislev and Cathay to the twisted, surreal realms of Chaos, the visuals bring the Warhammer universe to life. Unit designs are intricate, and the battles are visually thrilling, earning graphics a solid 9/10.

The sound and music are exceptional, with a powerful soundtrack that enhances the sense of grandeur and chaos. The voice acting, ambient sounds, and battle effects create an incredibly immersive experience. This aspect of the game earns a perfect 10/10.

Replayability is unparalleled, with a vast array of factions, each offering unique mechanics, units, and playstyles. The inclusion of the Immortal Empires campaign, combining content from all three games, provides a sandbox experience of epic proportions. Replayability easily scores a 10/10.

Innovation is present in features like the Realm of Chaos campaign, customizable Daemon Prince faction, and new mechanics for several races. While it builds heavily on the foundation of its predecessors, the additions keep the game feeling fresh and engaging, earning innovation an 8/10.

In summary, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a worthy culmination of the trilogy, delivering epic battles, diverse factions, and an expansive sandbox campaign. The inclusion of monsters and their impact on tactical battles make the combat far more intriguing and complex. For someone new to the fantasy setting of the Total War series, this was a surprising delight. With its stunning visuals, unforgettable soundtrack, and endless replayability, it stands as a crown jewel in the series and a must-play for strategy and Warhammer fans alike.

I tried to like it, I give it a shot. It is just not an enjoyable Total War game OR an enjoyable Warhammer game. Fanboys will crucify me but I just don't see the appeal. I understand that different people like different things but as a Total War AND a Warhammer fan I am a bit stumped that this game is a miss. 

Here are my gripes in a nutsell:

- Although units look diverse, they play and behave the same.
- The only valid playstyle is hyperaggression (I get it, it is Total War but in other titles at least you have time and a chance to build up your economy first/play defensive/responsive)
- Diplomacy/Vassalage/Trading etc. is very difficult, almost not worth the effort. 
- Incredibly convoluted building chains/building browser.
- Overpowered lords, making armies feel like mere decoration in the background. 
- Too many sieges, not many field battles.
- Convoluted UI.
- Due to the modern Warscape engine battle mechanics are dumbed down (HP bars, no armor, unit clumping, no charge weight).
- Units generally feel unresponsive and slow.
- No real difference between arrows and bullets, plays the same, looks the same.
- Battles end in 5 minutes or less, they all feel and play out the same. 
- Campaign gets boring and repetitive halfway through with all neighbours declaring war. 

Overall I do not recommend. I see that there is a division between the history and fantasy fans. Personally I prefer both, the problem isn't that it's Warhammer. The problem is that the game is dumbed down while also feeling very convoluted and unintuitive.

Total War: WARHAMMER III had a rough start. Initially it launched without its grand campaign mode, Immortal Empires, instead launching with a narrative driven campaign called Realms of Chaos. Realms of Chaos was not a bad game mode, but for those who primarily played Mortal Empires in Warhammer II, it was a very lackluster experience. 

After Immortal Empires launched, the game improved drastically, but there were other problems. For starters, many bugs that were originally fixed in Warhammer II suddenly came back, and unfortunately, did not get fixed quickly. There were also many new bugs, such as inconsistent unit pathing, poor performance, crashes, and some more serious bugs that effectively made certain factions unplayable. Over time, these bugs were fixed, but very slowly. So slowly, in fact, that the Community Bug Fix mod was practically a necessity for some players. 

Unfortunately, Warhammer III's problems did not end there. Starting in 2023, the price for DLC had a significant increase. While the cost in itself was not a big deal for some, what was a big deal was the lack of content contained in these DLCs and overall support. While you can refer to each DLC's page for more specific reviews, I personally thought the price was fair for all EXCEPT Shadow's of Chance, which is where Warhammer III's issues reached it's peak. 

When Shadows of Change launched, the game was in a poor state. There were MANY bugs that significantly affected the enjoyment of the game. Ranged units would refuse to fire, unit reactions to your commands were delayed, the AI on the campaign map was overly passive and would often refuse to attack the player even after they declared war, and so much more. All of this, in addition to the high price and lack of content in Shadows of Change, led to a massive backlash within the community. In nearly every social circle, from Reddit to the Creative Assembly forums, people made their disappointment known. The game and DLCs were pounded with poor reviews and the outrage reached a peak when the former Product Manager for Creative Assembly, Rob Bartholomew, low-key threatened to pull support for the game if Shadows of Change did not sell well. 

After the Shadows of Change fiasco, Creative Assembly promised to do better. I am VERY happy to say that they have. While DLC prices remain high at $25 USD, they contain significantly more content and have been broken down into three parts that can be purchased individually. They have put a lot more focus on bug fixes and quality of life changes, as well as put in a lot of "free" content that was completely unexpected. Shadows of Change had more content added to it, as well. They have promised reworks and updates to factions that have fallen behind since their release in Warhammer I and II, and so far, have followed through with these promises. 

The game still needs more work, but compared to a year ago, it is in a MUCH better state. Creative Assembly has established better communication with the community and bug fixes have occurred much more frequently. The more recent DLCs, such as Thrones of Decay and the upcoming Omens of Destruction, contain much more interesting new content alongside updates to existing factions and mechanics. There are still many bugs that need squashed, but there are very few bugs that significantly affect gameplay. 

A year ago I would have not recommended this game, but now I encourage you to get it. There is a lot of DLC, but don't be intimidated by that. It frequently goes on sale with deep discounts, and unlike games like Hearts of Iron 4 or Stellaris, these DLC packs do not contain necessary campaign-wide mechanics. You can buy them slowly over time, or not at all, if you are simply not interested in certain factions.

One of the worse Total War games by far. 

Half 60% of all playable races/lord are locked behind DLC content (~150€), and there are barely any races you can play together with your friends without having to pay an additional 10€ for a DLC (If you have more than one friend to play with, only Kislev and Bretonnia have 2+ Lords. Then there are Cathay with 2, Khorne with 2 and Nurgle with 2 playable lords if you only have one other friend.)

Other than the disappointing selection in playable lords after spending 25-60€ on this 2 year old game, (for which they still release DLC content actively), there are only 3-4 campaigns, two of which are very short (~3-10 hours each). Combined with the lack of playable lords, the game becomes stale very quickly if you want to play with friends.

The world is filled with uninteractable lore points, which don't give you any interesting stats or effects for being in your territory. You'll have a shrine dedicated to Ursun while playing Kislev, have a huge marker above it to read the lore, but not have any way to interact with it (via any bonus effects or special buildings). Makes me question the inclusion and effort spent besides simply lore dumping.

As for the battles, a lack of options for (special) formations, like in other games, makes you feel like most fights are simply a stat check. You can cheese the AI slightly by using cavalry to distract troops and use artillery to kite, but other than that even terrain barely gives noticable gameplay advantages. 

It's fun to play in a gaming landscape with barely any good games to play with friends, but that isn't saying much. I've been enjoying my time with it so far, but there are some short comings. I wish the game would at least have more than 2 playable factions for a party of 3-4 friends, without the need to buy a bunch of DLCs, especially when the base game is that expensive.

Das Spiel wurde seit der Veröffentlichung geupdated und neue Inhalte wurden veröffentlicht. Grundsätzlich braucht ihr kein zusätzlichen DLC. ABER es gibt einen versteckten Harken. Kampagne:
Der Bot kriegt Vorteile beim Unterhalt seiner Einheiten. Mit einer einzigen Siedlung (keine Stadt) in einer Normalen Kampagne hat der Bot während 2 Armeen ihn geplündert haben 1,5 Armeen ausgehoben! Do not let the high budget of the cinematic content and crowds of table-top fans convince you that this can easily fit within your economic budget. With this entire franchise's dependency on downloadable content in hindsight, it's clear Creative Assembly merely phones it in with continued patches.
Newer content comes at the expense of the player's wallet, older content comes at the expense of the player's wallet, the warnings have been present since the Chaos Warriors scandal. The new DLC monetization model may hold the attention of big spenders, but condemns newer players to buy new content for old content with no real depth.
The Fantasy gimmick doesn't hide the larger issues plaguing the Total War franchise's gameplay and engine.

Been playing since the release of warhammer 1 and iv'e probably sank over 1000hs into the trilogy and i can say with some confidence that ill be reaching 2000, the games just have so many features and replayability to keep you invested long term.  although warhammer 3 had a rocky start when it was released, in its current state thanks to the continued support by the developers has made it the ultimate way to play the game especially with the inclusion of immortal empires free to anybody who owns warhammer 3 without the need to purchase any of the other games although you will still need the other games to unlock optional factions and characters.

The game starts when you select your character which currently upon writing there is 100 characters! available to pick from from various factions in the warhammer lore each with unique faction and character mechanics.  there is 2 grand strategy elements in the game that define total war, the campaign map and the battle map.  the campaign map is where you'll be moving your characters around and building armies and upgrading settlements and the battle map is where you'll be using these armies to fight battles from small skirmishes to huge battles involving 1000s of units.  The difficulty of the game is upto the user and on the hardest difficulties the game can be very challenging where a single mistake can cost you dearly,  for new users the learning curve can be quite steep but it has a good tutorial campaign to guide you through starting off then the rest will come from playing.  

Onto the dlc's which seems to be what puts people off the most as there is alot but im not one of those that agree with the gripe as the dlc's have been spread over the course of 10 years of development and the base game comes with enough factions and characters to keep you playing for hundreds of hours.  If you decide you enjoy the game the option is there to purchase the dlc's you like in any order you like and also supports the development of future releases,  the prices i would say are not bad especially if you get them when on sale.

sound and music is one area of the game i would like to highlight as CA do a great job here,  each faction has its own distinctive music and it does a great job of getting you immersed into the game as all the scores feel very relevant to the factions

Graphically the game is stunning which will require a high end PC to run on the higher setting and i would say is my only gripe on this game as it could be optimised better for lower end PCs but i suspect this has something to do with the engine that runs warhammer, other than that i haven't had any crashes and ive seen very few bugs in the game.

Multiplayer - its there and there is a dedicated multiplayer community if you enjoy competing but i would say the single player campaign is the focus (you can also play this multiplayer)

To summarise i would recommend this game to anyone that is interested in grand strategy and RTS players and also just for the lore as this game sparked my interest in warhammer in general which then led to the discovery of the books and other games in the genre.

Seit ca. 20 bin ich ein Fan von GamesWorkshop Warhammer. Und seit 20 Jahren bezahle ich ein Haufen an Money für dieses Hobby.

Zur Sache: 
Das Spiel ist unbedingt zu empfehlen! DANK "Total War"! Bisher waren EgoShooter wie Firewarrior für Ps2 oder aktuell SpaceMarine die einzigen sehr guten GamesWorkshop Spiele.

Nach "Dawn of war" ist ein einzigartiges Spiel geboren, mit "Total War" Warhammer! Gefühlt tausend Variationen und Eigenschaften der Rassen. Ein wahres Festival für ALLE Fans der Warhammer Welt. 

Grafisch kann das Spiel locker mithalten, das Gameplay wird teilweise erleichtert um überhaupt das Konzept zu erfassen. Es ist sehr komplex gestaltet um Einzelheiten zu erklären, wie so oft von GamesWorkshop. 

Seit dem ersten Teil dieser Reihe wächst das Spiel unaufhörlig. Hier Knüpfe ich mal an:

Als eine Art der TotalWar Reihe ist das Spiel absolut zu empfehlen! Hier ist Strategie und etwas "Insiderwissen" gefragt. Erobert und baut globale Städte aus. Hier gibt es kein Fokus auf einzelne Helden, bis auf bestimmte, relevante Missionen. Jede Seite des Warhammer Universums kann gespielt werden, wenn nicht ist noch keine DLC erschienen! Jede Rasse mit ihren zugehörigen Hauptcharakter hat jeweils ein spezielles Gameplay und somit einzigartige Fähigkeiten sowie Truppen.

Man merkt es wirkt kompliziert mit  locker über 10 Rassen und jeweils bis zu 4 oder mehr Hauptcharakteren. Aber wie so oft, ist aller Anfang schwer! Ihr kommt schon rein mit etwas Geduld und Verständnis. 

Mich stören:
Extrem EXTREM!!!!! ÜBERTEUERTE!!!!!!!! DLC. Wer hätts gedacht, GamesWorkshop geht mal wieder voll auf Umsatz und verkauft, was die Fans als letztes Hemd haben. Das Balancing schwankt oft sehr stark, was auch mit den einzelnen Eigenschaften zusammenhängt. Trotzdem wird es nicht besser. In nahezu JEDER Kampagne kann man nicht mehr strategisch agieren sondern muss mit brachialer Gewalt und milliarden von Truppen einfach alles wegrammen! Das spielverhalten ändert sich im Laufe, was an sich geil ist, aber früher oder später gibt es keine interessanten Schlachten sondern einfach ALLES REIN WAS GEHT! 

Zusätzlich werden einige Rassen benachteilt und nicht weiter ausgebaut. Hier entsteht also ein weiteres Problem vom Balancing. Klar muss man hier bei dem komplexen Gefüge immer etwas nachjustieren, allerdings scheiße! Wenn man allein für eine handvoll und ein Kommandant ca. 20 EUR zahlt, erwartet man ein ausgereiftes System. Aber das wird GamesWorkshop niemals, NIEMALS schaffen.

Total War: WARHAMMER III

I've been trying to convince myself to play the WARHAMMER total war games, and every single time I give in and buy it; I inevitably find myself just... Not having fun.

Now, don't get me wrong; there's plenty here for people to enjoy, but as someone who played and loved Medieval 2, Shogun 2, Napoleon; hell, even Rome 2 after a few years of patching..., Warhammer 3, and honestly all the rest of the Warhammer total war games just don't do anything for me.

Sure, the game is very pretty, and the Warhammer setting is (probably) interesting, but the actual gameplay is... Honestly pretty bad. The overworld map gameplay is fine! It's basically just Rome 2, which itself is basically just Shogun 2. My problem is not with the campaign map. It's as 'fine' and 'good' as Total War campaigns have ever been. The inclusion of an actual storyline was interesting! Though the prologue itself was way too drawn out and slow. Other than that, perfectly fine.

My issue lies with the actual battle simulation mode. Its just not fun, and it's still got the exact same problems it's had since Warhammer 1, except that they finally made (some?) of the sieges not miserable.

The maps are painfully small. Noticeably so. It almost feels like a huge snap-back ever since Rome 2 had absolutely huge maps. Admittedly, there's very few maps that are just "Boring empty field", and there's lots of steep hills to provide cover and all that, and they're all very pretty and visually interesting due to the setting, but that isn't super important when the Total War AI is basically still the same as it's always been, and won't ever use any of this terrain to their advantage purposefully and will, 9/10, spawn in the middle of their spawn region and charge your frontline, while maybe sending out flying units or cavalry to flank around you.

Now, everything IS pretty. But when I'm playing Total War, I'm more likely to be zoomed in on my troops and trying to move them around; not staring at the scenery at the edge of the map.

Your artillery will usually have more than enough range to immediately start plinking shots at the enemy lines upon spawn. Missile units barely have to move forward to start firing shots at the enemy, and there's barely any room for any flanking maneuvers unless it's cavalry or flying units. Melee infantry also kind of feel like the most... Useless they've been in a long while. Many of the melee units (Atleast for the factions I played: Kislev and Cathay) seem to function more as mobile walls to soak damage and cover the flanks of your missile units and cavalry who actually get the real damage, while melee infantry don't do a whole lot. Perhaps that's merely a faction thing and I got unlucky by picking the two factions who happen to have bad melee infantry. The artillery is fine, the missile units function as expected, and it looks like they actually improved gunpowder units by forcing them to require a direct line-of-fire, which; as far as my memory serves me, in Warhammer 1, the gunpowder units functioned near-identically to archers and could actually arc their shots. Beast and special units are all fine-ish, I suppose,.

One of the more controversial bits that I personally don't enjoy (though I know a few people who do) is that I think "Hero" units, or "Single entity/model unit" just don't belong in Total War. They're too easy to use for cheesing, and just don't really add anything, and a huge chunk of their level-up development is just stat boosting themselves, or stat boosting their attached armies. A single man in a field (to me) is a lot less interesting than another 100+ men in a block.

Here's hoping Medieval 3 Total War doesn't follow in the footsteps of Warhammer 3.

Total War: Warhammer 3 – Licht und Schatten in einem
In seiner aktuellen Form (Dezember 2024) kann ich keine uneingeschränkte Kaufempfehlung für Total War: Warhammer 3 aussprechen. Das Spiel wurde 2022 mit zahlreichen Fehlern und Instabilitäten auf den Markt gebracht. Bis heute wurden einige dieser Fehler noch nicht behoben. Stattdessen verfolgt Total War: Warhammer 3 eine noch aggressivere DLC-Politik als seine Vorgänger und der Großteil des Inhalts ist mittlerweile hinter einer Paywall verborgen.
Als Total War: Warhammer 2 erschien, hatte man nie das Gefühl, dass dem Spiel etwas Wesentliches fehlte. Auch nach dem Erscheinen von DLCs war es nicht unbedingt notwendig, die neuen Fraktionen zu kaufen. Bei Warhammer 3 wurde das Konzept jedoch geändert: Der reine Inhalt ist deutlich geringer als bei seinem Vorgänger und die neue Fraktion „Chaoszwerge“ (25 € DLC) ist so mächtig, dass sie kaum zu bezwingen ist. Natürlich wurde diese Fraktion auf der Karte so platziert, dass man als Spieler ihr schnell begegnet und daran verzweifeln darf. Es scheint fast so, als wolle man den Spielern diese Fraktion regelrecht aufzwingen und zum Kauf animieren. Diese Vorgehensweise setzt sich kontinuierlich fort, insbesondere mit allen DLCs seit 2022. 
Obwohl Warhammer 3 zu Beginn weniger Inhalt bot als der Vorgänger, hatte es immerhin 6 Fraktionen, die jeweiligen Kampagnen und als kostenlosen Patch die „Immortal Empires“-Karte, die laut Entwicklern ursprünglich zum Release verfügbar sein sollte. Das war eine beachtliche Menge für 60 Euro. Heute kosten einzelne Fraktions-DLCs 25 Euro. Ist das Preis-Leistungs-Verhältnis gerechtfertigt? Nein, absolut nicht.
Trotz meiner persönlichen Freude an dem Spiel kann ich die aktuelle Entwicklung nicht gutheißen und kann daher keine Empfehlung aussprechen. Wer wirklich in das Warhammer-Universum eintauchen möchte, dem empfehle ich Total War: Warhammer 2, da es häufig zu reduzierten Preisen erhältlich ist, eine enorme Menge an Inhalt bietet und sich hervorragend eignet, um das Franchise kennenzulernen. Sollte man später den Wunsch verspüren, mehr zu erleben, empfehle ich, nur Angebote mit mindestens 50 % Rabatt zu akzeptieren. In diesem Preissegment wird das Preis-Leistungs-Verhältnis wieder angemessen. Leider wird auch hier seitens der Entwickler und Publisher das Modell der Paywalls und „Pay-to-Win“-Mechaniken in Spielen weiter unterstützt und ausgebaut. Eine bedauerliche Entwicklung.

Total War- Warhammer has two main problems that make me not want to recommend it even if you can get some enjoyment out of it. The first one is that it has the most insane monetisation scheme I've ever seen in any game ever released. The base game is bare-bones and offers only a small number of races. If you wish to have an actually complete experience you're expected to purchase a large number of absurdly overpriced DLCs that amount to a total sum of over 300€. Creative Assembly have even gone so far as to require you to own the previous two Warhammer games (including their DLCs) in order to access the full content. Some content is even locked behind requiring you to create a CA account and linking it to your steam account, something that isn't mentioned anywhere on the store page mind you. Not only are races and factions tied to DLCs but essential units as well. For example, you might be interested in playing as the Skaven after watching some gameplay on YouTube, so you purchase Warhammer 2 only for you to find out that their best and most exciting units, the Weapons Teams (Ratling Guns, Warplock Jezzails etc.), aren't even part of their base roster. So if you want to have the true Skaven experience you have to buy even more DLCs just to get their full roster. The game is essentially a big jigsaw puzzle where you have to buy each individual puzzle piece separately at ludicrous prices. Just to put this into context, the Chaos Dwarf DLC costs 25€. Half the price of a full game for just one measly race.

The second big problem with the game is that after all that you're left with a rather mediocre gameplay experience. I've played previous Total War titles extensively and I must say that the battle mechanics are incredibly watered down. Tactics barely matter (unless you count cheese) and it's mostly a stat game. The majority of battles revolve around you decimating the enemy with overpowered magic or artillery and any "tactic" you might use simply aims to abuse the AI and make them bunch up their troops in one big blob to make killing them easier or you dancing with a single entity unit in front of them to make them waste their precious ammo. What was once known as morale is now called leadership and basically doesn't matter anymore. Each battle is fought to the death as routing a unit from the battlefield is utterly impossible in most circumstances. Flanking and charging in the rear does nothing. Formations are gone, even something as basic as loose formation has been removed. The game has the depth of a puddle and can only be described as a glorified spectacle of explosions and magic fireworks. Some people like that. But if you're looking for something with strategic depth and more along the lines of a battle simulator packaged as a video game (which Total War aimed to be a long time ago) you'll be very disappointed.

After a rough launch and a few pretty big missteps along the way, Creative Assembly have brought Total War: Warhammer 3 into a much better state. 

Pros:
- A huge amount of factions and Lords to play, resulting in many wildly different play styles. 
- A giant sandbox campaign in Immortal Empires.
- Many different types of units, from standard infantry to monsters, dragons, zombies, ogres and dinosaurs. (No ratmen, though. There's no such thing as Skaven.)
- All the usual Total War stuff. Big battles, empire building, conquest etc.

Cons:
- Very poor AI. This is easily the biggest flaw of the game right now, in my opinion. Check out a few Youtube videos demonstrating the lackluster AI, if you're interested.
- Lame sieges. They're annoying and tedious. 
- The Realms of Chaos campaign is pretty poor. Immortal Empires is the much better experience.
- Lots of DLC, much of it pretty expensive. There's 3 games worth of DLC now, and it all really adds up. On the plus side, I'd say most of it isn't necessary. If you want the full experience, however, you'll be forking over a lot.
- Creative Assembly. I won't go into their many controversies here (Youtube has plenty of videos breaking them down). Just know that CA has screwed up big time in the past and may do so again in the future, although they seem to be doing pretty well at the moment.

Overall, despite the games issues, I'd recommend it to any RTS fan. The sheer diversity of play styles, coupled with the great unit rosters and huge sandbox campaign is enough outshine the poorer aspects of the experience.

I mean yeah, if you're new, you should buy it. But if you're new, you've waited this long, so wait for a real good sale on it, unless you got some serious $ to drop out the gate. Total War: Warhammer 3 ist ein Meisterwerk der Strategiespiel-Genre. Es verbindet die epische Größe der Total War-Serie mit der fantastischen Welt von Warhammer, um eine einzigartige und fesselnde Spielerfahrung zu schaffen. Die Detailtreue in der Grafik und die atemberaubende Gestaltung der Schlachtfelder bieten ein beeindruckendes visuelles Erlebnis.

Die Vielfalt an spielbaren Fraktionen und Einheiten ermöglicht es den Spielern, ihre eigenen Taktiken und Strategien zu entwickeln, was für eine immense Tiefe und Wiederspielbarkeit sorgt. Die Echtzeitschlachten sind nicht nur visuell spektakulär, sondern auch taktisch anspruchsvoll, was sowohl für Anfänger als auch für erfahrene Strategen gleichermaßen ansprechend ist.

Die Kampagne von Total War: Warhammer 3 ist reichhaltig und gut durchdacht, mit einer packenden Storyline, die im Warhammer-Universum spielt. Die Entwickler haben großartige Arbeit geleistet, die Atmosphäre und den Geist dieses Universums einzufangen und in das Spiel zu integrieren.

Besonders hervorzuheben ist die Balance zwischen den rundenbasierten strategischen Elementen und den intensiven Echtzeitschlachten. Diese Kombination sorgt dafür, dass das Spiel niemals langweilig wird und immer wieder neue Herausforderungen und Erlebnisse bietet.

Insgesamt ist Total War: Warhammer 3 ein absolutes Muss für jeden Fan von Strategiespielen und Warhammer. Es liefert ein tiefgründiges, packendes und visuell atemberaubendes Spielerlebnis, das seinesgleichen sucht.

Honestly? This is my first ever game of the genre, and lemme tell ya how much of a grand experience I have had with this game.

First of all, I'm a massive Warhammer nerd and am especially happy to see something on the fantasy side, considering that 40k has had no shortage of its own hits in recent years. And as a first-time player of any Total War game, this has most certainly piqued my interest in the rest of the franchise. Battles feel exciting and can be as challenging as you want them to be, with three different difficulty modifiers to help you find just what suits your playstyle the best, and the various models for all the units and lords in this game can be very immaculate. And don't get me started on just how many different ways there are to play the game. With almost every notable race and faction present in this game, you are certain to find a familiar face or hear a renowned name as a Warhammer fan. You want to play a straightforward and relatively simple campaign? Try the Greenskins or Khorne, who's entire goal is to just overpower the enemy with brute force. Want a more safe playstyle while keeping away from your opponent and rain hell from afar? Try Wood Elves or Cathay with their impressive ranged units that are nigh unmatched. Want to harness the Winds and devastate the frontlines with a myriad of spells? Try Tzeentch or the High Elves who have access to rather impressive arsenals of arcane arts. How about shatter both the enemy's morale and bodies? Then you'll love the monsters from the Lizardmen and Dark Elves, terrifying the weak links and slaughtering those who still stand. I could continue on and on, but this game has left a great impression on me and what already has incredibly replayability has been further enhanced by the dedicated and active modding community, so I'll leave it at that. 

TLDR: Lotsa cool factions and really fun game for any Warhammer nerd such as I.

This is the best strategy/RTS game I've ever played, nothing else comes close. I've been playing since Total War II ( I have 1,500 hours in that version ), and at this point in it's development, TW III is better, an amazing final chapter to the Total War series.
The combat is varied and thrilling, with huge armies clashing in all kinds of different terrain, and incredibly realistic scenarios developing in the chaos of combat. Some of my best memories in PC gaming come from TW battles that took an unexpected turn due to a tactical decision I made, where I turned the tide of battle at the last moment. So satisfying. 
Overall the game is very polished, with better graphics that prior versions and an expanded map to explore, along with many new factions. 
There are so many different factions with wildly different mechanics ( elves, orcs, dwarves, dark elves, undead.. the list goes on and on ). You could play 10,000 hours and still not master them all. I love all the new Demon units ( though I haven't played them, I do enjoy destroying them with my Vampire Count or Pirate Coast lords ).
The only downside with this version is that I liked the siege mechanic better in Total War II. In all fairness, I do need to play out more siege battles in this version to get used to the new mechanic ( I mostly auto-resolve seige battles now ), but I liked the more simple 'hold the walls' version in TW II. I've also run into the gate-pathing bug a time or two which prevented my large units who could not use ladders to scale the walls from entering besieged cities. This was frustrating, but I think CA is working on a fix. These are small things though compared to the overall quality of the game, and not enough to cause me not to recommend the game, as it is 99% amazing.

《全面战争：战锤 3》以其深度剧情导向的主战役，为玩家提供了一段紧张刺激且极具挑战性的冒险旅程。游戏不仅继承了系列作品一贯的高品质战斗体验，更在新派系和战役设计上做出了大胆创新，使得整个游戏过程充满了新鲜感与趣味性。

在本作中，玩家将参与到一场争夺恶魔亲王之魂的激烈竞赛中，这一设定赋予了游戏更快的节奏和明确的目标导向。虽然这种线性结构可能限制了一些自由度，但它有效地增强了故事的紧凑性和吸引力。尤其是在混沌魔域的部分，每个区域都有其独特的挑战和主题，反映了各自领主的个性特征。特别是高潮部分引入的新战斗形式——通过建立防线和呼叫增援来抵御敌人的潮水般进攻，这无疑为传统的《全面战争》玩法注入了全新的活力，令人耳目一新。

攻城战方面，《战锤 3》也进行了大幅革新，增加了更多战术层面的选择。新的外交选项简化了谈判流程，使玩家能够更加专注于战略规划而非琐碎的交流细节。例如，“快速谈判”按钮允许玩家迅速找到愿意签订贸易协定的对象；而“自动报价”功能则能帮助玩家更快达成和平协议，节省大量时间。这些改进不仅提升了用户体验，还促进了不同派系之间的互动合作。

说到派系，《战锤 3》带来了四个充满特色的全新阵营，它们各自拥有独特的能力和机制。色孽的魅力诱惑、震旦天朝的商队探险、恐虐的暴力美学以及混沌恶魔的高度自定义化，都为玩家提供了多样化的游戏风格选择。特别是混沌恶魔派系，其纸娃娃系统让每位玩家都能打造独一无二的角色，并享受“这是我的派系”的强烈归属感。其中，末日亲王Ragnarr的故事更是成为了游戏中的一大亮点，从序章开始便牢牢抓住了玩家的心。

《全面战争：战锤 3》凭借其引人入胜的故事情节、丰富的战术选择以及富有创意的新派系，成功地创造了一个既紧张又充满乐趣的游戏世界。对于喜爱策略游戏的玩家来说，这绝对是一次不容错过的精彩体验。即使是在等待未来更多内容更新的过程中，当前版本的《战锤 3》也已经展现出了足够的魅力。

To put it bluntly, this game is wildly broken. A game of this size and complexity will inevitable include encounters with bugs, but this game has so many obvious issues you can replicate without fail. However, the issues in this game are so prevalent you have to consider incompetency at a certain point.

All sieges are busted beyond reckoning with unit-path issues that range from comically bad to game breaking. It's not uncommon to take 200% more casualties than you otherwise should because your units bug out. When I first started playing this game, sieges were rough, but they were not THIS bad on a regular basis -- regular basis being literally every siege I manually fight. I just auto-resolve all my sieges now, which is not what I want.

Sieges aren't the only issue in manual battles, either. I've recently seen several times where I give a unit an order and it begins to swirl around into a vortex blob, which of course also happens in sieges. I'll frequently find my units will revert to walking speed when given an attack order, forcing me to babysit the unit with orders moving them near a unit before issuing an attack so they retain their speed and actually charge when close. I have had on multiple occasions my units blob up after issuing a move order, and then form some sort of moshpit that is unable to move because they have decided to clump. Even issuing each unit individual orders, they will still sometimes revert to this behavior. Then there's the issue of them just getting completely stuck on map objects, like at the base of a cliff wall, when I'm trying to reposition because they got too close, I guess -- who knows anymore.

Units frequently forget what they are doing, even mid-combat. They are often extraordinarily slow to react to any given order, especially ranged units. I give them a move order to move so an approaching enemy doesn't catch them, I give another units the order to intercept the approaching unit, and by the time either unit responds it is well too late for one to get away and the other to intercept. This is every engagement, regardless of how fast I make units, they simply don't respond to orders until it's well beyond the time you've wanted them to perform a task, and that's if they actually hold the order the whole time and don't forget what they were supposed to do. I've even adapted how I issue orders based on this information, to give plenty of time to react, and it just doesn't matter. The AI can micro every single entity on the battlefield at the same time, a human cannot. so issues like this can sometimes cost you a battle with your key units. Same with sieges.

I've also noticed recently AI entities don't seem to care whatsoever about what is in front of them, they'll move through my front line without any issue if they want to get to my backline. Not just large monster-type units, even basic marauders and dogs, small heroes, you name it. They don't get stuck in my units to any degree, unlike mine, which take about 40 to 50 clicks to get them to move through anything -- all the while spinning in circles because it's so confused about what I've just told them to do.

[b]I absolutely love this game, and it's been a great way for me to get into Warhammer Fantasy and it's always cool to see the monsters and whatnot look alive on the field. However, given how expensive this game is, there's no excuse whatsoever for there to be issues of this magnitude so prevalent within the game. I could not care less how much money was thrown away on development for failed projects, this title is released, and has been for multiple years now. This title needs to be supported, and it needs to be fixed. Especially if you're going to make people purchase a decade of DLC to have access to the full game.[b]

Where to begin? I want preface this review by admitting that this is the first game of its type that I have really enjoyed. Having no real experience with games of this nature, I decided to put it off until a friend bought it for me as a gift to play together. This game is great and I hate that I'm just now getting into it. I'm the one confused by the DLC you have to buy to enjoy the game with blood and being told "it's to protect the kids" when kids really shouldn't be playing this in the first place.

Pros: 
- This game is a joy to look at. The artwork is incredible and I take my hat off to the people that designed it.
- This game is great for beginners like me. The prologue, while not perfect, helped me understand the basics.
- The story is good so far. I've only beaten the prologue. The voice actors do a great job and the sound design is excellent.
- Controls are easy to use for noobs like me that don't play games with a mouse and keyboard. It's really got me into using them more.

Cons:
- Progression can be a little boring sometimes (i.e. building your cities). While I understand the premise, I wish they would have added more detail to them to make it look like they were living (kind of like Sid Meyers Civ, the closest thing I can think of to this game genre).
- There were times in the prologue where the difficulty spiked for me and I didn't realize it was because I really needed to progress my cities more before moving ahead. It would have been nice to let me know when it's a good time to fight and a good time to sit tight. Still, it helped me learn probably more that what the average Joe would need.
- The DLC is quite expensive and I still don't understand what they significantly offer. The blood DLC was confusing for me. I asked the friend that bought me this and he said they've always done this. Seems like a poor practice. 

Final Verdict:
- Even if you're new to the genre, you should give this game a chance. It's a lot of fun (but I'll warn you a game take a long time, think Risk). It is really fun playing with friends and learning what race you enjoy playing as. Thanks for reading my review.

I took my time learning every faction, how they play, the mechanics and some lore and checking out each units model. Pros:
- Rich lore
- Great gameplay (every faction has a different mechanic/playstyle)
- Great replayability.
- Still same Total War but with magic
- They are still working on the game and put out DLC.

Cons:

- Bugs. They're still updating the game. Hopefully they'll support the game for a long time. 
- Siege battles are a downgrade compared to Rome 2 (ass ladders). 

TLDR; Game is great but very expensive with all DLC. 
My advice; buy the base game first and try the unlocked/free faction. If you like the game and faction, buy the DLC of the faction. But don't get FOMO and think you HAVE to buy all the DLC to get the "complete" experience.

One thing you can't deny is that every flop that developer made they poured a lot of time and resources to fix. Even Thrones of Britania and the one that was called "Total War Troy DLC sold as full game" now according to reviews are fixed and fun to play as the titles in their own right. The community here is demanding. CA and Sega ask for a lot of money with their games and the price for complete versions with all DLC is insane. However community demands back for it so they stay on their toes to deliver even if from time to time they test the waters to check if we swallow garbage and pay for it. 

I have all 3 games with all DLC and A LOT of hours put into all of them and I can honestly say that WH3 is THE GO TO GAME for anyone who wants to experience grand fantasy battles with impossible number of different factions, all unique and catering to fans of different things. Vampires? Check. Pirates? Check. Elves of all kind? Sure. Dwarfs? Of course! Demons? Pick your color. And a lot, lot more. You need money for it though as to get full experience you need to buy not only dlc for 3rd game, but also for another two as the units and lords are unlocked through their respective DLC's in previous games. If you were to jump into it bare bones version with only basics of what WH3 has to offer - cool in the short term but you will crave much more so have wallet ready. You have been warned it will drown your money.

Blood DLC - this one is a hated joke, you need to pay separetly to unlock blood, gore and all adult effects. Up side? You do it once, not with all 3 games separetly. Another upside? They vowed to remove that ♥♥♥♥ going forward with future games. Downside? Yeah, it's still here right now. 

In simple words? When you take that game and a few mods for it you can sink years of your life into your campaings and still not have enough. That's how TW series draws you in and its a good thing as it's time well spent. Not much to ponder about, buy that game and jump right in as it's incredible fun and still a lot more to come on the horizon. But if you decide to join the community and immerse yourself in world of Warhammer Fantasy or Total War in general, remember to demand quality in updates, dlc's and communication as well as respect for your time and money. Total War- Warhammer is a great game that is worth playing. However, it has a main problem that makes me not want to recommend it even if you can get some enjoyment out of it. It has the most insane monetization scheme I've ever seen in any game ever released. The base game is bare-bones and offers only a small number of races. If you wish to have a complete experience, you're expected to purchase a large number of absurdly overpriced DLCs that total over $450. Creative Assembly has even gone so far as to require you to own the previous two Warhammer games (including their DLCs) to access the full content. Some content is even locked behind requiring you to create a CA account and link it to your Steam account, something that isn't mentioned anywhere on the store page mind you. Not only are races and factions tied to DLCs but essential units as well. For example, you might be interested in playing as the Skaven after watching some gameplay on YouTube, so you purchase Warhammer 2 only to find out that their best and most exciting units, the Weapons Teams (Ratling Guns, Warplock Jezzails, etc.), aren't even part of their base roster. So if you want to have the true Skaven experience you have to buy even more DLCs just to get their full roster. The game is essentially a big jigsaw puzzle where you have to buy each puzzle piece separately at ludicrous prices. Just to put this into context, the Chaos Dwarf DLC costs half the price of a full game for just one measly race.

For years I looked with interest at the TW:WH series and wishlisted it. The open world, immortal empire campaign, struggle of good vs evil, and offer of a majorly 'uphill battle' single player were super enticing. But it's nothing like other 'open world' games I loved- Civilization, the Age of Wonder series (up to #3), Dune Wars, etc. I am sure its amazing for some people but here's why -IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A FANTASY CIVILIZATION-LIKE EXPERIENCE- I don't recommend this:

1. The camera & colors - I know there's a mod(s) to help with this, but zooming- like in most full-world strategy isn't possible. You sorta can zoom - but its either too close or too far away to be useful. On top of that, the warnings weren't wrong. The exaggerated colors and vivid displays left my eyes hurting after a while. The graphical elements are so bright and pronounced they also tend to obstruct the UI buttons/unit interaction tags. 

2. The UI -  It doesn't use the same key movement scheme or unit selection that I thought was standard. Shift click quing- doesn't quite work like it does in most RTS. Unit selection is a bit different as well, double clicking doesn't let you pick all types of that unit- it just felt off.

3. The Over-the-top environment - In the age of wonders series, if I see a bleeding skull cut into the mountain- I can do something about it (raze and extinguish that feature).  Here, you can't- its just there. The enormous monoliths tower over the mountains, and chasims make no sense for their scope and scale- AND I GET IT'S AN ART FORM- but it just ruins the immersion for me. 

4. Empire Building - It feels like it has more of a mobile game the way the outposts are built. There's just a bunch of drapes to choose for upgrades, and slowly your city/outpost settlement changes. It reminds me of those old facebook games with farms or similar browser based games. Meanwhile, the focus on heroes is super intense- there's an INSANE amount of stats on them with upgrades to eek out whatever you'd desire. It's not focused on the empire. 

5. The On-The-Rails - You're not contemplating where to put cities, farms, resource nodes- in this game. It's all there for you already fixed in place! The fact that, apart from gold, you're not really sharing resources between different settlements adds to this. 

Anyways, if I am poking someone's personal favorite game- sorry. If you're a Civ Fan or similar 4x- you're probably not going to enjoy this like me.

If you enjoyed previous Total War titles or enjoy RTS games generally, I strongly recommend this game, even if you are not versed in the lore of the Warhammer Fantasy universe.

The only downside of this game is the sheer amount of DLC and how much you have to sink your wallet into the game if you want to explore every possible avenue the game has to offer. But even getting a couple adds SO much replayability + workshop adding even more variability to the game really just gives this game so much more compared to the other total war games. 


Overall, if you want a game that gives you every avenue to play your own way, doomstack your own way, or play to whatever variability, explore fantasy warhammer in a way you have never explored, no other total war, or game, or media will give you an even an ounce of content compared to total war warhammer 3. Una experiencia épica para los fanáticos de la estrategia en tiempo real, con un alcance masivo y un universo rico. El juego combina las clásicas batallas de Total War con las dinámicas propias del mundo de Warhammer, ofreciendo un sistema de combate detallado y profundamente táctico. Las batallas se sienten monumentales, con ejércitos enormes enfrentándose en escenarios llenos de acción. El manejo de las facciones es variado, cada una con unidades y habilidades únicas, lo que otorga una enorme rejugabilidad y flexibilidad en el estilo de juego, aunque a veces me parecía un poco complejo entender estos estilos de juego.
Las mecánicas de juego están pulidas, con un sistema de gestión de recursos que, aunque eficaz, puede resultar algo abrumador al principio debido a la cantidad de cosas que uno debe aprender. Las batallas son el centro de la experiencia, pero la interacción con el mapa de campaña, los eventos aleatorios y las decisiones diplomáticas enriquecen la experiencia global.
Gráficamente, Total War: Warhammer III sigue el alto estándar visual de la saga, con paisajes impresionantes y un diseño de unidades meticulosamente detallado. Los entornos son vibrantes y épicos, haciendo justicia a la magnitud de las batallas y a la estética del universo Warhammer. Sin embargo, algunas texturas y animaciones en las unidades pueden parecer algo estáticas o simplistas, especialmente en comparación con otros aspectos más detallados del juego.

Es un buen juego, pero con algunos problemas de rendimiento y no tan amigable para los novatos. A pesar de todo esto, es un título muy recomendable.

I am not writing this lightly. I very rarely write game reviews, and this is my first negative review ever. I am writing this as a long-term fan of the series: I have just shy of 470h on Total War Warhammer, just a bit more than 2300h on Total War Warhammer 2, and about 970h on this game. I also own all of the DLCs for all three games up to and including Thrones of Decay, i.e. everything up to October 2024. Obviously, even including the cost of all the DLCs, these games have provided good value for money in the past.

But things have changed: as of the second half of 2024, I am no longer able to enjoy this game. This is not me getting bored of it: I still enjoy the "instant of playing", so to speak. But a change in patching policy has made it impossible for me to reliably finish a campaign, and the frustration of having games killed by the developer midway through is, for me, high enough that I can't find the motivation to start a new one anymore.

Adding more details. This is a game where a single run through ("campaign") can easily take between 40 and 100 hours, depending on many factors. That means that it typically takes me between one and two months to complete a campaign. This is also a game where patches tend to break existing saves and the recommendation of the developer has always been to not even try to load old campaigns in a new version of the game.

The developer used to be very slow in improving the game, publishing patches along with DLCs about once every six to nine months. When they did, they tended to create a "beta" release targeting the previous version, so players were able to keep playing on the pre-DLC version for a while. I did not keep track of how long each old version remained, but it has historically been long enough for me to finish ongoing campaigns before installing the new patch and enjoying the new content.

Over the course of 2024, the company made two big changes, one very good and one very bad. On the good side, they started releasing much more frequent patches, listening to the community, and actually improving some aspects of the game instead of just producing new content. That is very good for the long-term health of the game.

However, at the same time, they decided to change the way they publish "betas" of old versions in a way that is completely unusable as a player. I have no idea how they came up with their current design, but as both a player of the game and a software professional who spent the last six years heavily involved in versioning questions for a big company providing foundational B2B software, it makes absolutely no sense and is completely useless.

From a practical perspective, they have completely stopped providing any way for players to keep playing an existing campaign when they release a new patch, which now happens on a much more frequent and much less predictable basis, with an average of perhaps once a month, and most often with no warning whatsoever.

I have tried raising this issue with the developer twice now, and each time my ticket was closed with no further comment beyond "the system is working as intended", which seems to imply the intent is that I no longer play the game.

If anyone from CA ever reads this, let me be clear that I will be very happy to remove this review as soon as you once again have a useful "old versions" policy. I'd really like to be able to finish my 5.3.1 campaign, and would be looking forward to playing other ones if I could believe you will let me finish them.

Unfortunately this game has so many bugs and so many broken ways in which it is patched that I cannot in good faith recommend it.

When it's at it's best, it is a ton of fun. Unfortunately it is rarely at it's best.

short summary:
-Ranged units are broken
-AI is bad, so they simply pump it with cheats on all difficulties
-Difficulty scaling is broken, other than small stat differences in units the differences between difficulty modes both in campaign and battle are unnoticable. Very hard is the same as normal, legendary is barely more difficult.
- Early game difficulty is monotonous, extreme and hairpulling, which rapidly transitions to mid to late game where its a boring steamroll
- lots of bugs 
- you pay a lot of money for factions that are overpowered or underbaked

- Ranged units are extremely buggy, even with a clear line of sight on completely flat ground they will often simply not fire. Even the amount of damage they do on unarmored units can sometimes vary wildly for no discernible reason. This means you can plan your tactics out all you want, and then when it comes time to fight you simply get rolled over because your units chose not to fight. If there are hills or trees, forget it, your ranged units will simply wait to be demolished. They also do not react well to be told who to fire on and will run into melee, stop doing anything, or take a very long time to reorganize themselves for no reason

- The developer has not been able to figure out a reasonable way to make the game difficult, and simply opts to give the AI more and more cheats. Even on normal difficulty, the AI pays nothing for units, pays nothing for upkeep, does not require buildings sometimes, builds buildings for free instantly, recruits instantly at times, and their lord can respawn with a full stack often instantly even without the ability on paper to do so (e.g. tamurkhan or some vampire lords.) This makes the game more difficult, but also feel more like an arcade game than a strategy game. Unfortunately the community loves this, as they are only interested in being challenged at any and all expense to realism. So this isn't going to change. Additionally the AI has super powers of dodging artillery and magic that even advanced players do not have -this is true on normal and it does not even get better at it on very hard, as it has already mastered the ability on normal mode.

- Differences between normal, hard, very hard are invisible. It's the same mode. The AI acts the same way, recruits the same way with the same cheats etc. there are minor stat bonuses you can scale on units but in practice they don't matter much. As a result the community likes to play on very hard and pretend they are very good at the game even though its the same broken setting as normal mode. In reality there are only three difficulty settings: easy, normal and legendary. legendary is harder but arcade-y for the AI and is not a more immersive experience. The AI simply is not affected by mechanics of your faction, by money, or by losing. They simply spawn endless stacks of enemies like the arcade game alien invader. it is definitely a challenge, but not a strategy game. You might play a faction and be excited to use their mechanics on the enemy. You will be disappointed. Only damage dealing units matter on legendary. Do not bother picking targets. It is an arcade mode.

- Early game regardless of setting is extremely frustrating, as you are forced to min-max and choose the correct target or you are completely screwed because you chose a faction that has multiple stacks of armies in the first few turns. As a result you will likely start and end campaigns multiple times using the same boring weak units. Once you pick the correct choices and survive to turn 10 to 20, you will begin steamrolling with your high level units and fighting will not matter. as a result you will be less inclined to see your high level units in action. the difficulty curve is cartoonish here and not fun. it immediately goes from exhaustive and not fun, to far too easy and not fun. This is true regardless of whether youre on normal or legendary difficulty setting. Because of the way difficulty has been implemented for the AI in a broken manner.

- there are a lot of bugs besides ranged units (though those I found the most frustrating). camera sometimes acts wonky, a unit I defeated all units to 0 hp simply continued to exist and walk around with a full stack army at full health, sacked a settlement once and received nothing even though the menu said I would receive some 10,000 gold. It isnt super buggy mind you, most of the time its fine. but once in a while when youre dealing with other things it gets frustrating. there are mods that fix these things but it should be fixed by the developers.

- Some of the factions which they still charge a lot of money for seperate from the game are either far too powerful and youre simply paying to win as they give the AI more and more cheats, or they are underbaked and have no mechanics, poor animations etc. and you will wonder what you paid for. Some of the DLC is fairly priced but a lot of it is not.

Da migliorare: 
il gioco, nonostante requisiti minimi abbordabili diventa instabile per piattaforme non all'avanguardia, presentando fin troppi crash.

A livello di battaglia (tempo reale) :
è estremamente difficile controllare le truppe che spesso ingaggiano combattimenti non voluti o si mettono a inseguire nemici in fuga, gli appositi settaggi per evitare che ciò accada di default causano simili problemi di gestione (truppe che si riposano o che subiscono attacchi a distanza da ferme o che attaccano nemici che non abbiamo richiesto di attaccare, ecc).

Nonostante il dettaglio nelle cose da migliorare, segno solo della mia grande passione per questo gioco e per il mondo che esso racconta, il mio giudizio è estremamente positivo e non vedo l'ora che vengano aggiunte altre razze o nuovi engine per l combattimenti su vasta scala. Honestly this iteration Total Warhammer is a mixed bag for me, as well as a lot of the community with ~80% recent and ~70% overall, but I do recommend it.

The game has undergone a massive face-lift since TW2 and it really shows.
[list]
    [*]Auto-resolve tells you what units die in battle now. WHY DID IT ALMOST TAKE 2 DECADES FOR THIS TO BE ADDED??? Playing any other Total War for me now feels absolutely awful when I have to quick-save and guess what units may die.
    [*]The new factions are magnificent, extremely versatile in their gameplay which is my main draw in playing other factions. A pretty decent stream of content from DLCs means there are a few new leaders to play every year or so, and with some factions getting a face-lift(chaos my beloved) it makes playing them feel like a brand new experience that dwarfs my enjoyment of them from TW2.
    [*]With new factions they also revamped the alliance system in fantastic new ways, mainly the outpost/war coordination system. Being able to simply *direct* allies as to how to conduct the war is a huge boost as I can, in theory, tell them to defend one front while I attack somewhere else. The outpost system also allows faction variety beyond the base faction system, allowing vampires to get siege weapons or skaven to gaet *actual* late game infantry, which is wonderful in expanding an army roster list.
    [*]Siege battles have been drastically improved in terms of variety of maps and simple changes never made in TW2; highground inside cities so your artillery can fire at an assaulting army, heavy gunner units can mount walls, and siege points that can be used to build defenses inside the city after the walls fall. All of these things seemed like a no-brainer for siege defenses, but were never implemented in TW2 outside mods.
    [*]The new Immortal Empires map is MASSIVE, with so many factions available(especially with faction unlockers) that you could probably play tens of thousands of hours and still not get full campaign experiences for every little faction. The changes to some starting locations is also appreciated, allowing me a refreshing experience with some faction leaders in newer locales compared to TW2.
    [*]The new factions are magnificent, extremely versatile in their play-ability which is my main draw to play other factions. A pretty decent stream of content from DLCs means there are a few new leaders to play every year or so, and with some factions getting a face-lift(chaos my beloved) it makes playing them feel like a brand new experience that dwarfs my enjoyment of them from TW2.
[/list]

[h1][i]But...[/i][/h1]
At the same time many of these positives come with direct downsides linked to them.
[list]
    [*]Auto-resolve is just terrible if you pick certain factions. I was playing Ogre Kingdoms and was about to suffer a 90% loss of units in my army against Skaven(genuinely only clanrats/skaven slaves in the armies). We played it out manually where we literally right clicked the Skaven and walked at them. 34 deaths(our army consisted of ~800) to 2000 kills. There are about half a dozen factions where auto-resolve just isn't an option, even on the lowest difficulties. I now use a mod to slightly adjust auto-resolve so I don't waste dozens of hours fighting early game infantry battles.
    [*]The DLC-spam has become notorious in the strategy game community. Paradox is the prime example in this monument to greed and Creative assembly seems to be going down the same route. The DLC that get put out are often half baked and overpriced beyond any reasonable doubt. I don't mind purchasing dlc that add dozens of hours of game-play, but when they are [i]abysmal[/i] on release and only become playable years later(looking at you Ogre Kingdom) then it just shows how little effort CA is willing to put in to shave a little money off its community.
    [*]The outpost/war coordination is just pretty poorly implemented. Constructing outposts costs a ton early/requires you to trust 1 of their cities, unless it is a massive capital like Skavenblight be ready to rebuild it when their city gets taken/razed. Ever ally with someone but don't want an outpost? Enjoy clicking a bonus notification button *every turn* to ignore building an outpost, even if they are the same race as you and give you no new units in any of their cities. The war coordination system seems good on paper, but it won't stop your allies from taking territory that is clearly in your path, nor will it stop your allies from drip-feeding their armies into a stronghold and never capturing it without you paying war-coordination money to turn their brains on. I want to like the system, but whenever I say 'Hey I can use the war-coordination system for this' I can, indeed, not use the war coordination system for that or I can do it faster myself.
    [*]Many of the sieges that are available I just skip. In the game's beta-immortal empires form it felt more forgiving and nuanced, with rebuild-able defenses that made a running defense of your city viable so long as your army didn't break. Most of the time I kind of groan when I have to play one out because I rarely feel that I out-maneuvered or outsmarted the opponent, but rather the enemy decided to slowly scale walls while being shot or funneled into a super tight choke-point with a tier 4 defense tower bombarding them. Basically TW2 sieges felt so cool because the walls and chokes meant so much in terms of tactical advantages, now you just toss units around to provide the bare minimum for resources and hope the enemy dies of cringe enough to shatter.
    [*]The new map is big, but it is so big that it ends of being its downfall. With 554 settlements and 278 factions at the start the developers have taken a step back and gone 'this isnt viable for our players to be expected to conquer most of this' and taken the piss out of long victories. In TW2 a long campaign victory really FELT like you had the world in your hand, making you conquer enough in most cases that your victory was all but assured after the fact, now many factions just say 'raze/conq/sack 60 settlements+get a resource to lvl 3 of 5'. With that shortened win condition in play they also added a system to challenge the player more in the short term to balance out the removed late game difficulty, [b]the anti-player bias[/b]...
    [*][b][i]I despise the anti-player bias.[/i][/b] It is a value hard coded into the game that does as it suggests. Your allies will falter, your neighbors want [i]YOUR[/i] stuff over all worldly possessions, and you are sitting there trying to wonder why a game that makes you fight 5 random factions at the same time is a 'fun' experience. TW2 didn't need this in the game and there is diplomacy for exactly this reason. Someone strong? Make a treaty with them. They don't accept? Ask your neighbors to join a defensive pact. They declare war? Bribe other factions to join or beg your allies to intervene. Instead we get the 'free thinkers' iRobot meme the second the player gets beyond 10 settlements. I use a mod to turn this setting off and the game is genuinely frustrating without it.
[/list]
 
I do really like this game and recommend it as probably one of the best total war games ever made simply because they have directly improved the Total War formula so much, but understand that there are very solid reasons why people don't recommend it.

[h1]Bonus[/h1]
I really didn't go over *all* of the QoL differences between the two games, but they are so numerous 'itsmehawkeyeg' made a 27 minute video breaking down how much they worked on improving the base experience. If you are a fan of the Total War games, this one is a must have.
