I really wish I could in good conscience make this a positive review. I've secretly been sustaining a "next patch will be the one" mentality, but after THREE YEARS in this third part of the trilogy alone, I'm out of hopium. 

[h3]I think a good summary is a thought that boiled up the other day: playing WH3 feels to me like I have a "minutes since the last substantial bug/balance issue" wall counter, and it never takes too long to reset to 0.[/h3]
Especially if you trained your eye by meddling with the game in terms of modding, you can spot them everywhere, and each patch is at best a one-step-ahead-one-step-behind situation where they fix a bug or introduce a good thing, but break something else. 

[h3]It's three years in WH3 and NINE YEARS in the trilogy[/h3]and we still have to deal with stuff like units forgetting orders, ranged units refusing to fire for no reason, single-entity or chariot-like unit performance that is way too relative to their animations (in either direction) compared to just their readable stats. 

WH3 launched in a super buggy state with a narrative campaign that hardly anybody plays more than once, as if oblivious to the fact that the same happened with WH2 (more context to it but eh), and a siege rework that can be summarized with most people autoresolving every single siege map. Similarly to how many admit to autoresolving fights against characters that are completely overpowered and/or obnoxious to fight manually. 
[h3]The game also maintains a steady story with unrepentant powercreep and "how did you honestly think this was a good idea" features/power levels, which coupled with insufficient QC means there's always more to fix.[/h3]

I could rant for hours. I want to love this game, I'm not insane enough to be still modding it if I didn't. I know there are good eggs at CA, I know they stepped up since the Shadows of Change outrage, and I don't lack "oh that's cool" moments towards gameplay or modding, but there's just so much still going the other way that I can't stay positive.

[h3]Another summary: TWWH is a fantastic spectacle and a great RTS/RTT held more or less together with duct tape, and no other game I played in the past few years managed to give me a comparable sense of lack of polish.[/h3]

Get the game and any DLC you really want at deep discount, and hope that CA gets some serious competition soon for a much-deserved wake up call.

Okay, I don't want to take much of everybody's sweet time so I will try to make this as clear as I can while writing an essay:

First off, this game is part of a trilogy of games, which they are all sort off the same, it feels like the iterations  of one single game over the years personally, with Warhammer I being like a Prototype, Warhammer II is a more solid thing, like a 1.0, and Warhammer III is a 2.0. In other words, I dont reckon you buy the other two and stay with this one instead.

Now, If I had to choose TWO strategy games to play for the rest of my life, this would be it, no overthinking, one of them would be Total War Warhammer III ( the other is Age of Empires 2 Definitive Edition ).

It is the ultimate real time tactics strategy / turn based game, the scale of a lot of things is just superb, the amount of factions, leaders, units, mechanics on another level I reckon. You MIGHT initially get lost with the quantity of features to understand, however here is the catch: 

There are factions that are easier to understand and others that are more complicated, with all factions sharing most of the same concepts ( lords, units, cities, heroes, money ) but each faction will have different mechanics from the others to achieve their goals in game. 

and Please, my main suggestion to get you into the game is PLAY the Prologue before going into any other mode the game offers you to play, it will give you a rundown of how MOST of the game works in around 2 hours and also if you are interested, gives you a bit of lore of what is going on the world the game is set in. After that, I suggest Bretonnia ( Repanse as Lord ) , High Elves ( Tyrion as Lord ). and after those campaigns if you enjoyed them, you can try other factions later on, WHICH takes me to the BIGGEST issue that CA has with ALL their games and the current problem in game marketing and design:

Every single one of their past titles have a lot of content blocked behind a Giant Golden Paywall, in other words, when you buy Warhammer III you only have a mere fraction of the factions that are available to you on the get go, and the rest you buy DLCs for them.

Sure, you can have some fun with the factions that are in the base game and then later if you enjoyed the experience, you can buy more factions, sounds fair enough, but in general the DLCs average $8-$30 ( australian dollars ) and even I have no plans to buy all of them for the lack of interest in some of the factions, but the major problem is that some units will not be available to you if you dont get the DLCS and some DLCS are just extra gore and blood effects added to the game. 

SIDENOTE: For the owners of Warhammer I and II and you paid for the DLCS back then, they carry over to Warhammer III, because at the end of the day, the trilogy are KIND OFF the same game, but with improvements, tweaks and adjustments over the years.

As big as the universe and the lore is, there is ABSOLUTELY no need for you to be a fan of the Warhammer lore previously to play the game, neither understands any previous, current or future lore to play it. I literally started playing because it was recommended to me by my cousin as a solid turn based strategy game.

With all that being said, I still like this game a lot and I know it will give me hours and hours of great content, my last campaign with Karl Franz was one of the best strategy game experiences I had in my life.

Also note, this game has a Mod community / Workshop on Steam, past the first experience you have, go and have a browse there, because I thank the Mod community for pumping this game with FREE content!

And as well, because of the amount of DLC that you can buy ( and if you are interested ) just wait for a solid discount during July or end of the year so you can grab the game at a fair discount.

It was a welcoming surprise to me on a very weird and complicated time of life, and I thank my cousin for introducing me to this franchise, love ya!

NOTE: After reading through the review and some notes about the game on other player's reviews, I do 100% agree that some campaigns are MUCH better played on previous iterations of the game. ( such as playing Repanse de Lyonesse, a Bretonnian Lord, in Warhammer II but not Warhammer III, similar to Eltharion and Grom the Paunch, Lords which their campaigns make WAY more sense if you play on Warhammer II, and so far, they have been just thrown into the Warhammer III mix with no future plans ).

Also yes, Snowballing on this game becomes a thing as soon as you start understanding the game mechanics, which makes most of the game experience kinda the same for all the factions you play, but that does not stop it from being fun ( after all, snowballing also happens in many other Total War games and they didn't stop being fun to me at least ).


Personally I think that the campaigns / Lords that are more fleshed out than others right now are: Karl Franz ( The Empire ), Malakai Makaisson ( Dwarfs ), Tzarina Katarina ( Kislev ).

Total War: Warhammer III — це справжній тріумф стратегічної думки й творчої фантазії. Гра піднімає планку не лише для всієї трилогії, але й для жанру глобальних стратегій у цілому. Вона поєднує у собі масштаб епічних битв і глибину дипломатичних маневрів, занурюючи гравця у похмурий, але захопливий світ Warhammer Fantasy.

Кожна фракція — унікальна й продумана до найменших деталей. Від демонічних орд до імперій смертних — усе має свій характер, стиль гри й глибину. Особливо вражає кампанія за Дао Цзінь, де містика Сходу поєднується з воєнною майстерністю.

Візуально гра виглядає приголомшливо. Дизайн юнітів, анімація битв, атмосфера — усе це викликає справжнє естетичне захоплення. Саундтрек доповнює загальну епічність і підсилює відчуття занурення.

Так, гра має свої недоліки — іноді штучний інтелект діє нелогічно, а інтерфейс може видатись складним новачкам. Проте все це відходить на другий план, коли ти опиняєшся в серці битви, керуючи армією з тисяч бійців.

Total War: Warhammer III — це не просто гра. Це досвід, у який хочеться поринати знову і знову. Вона дарує емоції, які залишаються з вами надовго.

Оцінка: ⭐ 9.5/10

I am a very long-time Total War fan, and a very long-time Total War Warhammer trilogy fan. These have quite possibly been my favorite games of all time.

So it is genuinely heartbreaking to say that I cannot in good conscience recommend this game.

On the one hand, its potential for fun is very high. I enjoy it every time I play, and I will continue to play!

On the other hand, it is largely broken, being held together by duct tape and faithful community mods.
Considering the VERY HIGH cost of entry, customers are certainly entitled to a quality and complete product, but in truth that is not what they are getting. Legacy bugs that have been present across multiple iterations of the games; new glitches and (sometimes gamebreaking) bugs every time they release another DLC and update the game; very broken or ridiculous mechanics that fans have nearly universally indicated are just bad (siege battles being the most obvious offender); repetitively questionable or straight-up unethical DLC and community management practices; the list goes on and on…

All these things paint a pretty bleak picture in terms of the value of the Total War Warhammer trilogy as a product.

If you are a person who has cash to burn and for whom this game looks particularly fun, then go for it. You probably will have fun. But now, you’ve also been warned: This is simply not a high quality product for the amount of money you will pay in order to ensure the most complete experience. There are much more quality gaming options out there that will deliver a cleaner, higher-value experience for your hard-earned cash.

I feel so let down, disillusioned, disappointed about the shattered potential here. The leadership culture at CA has guaranteed that this title will probably always be a tragic shadow of what it so very well could have been.

Things need to change at CA, big time. Until they do, I cannot, with a clear conscience, continue to support their practices financially as I have so very eagerly in the past, nor to recommend others buy in. This is FAR deeper than demanding they fix things up this one time. Because there is always a next time. And I’m not talking about fixing up little annoyances or prioritizing simple game balance issues. I am talking about the baseline ethics of a company ensuring that their customers receive a quality product for their money. And that is CLEARLY not something CA cares about, at all.

They can’t even humble themselves enough to issue a proper apology without gaslighting the entire community, ridiculous PR euphemisms, not-so-clever equivocation, shifting blame, horrifically unethical and arrogant attitudes, etc… much less prioritize putting out a baseline quality product.

So, so sad.



[i]original review[\i]:
The Total War Warhammer series is probably my favorite set of games of all time. It's kinda hard to judge them as three separate games because they are all so intimately linked in so many ways.

There are certainly some legacy issues, kinks, and annoyances. And CA as a developer is not the greatest but also not the worst.

Overall this game is more than able to provide thousands of hours' worth of very thorough enjoyment and I would STRONGLY recommend it to any strategy game lover.

The DLC could be extremely expensive if you wanted everything in the game, but then again not everything is necessary in order to play and have all the fun. I would STRONGLY suggest to anyone considering this game that you buy the base game (or, perhaps, the three main titles in the series) to begin with and WAIT on any DLC. Your experience will still be very complete without any DLC, and you can always pick up some on-sale DLC later, AFTER you have gotten into the game and begun to learn what you most enjoy or don't. If you buy too much DLC up front, I can almost promise you that you will find you have wasted your money for absolutely no reason.

In my experience, most of the DLC is well worth the price ONLY if you already enjoy that particular race or play style, which you can only know for sure after you played for quite a while.

Personal opinion, not a technical critique

Let me start by saying: Total War, Warhammer is a well-made and impressive game. It’s packed with content, the factions feel unique, and Creative Assembly has done an outstanding job bringing the Warhammer universe to life. The way they’ve handled expansions makes sense, and the ability to play with a full group of friends is fantastic, something I really miss in the historical Total War games.

That said, I have to be honest: I just can't enjoy Warhammer in the Total War format. This isn't the game's fault, it's simply a matter of personal taste. I've always loved the historical aspects of the series, real empires, real battles, and historical tactics. Warhammer removes all of that, and for me, it makes it difficult to get truly invested, even though I’ve given it multiple chances.

So yes, this review is negative, but only because it’s not my kind of Total War. I understand that I’m in the minority here, and that’s completely fine. If you enjoy fantasy, magic, and epic heroes, this game is absolutely for you. But if, like me, you prefer grounded historical warfare, this one might not hit the mark.

The Tome of Endless War: A Chronicle of Total War: Warhammer III
Penned by Marcius, Keeper of Legends and Chronicler of the Great Cataclysm

In the dying light of an age wracked by sorcery and steel, I, Marcius, set quill to parchment to record the great and terrible saga known henceforth as Total War: Warhammer III.

Harken, ye wanderers and warlords, to this solemn account:
a world set ablaze with ambition, blood, and magic, where might and madness entwine and no soul — mortal or monstrous — escapes the call to arms.

Upon this vast and battered sphere, the mighty and the monstrous march side by side:

The stoic Dwarfs, grim sons of stone and stubborn will.

The insidious Skaven, gnawing at the roots of creation with verminous cunning.

The rampaging Orcs, whose WAAAGH!s thunder across the fields of men.

The deathless kings of Nehekhara, who stride from their sun-blasted tombs in eternal defiance.

The Empire of Sigmar, steadfast halberdiers and thunderous hellfire rocket batteries, crying to the heavens,

"FOR SIGMAR! FOR THE EMPIRE!"

And amidst them all, the blasphemous hordes of Chaos, whose unholy rites seek to shatter the very fabric of reality.

The world is a living dream — or a nightmare —
where magic rends the heavens,
where monstrous engines reap harvests of flesh,
where heroes rise like stars and fall like stones into the abyss.

Raise thy banners.
Muster thy armies.
Crush thine enemies and carve thy legend across the shattered lands.

Yet even the mightiest tapestry bears its rents and tears.

The sieges, though grand, oft favor brute breaches over cunning.
Diplomacy, though improved, remains at times a blunt tool; the councils of kings lack the serpentine craft and perilous depth they ought possess.
The AI, fierce at moments, yet sometimes stumbles — besieging without purpose, withdrawing without reason.
And though glory blooms across the campaign, there are places where repetition gnaws at the spirit:
the Realm of Chaos, though rich in vision, oft interrupts the flow of mortal conquest with rift and ruin.

Performance falters too, where the snows of Kislev and the tundras of Norsca slow the march of armies not through might, but through unseen sorcery of the engine.

Yet for all this, Total War: Warhammer III remains a wonder:
a realm of infinite war, where no victory is certain and every fall is a legend in itself.

For what sweeter triumph than to hold fast as the tides of darkness rise,
thy banners torn, thy warriors bloodied — yet thy spirit unbroken?

Virtues of the Great War (Strengths +):
⚔️ Epic scale and diversity: Each faction — from Dwarfs to Demons — offers distinct mechanics, units, and strategies.

🌍 Immortal Empires Campaign: A vast fusion of the three games' maps, uniting the whole world into a boundless arena of conquest.

🎨 Visual and sound excellence: A world of magic, horror, and wonder, rendered in breathtaking beauty and dread.

🛡️ Improved diplomacy mechanics: Balance deals, outpost construction, and more nuanced alliances enrich the political dance.

🌋 Endgame Disaster system: Breathes peril and excitement into the late game, preventing stagnation.

⚔️ Dynamic battlefield tactics: Tactics matter — terrain, magic, morale, all can turn the tide.

🤝 Strong multiplayer options, including co-op campaigns and survival battles.

Flaws Carved in the Stone of War (Vices −):
🏯 Siege battles, though imposing, often lack complexity and rely too heavily on simple breaches rather than tactical depth.

🧠 AI behavior, both in diplomacy and battle, can be inconsistent — clever at times, baffling at others.

🗺️ Performance issues: Frame rate drops plague the great northern wastes of Kislev and Norsca.

🕳️ Realm of Chaos campaign structure, while ambitious, disrupts the flow for many, feeling repetitive and intrusive.

⚖️ Faction balance: Certain powers may snowball too easily if unchecked.

🎯 Limited unit diversity for some factions, leading to a feeling of sameness in long campaigns.

📜 Steep learning curve for newcomers, with systems layered thick as the walls of a Dwarfen hold.

Final Inscription of Marcius:
Total War: Warhammer III is a realm without equal —
a battlefield where gods and mortals clash,
where ambition is a blade and survival itself a triumph.

Though its vast tapestry bears a few rents and stains, its majesty is undeniable,
and its call irresistible to all who dream of empires forged in fire, blood, and sorcery.

Whether thou art a grim Dwarf, a scheming Skaven, a deathless Pharaoh, or a paladin of Sigmar —
thy saga awaits.

Raise thy standard, sharpen thy blade — for the world shall not conquer itself!

This game has had its fair share of controversies, and some of the business practices of those at Creative Assembly have been rightfully criticised in the wake of several DLC launches. It's important to speak up as a community and let companies know when they're crossing lines or taking the wrong approach, and CA's negligence and greed at times has been outrageous, and does seem to have been genuinely recognised and tackled by the developers - albeit more slowly than it should have been.

That being said, at its core, Warhammer 3 - and in particular Immortal Empires - feels much like an 'Avengers: Endgame' scenario: the culmination of years of work, build-up, adjustment, and growth. Seeing the many, many diverse races become more and more fleshed out across the trilogy, watching entire mechanics come and go as others are refined, experiencing something so ambitious in scope gradually become realised... it's been quite amazing.

I'm a long time fan of the Total War series, with one of my first ever PC games as a kid being Rome: Total War. I've seen the highs and lows of the franchise, I've put thousands of hours into these games over two decades. The Warhammer Total War trilogy (and therefore this current, ultimate iteration) has, in my opinion, blown the entire series out of the water in a transformative way. Not necessarily in polish, in fact it's been one of the jankier rides in the franchise's history. But marrying the Total War formula to a fantasy setting has been like unlocking a new power level. The freedom provided has led to the kind of scale, variety, creativity, originality, outlandishness, and spectacle that is simply not possible in a historically grounded setting. That's not to say their historical games suck, but I have genuinely found it difficult to enjoy them since this particular genie has come out of its bottle.

Such spectacle and variety have made the Warhammer trilogy of Total War games feel infinitely more replayable, refreshing, and downright fun that any other entry in the series for me personally. In fact, I'd go as far to say it may be the single most replayable strategy game I've ever played, rivalled only by Civilization V.

It isn't perfect, and CA should continue to be held accountable for their slip-ups. A recent bug made the game unplayable for me for four whole months before it was finally fixed, and that just isn't good enough. But I also believe this is one of the current gold standards in strategy gaming, and has set several bars that will be VERY difficult to surpass. I could see myself clocking in 3-4 thousand hours before I even begin to get bored. My only hope for this game is that the developers see their vision through to completion before moving onto the next fictional Total War project (Warcraft please), and that includes revisiting the idea of including Araby, as well as potentially Nippon, Albion, and/or Ind. Regardless, I can't call this a masterpiece, but I would call it a stunning accomplishment.

This game is a recommend with a lot of caveats. While the game itself is usually fine, minus some minor bugs or miss-balancing that is usual of the RTS genre. The main point of contention has always been the price versus content.
While I don't think this game is lacking in a major way, there are small points here or there that game feel too empty.

A main point to this is the constant updates that happen after either a game release or DLC release.
Though on the surface this may seem really good, the main problem is that whoever is responsible for the final calls on the direction of DLC and main game releases seems not to understand what the playerbase enjoys.
There have been some amazing DLC releases with a lot of praise going to them, then the next DLC has the same faults they had with other DLC before the last. Not to mention the main games themselves always come out in a buggy, unfinished in some parts, or excessive way.
And while maybe if this was the first game they ever made it would be fine, they seem to treat every sequel, DLC, and spin-off or new series as if it was their first time creating a game.

To point out a way this main game came out in an excessive way is the realms of chaos campaign. In all honestly there was and is no excuse that this was the first thing they focused on despite no one asking for or wanting it.
While some players say they like Realms of Chaos, the truth is they were not asking for it pre-release either, to them it was simply a happy surprise. However to the rest of the fans of the series, the lack of Immortal Empires from the games start was a huge blow to everything.
And again if this was the first game that may be fine, however even knowing that the majority of the community loved the large map with faction objection system in 2, they chose Realms of Chaos.

To the credit of the developers they did eventually ad Immortal Empires as promised, however it came much to late, and instead of further leaping from a high point, they were made to climb back up the ladder just to jump again.
if this game was 20, no even 30-40 dollars this may have been forgivable. Yet they priced this game at full triple A price. While now after everything it may be worth close to that, there are still many problems or points of contention that make the game fall just short.

Now the actual game-play as of right now is perfectly fine. There may be systems people wish were in this series, or that they hope would be removed from the series. However this is not a killing blow to many of them. The major boon this game truly provides, aside from it's slightly non-standard perfectly servicable RTS systems, is the art direction.
I do have to give a hand to the art team, as the models, animations, and look of the maps are beautifully done (even if the maps themselves are hit or miss.) The music doesn't lose out, and is quite fun to listen to (though of course 50 turns in you may switch to other music until you play with a new faction haha)
The cinematic camera combined with the detail of the arrow trail and impacts are amazing. The magic effects are really something special, especially when you use them to full effect and characters fall to their knees, are blown away, or blown to smithereens as you cast your spells on them.
The different factions, and for the most part the models and units they decided to include in the game is honestly a ton of fun to look at and play with.
The lords and their voice acting and personality is really something that brings you to either love or despise the characters, which lets you get even more invested into your favorite races.
Even the spread of races themselves (again though the price of entry is a major pain point) is quite good. from chaos to order, dwarves to elves, orks to scaven, even ogres and vampire kingdoms and pirates.
The wide spread is genuinely a nice addition to this game.

Over all while I do recommend this game and this series, I also say maybe only buy full price if you are really wanting to play a new RTS or just get hooked on a certain something the game contains.
Otherwise i would recommend waiting for a 20-30% sale for all parts of the game. not just the main game itself but the DLC as well, as they can feel over-priced and leave you slightly disappointed at what wasn't in the game in the first place, an just how much it costs baseline to add them in.

The Total War series and I have had a strained relationship over the past decade, but Total War: Warhammer 2 and 3 are the only ones I keep coming back to year after year. I am by no means a super-fan or expert in the Total War franchise, but coming to it as a massive Warhammer Fantasy fan, it's the best way to experience the most the setting has to offer. Unfortunately, there really aren't a lot of other video games set in this universe. Vermintide 1 and 2 come to mind, but not many others. Those are both excellent, but provide a pretty small window into the fiction being so Empire and Skaven focused, and if you don't like first person hack-and-slash games, you might not get a lot out of them.

I can't really sugarcoat this next part. This game is complicated, difficult (for me personally), and kind of hard to get into as a newcomer - both in terms of Total War games or the Warhammer Fantasy setting. If you can get past that initial barrier of entry, it has so, so much to offer. The amount of content on display is honestly shocking. So many factions, so many unique campaign playstyles, and so, so many cool units to do battle with!

It's far from perfect. Bugs still exist in this game that date back several years (looking at you, siege gate bug), and Creative Assembly have had their fair share of controversy with pricing models, DLC issues, and questionable responses to community feedback.

But... there's nothing else like this out there. No other game can scratch the itch this one does. That's special, and means a lot to me in a gaming market so oversaturated with bland hero shooters, mobile game shovelware, low effort, garbage, derivative, """AAAA""" games from billion dollar companies, and the growing issue of AI slop.

I like the game, but I wish there was an "ish" button for the monetization, because it honestly brings a brilliant game down.

World-building: brilliant, absolutely love it. The world is rich with lore for races, units, geographical areas and play styles, etc. This game is dripping out of the seams with some incredible world-building that I absolutely love. 

Economics and campaign: these are both great. Every race functions differently and operates in a way that makes sense lore-wise and fits their overall playstyle, and the unique variations for each race is just incredible. And the way that the economic and city-building structure of each race works seamlessly with the overall function and style of each group is *chef's kiss*.

Combat and balancing: This can be a bit wonky now and then, but is overall pretty solid. I do wish that the auto-battle feature were a bit more balanced sometimes, as it's generally not bad but there are times when it'll give you a "valiant defeat" but if you manually play it it's easily a "valiant victory." Like the second battle as Tzeench is an easy win, but the game freaks out and thinks you'll lose it for some reason, this coming from someone who isn't a competitive or top-tier player. Otherwise the way you can build armies, pros+cons, make ridiculous builds and absolutely fall on your face if your build is bad is a really great aspect of the game.

PvP: there is a PvP scene that's kept alive pretty much exclusively by passionate content creators that are invested in the game. No dedicated servers, it's all peer-to-peer. Unit balance is an ongoing project, and some races tend to do much better than others, at times due to balancing and at times due to technical difficulty. But the balance of races in many ways comes down to your wallet, as so much is locked behind pay walls, so I suppose it's time to bring up the elephant in the room: monetization.

Monetization: as of writing this all DLC comes out to $320 USD. Yes, $320. There is a lot in the base game and you can absolutely have a blast with that alone, but the Dark Gods forbid if you want to keep up with this game in the long run because it will cost you your first born child. I understand that it takes money to make money, but this amount just seems predatory and hurts the hardcore fans more than anyone else. If you want to get into PvP, explore the full breadth of the campaign settings, or really get into the many different ways of playing that are available you'll need to fork over some really significant cash, and the monetization continues in these series until the next in the series is made, meaning that I fully expect the full price to go well above $320 before it's said and done. It's just unfortunate, really, as it casts a dark shadow on an incredible world and overall game. And if you're looking for an example of just how high the DLC can get check out Total War 1 and 2 then adjust those DLC prices for inflation.

混沌狂潮中的史诗咏叹.

作为系列终章，《全面战争：战锤3》以磅礴的野心将玩家抛入一场混沌与秩序的终极对决。初入震旦天朝，水墨风界面与文言旁白交织出东方史诗的厚重感，而“阴阳宁和”机制则如治国之道般深邃——平衡建筑、科技与兵种的阴阳属性，方能解锁震旦的巅峰战力。玉勇枪阵稳如磐石，龙弩齐射如暴雨倾泻，但面对混沌巨兽的冲锋，这份平衡又脆弱如薄冰，逼玩家在扩张与固守间反复权衡。  

混沌魔域战役是游戏最惊艳的篇章。踏入恐虐的血腥竞技场，杀戮的狂热裹挟着每一支军队，而色孽的诱惑迷宫则让胜利与贪婪的抉择如刀刃割心。每一场魔域试炼不仅是战术的考验，更是对玩家欲望的拷问——是攫取邪神赐福的即时快感，还是为终局之战克制隐忍？这种叙事与策略的深度交融，让战役节奏如交响乐章般跌宕起伏。  

然而，混沌的狂欢下亦有裂隙。恶魔亲王的养成系统虽充满RPG式的自由——通过献祭四神定制肢体与技能，但前期孱弱的兵种与四面楚歌的地理位置，让每一场战斗都沦为手操炼狱。优化问题如幽灵般缠绕：后期大地图掉帧、偶发的读条卡死，以及国服服务器的缺席，让沉浸感在硬件门槛与BUG中片片剥落。  

外交与联机的革新是暗夜中的星光。哨站系统让盟友不再是纸面条约，臣道值可招募异族精锐，甚至将边境孤城化作战略缓冲带。八人联机战役的混沌狂欢虽因网络延迟常沦为“PPT式团战”，但同一回合行动的设计终让协作有了史诗的实感。  

若将《战锤3》比作未完成的混沌祭坛，它已堆砌了足够瑰丽的颅骨与宝石，但祭火的灼热与烟尘亦刺痛着信徒的双眼。它既是策略迷的饕餮盛宴，亦是一面镜子——映照出CA在野心与细节间的摇摆，以及玩家对完美终章的永恒渴求。

Rezension: Total War – Warhammer III
Total War: Warhammer III ist ein beeindruckendes Strategiespiel mit enormer Vielfalt, hohem Wiederspielwert und vielen verschiedenen Spielstilen.

Das Gameplay ist zweigeteilt: Auf der rundenbasierten Kampagnenkarte trifft man strategische Entscheidungen, während in Echtzeitschlachten Taktik gefragt ist. Wer auf der Karte klug agiert, wird mit spannenderen Schlachten belohnt.

Der Schwierigkeitsgrad ist flexibel: Einsteiger finden leicht Zugang, während erfahrene Spieler mit dem legendären Modus oder herausfordernden Mods voll auf ihre Kosten kommen.

Die Hauptkampagne wirkt jedoch schwach und bietet wenig erzählerischen Tiefgang. Die wahre Stärke des Spiels liegt im "Reich der Unsterblichen" (Immortal Empires): eine gigantische Karte mit 24 Fraktionen, die jeweils eigene Spielmechaniken, Kommandanten und Startpositionen bieten. Diese Vielfalt sorgt für enormen Langzeitspaß.

Technisch läuft das Spiel stabil, auch auf Mittelklasse-PCs. Die Grafik ist gelungen, nur die Ladezeiten zwischen Welt- und Gefechtskarte könnten kürzer sein.

Fazit:
Mit über 348 Stunden Spielzeit begeistert mich Warhammer III immer noch. Die riesige Welt, die Vielfalt der Fraktionen und der gelegentliche Multiplayer sorgen für langanhaltenden Spielspaß – trotz schwacher Hauptkampagne.

Bewertung: 9,3/10

After wasting far too many hours of my life on this thing, I can't do it anymore. Conceptually, this is one of the most amazing games ever made. Three games' worth of content and several years of substantive DLCs all in one package makes for a massive (and expensive) experience.

It's the little nitpicks of unfairness that eventually drive me insane. This game can be really easy to cheese if you choose to exploit it. I'd rather try to play it the way they intended and really, you suffer for it. The way the AI moves on the campaign map so they're either always just out of reach or blunder directly into your superior army bugs me. I still don't know how the hell ambush detection works except that if you really don't want to be seen, you will be.

Diplomacy is largely pointless depending on the race you play. In general you're either surrounded by people that love you and always will or people that hate you and will never stop trying to kill you. This would get pretty old pretty fast if the map and number of playable factions on Immortal Empires weren't so huge.

In battle is where the AI cheese really gets me because it can do things you simply cannot. Which in my opinion, invalidates the concept of strategy in a game. Some ranged units require direct line of sight to attack, which you'll notice because yours will never fire unless they're on a flat plain with nothing else remotely nearby.

If so much as a squirrel runs across their path, they all panic and give up on the idea of war entirely. Meanwhile, the AI's LOS ranged units can find the barest sliver of an opening and launch a full volley at you. Sometimes they'll even shoot over their allies' heads to hit your troops, which should be impossible. How the hell do you shoot a flamethrower in an arc?!

If the AI has cavalry, they're going to hit you in the back. They just do. They can turn on a dime, disengage as they please, and somehow run in an arc faster than your anti-cav units can turn around while standing still. Your cav on the other hand, move like they're trapped in mud. If even one entity from the unit gets hit in the back trying to run away, all of them will stop and stare at the sun while you frantically click and swear at them.

Are there ways to overcome these things? Sure, sort of. You can simply never use cavalry. You can squeeze one of those little rubber balls until your hand cramps up. But usually, most of the tools aren't available until the mid-game when you've probably gotten bored with fighting battles anyway.

Eventually if you can stomach the annoyances and move beyond the challenging but interesting parts of the early game, it becomes paint the map. Make numbers go bigger. The loading times for battles are so long that you mostly resort to auto-resolving, which eliminates a rather large portion of the game.

The alternative is rolling your veteran army of doom into whatever dregs the AI can still muster after you break their momentum and you just win in a few minutes anyway. They've tried to vary this up for some factions by giving them win conditions based around doing specific things, but for the most part I think campaigns get really boring after turn 60 or so.

At the end of the day there's a lot to love and a lot to hate, depending on what you're into and what bugs you in a video game. I've dropped over 2,000 hours into this trilogy so I've gotten my money's worth, but I've hit the point of being annoyed more than I'm having fun. I would probably give it a mixed recommendation overall, but the opponent getting pinpoint precision while I'm a lumbering doof is why I don't play Monster Hunter.

I am once again reminded of how frustrating and narrow Total War games continue to be. These games overwhelm you with visual finesse in the hopes that it might smooth out the constant head-slapping that you have to do to slog through it. The problem is a lack of strategic ability in the campaign map. There is none. It's a game where you and the AI mass up endless 20-stacks and throw them at each other like bowling balls so that you can play the same 2-4 battle maps a hundred times in a row. Chokepoints? Geography? Meaningless on the campaign map. It might as well be an arcade-style battle arena game. 

WH3 seemed to introduce reinforcement delays. So now your reinforcing armies arrive 6 minutes after the start of a battle that will probably not last longer than 3 minutes. Want to defend a settlement? Too bad, your armies will sally out into the field for some reason.

In old WH, retreating armies used to somehow walk inter-continental back to Timbuktu. Now they retreat four and a half steps, guaranteeing their final destruction in the same turn. This results in a make-or-break type of gameplay experience.

 The game isn't bad.  The graphics are lush, it runs well on my new PC with minimal delays after battles and on enemy moves.  Even with no expansions bought yet I've got a huge diversity of armies available because of owning Warhammers 1 and 2 and a lot of the DLC.  Diplomacy is streamlined in a good way.

  I've won a credited campaign as Dwarves (first time I've won with Dwarves) and an uncredited short campaign as the Empire.  Now I just need to "persuade" the Ogres and Wood Elves with whom I signed multiple treaties when I was fighting for my life versus Undead and Skaven, to leave the Empire provinces.  Perhaps they swap for some French, sorry Bretton, lands I seized from the ghouls and the rats ?

  So why the negatives  ?  A couple of reasons but they are major issues.

  Warhammer 2 was mercilessly hard.  On medium level campaigns if you ran into Grimgor or Van Carstein early in the game when they were stronger then you you could pretty much kiss your derriere goodbye.  Grimgor on Waaagh (spellings differ) got double armies for free, Van Carsein could have an army wiped out and be fully replenished two turns later.  Auto battle was fair in that it enabled you (indeed was the only practical way) to wipe out enemy forces when you were much stronger but for more even battles player control was better.

 In Warhammer 3 autobattle massively favours my armies.  I've heard tales that autobattle ignores magic and over values armour but it means that I'm taking autobattle wins on fights that legitimately I should be losing.  The worst injustice was when defending dwarves totally wiped out two attacking Skaven armies in a siege battle.  What ?  Not a single Skaven escaped the battlefield !  This should have led to a real life plague like the one that hit London in 1665.

 Bearing in mind that battles are the meat and drink of the game this means I'm not really playing the game because I'm taking the super bonuses from Auto Battle instead.  Game balance is broken and that's unforgiveable.

  Which, in perhaps a connected step, takes us to the second major problem.  Melee combat doesn't work properly.  Units clash in melee and then remained fixed there with nothing much happening.  Your troops ordered to attack a particular enemy will sometimes just stop and do nothing instead.  This is huge.  No matter how large the map and how diverse the units if combat doesn't work properly the game is broken.  I've played a huge amount of Total War - Shogun, Rome, Rome Barbarian, Medieval 2, Shogun 2, Empire, all three Total War Warhammer and it's the first time that combat has felt wrong.  And that's without later tier Skaven armies play like the Skaven are World War 1 equipped troops facing primarily Medieval opposition with expected results.  They need a major nerf.

  Creative Assembly - you know that this game is badly balanced on Auto Battle and that the melee combat isn't working properly.  Please fix.  Once you do it will be a great game.  Until then it's broken and I can't recommend it.

As more factions get added to the game, the game pacing increases drastically. The map becomes super cramped with all the bordering legendary lords with the biggest examples being Lustria and the Southlands leaving you little to no breathing room after you take out a very strong threat early unless you play absolutely perfect and/or cheese the AI. 

The entire game is basically a snowball check, there Isn't a huge amount of strategy involved in the Grand Campaign aspect due to anything interesting you can do like trying to cause unrest in opposing factions regions is entirely mitigate by AI cheats on the higher difficulties.

Settlements and provinces become extremely cookie cutter as most factions have an objectively correct set of buildings due to the restrictions imposed on the player such as settlement slots, public order penalties, supply lines etc.

Sieges are an extremely mixed bag, if a lot of the bugs were fixed such as unit pathing and responsiveness, Pocket ladders, the gate bug etc. maybe they would be fun? It's honestly hard to say since these seem to be a very baked in issue for the last 3 games with little to no progress being made to address any of it. Previous games such as Three Kingdoms and hell even Rome: Total War 1 had more interesting sieges.

The lack of a good narrative campaign really does hurt this game a lot, the Vortex campaign in Warhammer 2 is multitudes better than the Realms of Chaos in 3 not to mention some of the best DLC campaigns such as Grom & Eltharion were played via it. Eltharion in Immortal Empires (Warhammer 3) is a shadow of what he was since the Rivalry between him and Grom was Absolute Cinema and now they Exist almost half the map vertically away from each other with chances being he gets taken out by The Lady, Louen or Orion.

The best thing CA could add are smaller campaigns with select factions in zoomed in more detailed sections of the map such as a Thematic Campaign built around the 3 factions that have Karak Eight Peaks as their main objective, or the aforementioned Grom and Eltharion, pretty much ANY DLC that came out prior with linked factions.

While I do not regret my hours in the game nor will I drop the game completely, I find it hard to recommend the game to others with it essentially being a Sandbox of cheese at Legendary/Very hard and a trivial steamroll at lower difficulties with an extremely hefty price tag for the "complete package". While not a major focus, a lack of a narrative focus genuinely hurts a game in a setting with rich lore and currently the bloodbowl of factions is not being addressed with how uncomfortably cramped the map is getting.

玩了《全面战争：战锤 3》一段时间了，必须要来给它一个好评！​
这游戏的玩法简直丰富到爆炸。在这个奇幻的中世纪世界里，你能操控一支独特的军队，地图超广阔，探索起来乐趣无穷。不管是在 3D 环境的地图中穿梭，规划行军路线，还是管理自己的 settlements ，都让人沉浸其中。战斗的时候，那种排兵布阵、指挥作战的感觉，爽到飞起！而且，它的 turn - based 系统非常容易上手，每个回合都充满了策略性。你得根据敌人的情况，合理安排自己的行动，决定是进攻、防守还是与盟友协作。有时候，以弱胜强的关键就在于巧妙的策略，这种运筹帷幄的快感真的无法言喻。​
从策略深度来讲，《全面战争：战锤 3》堪称一绝。面对不同的敌人和战场形势，你得绞尽脑汁去思考对策。比如，当你的军队实力不如对手时，就需要通过奇袭、利用地形等方式来创造优势。而且，游戏中的盟友也不是摆设，他们能极大地影响你的战略布局。和盟友一起制定联合进攻计划，或者在关键时刻互相支援，都能让你感受到团队作战的魅力。​
画面和音效方面，游戏也表现得十分出色。地图场景制作得极为精细，无论是寒冷的北方雪原，还是神秘的奇幻森林，都栩栩如生，仿佛让人置身其中。战斗时的特效和动作也非常流畅，给人强烈的视觉冲击。音效更是为游戏增色不少，激昂的战斗音乐、士兵的呼喊声、武器的碰撞声，都营造出了极其紧张刺激的氛围。​
另外，游戏还在不断更新和完善。就拿联合大地图的推出来说，这无疑给玩家带来了更多的玩法和挑战，也大大延长了游戏的寿命。​

I guess that hardest part was deciding which faction to play after the prologue. Why? Because it's an investment of time. Yet the stories behind the factions are fun.  I am not going to tell you which faction to play because you should play what you like--each faction is unique, you are NOT playing a cookie cutter faction with just skins.  So far, my conquest of the world and giving it to the Chaos Gods is my cup-o-tea, witch a nice crumpet made from the tears and suffering of my enemies.  

This is more than just fighting. There is diplomacy. . .and the game pays attention to some things that you might not appreciate until it's too late! 

All in all, this is a fantastic game that captures warfare in a fun way and captures that Warhammer feel in a way only it can. Die „KI“ in Total War: Warhammer 3 ist eine Illusion.
Es gibt keine intelligenten Gegner – nur Skripte, massive Boosts und willkürliche Vorteile.

Aktuelles Beispiel aus meiner Kampagne (Schwierigkeit: Normal):
Die Frostkönigin (Charakterstufe 19) hat im Khorne-Reich innerhalb von nur vier Runden sämtliche notwendigen Kämpfe gewonnen – ohne ein einziges Regiment zu verlieren.
Ich war zeitgleich mit Skarbrand (Stufe 11) und einer Khorne-Armee im selben Reich unterwegs und kämpfte gegen dieselben Gegner – dabei verlor ich regelmäßig 10–30 % meiner Truppenstärke.

Sie sammelte also völlig problemlos die Chaos-Seele – und warf mich automatisch aus dem Reich.

Ich lud daraufhin einen älteren Spielstand, schnitt ihr den Weg zum Messingturm ab, erklärte ihr den Krieg und griff in der folgenden Runde an.
Ergebnis: Ihre gesamte Armee wurde bis auf drei Regimenter vernichtet.
Meine Armee verlor lediglich ihren Anführer – der Rest nahm nur 20–40 % Schaden.

Und das war dieselbe Armee, die angeblich zuvor mehrere Dämonenarmeen am Stück besiegt haben soll?

Auch die Schlachtvorkalkulation von Warhammer 3 ist unbrauchbar.
Wie das Spiel zu seinen Bewertungen kommt, ist völlig unklar – selbst bei der schlechtesten Prognose habe ich schon Kämpfe fast ohne Verluste gewonnen.
Automatisch berechnete und manuell geführte Schlachten haben nichts mehr miteinander zu tun.
Früher waren die Werte wenigstens grob nachvollziehbar – heute wirken sie völlig daneben.

Das hat nichts mit KI zu tun.
Das ist ein Skript.

Strategie wird hier durch vorgefertigte Drehbücher ersetzt.
Spannung entsteht nicht durch kluge Gegner, sondern durch erzwungene Ungerechtigkeit.

Ja, es gibt Mods, die das reparieren – aber wenn ein Spiel nur mit Community-Fixes überhaupt spielbar ist, dann ist es nicht fertig.
Dann verdienen die Entwickler auch keine DLC-Verkäufe mehr.

Ich habe genug gesehen.
Das ist kein Total War – das ist Theater.

I have two main reasons for this and it's both the dlc and micro transaction policy. Firstly, and most easy. DLC factions are way too powerful. This seems to all be determined by GamesWorkshop. But to play the full game of Warhammer 3 you must own Warhammer 1 and 2. You don't even need to play them, just own them. Warhammer III is exactly what it was meant to be. It’s both an immersive campaign style game, if you prefer diplomacy and auto-resolving battles, while also giving you the option to micromanage your forces by fighting the battle individually if you prefer a more combat driven style of game. I find this to be brilliant because sometimes I just like to sit back and watch the world unfold, while other times I feel like getting my hands bloody.  

I have a healthy appetite for additional paid content, but I appreciate that CA and SEGA do not over-provide. I don’t feel overwhelmed by the releases, which are averaging a modest twice per year. 

A final note, I’m an Oldhammer guy if you’re familiar with the term. Years ago, Games Workshop had to move away from the original content this game is based on. Without the hard work by CA and SEGA we wouldn’t have a current table-top release for Cathay for example. So, thanks to these guys for basically curating and saving the entire hobby line. You’re good lads.

I’ve been playing since the first Total War: Warhammer and have been a fan of Total War games since the original Medieval (at the time, the first Shogun was way too demanding for my hardware 😅).

Yes, the game has its ups and downs. Sometimes it tends to snowball in one direction or the other—but that’s to be expected with so many legendary lords and heroes. For me, the magic lies in how well it lets me “tell my own stories.”

I love the fact that Creative Assembly is still adding new content. Sure, it’s kind of expensive if you try to buy everything at once—but that’s what happens when you’re buying years’ worth of DLCs.

What I don’t understand is people who think they’re entitled to older content for free just because they decided to buy the game now. Older doesn’t mean free. It doesn’t work like that in any other industry—try telling a book publisher that just because you bought book #15 in a series, you should get the previous 14 for free and see what happens. 😄

If anything, new players get it cheaper than veterans who bought everything at release, especially with regular sales throughout the year. So really—stop whining.

That being said, the price tags on some of the newer DLCs do feel a bit steep. I like the new option to buy parts of a DLC if you're not interested in all included factions. (Personally, I never bought the Vampire Coast DLC—just not into VC at all.)

I still hope we’ll eventually get more minor factions like Araby or Tilea (even though I know it’s unlikely). And I’m dreading the End Times—I really hate that part of the lore. It basically destroyed my favorite universe based on a predictable fan poll, and I still try to pretend it never happened. 😅

All in all, though, I absolutely love this game.

Buenas, con más de 2000 horas entre los juegos y habiéndome pasado prácticamente todas las campañas en muy difícil o legendario puedo hablar de mi experiencia en Total War Warhammer. 

El juego es increíble, muy bien logrado y con detalles geniales. Está muy completo y refleja a la perfección todo lo que el mundo de warhammer (fantasy) ofrece. Los señores y héroes se presentan de forma idéntica a lo esperado en las novelas y cuando juegas sus campañas de verdad sientes esa conexión con la facción y líder escogido.

Para mi, el juego es un verdadero 9,8 ya que tiene un par de cosillas que serían mejor de otra forma y pueden resultar tediosas si juegas en dificultades muy elevadas.
Un ejemplo de esto son los parches con nuevos señores (dlcs) incluyendo nuevas unidades que no están para nada balanceadas. Esto provoca una marea de ejércitos brutales y muy sin sentido de la IA (Imperio: Un señor y 19 barcos de tierra). Estos ejércitos son muy muy difíciles de ganar en batalla, se spamean mucho y pueden hacer que facciones como Norsca u Hombres Bestia no tengan ninguna posibilidad de ganar.
Lo curioso, es que este problema puede solucionarse habilitando un tope de mantenimiento por ejército y no un tope de 20 unidades. Esto acabaría con ejércitos de Condes Vampiro con 1 señor y 19 dragones entre otras cosas similares a casi todas las facciones. Además promovería una mayor variedad de unidades en cada ejército.

Por este motivo y otros relacionados al multi-jugador no puedo darles un 10 de nota (cosa que desearía).  
Para finalizar, me gustaría señalar de nuevo que el juego merece la pena para cualquier jugador de warhammer y/o gente que le guste todo lo relacionado con la estrategia. 
"Los necios desprecian la guerra, hasta que el Caos les enseña su verdadero rostro."

Total War: Warhammer III, Creative Assembly’nin yıllardır geliştirdiği Total War serisinin fantezi temasındaki zirvesi. Warhammer evreninin kaotik, karanlık ve olağanüstü dünyasını, devasa savaşlarla ve derin stratejiyle buluşturan bu oyun, serinin en kapsamlı, en yoğun ve belki de en iddialı yapımı.

Oyun Dünyası ve Fraksiyonlar: Warhammer III, daha önceki iki oyunun üzerine kurulu bir evren sunuyor ve bu sefer olayların odağında Kaos Tanrıları’nın diyarı bulunuyor. Oyunun ana senaryo modunda (Realm of Chaos), Kislev, Grand Cathay, Ogres, dört Kaos Tanrısı fraksiyonu (Khorne, Nurgle, Tzeentch, Slaanesh) ve kaotik Daemon Prince liderliğindeki özel fraksiyonla oynayabiliyorsunuz. Her biri hem oynanış mekanikleri hem de estetik tasarımları açısından oldukça farklı.

Fraksiyonlar sadece tematik olarak değil, mekaniksel olarak da çeşitlilik sunuyor. Örneğin:
+Kislev, güçlü savunma hatları kuran ve moral değeri yüksek birliklerle öne çıkıyor.
+Grand Cathay, denge üzerine kurulu, ticaret ve uzun menzilli savaş yetenekleriyle oynanıyor.
+Kaos fraksiyonları, farklı oyun felsefeleri sunuyor; Slaanesh hız ve manipülasyonla, Khorne doğrudan saldırganlıkla ilerliyor.

Savaş Mekanikleri ve Strateji : Savaşlar hâlâ Total War'un klasik yapısı üzerinde ilerliyor: devasa gerçek zamanlı savaşlar, birim yerleşimi, moral dengesi, çevresel avantajlar ve kuşatma stratejileri önemli. Ancak Warhammer III ile birlikte savaşlar daha da kaotik, daha büyük ve görsel olarak daha etkileyici hale gelmiş durumda.

Özellikle Kaos diyârında geçen görevler ve "sürreal" savaş alanları, klasik Total War atmosferine farklı bir hava katıyor. Yalnız şunu belirtmek gerek: Bu oyunun zorluğu, zaman zaman sınayıcı düzeyde. Birim yönetimi ve savaş alanı takibi, özellikle yeni oyuncular için oldukça yoğun olabilir.

Kampanya Haritası ve Diplomasi: Kampanya haritası oldukça geniş ve detaylı. Her bölgenin kendine özgü yapısı, tehditleri ve stratejik önemi var. Diplomasi, önceki oyunlara göre daha anlamlı ve aktif kullanılabiliyor. Ticaret, askeri anlaşmalar, ittifaklar ve entrikalar stratejik derinlik sağlıyor.

Warhammer III ayrıca, Immortal Empires adlı devasa birleşik kampanyayla Warhammer I ve II oyuncuları için eşsiz bir “tüm dünya haritası” deneyimi sunuyor. Bu, serinin belki de en sevilen ve tekrar oynanabilirliği en yüksek parçası.

Grafik ve Performans : Görsel olarak oyun oldukça güçlü. Birim tasarımları, büyü animasyonları ve savaş alanları detaylı ve atmosferik. Ancak bu detay, performans gereksinimini de artırıyor. Özellikle büyük savaşlarda, sisteminiz güçlü değilse FPS düşüşleri yaşanabiliyor. Oyunun teknik optimizasyonu çıkışta bazı sorunlar yaşasa da güncellemelerle büyük ölçüde iyileştirildi.

Öğrenme Eğrisi ve Kullanıcı Deneyimi: Total War: Warhammer III, yeni başlayanlar için karmaşık olabilir. Her fraksiyonun farklı mekaniği olması, oyunun öğrenme sürecini uzatıyor. Ancak bu, aynı zamanda oyunun tekrar oynanabilirliğini de artıran en büyük unsur.

Yapay zekâ zaman zaman garip kararlar verebiliyor, özellikle diplomatik alanda tutarsız davranışlar görülebiliyor. Ancak genel olarak düşmanlar, özellikle yüksek zorlukta, ciddi tehdit oluşturabiliyor.

Total War: Warhammer III, strateji ve fantezi sevenler için benzersiz bir deneyim sunuyor. Geniş kapsamlı fraksiyon yapısı, etkileyici savaşlar, detaylı kampanya haritası ve Warhammer evrenine duyulan saygıyla hazırlanmış içerikleriyle türünün zirvesinde yer alıyor. Yeni başlayanlar için karmaşık, deneyimli oyuncular için ise uzun soluklu ve derin bir strateji oyunu.

Es la saga a la que más horas le he dedicado en toda mi historia jugando videojuegos (En el Total War: Warhammer II tengo 2k horas). 

Primero que nada, yo sé que no es un juego para todo el mundo. 
Pero aquí va mi reseña (la primera que hago) 

Lo que me ha maravillado del juego es la variedad de facciones y razas con las cuales se puede jugar y la mentalidad con la que se juegan las mismas. Son muy inmersivas.

Un ejemplo. Para mi no es lo mismo jugar con facciones de bien; humanos, enanos, elfos, etc. A jugar con facciones más grises o malas. Pues la vida de un soldado en las facciones de bien nunca tendrá el mismo valor que el de una gris o malvada (que es básicamente nulo). Mientras que no puedo mandar a mis tropas a morir a lo loco con las facciones de bien (no me nace hacer eso), la verdad es que la vida de un montón de esqueletos, orcos sedientos de batalla, ogros con un hambre insaciable, hombres bestia y criaturas marcadas por el caos no vale nada para mi. Por ende mi estilo de juego cambia.

Las diferentes habilidades de cada raza y facción también le añaden bastante encanto al juego y muchas veces me han empujado a rejugar algunas partidas de lo bien que me lo pase.

Ahora, si de verdad quieres jugar con una facción en su máximo esplendor, si vas a necesitar comprarte uno o dos DLCs, por no decir que si quieres tener acceso a algunas facciones de razas de juegos anteriores vas a tener que comprarte dichos juegos. Así que, piensa bien que quieres jugar, porque lo más probable es que cueste dinero.

Listen up, future warlords of the digital age—this game is like crack, but with more dragons and slightly less legal trouble. I came for the big battles, stayed for the lore, and now I’m trapped in a never-ending cycle of "[i]just one more turn[/i]" until the sun comes up.

[h2]The Good (Which is Most of It, Honestly):[/h2]

[h3]Factions?[/h3] You mean my new hyperfixations?

[b]Skaven:[/b] YES-YES! Backstabbing, nuke-spamming, rat-men who shouldn't exist but somehow rule the under-empire.

[b]Kislev:[/b] Bears. More bears. Bear cavalry. BEAR SUPREMACY.

[b]Cathay:[/b] "Oh wow, a balanced, disciplined faction—" PSYCHE, here’s two dragons who hate each other.

[b]Empire:[/b] "SUMMON THE ELECTOR COUNTS!" (I have this macro’d to my keyboard now.)

[b]Vampires:[/b] Goths who took "raise the dead" way too literally.

[b]Chaos Dwarfs:[/b] Evil steampunk slavers. My moral compass: [spinning like a top]

[b]Dwarfs:[/b] "THAT’S GOING IN THE BOOK!" (They have a book. For grudges. It’s hilarious.)

[b]Lizardmen:[/b] DINOSAURS. RIDING. DINOSAURS. Need I continue?

[b]Ogre Kingdoms:[/b] "MEAT." – Ogres, explaining their entire political system.

[b]Wood Elves:[/b] If elves were Texas Rangers but with more trees and less guns.

[b]Khorne:[/b] BLOOD. SKULLS. ANGER ISSUES.

[b]Nurgle:[/b] Papa’s happy plague family. They’re disgusting. I love them.

[b]Tzeentch:[/b] "Just as planned." (Translation: "I have no idea what I’m doing.")

[b]Slaanesh:[/b] "Excessive perfection." (Also, why are the daemonettes like that?)

[h3]DLCs?[/h3] Worth it. Thrones of Decay? Omens of Destruction? More like "Omens of My Wallet Crying But I Don’t Care." Unique mechanics, new toys, 10/10

[h3]Lore & Story?[/h3] Chef’s kiss. I’m out here quoting Warhammer like it’s Shakespeare while my cat judges me.

[h3]Multiplayer?[/h3] Absolute chaos (pun intended). Nothing like watching your buddy’s elite army get wrecked
 Only downside? No in-game voice chat. [b]CA, it’s 2025![/b]

[h3]Tzeentch’s Trial Battles?[/h3] Genius. Like a fantasy battle royale, except instead of a victory royale, you get the sweet taste of [b]Defeat[/b]

[h2]The Not-So-Great:[/h2]

[h3]Tomb Kings?[/h3] Look, I love my skeletal kings in theory, but their campaign is slower than a college student on a Monday morning. Wake me up when Settra remembers what "haste" means.

[h3]Achievement hunting?[/h3] Did it. All of ‘em. My reward? A sense of pride, accomplishment, and a Steam profile that screams "I need sunlight."

[h2]Final Verdict:[/h2]
If you love strategy, fantasy, or just watching tiny digital men beat each other up in glorious detail, BUY THIS GAME. It’s got more content than my grandma’s fridge after Thanksgiving, and the community’s awesome.

Total War: WARHAMMER III has an incredible amount of content, but some design decisions still hold the campaign back.

One of my biggest complaints is the infamous “magic ladders” during sieges. Units being able to pull ladders out of nowhere completely undermines siege preparation and makes walls far less meaningful than they should be. Ladders should have to be built before the battle, forcing the attacker to actually prepare for an assault.

Another major issue is the unfinished southern part of the campaign map. The map clearly has room to expand, yet large areas remain inaccessible. For a game of this scale, especially after years of DLC and updates, the world still feels incomplete. Opening and developing those regions would make Immortal Empires feel much more like the enormous global campaign it is supposed to be.

But my biggest problem is the lack of a truly living world. The AI factions often feel like they exist mainly to react to the player rather than pursuing their own ambitions. I want to see factions building empires, fighting major wars, forming rivalries, betraying alliances, invading distant territories, and becoming major powers regardless of what I am doing.

The campaign should feel like a world that keeps moving without me. If I spend 50 turns focused on one corner of the map, I want to discover that somewhere else an unexpected faction has conquered half a continent, another empire has collapsed, and completely new political situations have emerged.

WARHAMMER III has the content and scale to create that experience. What it still needs is better siege mechanics, a truly completed campaign map, and above all, an AI-driven world that feels alive instead of a world waiting for the player to interact with it.

I don't recommend the game in its current state because these problems affect the core campaign experience, not just minor details.

Total War: Warhammer III ist das epische Finale einer der ambitioniertesten Strategiespiel-Trilogien überhaupt – und es liefert auf ganzer Linie. Die Tiefe, der Umfang und die kreative Vielfalt der Fraktionen sind schlicht überwältigend. Ob Chaosdämonen, edle Hochländer oder untote Herrscher – jede Fraktion fühlt sich einzigartig, lebendig und taktisch anspruchsvoll an.

Das Spiel glänzt nicht nur mit seiner komplexen Mischung aus rundenbasierter Strategie und Echtzeitschlachten, sondern auch mit einer enorm lebendigen Welt voller düsterer Fantasy-Atmosphäre. Besonders beeindruckend ist die Immortal Empires-Kampagne, in der alle Karten und Völker der gesamten Trilogie vereint werden – ein echtes Mammutprojekt, das Fans stundenlang fesselt.

Einziger Wermutstropfen: Die DLC-Politik. Viele Fraktionen, besonders beliebte wie die Chaoszwerge oder einige legendäre Kommandanten, sind kostenpflichtig – und das kann schnell teuer werden. ABER: Wenn man sich die DLCs über seriöse Keyseiten besorgt, bekommt man sie oft deutlich günstiger. In diesem Fall lohnt sich die Investition absolut, denn jeder DLC bringt echtes Gameplay und keine oberflächlichen Skins.

Ein Wunsch an Creative Assembly: Es wäre großartig, wenn man neue Fraktionen für eine Stunde kostenlos anspielen könnte – etwa im Stil einer Testphase. So könnte man ausprobieren, ob einem eine Fraktion wirklich liegt, bevor man zuschlägt. Das würde Spielern noch mehr Sicherheit geben und zugleich das Vertrauen stärken.

Fazit: Wer sich für Fantasy, Strategie und gigantische Schlachten begeistert, kommt an Total War: Warhammer III nicht vorbei. Mit ein wenig Geduld und Schnäppchenjagd bei den DLCs entfaltet sich hier eines der besten Strategiespiele der letzten Jahre – gewaltig, herausfordernd und absolut faszinierend.

Bigos tradycyjny wychodzi bardzo aromatyczny, wyrazisty i sycący. Zdaję sobie sprawę, że tak jak w przypadku np. rosołu każdy od lat ma swój sprawdzony przepis i nie wyobraża go sobie robić inaczej. Jednak w tym wpisie chciałabym Was zachęcić do zapoznania się z moją recepturą na przepyszny bigos z dużą ilością mięsa przełamany słodyczą suszonych śliwek i aromatycznych przypraw.

Bigos z kiszonej kapusty
Przyznaję, że mój bigos składa się tylko z kiszonej kapusty (ja nie używam świeżej kapusty). Do tego używam zawsze sporej ilości mięsa wieprzowego (karkówki, schabu, kiełbasy, boczku surowego i wędzonego, a nawet żeberek wędzonych). Poniżej są przykładowe proporcje, które nie muszą być użyte co do grama tak samo jak u mnie (to nie ciasto, gdzie konkretne gramatury mają duże znaczenie). Jeśli szukasz postnego bigosu to koniecznie odwiedź mój przepis na bigos wigilijny.

Z czym podawać bigos?
Bigos najczęściej podajemy z chlebem lub innym rodzajem pieczywa. Możemy jednak podać go również z ziemniakami lub nawet makaronem – rzadziej spotykana wersja, ale pasują do bigosu np. z łazanki. Moim zdaniem, ciekawym dodatkiem do bigosu mogą być też kopytka.

Czy można zamrozić bigos?
Tak, jak najbardziej bigos można mrozić. Pamiętajmy jednak, aby przed włożeniem do zamrażalnika był całkowicie przestudzony. Polecam użyć do tego plastikowych pojemników lub specjalnych woreczków do mrożenia. Nie polecam do mrożenia w szklanych pojemników lub słoików, ponieważ jest ryzyko, że pękną.

Jak przechowywać bigos po ugotowaniu?
Bigos możemy przechowywać po prostu w lodówce do tygodnia czasu, jeżeli mamy zamiar go w tym czasie zjeść w całości. Jeżeli mamy większą porcję, to możemy go zamrozić i przechowywać go w zamrażalce do 6 miesięcy. Ostatnią opcją jest pasteryzacja w słoikach – w ten sposób możemy przechowywać bigos do 3 miesięcy.

Pasteryzacja bigosu
Bigos możemy pasteryzować w słoikach i przedłużyć jego zdatność do spożycia. Możemy napełnione bigosem, zamknięte słoiki zawekować gotując je w garnku przez 20 min, licząc od rozpoczęcia gotowania, pasteryzować w piekarniku przez 30 min w temp. 120 stopni lub włożyć je do zmywarki i nastawić program o najwyższej temperaturze.

Przepis na: Bigos tradycyjny

400 g kiełbasy zwyczajnej
200 g surowego boczku
200 g boczku wędzonego lub żeberek wędzonych
2 kg kiszonej kapusty
1/2 łyżeczki ziela angielskiego
7 liści laurowych
kilka suszonych śliwek
1/2 łyżeczki pieprzu
opcjonalnie 1-2 goździki
1/2 łyżeczki majeranku
opcjonalnie 1 płaska łyżka powideł śliwkowych
1 szklanka czerwonego wina wytrawnego

Bigos tradycyjny 
Do przygotowania bigosu będzie potrzebny większy garnek (np. żeliwny lub po prostu jakiś z grubszym, nieprzywierającym dnem – o pojemności tak około 6-7 litrów, choć łatwiej będzie mieszać w takim 8 litrowym).
Jeśli nie potrzebujesz takiej ilości bigosu to zrób z połowy porcji lub analogicznie podwój proporcje jeżeli spodziewasz się wielu gości (czy chcesz po prostu sobie część bigosu poporcjować i pomrozić).

Suszone grzyby (30-40 g) zalewamy ciepłą wodą (tylko tyle wlewamy, aby grzyby lekko w niej pływały) i odstawiamy na minimum godzinkę, choć można zostawić na całą noc. Po tym czasie je odcedzamy i lekko siekamy (wodę z namoczonych grzybów użyjemy później).

Kapustę kiszoną (2 kg) odciskamy z nadmiaru słonej wody i lekko ją siekamy.

Surowe mięso, czyli karkówkę (600 g), schab (400g) i boczek (200 g) kroimy w kostkę. To są zaproponowane przeze mnie proporcje i rodzaje mięsa, ale jeśli wolisz to użyj samej karkówki, łopatki czy schabu. Raczej w bigosie zawsze korzystam z wieprzowiny, a unikam wołowiny czy drobiu.

Na średnią lub większą patelnię wlej odrobinę oleju i smaż pokrojone mięso przez 30 minut (na małym lub średnim ogniu). Co jakiś czas mieszaj.

Po tym czasie, w dużym garnku zaczynamy gotować kapustę kiszoną (wlewamy około 350 ml wody) wraz z przyprawami i ziołami- ziele angielskie (1/2 łyżeczki), liście laurowe (7-8 większych liści), pieprz czarny mielony (1/2 łyżeczki), a także opcjonalnie 1-2 goździki czy ziarna jałowca  (1-2 szt). Dodajemy posiekane grzyby wraz z wodą po tych grzybach. Całość mieszamy.

Dodajemy mięso z patelni (jeśli puściło sporo wody na patelni to raczej polecam ją wylać). Mieszamy i gotujemy pod przykryciem przez około pół godziny na malutkim ogniu. Co jakiś czas mieszamy i pilnujemy żeby bigos na dnie się nie przypalił.

Na patelni podsmażamy na małej ilości oleju posiekaną drobno cebulę (2 szt) wraz z kiełbasą (około 400 g) i boczkiem wędzonym (200 g). Jeśli wolicie to możecie użyć żeberek wędzonych i wystarczy je włożyć po prostu do gotującego się bigosu.

Dodajemy do bigosu wraz z posiekanymi suszonymi śliwkami (kilka szt), można też opcjonalnie dodać odrobinę powideł śliwkowych (najlepsze te domowej roboty) i majeranek (1/2 łyżeczki). Wlewamy wino czerwone (1 szklanka) i całość mieszamy. Gotujemy na malutkim ogniu przez 4-5 godzin (pod przykryciem), co jakiś czas mieszając. Następnego dnia ponownie gotujemy na malutkim ogniu przez 2 godziny. Jeśli chcecie to czynność można też powtórzyć trzeciego dnia np. przez godzinkę.

Bigos tradycyjny najlepiej smakuje na drugi czy nawet trzeci gotowania. Podajemy z chlebem.

Pierogi z mięsem
Domowe pierogi z mięsem, to świetny pomysł na pyszny obiad dla całej rodziny. Zapraszam po mój sprawdzony przepis na ciasto oraz na najprostszy farsz z mięsa wołowego z bulionu.

- dokładny opis wykonania plus zdjęcia kroków
- idealne ciasto pierogowe z dodatkiem oleju
- kilka propozycji na wzbogacenie farszu

Czas przygotowania: 1 godzina 30 minut
Liczba porcji: 70 małych pierogów

Składniki na ciasto na pierogi

500 g mąki pszennej np. typ 500
1 szklanka gorącej wody - 250 ml
4 łyżki oleju roślinnego - 50 ml
pół łyżeczki soli

Farsz na pierogi z mięsem

800 g mięsa wołowego z bulionu
2 średniej lub większe cebule - do 400 g
4 łyżki oleju roślinnego - 50 ml
przyprawy: 1 płaska łyżeczka soli; pół łyżeczki pieprzu

Pierogi z mięsem
Szklanka ma u mnie pojemność 250 ml.

Do zrobienia pierogów potrzebujesz również: czysty blat lub stolnica do wałkowania ciasta; wałek; okrągła wykrawaczka do pierogów o średnicy około 6,5 cm; bawełniana ściereczka; szeroki garnek; cedzak do łowienia pierogów.

Kalorie policzone zostały na podstawie użytych przeze mnie składników. Jest to więc orientacyjna liczba kalorii, ponieważ Twoje składniki mogą mieć inną ilość kalorii niż te, których użyłam ja. Podczas liczenia kalorii nie uwzględniłam dodatków w postaci cebulki podsmażonej na oleju, której użyłam do okraszenia ugotowanych pierogów. Z podanej ilości składników wyszło mi 70 niewielkich pierogów szykowanych na cienkim cieście. 

UWAGA: Do zrobienia farszu użyłam mięsa z przepisu na bulion wołowy. Zmieliłam całe mięso, ale już bez warzyw i wyszło mi trochę ponad 800 gramów mięsa. Polecam zatem dzień przed szykowaniem pierogów ugotować bulion. Z wywaru zrobić rosół lub pomidorówkę, a mięso odłożyć do zmielenia na farsz do pierogów. 

Pierogi z mięsem przepis
Do farszu używam mięsa wyłowionego z bulionu. Bulion wołowy - pod linkiem dokładny przepis. Z podanej ilości mięsa powinno wyjść około 800 gramów mięsa gotowego do zmielenia (Mięso mieliśmy razem z ewentualnymi skórkami, miękkimi żyłkami itp. Oznacza to, że wyrzucamy tylko kości). Tym razem do bulionu użyłam około 500 gramów karczku wołowego oraz po około 250-300 gramów szpondra i pręgi wołowej. Bulion gotowałam dzień wcześniej. Wyłowiłam mięso, które odłożyłam po przestudzeniu do lodówki, a w dniu szykowania pierogów zmieliłam je w maszynce, na średnich oczkach razem z podsmażoną na oleju cebulką. 

Jak przygotować cebulę do farszu: Dwie cebule obierz i poszatkuj (u mnie jedna zwyczajna i jedna czerwona). Możesz też użyć kilku mniejszych sztuk o łącznej wadze do 400 gramów. Na nagrzaną patelnię dodaj cztery łyżki oleju roślinnego do smażenia. Dodaj poszatkowaną cebulę i podsmażaj na średniej mocy palnika przez około 10 minut (ma się zeszklić, ale nie rumienić zbyt mocno, by nie wyszła gorzka). 

Tym razem nie mieliłam warzyw z bulionu, ale można to zrobić. Otrzymasz więcej farszu, który będzie przy okazji bardziej wilgotny. Po zmieleniu mięsa z cebulą sprawdź smak farszu i zdecyduj ile dodasz do niego soli i pieprzu. U mnie była to płaska łyżeczka soli i pół łyżeczki pieprzu. Farsz jest już gotowy.

Porada: Do farszu można też dodać podsmażone na oleju i poszatkowane lub zmielone razem z mięsem i cebulą pieczarki. Jeśli wolisz farsz z mięsa wieprzowego i kapusty kiszonej, to polecam farsz z przepisu na naleśniki z mięsem. 

Przygotuj ciasto na pierogi z mięsem. Do szerokiej miski przesiej mąkę (najlepsza będzie poznańska typ. 500). Pół kilograma mąki, to połowa standardowego opakowania o wadze jednego kilograma. Dodaj pół łyżeczki soli oraz cztery łyżki oleju roślinnego. Wlej szklankę gorącej, przegotowanej wody i zamieszaj ciasto łyżką, a następnie zacznij je wyrabiać. Można też śmiało wyrabiać je w maszynie np. w Thermomix. Ciasto powinno być miękkie, plastyczne i elastyczne. 

Gotową kulę ciasta zawiń w folię i odłóż na 30 minut. Ciasto po leżakowaniu nie będzie się kurczyć podczas wałkowania.

Po tym czasie ciasto odwiń z folii i podziel na 3 części. Dwa kawałki odłóż na bok i przykryj bawełnianą ściereczką, by ciasto nie obsychało. Jeden kawałek rozwałkuj cienko na stolnicy lub na blacie lekko oprószonym mąką. Przy pomocy wykrawaczki o średnicy około 6,5 cm wycinaj okrągłe placki pod pierogi. Na środek placka nakładaj farsz mięsny. Daję zawsze sporo farszu. Kulkę farszu lekko spłaszczam na kształt wałeczka, by idealnie wypełnić wnętrze pieroga. Pierogi składaj na pół i sklejaj boki. Po sklejeniu łączenia polecam wykonać dodatkowo falbankę. 

Resztki ciasta po wykrawaniu pierogów zbieraj i na koniec połącz w jedną kulę. Ponownie rozwałkuj ciasto i wycinaj placki pod pierogi.

Porada: Moje pierogi były dość małe, dlatego też wyszło mi aż 70 sztuk. Placek na pieroga ważył około 11 gramów, zaś porcja farszu 10-13 gramów. Można śmiało lepić trochę grubsze pierogi i o większej średnicy. Wyjdzie mniej sztuk, ale zużycie farszu będzie podobne, ponieważ do jednego pieroga dajemy go wówczas znacznie więcej.

Pierogi układaj obok siebie na stolnicy. Aby oczekujące na gotowanie pierogi nie schły, przykryj je lekko wilgotną bawełnianą ściereczką.

Każdą serię umieszczaj w garnku z osoloną, gotującą się wodą. Woda nie powinna gotować się ani za mocno, ani też tylko lekko "mrugać". Pierogi wyławiaj po około 3-4 minutach od ich wypłynięcia na powierzchnię. W ten sposób ugotuj wszystkie pierogi (każdą partię gotujesz na tej samej wodzie, nie wymieniasz jej).  
Gotowe pierogi z mięsem polałam zeszkloną cebulą z dodatkiem szczypiorku. Taką okrasę szykujesz identycznie, jak cebulkę na oleju, którą wykorzystujesz do zrobienia farszu na pierogi z mięsem. Na koniec dokładasz tylko garść szczypiorku. 

Pierogi z mięsem można mrozić zarówno surowe, czyli takie od razu po sklejeniu, jak i ugotowane. 
Ugotowane pierogi odcedź dokładnie i delikatnie wysmaruj olejem. Większą deskę lub tackę (deska powinna mieć taką wielkość, by bez problemu zmieścić się w zamrażalniku) posmaruj cienką warstwą oleju. Wyłóż na nią pierogi: jeden obok drugiego. Pierogi nie powinny się ze sobą stykać. Tackę z przestudzonymi pierogami umieść w komorze zamrażalnika na 90 minut. Tak samo mroź pierogi surowe, których nie trzeba już smarować olejem przed mrożeniem. 

Przymrożone pierogi z mięsem możesz przekładać do woreczków do mrożenia lub do pudełek. Takie pierogi można już kłaść jeden na drugim. Podpisz woreczki i odłóż do zamrażarki. Tak przygotowane pierogi nie będą się już sklejały i po wyjęciu z zamrażalnika będzie je można wyjmować z pojemników/woreczków sztuka po sztuce. 

W momencie, gdy zapragniesz zjeść zamrożone wcześniej pierogi z mięsem, wystarczy wyjąć odpowiednią ich ilość z zamrażalnika i jeszcze zamrożone umieścić w garnku z wrzątkiem. Gotuj je na małej mocy palnika do miękkości ciasta. Jeśli chcesz zjeść pierogi podsmażone na patelni, to wyjęte z zamrażalnika ułóż na szeroki talerzu. Po naturalnym rozmrożeniu możesz je już podsmażać na rumiano i podawać.

Total War: WARHAMMER III — 1 336 h played  
Score: 9 / 10

The definitive Total War sandbox: Immortal Empires unites three games’ worth of factions on one gargantuan map, while overhauled sieges and continuous DLC support keep the meta evolving.

ANALYTICAL HIGHLIGHTS  
• Unparalleled faction variety — 30 + launch & DLC factions span daemon legions to ogre mercantile empires; each features bespoke campaign mechanics, tech trees, and battle rosters.  
• Immortal Empires — A combined-world map that dwarfs anything in the genre, enabling truly emergent grand strategy and eight-player co-op campaigns.  
• Battle improvements — Redesigned siege layouts, minor-settlement street fights, and expanded magic lores add tactical depth without sacrificing clarity.  
• Live-service cadence — Quarterly balance patches, free LC lords, and saga packs (e.g., *Thrones of Decay*) demonstrate sustained Creative Assembly commitment.  
• Quality-of-life tooling — End-turn times, diplomacy filters, and auto-resolve previews have all improved markedly since launch.

OBSERVED LIMITATIONS  
• Realms of Chaos narrative campaign remains polarising; many veterans skip straight to Immortal Empires.  
• Path-finding and unit spacing can still misbehave on multi-tier siege maps.  
• Heavier performance load than WARHAMMER II; large battles demand modern hardware (runs well on Core i7-11700K / RTX 3090 at 1440p “High”).  
• DLC pricing has crept upward, so completionists may feel nickel-and-dimed.

FINAL ASSESSMENT  
If you crave a grand-strategy experience where every faction is its own game and the tabletop’s full lore catalogue is in play, WARHAMMER III is indispensable. Expect to lose entire weekends to Immortal Empires—and keep 30 GB spare for the inevitable next patch.

Я давно знаком с серией Total War и с интересом ждал третью часть Warhammer-трилогии. В целом игра оправдала ожидания: масштабные битвы, разнообразные фракции, мощная атмосфера мрачного фэнтези — всё это на месте и выполнено на высоком уровне. Кампания за Царства Хаоса и другие расы предлагает массу контента и стратегических возможностей. Особенно радует внимание к деталям и стильное визуальное оформление.

Однако у игры есть ряд недостатков, которые мешают в полной мере наслаждаться процессом. Во-первых, интерфейс временами перегружен, особенно для новых игроков. Во-вторых, оптимизация оставляет желать лучшего: даже на довольно мощных ПК случаются просадки FPS и подгрузки. Баланс между фракциями местами хромает — некоторые кампании ощущаются слишком простыми или наоборот, излишне сложными. Также ИИ на стратегической карте временами ведёт себя странно и непоследовательно.

В целом, Total War: Warhammer III — хорошая стратегия для фанатов жанра и вселенной Warhammer, но не без шероховатостей. Надеюсь, с будущими патчами и дополнениями игра станет ещё лучше.

I really tried to like it. But no, despite the hefty pricing it has very deep design issues in its very core:
1) Due to all factions starting with only one region and starting right next to each other (as with all new Total Wars) there is no build-up phase. While in older Total Wars there were rebels and neutral cities, here everything belongs to a faction. 50% get removed in the first turns and then starts the snow-balling. Meaning: The game is decided in the first 15 turns. While it is important that no faction starts overpowered, a build-up phase usually creates the first decision layer (see RTS like Age of Empires, the decision between resource Accumulation and rushing. This game here however, is only rushing)

2) Magic, flying units, monstrosities are cool, but create additional layers for the balancing. Now coming back to issue number 1: There are very clear factions that will survive and those that are doomed to fail. The balancing in many cases does still not work. Add then random events like earth quakes at the wrong time and boom, you lost your time window for expansion and get steamrolled.

3) The late game is also weak due to the game's simplification in regards of politics and economy. There are clear builds for settlements for each faction that you then just repeat, while your armies are painting the map in your colour. Isn't that the pinnacle of excitement?
Oh and the lategame crisis are the laziest attempts I have ever seen in a game. Just a random invasion in an area that was most likely already pacified.

4) Sieges are still broken as hell. Or to use the wording of a YouTuber: "Ass-ladders". That units can spawn ladders out of thin air makes walls completely useless .

Do yourself a favor and play the other TW-titles if you are looking for a good time. if you want the full portion of Warhammer-atmosphere, than this one only wins bcs of lack of competition.
