I would recommend this game and the Total Warhammer series. 

But with caveats. 

I began my days playing TW with Shogun 1 on a Gateway PC when I was a kid. When I first played the Warhammer games, I truly felt lost and did not enjoy them much. The balance is at times abysmal. The game almost requires you to play totally different than what you'd be used to if you've played the series from an early point like I did. 

Having grown up with historical strategy Total War games, I couldn't get into this game for a while because of how much the game can and will punish you for doing what works and what makes sense in historical titles. I especially always loved to play a formation focused command style, letting the enemies break on a well built formation. But that only works in some situations in this game and there is a lot more sub systems you need to learn in order to play it efficiently. Even then, the power creep and broken lords/units is a major issue with the game. Some units, while it may be lore accurate for them to be this way, are utterly ridiculous and/or broken against units that you might build all your armies around. So if you don't know exactly what to ignore and what to recruit, you have little space to learn by trial and error. The game punishes you badly for trying to just learn the game by playing it and it really is something you need to learn before you start if you want to play on normal or higher. 

But if you can accept that and if you can give it a chance to learn it, it really is fun. It's got problems but, honestly, every TW game has had problems. All of them also have doom-stacks as they're called. They all have broken mechanics and ways to cheat the AI. This game, though, seems hell bent on forcing you to play the game in a way that cheats the AI especially on higher difficulties and it's bad game design. It's also faux variety because the fact that the factions all more or less force you into playing them in specific ways, it's got little to no more variety than any other game in the series.

I wish though that CA would have done to a Medieval or Empire game what they did with this series and built upon it over multiple games. Being able to have a massive world with so many factions is truly awesome. No other game in the TW series is close to what Warhammer 3 offers. But, it offers all that at a very steep cost. 

If you want to play the full game and all of the content, it's going to cost you an entire damn pay check. It's ridiculous and don't pay for the DLCs at full price. You're a fool if you do and you're not encouraging good business practices. The game also is still to this day in dire need of fixing for a lot of it's core mechanics and AI. But they are slowly working at it at least, it's just a bit hard to excuse how long it's taking and how much is still busted while they continue to pump out high priced DLC.

I would recommend the games, get the full trilogy and then whatever DLCs you'd like to get. Get them on sale though, don't get them for full price unless you're loaded with money burning a hole in your pocket. 

And even then, I wish people wouldn't because the prices for the DLCs are not reasonable and you shouldn't encourage this crappy DLC pricing. The DLCs are really worth about half of what they charge for them so I wouldn't buy them for anything but 50%+ off. 

Each faction does play pretty distinctly but not overly so, honestly. They still are all fairly similar in a lot of ways but there is definitely a lot of variety to it, it just is less than people act like it is because many of the factions have to be played a specific way to succeed. Or, you have to play them on a low difficulty to play them how you want to play them if it's not a meta play style.

You do still get a lot to play with if you get the trilogy but I honestly don't even know what all you get with just Warhammer 3. For what it is though, having the trilogy and just the free DLC for now, it's really a lot to play with and there's so much more to play in the future as I decide to get DLCs. And at first I didn't like facing the DLC factions but they have made me want to experience playing them so, it's a solid little trick to get you to want to buy them.

I knew nothing about Warhammer and still know very little and that is definitely part of why I didn't enjoy this series to start. I didn't care about how the lore dictated that Elven melee units sucked compared to Orc melee units, I just was pissed off that I wasted hours buying a bunch of useless units that ultimately let me down in every battle. Until I learned more about the game and how you just have to focus on certain units for a lot of the factions, I just didn't enjoy it. I thought it was just horrifically balanced, which it kind of is. But it is intentionally for a lot of the factions. Unit quality has always been something that can vary, but it was often offset by higher numbers. But in this game that doesn't matter. A unit of Black Orcs will pretty much beat any Elven infantry and it takes time to learn why. And then you need to learn how to avoid player traps and even then you'll probably still fall into player traps since the game is filled with them, intentionally or not.

But, yeah, it's a good game. It's not as bad as some people act but it's also not nearly as varied as some people act too. It's a solid modern Total War game and if you're more into fantasy than history or if you're into a blend of history and fantasy then you'll find this game enjoyable. If you're more historical leaning like I am, you have to go into this knowing that it will not be like the other TW games. If you want to play the game the way YOU want to play it, you pretty much have to play it on easy difficulty. 

To some degree, that was true for all of the TW games but it just seems like everything is taken to a higher extreme in this series. For better and for worse. But it's full of it's own charms and has it's own identity. You'll either really enjoy it or you won't. 

But if you don't, give it another chance after you go and learn some more of the game's mechanics and systems at play. It's more complicated and I can at least say Warhammer 3 definitely does a better job at explaining what mechanics/stats play well against specific units. But it still leaves a lot to be desired.

I would give the trilogy, which gives you a gigantic map with many factions, a solid 7.5 out of 10. I would recommend the trilogy to start. All the factions are fun and they all have unique campaign mechanics. On the battlefield, the factions all play fairly similary since there's only 5 or 6 unit archetypes. But that's not to say they don't have distinctions. But I wouldn't say they are any more distinct than factions in Shogun 2, for example. They just have differnt skins, number of entities and stats. But at the end of the day there is just infantry, range, cavalry, range cavalry, monsters, flying and heroes/lords. So there's not as much variety as people try to say there is. 

I would say there's like 25% more variety to the factions than a typical TW game on the battlefield. But for the campaigns, there is a lot more variety to that aspect. Some factions do almost no diplomacy, some do a ton of it. Some factions will never fight certain other factions and will always fight certain other factions. But at the same time, it leaves little room for unlikely friendships. So it's really just a different kind of variety, not more varied. How many times can I say variety in this review? I don't know, but I am sick of people justifying why historical TW games are worse because they don't have variety when they're legitimately every bit as varied as these games. They just aren't 3 games worth of content + DLC like this is.

To sum up the review, get the trilogy. Warhammer 1, Warhammer 2 and Warhammer 3 and see what you think. If you enjoy it, then get some DLCs if you want more.

Total War: Warhammer III est une véritable perle pour les amateurs de stratégie et de l’univers de Warhammer. Le jeu propose une profondeur tactique impressionnante, des batailles spectaculaires, et un mode Immortal Empires d’une richesse inégalée qui fusionne les trois opus en une gigantesque campagne sandbox. Les factions sont variées, magnifiquement conçues et offrent chacune un gameplay unique.

Cependant, difficile de ne pas ressentir une certaine frustration face à la politique commerciale de Creative Assembly. Le nombre de DLC payants — parfois à des prix élevés pour un contenu limité — donne l’impression que l’expérience complète est fragmentée et vendue en kit. Cette approche peut décourager les nouveaux venus et frustrer même les fans les plus fidèles.

Malgré cela, le cœur du jeu reste exceptionnel. L’ambiance, la direction artistique, la bande-son et l’équilibre progressif des factions rendent chaque campagne unique et épique.

En résumé : un monument du jeu de stratégie, sublimé par son contenu… mais dont l’accès complet ressemble parfois à une chasse au trésor payante.

Soy un gran fan de los Total War:Warhammer, y sinceramente, versión tras versión de este juego, lo que veo es un declive ofrecer un juego para divertir a tu público y orientarlo a ser una máquina de dinero. 

Al margen de los gráficos, que está bastante bien, dependiendo del ordenador que tengas, la potencia,  etc. Esa parte más técnica se la remito a alguien que tenga más conocimiento. Lo que yo veo es que con este juego vendieron la idea de hacer una campaña masiva en el mundo de Total War Fantasy,  en la que casi 300 facciones se pelaban por el control del mundo, y el jugador toma partido de una de ellas para llevarla al éxito.

El problema principal que llevan arrastrando desde la primera entrega, que a mi parecer es bastante grave, la IA. Tiene una ambición y una fantasía demasiado arraigada por acabar a toda costa con el jugador; traspasan territorios de enemigos, usando cientos de agentes constantemente y formando ejércitos en apenas 1 turno.  Alianzas incoherentes y ejércitos que te obliteran en 1 vs. 3. Lo que al final te expone a la obligación de poner mods creados por la comunidad, para compensar y que no seas la diana de todas las facciones, aparte de crear un equilibrio en las partidas, que, a mi parecer, debió ser ya aplicado por los desarrolladores cuando hicieron este juego. 

No lo vería tan negativo, si fuese un juego completamente terminado o si se estuviesen centrando en mejorar la calidad de las partidas. El  problema es que, después de 28 Dlcs de pago (que oscilan entre los 9 y los 20 euros), sigue siendo el mismo juego que el TW: Warhamer 1 con la misma IA mediocre, incoherente y completamente ilógica.

I never played a TW:WH title before this one, so to all new players (and I'm sure the rest of the commenters mention this), to play a lot of the factions you're going to want to play as, you're going to have to shell out serious cash beyond the title itself. This has been discussed and lamented and argued so much by the community that I won't get too far into it, but a serious caveat to playing is you will end up spending several times the actual title's sale price to play fun factions. There are several that come with the game and they are unique and rewarding to play, but as it's a fantasy game and in many ways an RPG, if they do not conform to how you want to play, set an alert to let you know when the expansion content goes on sale, when they are quite reasonable (I bought all of the WH3 expansion content for roughly the same price as the base game). Now onto the review:

This is one of the most engrossing, rewarding, and fun strategy games to play. There are important consequences to how you develop your tech tree, economies, unit producing structures (unit... allowing? structures), who your neighbors are, what their alignments are, your settlement defenses, your heroes, your lords, and basically every other choice you can make. There are factions for whom some of these choices are less and more important, however in general, this game will punish and reward you alike for your decisions.

You are somewhat limited by alignment, chaos-aligned and non-chaos-aligned factions will almost never be friendly unless they are being destroyed in a war and can afford to pay the other off, however there are exceptions and this largely serves as a difficulty setting for certain starts.

As for the difficulty itself, the difficulty level you assign to your campaign will essentially serve to reduce/bolster the incomes and attitudes of your neighbors and settlements. I have only ever played on Hard and there does seem to be a bit of an issue where a faction reduced to a handful of settlements can recruit heroes and lords and units at an insane pace (especially early in the game when this will be much harder for you) but it does provide a challenge for those seeking it. For reference, I once assimilated another faction through confederation and my income went from ~+2000 to ~-20,000, so they are getting a rather large advantage. If you're uncomfortable with that, or don't like the way it plays there is always normal.

The battles are a large part of the appeal of the game, they are deeply tactical and require a lot of thought and engagement throughout, however there is no better feeling than winning a battle manually that the computer deems a decisive defeat against you. It is imperfect, at higher levels your units take damage on auto-resolve that they wouldn't if you fought them yourself, however the battles are quite long and unless you have a lot of time on your hands you probably won't be fighting all of them yourself.

Everything in the game does take quite a lot of time, however as you get better you can streamline turns and battles, and besides this game is the rare gem that makes the time consumption enjoyable. I can't recommend it enough. If you have deep enough pockets, it provides a ton of content and potentially thousands of hours of enjoyment.

After 1000 hours and every bit of content Creative Assembly has put out, I can say Warhammer III is a phenomenal strategy game with some persistent flaws. It’s the most ambitious Total War game ever made, packed with depth, variety, and spectacle. It’s also bloated, sometimes broken, and occasionally infuriating.

IE is the heart of the experience. This massive campaign brings together all factions from Warhammer I, II, and III into a single map. With it, Warhammer III becomes a proper sandbox. No other game offers this much variety in how campaigns play out. Every faction has unique mechanics, campaign objectives, and unit rosters. Playing as Kislev is nothing like playing Skaven. Tzeentch’s teleportation and manipulation is a completely different game from Nurgle’s attrition and slow deathball. It’s a real achievement in asymmetric design.

I haven't really dug into the multiplayer battle experience, but this still has a huge following on youtube and twitch similarly to to the IE campaign mode. That said I have done quite a few multiplayer IE campaigns, which have their own struggles. This has been worked on significantly. 

The battles are still excellent. The animations are full of character. The sound design brings the Warhammer universe to life. The scale of the fights, combined with the fantasy unit variety, puts it miles ahead of historical Total War entries. Magic, monsters, and artillery all play distinct roles. When it works, it feels brilliant. This is why for me personally I play this title vs the others in it's category. I like the fantasy!

The DLC content is a mixed bag. Chaos Dwarfs are one of the strongest additions. Thrones of Decay added interesting lords and brought needed attention back to older factions. But Shadows of Change launched with far too little content for its price, prompting a community backlash that forced Creative Assembly to apologise and promise more value moving forward. Not every DLC is essential, but the best ones significantly improve replayability. I have tried to play all of the lords for at least a campaign. 

There are issues. The campaign AI is inconsistent. It sometimes declares war for no reason or fails to manage its armies properly. End turn times get long in the late game. The UI starts to feel sluggish when your empire scales up. Factions from Warhammer I still feel a bit dated compared to newer releases. And multiplayer, while improved, remains unreliable. The constant updates are good, but they'll break mods (to be expected, just a little annoying)

Despite all that, Warhammer III is still the best fantasy grand strategy game on the market. It offers more faction depth, replay value, and cinematic spectacle than any other Total War. It’s easy to get lost in the story of your campaign, whether you’re dominating as a god of plague or scraping together a defence with a band of stubborn dwarfs.

If you are interested in strategy games or the Warhammer setting, it’s worth the time. Just be prepared to mod a few things, tolerate the AI, and expect occasional growing pains with new content. The core experience is strong enough to shine through the noise.

This is a difficult game to review, since Steam doesn't allow for a middle-ground option and since i think there are two very different groups in the area:

If you never played a Total War game before (or if you played the ones from Rome 2 forward),  
Total Warhammer offers great fun with your favorite Warhammer Fantasy factions, with a lot of the models from the war game being recreated for the PC.

 Total Warhammer III is brings an end to the ambicious trilogy, with the Immortal Empires Campaign(which puts the maps of all three games together for a massive campaign), a story-based mini-campaign for Kislev and regular campaigns for a lot of different factions. There will be a lot, if not all of the factions from the Fantasy Warhammer Battles. Magic is powerful, some heroes can punch a hole through a whole army, and generals and wizards can cast powerful buffs and debuffs that change your and your enemies stats. The game is pretty, but it's also the most egregious case of CA's  nasty chasm of micro-transactions, with more than 2/3 of the factions being locked behind paywalls, which force you to buy the previous games and their DLC, all at absurd prices. The content for the third game of the series is sometimes very small for some of the most expensive dlc from CA to date. Total Warhammer III, like pretty much all of the other CA's games are never to be bought at full price, specially since they almost never lower their prices, even for games that are more than 10 years old.Never buy at full price.

If you are a fan of older Total War games, this is a totally different beast, and can be quite the disappointment if you come waiting for the things that made the series great: prepare for all of the problems that have been killing the series since Rome 2: lot of issues with units pathfinding, lack of reloading animations,physics not being relevant anymore and most combats devolving into meaningless blobs of units,deprived of unit cohesion and with positioning and actual tactics being substituted by raw statistics that don't make sense. Higher difficulties >do not< mean more difficult A.I, but rather cheap stat boosts to the AI. 

For new players who warhammer enthusiasts, TWIII has a lot to offer and can be tons of fun, but if you are someone who enjoyed Total War games and was looking to see something new for the series, you should go look somewhere else.

This game is WILDLY unstable (CTD), and is only getting worse as more updates come out.  It crashes on loading (I often have to launch the game three or more times just to get to my campaign).  It crashes if the camera zooms too quickly over the campaign map (disable all out-of-turn cameras showing other faction activity, and download the mod that disables zoom to diplomatic target).  Even with all cameras disabled, it will often crash when another faction makes a move within your line of sight (this one is particularly bad, because it often happens after a battle, which you must then replay because you can't save after).  Worse, while it doesn't always do this, it does so consistently--meaning that if it crashes at a particular point once, it will do so again and again if you reload, so there is no way to advance past it.  It is effectively unplayable.  And it's not just me, the steam community is full of threads from other people with the same problems.

Even if the game functioned, though, it has very little to recommend itself over Warhammer TW II.  New factions, obviously, but I for one don't find them terribly compelling.  Ditto for the new campaign storyline.  Diplomacy and siege battles have been moderately revamped, but these are pretty minor additions.  They added a "Rematch" button to the battle conclusion, which is a godsend (previously, if you wanted a do over you had to load the battle summary screen, then quickload the prebattle screen, then load the battle itself--and that's if you quicksaved in the prebattle scene, if you didn't you'd also have to load the pre- and post-battle campaign map for a total of 5 load screens when you only needed 1!), but they also inexplicably removed the key binding for pausing.  But basically you're paying more money for the same game, only it crashes more (seriously, mine's crashed three times in the last hour).

At its core, Total War: WARHAMMER III is an incredible strategy experience.
Immortal Empires is massive, the factions are diverse, the battles are epic, and the modding community is doing heroic work keeping everything alive. There’s a ton of content, and if you love Warhammer or Total War, there’s nothing else like it.

But damn… the way CA handled this game post-launch hurts.

The price hikes, the silence, the DLC mess (Forge of the Chaos Dwarfs, Shadows of Change), the drip-fed content, and the feeling that the community’s passion is being milked instead of respected — it all casts a shadow on what should be the crown jewel of the trilogy.

The game didn’t die — it just lost its soul somewhere along the way.

And it’s frustrating, because despite all that, I still enjoy playing it.
I still launch campaigns. I still sink hours into tweaking builds and reading lore.
But every time I do, there’s this lingering thought: it could’ve been more.
It should’ve ended on a high note. Instead, it’s limping, carried by fans more than by the devs.

So yeah — I recommend it.
But know what you’re getting into. You’re buying a great game surrounded by disappointment.

I have always been a player of historical Total Wars and loved them, but I was very hesitant to play the Warhammer ones. Not only due to the differences in starting points, but also because I didn't know if the scenario would suit my taste. But as historical Total Wars have really been a disappointment recently, I picked them up in the last Steam sale. What I got was a decent Total War in a great setting with mediocre gameplay and a really big downside to non-Windows players.

To me the strengths are the battles and the setting. The Warhammer lore actually makes me want to engage with the campaign, although it often is quite cheesy of course. The battles also mostly have a great pacing and good mechanics that especially work well for Warhammer.

However it feels to me that campaignwise CA abandoned every ambition to make a great campaign map with detail as there really is little depth to building up cities or most gameplay features in the campaign mode. They obviously don't want to go down the Paradox-road and I actually don't get why. Paradox games are much more successful, offer more replayability and they last for years, which should be great for any video game company. If you take the advantages of Total War and put it in a real 4X-strategy game, it would be great. In this game the singleplayer campaign mostly is mindlessly building up everything you can to get the strongest units and then pumping them until you win, no matter the tactical approach (that's as far as I have seen it).

But what I am really really upset about is the multiplayer for non-Windows users. The singleplayer is ok for like 50 to a hundred hours of playtime but in the multiplayer the real fun begins. I did not suppose there would be no crossplay between OS/Linux and Windows, especially as CA is marketing the game for Mac, especially with the rise of the Steam Deck and with Apple continuing its pro-gaming approach. You might think, no crossplay would be no problem, but it essentially means that there is no multiplayer if you do not play on an Windows PC. I am really unhappy about that, as other games have no problems at all with that really basic feature. Windows players get a decent Total War and probably the best one of the recent years, as historical Total Wars sadly really sucked, but I can not recommend the game to Linux and Mac users at all.

In Immortal Empires campaign (generally, the main selling point) at the hardest difficulty on battle, normal on the campaign map, which means everyone being equal, nothing else, here are the issues with this game (Played as the Empire, Tomb Kings )
- Empire campaign (Franz) is designed to show how difficult the situation is, enemies everywhere (this is fantastic). However, no one tells you that you're supposed to watch youtube playthroughs (or figure them out yourselves) for the exact movements and specific battles you need to fight for the first 20 turns otherwise campaign is a sure bust because everyone is after you.
- Tomb Kings (played as Settra) is a more approachable campaign (seemingly) if you cheese the first actual enemy you have to fight (discount Carstein, not the single settlement one), and then you wait.
- You can gift liberated settlements to other factions to befriend them so they can also create a buffer zone (especially if they are not at war with whatever enemy you are fighting).
- What happens near the 100th turn if you make it that far, is you'll start to notice some patterns.
   o Factions with defensive alliance (or near to making one) to you start to drop like flies, factions below such a standing do pretty well. The worse, the better. Aside from prob set scenarios (like Vlad having to be an initial problem), this always seems to happen.  You conquer almost all of middenland, give it back, they'll certainly lose it. Conquer most of whatever that french shoreline is called, give it back, they'll lose it. In fact, they lost almost all of the peninsula to a settlementless vampire guy (Kemmler) I thought was doomed for sure. When I took a look after handling Vlad, I was absolutely shocked that not only did they lose everything, Kemmler was about to push towards the passes. They are not like this when I played as Settra. Nuln, which gets smacked eventually by Vlad is always the strongest in most campaigns.
   o Other factions go out of their ways to beeline towards you to be able to pressure you somehow and eventually attack. You'll see Elves, when playing as Franz (an example), declaring war on you when they are already at war (they have to cross other factions to get to you), there's generally no reason for this but they'll cross all that way to try to beeline towards Altdorf (You have nothing beyond the passes and it's all different factions doing their thing there)
   o Endgame event happens where one of the factions goes bananas and declares war on all of their neighbors where they spawn (without meaning) multiple stacks of max rank full stack quality troop armies. I never saw this actually happening when playing as Franz on multiple runs but on Settra I saw the dwarf one actually happen. I don't know how many stacks the game creates but I saw 7 full stacks.

Let me give an example;
On a Settra Campaign, all is going well, neighboring iron something dwarves really like me, orcs and the chaos at south has just been cleared. North is calm with the normal ogre faction (not the repulsive santa one), Nuln somehow took over a straight line of settlements to be 1-2 settlements away from me (it's unbelievable), the sigmar folks and the french are doing their thing fighting Skaven (somehow they suddenly appeared). My east is the dwarf folks completely (they are pretty big). At this point, I have around 8 (maybe more) stacks as well in total (research and awakening) fully upgraded towns, etc. I was preparing to hit the demon gate castle at the south to end chaos presence and then the dwarf end game happens. The game did notify that something was going to happen in 10 turn involving them but my standing was very good so I didn't think at least I would be a primary target. The event starts and I immediately get a war declaration. Well, I had 3 stacks back at home (from a defence with the unnecessary war with the ogres) so I figured they'd not dare since they had a smaller strength than mine. I saw that they only declared war to me, Nuln, some elves and the empire lol. When I used the prince agent to maybe check what they are doing, I saw multiple stacks going north towards Nuln (which makes sense) and then around 2 stacks pushing into my empire from my north 2 running around their settlements meaninglessly, 3 pushing from south. I knew something was wrong when I followed their main north group up, they were standing within attacking distance of Nuln armies (ones they could easily destroy) but not attacking. They ran around each other's armies without doing anything and the 5 stack eventually started coming back down without doing anything north (they could have taken a lot of Nuln territories).

I did beat them eventually as there's no need for many settlements when playing Settra aside from having a few, retook everything and stopped to check the map.
West, Skaven are rampaging. They are at war with everyone there but instead of fighting them, all 2 factions (sigmar fanatics and the normal ogres) are keeping 3 stacks each, right next to my capital (this is just meaningless). I have nothing nearby to cause this when they have lost half of their domain.
Since I couldn't wait 2-3 turns and had to rush back up asap, chaos took over the southern  most point (a boring slog to retake everything). They have the light elf guys RIGHT next to them with a single settlement  but they attack me instead. Nuln is just ridiculous, their armies are ALL OVER the place but doing nothing, taking settlements, losing them 2-3 turns later, coming back to take them again, losing them again. It's incredibly boring to see this.

I stopped playing this game when the Sigmar fanatics were cool with the vampires up north because reasons. I'm sure they'll ally with Skaven too if it means attacking me eventually, which is just supremely dumb. Nuln, was at war with everyone  (yes, everyone) but they still sent me 3-4 stacks when they are surrounded at all sides. Yes, they sent 4 stacks ALL THE WAY TO comparable South Africa from Finland by land while at war with all of Europe, Middle East, north of Africa, all of Asia and possible for whatever reason, all of South America as well. By the way, the reason for this war was they demanded 9k gold and I said no. LOL


TL;DR; game adapts if you are in a positive outlook. Not in a normal way, your allies make unbelievable errors (somehow lose 2-3 stacks to one stack of enemy) and get annihilated. If they are your enemies, the same faction never does that. Your enemies always bloat and you have to be the one clearing them. They'll always try to attack you and only fight each other if you are not reachable in 2-3 turns yet (they'll find a reason to declare war on you). I had enough of this boring slog unfortunately. This game is not fair and does not abide by its own rules BUT it is fun.

Very fun game, oddly a lot more enjoyable than Stellaris and such. Somehow the mechanics are more interesting than in for example Stellaris DLCs where so much is largely the same no matter whom you play. In this game  playing a different race (and sometimes even faction) makes a huge difference in how the game feels. Eg play as that "destroy everything" demon (Kohrne).

You don't build up settlements into  economies, you don't bother with manually occupying. You may try, but you will fail. You will succeed if you economy is deep red, but you keep looting and slaughtering fast enough, accumululating riches that way.

Or you play beastmen not caring about settlements at all, or you play Wood Elves, completely opposed to anyone entering their forests. It's really fun to "get" a race/faction.

Or you play Slaaensh and seduce everyone, or ratman, build undercities and ambush whenever you can. play Nurgle, spreading disease, Dark Elves, enslaving the world having big arches that are cities floating over the water.

Also starting out with 300 factions, actual factions, not slight variations (mostly) is just fun.

And so is learning the map, that actually does affect things, from barriers, to attrition, passes guarded by massive garissoned gates.

 If you pick it up, just play Immortal Empires. The Realm of Chaos is a failed attempt of cramming in a story with mechanics. Maybe cool idea, but its mechanics just don't git in.

If you are unhappy about victory conditions of Immortal Empires, want more lore, story, etc -> there is mods for that. I'd strongly recommend starting without and personally would recommend skipping everything that is "evening out" army rosters. I think it's likely destroying the mentioned "having fun understanding a faction". The fact that they re so different to me is the greatest feature of this game.

Lastly, when starting out and messing with settings:
- There are battle and campaign difficulty settings. It can be very confusing to end up only setting one and then being in weird situations like the autbattle suggesting it's an easy victory while when going into battle things being unwinnable. This can be frustrating. Either leave as is or look up YouTube videos on that topic. Also even though it can be overwhelming: Actually do battles. You are meant to turn things around that way at times. 
- In graphics settings you have unit size or something like that, increasing how many enntities exist. The game is largely optimized for the biggest two settings. There are things where this really matters since each entity is actually meaningful and not just graphics. Starting out it's also just for show and pretty might make this confusing.

lastly, do experiment. Do click on units, do notice that if you hover over the unit size there will be stuff like mass. Do notice that if you hover over stats it will show you why they are so scared and always run off. But also keep in mind it might just be normal for your faction, to be on the more cowardly side (eg Skaven).

A fantastic strategy game if you can stomach the extremely high price for the full experience. Comes with  a variety of different factions, all with completely unique unit rosters, playstyles and deep gameplay mechanics. The unit variety is immense. For the complete package with all factions, lords and units you need to own not just all DLCs but also Total War Warhammer 1 & 2. The Realms of Chaos story campaign is a bit grindy and VERY repetitive, but the true Warhammer experience comes in the form of the Immortal Empires sandbox campaign. The game also has some great mods. As a bonus, the game runs very smoothly on my system. Complete crashes are rare, at least in my experience (which is an achievement for a large and complex game such as this), but are not a big deal anyway if you save often. I wish the AI was more intelligent- it is unfortunately very predictable, mostly passive and easy to exploit. Difficulty scaling is heavily based on AI stats boosts, but those can be overcome on higher difficulties by player efficency (or cheesing, if you wish).

Listen...

Warhammer 3 is a FUN game, no doubt about it.  

However it is a fundamentally poorly designed and executed game.  It's biggest gameplay crime is that the core mechanic of having armies of soldiers smash into eachother just doesn't work... in order to succeed at the game the player must do their best to avoid direct infantry combat (unless they are playing the privileged few factions who break the system).

This alone is not enough to not recommend the game as it does lead to some fun and interesting scenarios despite undermining the vibe of a mass-combat game.  Ultimately why I can't recommend the game is the pricing for the DLC.  A large number of critical features are gated by DLC and the overall cost of the game is just too much for a game with so much imbalance and questionable design choices.

That said if you are a die hard fan of the genre and warhammer fantasy and have some cash to burn then this game is for you!

This game is amazing and full of detail. I’ve never played a Total War game before, and this was my first step into the series. It took some time for things to “click,” but once I started learning the mechanics, it became incredibly rewarding.

Things to know if you’re new:
Time investment – This is not a “play for 15 minutes and quit” kind of game. Campaigns take time, but the payoff is worth it.

DLCs matter (sometimes) – There are a lot of DLCs. Some factions (like Bretonnia) are complete with their base game release (and its a free DLC for warhammer 1), while others (like Nurgle) feel much better if you add certain DLCs (e.g. Champions of Chaos, Tamurkhan). Even if you own all three base games (Warhammer 1/2/3), some iconic races like Tomb Kings or Vampire Coast are still locked behind paid DLC. Creative Assembly (CA) did launch free content, so make sure to get the same via steam / linking your account with the CA website.

Best way to start – Just grab Warhammer 3 and try a Cathay campaign. If that doesn’t click, try another faction. For me, Nurgle (Ku’gath) is what hooked me. Don’t worry about “Legendary” difficulty — start on Normal, make mistakes, and learn. 150 hours in and im still learning normal / making mistakes.

Buying DLCs – Focus on the factions you actually want to play. DLC doesn’t restrict the AI, so even if you don’t own a race, you’ll face it in Immortal Empires. Sales are your friend – If you plan on buying multiple games or DLCs, wait for a sale. If you can’t wait, just start with Warhammer 3.

Account note – To unlock all factions / all content in Immortal Empires, make sure your Warhammer 1/2/3 + DLCs are on the same Steam account.

My journey as a newcomer:
- Bought Warhammer 1/2/3 on sale.
- Started with Cathay (too overwhelming at first).
- Switched to Lizardmen (Gor-Rok) → learned mechanics.
- Tried Dwarfs → loved them.
- Discovered Nurgle and Ku’gath → completely hooked. The plague mechanic is brilliant once you get used to the rough start.
- Ended up buying DLCs like Vampire Coast, Silence & the Fury, Norsca, Twisted & the Twilight, Ogres, and Tamurkhan. Next on my list: Champions of Chaos, Tomb Kings, and Chaos Dwarfs.

Verdict:
If you’re new, Warhammer 3 is the best starting point. The learning curve is steep, but once it clicks, it’s one of the most rewarding strategy experiences out there. Just be mindful of DLCs — buy what suits your playstyle, and pick them up on sale if possible.

[b]Total War: WARHAMMER III[/b] is the final chapter in the Total War trilogy dedicated to the world of Warhammer Fantasy. The game is a combination of a turn-based 4X game where you manage your empire on a strategic map and real-time battles that take place on smaller arenas. Although I've never been a big fan of turn-based strategy games, I couldn't put this title down for a long time (as you can see from the number of hours I've spent playing it). The universe itself is incredibly varied and rich, which is accurately reflected in the games – often after longer sessions, I would spend hours browsing the internet, delving into the world's history and the characters' backstories.

Upon launching the game, we have access to several choices for gameplay - an excellent prologue that serves as a tutorial (a huge plus for this), the main campaign available at launch - "The Realm of Chaos," and the creme de la creme, the "Immortal Empires" campaign, which brings together all three games, giving access to a HUGE map and over 24 races to choose from (where within each race we have access to several factions, each with their own strengths/weaknesses and certain gameplay modifications). Speaking of races I have to mention about a very controversial way of monetization, introduced by Creative Assembly in Warhammer I and II but that will be covered in a separate paragraph. Of course, we can play both of these campaigns with or against another player while online or test our abilities as commander in a quick battle, both in online multiplayer or against AI.

As I mentioned a moment ago, the gameplay is incredibly diverse, mainly thanks to the dozens of factions - each has unique mechanics, objectives they must complete to achieve victory, and most importantly, each has access to different unit roster. Anyone will find something to enjoy here. Are you a fan of balanced armies? Choose the Empire, where you can support close-combat infantry thru ranks of crossbowmen and artillery stationed in the rear. Do you prefer to destroy your foes with a swift and crushing cavalry charge? Choose Bretonnia. Or perhaps you are keen to lead hordes of demons, spread corruption and take over the world of the living? You have the option to pick one of four Chaos Gods, each different from one another - Khorne focuses on direct combat and bloodshed, while Tzeentch plots and sets factions against each other. My favorites are the Skaven, cowardly rats with endless armies where you don't care about losses because the units themselves are cheap to recruit (well most of them are cheap) - yet, despite their looks, they are extremely advanced technological race, with access to devastating artillery units, miniguns, and freaking ATOM BOMBS.

Managing the kingdom is the same as in the previous two titles - the world is divided into provinces, each consisting of several regions. You develop each region by constructing buildings and research of the technology. With time you gain access to higher-tier buildings, which allows you to recruit elite units that have superior combat capabilities. On the strategic map, we can also engage in diplomacy - compared to other titles in this genre I would say that diplomacy here is... basic, but it entirely fulfills its purpose - we can form military alliances, trade agreements, or most importantly, declare wars. Wars which are resolved by RTS-style battles. They're really good here. Because of the universe we are in, fights are feast for the eyes. Melee units, ranged units, artillery, various types of monsters or magic spells – all of which play distinct role during combat – that’s why this game is so addicting and fun! And even when you get tired of a fights you can use auto-resolve option which calculates your chance to win and casualties taken by both sides which allows you to skip some very easy and boring fights – it’s especially useful when your end-game army have to conquer tier 1 settlement with 5 basic units. To summarize gameplay I would say the game itself can initially be overwhelming to new players due to the sheer amount of content, the multitude of units, settlement development options and technologies to research, but in my opinion, it's an easy-to-learn but hard-to-master title.

As for the technical aspect I would say it's good. The models of the heroes leading the armies, as well as the units themselves, are very nice, full of details and excellently animated - sometimes instead of commanding the army I zoom the camera toward the fighting units, turn off the interface, and watch them battle each other. At the same time I don't recommend playing on the highest graphics settings unless you have a computer from NASA. Loading screens can also be excruciatingly long, especially during longer sessions - here I would recommend to frequently delete game saves from completed campaigns – it greatly improves overall performance. As for the sound design I would say that it is acceptable - it's a typical soundtrack that you would expect in a fantasy game – nothing fancy, just okay. There are plenty of different music themes but in a long run they can get a bit repetitive. Also lords and heroes “battle screams” can get a bit annoying especially after intense micro management. Additionally I have to mention about AI and its behavior. Sometimes factions lead by computer can make a very stupid decisions or just freeze and ignore that you are just bombarding them with your devastating artillery attacks. You can notice that mostly during siege battles when enemy ignores that one of his units got almost wiped out and he sends another one just to meet same fate as previous one. Changing difficulty doesn’t help since its only affects enemy stats and bonuses he receives.

A separate paragraph must be dedicated to monetization. New races and factions are released as DLC. Unfortunately, they are not among the cheapest - a pack of 3 new factions costs around 23$ while the new race, Chaos Dwarfs, costs 25$. In my opinion, these prices are definitely too high considering how few new features they offer. After release of TW:WH 3 they also raised the prices of the add-ons charging more while simultaneously lowering the quality. Of course, it's important to remember that if you want to access the races and factions from the previous two parts, you also need to own them on your Steam account. Whole collection costs now around 390$ (including base game) which is a small fortune for a video game – of course it’s not mandatory to buy all of this at once – you can wait for frequent sales and get DLCs one by one but I feel obligated to mention this. If I were to start from scratch I would buy base game, then if I liked the default campaign I would buy previous 2 main games and have fun playing “Immortal Empires” campaign. Then I'd gradually buy the DLCs with different races that I'm interested in.

In summary, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a title you sit down to play in the evening thinking you'll have a two, maybe three hour session, and you end up playing until it’s five in the morning. In my opinion, the best game in the Total War franchise, addictive, providing immense enjoyment and plenty of possibilities to have fun BUT not without a flaws.

[b]Final grade: 8/10.[/b]

I thought Total War: Warhammer III would be a fun way to relax after work. Big mistake. Instead, it’s a cruel machine designed to drain every last braincell from your skull while locking you in a cycle of endless campaigns you can’t escape.

The sheer amount of thinking this game demands is absurd. I didn’t sign up to run a calculator factory. Every battle feels like I’m solving an advanced chess puzzle while someone screams at me to do my taxes. By turn 50, I’m convinced I’ve aged ten years.

And then there’s Cylostra Direfin. Her voice lines—oh god, the voice lines. At first they’re quirky, even funny. But after the hundredth time she shrieks about the sea or curses in that ghostly opera voice, it drills directly into your brain. Combine that with the stress of micromanaging armies and you’ll find yourself haunted in real life. Sometimes I hear her voice even when the game isn’t on. I’m not okay.

The worst part? This game traps you. Once you start a campaign, you can kiss your freedom goodbye. You’ll sit there in your room, promising yourself “just one more turn”. Next thing you know, it’s 4 AM, you haven’t eaten, and you’re strategizing how to defeat demons instead of handling your real-life responsibilities. It’s less of a game and more of a prison sentence you willingly signed up for.

Verdict: If you value your sanity, your free time, or your last remaining braincells, avoid this game at all costs. Otherwise, enjoy your new life locked in a dark room, whispering back to Cylostra like she’s your only companion.

I've played TW games since Rome TW - and I love them.  Their emphasis on grand strategy, the fact that buildings constructed in the campaign map were present in the battle map, the massive battle maps that allowed for practically unlimited maneuverability, the ability to turn any village into a culturally unique thriving metropolis, and the fact that an army's position in the campaign map directly translated to their position in the battle map - all combined to simulate the growth of empires and a feeling of realistic warfare where battles took hours rather than minutes.  Those early TW games gifted us a true approach to simulated warfare rather than a mere digital game-board.  

Unfortunately, the keystones of what made those earlier TW games so special have consistently been eroded in favor of game-board strategies that emphasize balanced maps, actions per minute, and micromanaging lords and heroes.  

The maps are tiny as compared to their forebears.  
The cities do not alter their cultural identity in accord with their owner.  
The buildings you build in the campaign map do not exist in the battle map - at all.  
Placing your army on a hill or bridge in the campaign map does not translate into a tenable position on the battle map. 
 There is no way view your city as there once was.
The maps are designed for balanced and competitive play rather than a simulation of the real lopsidedness of warfare.
The focus on lords and heroes is obscene to the point that a one-man doomstack can wipe out an entire army.

The emphasis on releasing more and more DLC ignored the core mechanical failures that this game encounters.  For example, units often cannot see what is clearly right in front of them.  Ranged units are often blocked from firing by the units in front of them.  When ranged units are ordered to direct fire on an enemy, they often think that they need to charge or move closer, or turn, - rather than simply open fire - thus exposing those troops to annihilation (even though they can clearly see - yes I checked).

Further, heroes and lords, more often than not, will find themselves patiently standing in the midst of the enemy while they wait for the attack animation - and the enemy soldiers stand still in a circle around them - like something out of a bad kung-fu movie.  (the focus on complex graphic design re the attack animation is simply too clunky for what it needs to be - a simple slice of the sword etc.)

Overall, the game shifted from grand strategy to an emphasis on actions per minute, micromanaging units, balanced maps, competitive play, and lost its unique flavor by joining the horde of digital game boards that already dominate the RTS industry. 

I wanted to love this game.  I tried again and again.  Unfortunately, I could only play for a tiny portion of time before I became utterly bored (unlike every other TW game that I've played).  I hope that the TW series will return to their roots in the future in a true attempt to simulate the creativity and lopsidedness of real warfare, empire expansion, and city building - rather than a simple reskinned cashgrab of their more recent games.

There is one feature of this game that makes it truly special - the coop campaigns.  The creation of simultaneous turns is revolutionary (though a plainly obvious next step) for enjoying this game with friends.  Hopefully, this positive asset will play a future role in TW games and will be expanded upon.  (Unfortunately, it is currently still subject to bugs and disconnections despite ample internet connections from both parties).

Overall, I would not recommend this game because it ignores those facets that made the earlier TW games so special.  The sole redeeming quality is the possibility for coop campaigns, but that quality cannot undo the damage.

[h1] Total War: Warhammer 3 - A Legendary Triumph of Strategy and Fantasy [/h1]

[b] Total War: Warhammer 3[/b] is the crowning jewel of Creative Assembly’s Warhammer trilogy, masterfully blending the strategic depth of the Total War series with the vibrant, chaotic lore of the Warhammer universe. By combining the content of all three Warhammer titles into one colossal package, this game delivers an unparalleled experience that captivates both newcomers and veterans with its scope, polish, and replayability.

The [b] Immortal Empires [/b] mode is the heart of this triumph, uniting the maps, factions, and mechanics of Total War: Warhammer 1, 2, and 3 into a massive, sandbox campaign. With [b] 24 unique races [/b] to choose from—each featuring distinct game mechanics, unit rosters, and campaign objectives—players can command diverse factions like the stalwart Kislevites, the malevolent Chaos Gods, or the cunning Skaven, ensuring every playthrough feels fresh and deeply engaging. From the necromantic powers of the Vampire Counts to the savage hordes of the Greenskins, each race offers a tailored experience that rewards strategic creativity. Immortal Empires also supports up to 8-player co-op, allowing friends to team up or compete across the vast Warhammer world, with simultaneous turns ensuring smooth, fast-paced multiplayer sessions.

The end-game crisis mode in Immortal Empires adds thrilling unpredictability, introducing world-shaking challenges like Chaos invasions or other cataclysmic events that test your strategic prowess and keep campaigns dynamic. The game’s mod support on Steam Workshop further elevates the experience, empowering the community to create game-changing content. One standout is SFO: Grimhammer III, an incredible total overhaul mod that reworks every facet of the game to align closer to Warhammer lore, adding over 150 new units, smarter AI, rebalanced economies, and immersive faction mechanics for a grittier, more strategic experience. Mods like SFO, alongside others such as Radious Total War and Mixu’s Unlocker, bring fresh content and customization, ensuring the game evolves with player creativity.

The Chaos Realms campaign delivers a gripping narrative, with stunning cutscenes and voice acting that immerse you in a world of gods and daemons. Combat is a visual and tactical spectacle, with meticulously detailed units, dynamic siege battles, and a smarter AI that rewards clever strategies. The campaign map is a strategic masterpiece, with an enhanced diplomacy system that adds depth to alliances and rivalries. Performance is silky-smooth, handling even the most chaotic battles with ease.

Multiplayer shines beyond co-op, with competitive modes like Domination keeping battles intense and strategic. Total War: Warhammer 3, with its 24 unique races, unified trilogy content, 8-player co-op, robust mod support including the phenomenal SFO: Grimhammer III, and thrilling end-game crises in Immortal Empires, is a strategy titan. It’s a must-play for fans of Warhammer and strategy gaming, offering endless hours of conquest and creativity in a breathtakingly realized world.

Un putain de bon jeu, mais accrochez-vous.

C’est violent, c’est stratégique, c’est complexe. Au début, vous allez vous faire rouler dessus. Chaque faction a son délire, son style, ses galères. Y’en a des plus faciles, mais aucune n’est "gratuite". Faut apprendre, galérer, recommencer. Et ça fait partie du kiff.

Si vous débarquez comme moi dans la série des Total War : commencez en facile. Sérieux. Prenez le temps de capter toutes les mécaniques, y’en a une tonne. Et une fois que vous maîtrisez, là ça devient jouissif.

J’ai surtout joué en solo (c’est mon trip), mais le multi est pas mal aussi. Niveau graphismes, c’est une boucherie visuelle. Les combats sont magnifiques, ultra dynamiques. Parce que c’est ça, l’âme du jeu : foutre le feu à la plaine avec vos troupes, envoyer les monstres éclater des lignes, voir le sang gicler dans tous les sens. Si vous skippiez les batailles... vous êtes passés à côté du délire. ( Arrêtez de passer les combat, parce que honnêtement pourquoi acheter ce genre de jeu alors ? ) 

Côté technique : j’ai une 5070, et y’a encore des moments où ça rame. Le jeu est pas encore bien optimisé pour les nouvelles cartes, apparemment. C’est pas la mort, mais un peu relou quand même.

Le plus gros point noir ? Les DLC. C’est cher. Trop cher. Et pour avoir toute l’expérience complète, faut raquer. J’en ai pris deux + le DLC pour avoir du sang (obligatoire pour un jeu comme ça !), mais le reste attendra les soldes. Heureusement, y’a une putain de communauté de moddeurs qui balance des trucs incroyables. Franchement, allez mater des vidéos sur YouTube, ça vaut le coup rien que pour savoir quoi ajouter ou quel DLC vaut vraiment le prix.

Bref, si t’aimes les guerres épiques, les armées qui s’étripent, les monstres dégueulasses et la stratégie bien sale : fonce.

Maintenant, j’ai des vampires à démembrer.

Well......I certainly got MY money's worth out of the game but as a new player trying to get in....dang it really is a lot of money, sort of like a Paradox game with a million DLCs. I bought all this stuff drips and drabs over the last 8 or 9 years. But to buy this all at once? Yeesh. You will want the first two games as their content all snowballs into this title; meaning the races introduced in the first two games and whatever dlcs you picked will be playable right out of the box in addition to the warhammer 3 base factions if you buy this game (you don't need to keep warhammer 1 and 2 installed at least, thank goodness). If you don't own either of the first two you will only get the base warhammer 3 factions. As such, I can really only recommend this game on sale simply because there is just so much to buy. A good chunk of the DLC factions ARE pretty good too.

 The modding scene is really good on these games and I HIGHLY recommend the SFO mod. Just filter by "top rated all time" in the workshop and there's easily 5-10 pages of 5 star mods to look at. SFO is a great one-stop compilation though, doesn't add a bunch of useless fluff for the sake of adding it either; its all tasteful stuff in my opinion. Theres a lot of modded races you can add as well if you can't afford the DLC factions. Cataph's mods, Mixu's faction unlocker, Immortal Empires Expanded, The Old World Campaign, SCCP additional factions, OVN Lost factions. Hell there's a mod to be a nation of giant crabs. Get the Better Camera mod too, thank me later.

So what of the actual gameplay? These games takes place in two distinct spheres; the campaign map and the battlefield. The campaign map is a turn-based affair where you will manage your towns by constructing buildings in your allotted building slots, the number of which are governed by your population size/growth. So you have to decide do you want buildings that produce trade goods versus expanding the types of troops you can recruit as an example. Your towns themselves have to have their public order managed on a sliding scale of -100 to +100, and many factions have a corruption type and environment that they naturally spread/prefer to kinda terraform the land to their liking in a way which is pretty interesting. A couple of towns together in pre-determined geographic areas make up "provinces" and once you control all towns in a province you can issue an edict to give that whole province a buff. The capital town/city of each province can become bigger and have more building slots and get better defensive walls and higher-tier units. On the campaign map you will also recruit troops which go into army "stacks" that must be headed by a "lord". Each troop stack can have 20 units, including the Lord. These stacks can be moved around the map and even enter different stances so you can force-march them to get a bit more movement range, a raiding stance to steal gold or food in enemy territory, an ambush stance in difficult terrain to get the jump on the enemy......stuff like that. You can research technologies and engage in diplomacy with different tabs on the campaign map. You can also level up and equip gear to the Lords leading your armies.

When your stack(s) bump into enemy stacks, a pitched battle on that physical spot of earth takes place in that the game will send you through a loading screen and then into a whole other half of the game where you assume command of your military stack in real-time and guide them to victory. This is really where the Total War franchise has always stood out; offering battles the scale of which no other games really even get close too. Your units that you built and shoved in here? Oh yea, ONE unit might be 120 dinosaur-men wielding axes or spears. Another unit might be just one guy but its a whole entire dragon at your command. Maybe you built some sick siege equipment. Some factions get some crazy ish like warp lightning cannons (great for taking out aforementioned dragons heh) and my personal fave: Hellstorm Rocket batteries lolol. You can have FORTY units on screen under your command at once and thats not even including whatever the enemy is throwing at you so you could easily have 6000 - 8000 models on screen at once all INDIVIDUALLY fighting each other to where you can zoom in to their perspective on the ground and watch them fight and see their individual animations. It's insane. Zooming in to watch your undead Cairn Wraiths, ghost mfers with scythes riding skeleton horses, charging in to a flank and just demolishing some poor infantry unit. Or watching the previously mentioned siege equipment bombarding the enemy from their own perspective never gets old. In a rather loose way; its a rock, paper, scissors formula in that spearmen beat cavalry, cavalry beat infantry that dont have spears, missile units tear up anything until something gets in their face, heavy infantry can beat most other things once they bog them down enough but can be flanked and beaten by other things. Flying units are generally susceptible to missiles but scare the piss out of infantry when they land and start whooping ass. But then again.....this game has so many factions with weird niche exceptions and specialist units that its a little more complicated than that. You'll get the hang of it. It can be quite a bit to manage because on top of all these units....your Lords have special abilities and you may have a mage or two in your stack that can straight up cast spells. 

I could go on all day about this game. Graphics are good, performance is good untill you break the game with so much crap on screen it slows everything down lol. Audio is good for sound effects and forgettable for actual music. The faction variety gives a ton of replayability because of their wildly differing unit rosters and faction mechanics that have gotten better and better over time from Warhammer 1 until now.

Two last points. First, I have had an enormous amount of fun playing multiplayer co-op campaigns and if you have a good friend, or THREE who will spend the time with you, its friggin awesome. You all take your turns simultaneously now which is a huge improvement over warhammer 1 and 2. When your buddy wants to fight a battle on the battle map, they can gift you units to control so you all can actively participate and not sit there bored. Its actually a great way to learn to mico units by having your friend give you just the spellcasters or just the cavalry to manage. 

Last point; USE THE FOLLOWING DIFFICULTY SETTINGS!!!! For Campaign difficulty set it to easy or medium to learn the game. But for the battles, you should set it to Normal or Hard. It is crucial you DO NOT EVER SET BATTLE DIFFICULTY TO EASY! Why? Because it doesn't actually change the difficulty of the AI, all it does is make your auto-resolve battle option ridiculously easy by effectively multiplying the power of your army by a factor of 2.5 or 3....why is this bad? Because then when you go try to fight a battle yourself, you no longer get that multiplier, it ONLY applies to how your auto-resolved battles will go. This means, that as a new player you will get a worse result commanding the battle yourself EVERY TIME and discourage yourself and/or resign yourself to NEVER commanding any of the battles, meaning you effectively miss out on learning HALF OF THE GAME! Note; Normal battle difficulty has this problem as well but less so, it gives you like a 30 or 40 percent strength calculation for auto-resolves. Thus the recommended battle setting is actually HARD so the auto-resolve calculator finally tells you the damn truth about your chances commanding it yourself.

There are several great features to this game - which is good considering the expense of getting into it with all the dlc's and stuff.
First off, you have single player and multi-player competitive and co-op. I recommend checking TotalTavern if you want to get into the competitive scene or check out some of the content creators and ask them how you can join one of their tourneys - many hold some for newcomers specifically as well as others open to veteran players.
The game is a mix of turn-based and realtime strategy done very well. No getting distracted in the middle of epic combat to put an scv or villager back to work or make 5 more of them. That's all done in turn outside the realtime combat portion of the game. When it is time to fight, you get to really fight. Tons of great looking units, magic abilities, activatable items, terrain that actually matters for strategy, and big freakin armies. Micro matters, but you don't have to worry about losing half your army to a siege onager instantly; 20 slots for your army where each slot could be a lord, hero, or single entity monster, a small elite force of units (16+) or a big brick of lower tier units (80-120ish).
Balance isn't perfect. Any content creator will tell you that. But that shouldn't scare you. This game has many stats and balance features which give depth that other games do not. For example, you have leadership. Run a low leadership unit that is heavily damaged into a big scary enemy? They might flee. There's also armor piercing damage, anti-large, anti-infantry, and attack vs weapon strength to consider. This is a GOOD thing because it allows for more balance diversity than something like AOE2. For example, you could have a unit with 30 atk 40 weapon str, 30 atk 40 weapon str (10 armor piercing), and 20 atk 40 weapon str (30 armor piercing). Depending on if you're against a zero armor, low armor, high armor enemy one unit will be more effective than another. This means different army compositions are more effective or less effective depending on what they're up against. Instead of just spamming palladins or mammoth tanks to kill everything. Build a diversified army and pit the right types of units against the correct enemies for max effect.
There's also magic. Burn your foes. Freeze them. Infect them with plagues. Etc. And don't forget about your lord. Level them up. Use the tech tree to buff your forces or to turn them into an even bigger raid boss. Get elite gear for them to wear that buffs them even more and dominate the world.

Total War: Warhammer III is a grand strategy game where you plan an empire, manage diplomacy, fight epic battles… and then accidentally stay up until 3 a.m. because “this turn is important.”

What It Does Incredibly Well:
Immortal Empires is massive. Unreasonably massive. You could lose a small nation in this map.
Every faction feels wildly different. Demons play nothing like humans, and that’s the point.
Battles are cinematic chaos: dragons, artillery, magic, and units refusing to break because vibes.
The soundtrack and voice acting go hard. The game sounds expensive.

Where the Pain Lives:
The learning curve is a cliff. The tutorial helps, but the game still whispers “figure it out” and pushes you.
AI diplomacy can be… creative. Allies declare war because Mercury is in retrograde.
Late-game turns can feel long, especially on big campaigns.
Balancing changes mean your favorite unit might go from “unstoppable” to “why does this exist?” overnight.

Tips for New Warlords:
Start with a simpler faction (Cathay or Kislev) unless you enjoy suffering.
Economy > conquest early. A broke empire is a dead empire.
Auto-resolve lies. Sometimes it’s honest. Sometimes it murders your elite units for fun.
Save often. The Chaos Gods respect nothing.

Final Verdict:
Total War: Warhammer III is huge, complex, sometimes overwhelming, and incredibly rewarding. When everything clicks — battles, economy, diplomacy — it’s one of the best strategy experiences out there.

Игра оставляет после себя смешанные впечатления из-за ряда проблем, которые существенно влияют на игровой опыт. Хочу выделить несколько ключевых недостатков, которые требуют внимания разработчиков.
Вы серьезно? Платные DLC и их влияние на игру.
Политика платных дополнений в Warhammer 3 вызывает серьезные вопросы. Значительная часть контента, включая новые фракции, лордов и механики, доступна только через DLC, что делает базовую игру ощутимо неполноценой. Например, такие фракции, как Хаос Неделимый или определенные легендарные лорды, требуют дополнительных покупок, что может разочаровать игроков, уже заплативших полную цену за игру. Более того, стоимость DLC зачастую не соответствует их объему: некоторые дополнения добавляют лишь косметические элементы или минимальные нововведения, что воспринимается как попытка монетизации ради монетизации. Было бы справедливее включать больше контента в базовую игру или предлагать более сбалансированную ценовую политику.
Отсутствие баланса
Баланс в Warhammer 3 остается одной из самых слабых сторон. Разные фракции имеют слишком неравные стартовые условия и механики, что особенно заметно в кампании Immortal Empires. Некоторые фракции, такие как Тзинч или Слаанеш, обладают мощными механиками, которые дают им явное преимущество, в то время как другие (например, некоторые людские фракции) ощущаются недоработанными и менее конкурентоспособными. В мультиплеере дисбаланс также проявляется: определенные юниты или способности доминируют, что снижает разнообразие тактик. Патчи выходят регулярно, но их темп и эффективность пока не решают проблему полностью. Хотелось бы видеть более тщательную работу над балансом, чтобы каждая фракция была интересной и играбельной. Перегруженный интерфейс  
Интерфейс игры, несмотря на свою информативность, часто кажется громоздким и неинтуитивным. Огромное количество информации, отображаемой на экране, может запутать даже опытных игроков. Меню кампании, управление армиями и дипломатия перегружены мелкими деталями, которые не всегда логично организованы. Например, отслеживание эффектов построек или глобальных баффов требует лишних кликов, а всплывающие подсказки не всегда дают ясное представление о механиках. Для новичков это создает высокий порог вхождения, а для ветеранов — раздражение из-за неудобства. Упрощение интерфейса или добавление опции кастомизации могли бы значительно улучшить ситуацию.
Технические проблемы и подлагивания
Несмотря на многочисленные обновления, игра все еще страдает от технических недочетов. Подлагивания, особенно в крупных сражениях с большим количеством юнитов, заметно портят динамику боя. Проблемы с оптимизацией проявляются даже на мощных системах: долгие загрузки, падение FPS на глобальной карте и случайные вылеты встречаются чаще, чем хотелось бы. Также замечены баги, связанные с ИИ (например, некорректное поведение союзников в кооперативной игре). Эти проблемы не критичны, но они нарушают погружение и требуют доработки.

It took a long time. A long, long time...

...but this game is actually really, really good now. If you are scrolling through reviews to know if it's finally worth playing, yes, this is the definitive Warhammer: Total War experience at last... with a slough of DLC of course but you know what you're getting into.

Pros:

Immortal Empires is an amazing campaign mode. It is the ultimate sandbox experience and it's hard to go back once you truly realise the length and breadth of the full campaign map. Honestly, the game was incomplete until they added this and Realms of Chaos is now a distant conflicted memory.

There are so many factions in this game and they are all suitably unique and flavourful. The older DLC lords that were broken with the transition from 2 have all been fixed. You no longer have to feel stupid for buying the N'kai DLC only to learn his campaign is broken. Instead the legacy factions have been consistently updated and even expanded upon with factions like the Empire feeling completely revitalised. You are spoiled for choice and most of them are good ones.

Combat feels good. The sluggish movements and awkward pathing hasn't been hammered out completely but it's been vastly improved and now feels about on par with Total War: Warhammer 2. All the better that we have a bevy of wild and ridiculous monsters to play around with. The urge to Auto Resolve everything is no longer as strong.

The gameplay loop of Total War is as strong as ever, and with so many factions to master and locations to spawn and army types to build... the experience will melt away the hours like nothing. This game can completely absorb you if you let it. I have poured more time into this series that I like to think about and I will definitely pour many more.

Cons:

The lighting and colouring of this game still feels weird. It's a lot brighter and more saturated. It's not really noticeable with the newer lords designed with it in mind, but it looks really ugly on some of the older lords and units. If you liked the gritty aesthetic of the previous two titles then you might be a little disappointed but it's a small gripe. At least the entirety of the UI across all factions isn't blood red anymore.

The game still has a trove of minor bugs. Mostly small visual errors or abilities not doing everything they should. It's barely noticeable in most campaigns but, with so many factions, new bugs pop up with every update and can take a while to get fixed if ever.

Realms of Chaos still sucks. CA knows it and, while the campaign has been updated since, almost all developer attention is on Immortal Empires as it probably should but, if you're a Realms of Chaos fan.... well, sorry.

DLC. There's a lot. I own all of it because I've been following from the start but, looking back over it all, I have poured a LOT of money into this game. I'm glad to say I don't regret it as the scope of this game firing with all cylinders included is absolutely magical. But coming in new, there's a lot to parse. Buying all of it feels ludicrous but where do you even start if you just want a few. Buying the previous titles is a good shout as they are effectively super high value DLC nowadays. There are very good buyer guides online but it can be a headache. An expensive headache.

tl:dr

This game is an expensive, somewhat buggy masterpiece that has outgrown the kinds of growing pains that would have landed other games in the cancellation bin and instead become everything it always should have been from the beginning: the ultimate Warhammer Fantasy video game experience.

Se os Total War já eram conhecidos por misturar estratégia em turnos com batalhas em tempo real, o Warhammer III decidiu que isso não era suficiente e jogou no caldeirão: demônios, dragões, magias absurdas e exércitos tão insanos que fazem a Batalha do Abismo de Helm parecer uma excursão escolar.

Aspectos técnicos:

Mapa de campanha: gigantesco, cheio de facções com estilos únicos. Desde os mortais pragmáticos de Kislev até as hordas de Khorne que acreditam fielmente que diplomacia é um verbo proibido.

Facções assimétricas: cada raça é um jogo diferente. Jogar com Cathay é sobre equilíbrio e comércio; com Nurgle é uma simulação de doença pandêmica; e com Slaanesh… bem, digamos que é o marketing mais honesto que o caos já teve.

Batalhas em tempo real: milhares de unidades na tela, magias que viram o campo de batalha de cabeça para baixo, e aquele momento mágico em que seu general morre porque você esqueceu ele sozinho no meio de 200 ogros.

Sistema de Realms of Chaos: a campanha principal gira em torno de abrir portais para dimensões demoníacas, o que garante caos, eventos imprevisíveis e crises existenciais sobre se você realmente deveria ter clicado naquele portal brilhante.

Multiplayer: caótico, mas incrivelmente divertido. É onde amizades vão para morrer e pactos de não-agressão duram menos que a bateria de um controle de Steam Deck.

A experiência prática:

Primeiro turno: “ok, vou expandir minha economia com calma”.

Terceiro turno: invasão demoníaca, rebelião interna, seu aliado declarou guerra e ainda tem um dragão cuspindo fogo na sua capital.

Resultado: 3 horas depois, você percebe que está falando sozinho, planejando rotas comerciais como se fosse ministro da Fazenda de uma nação imaginária.

Diferencial do WARHAMMER III na trilogia:
É a culminação de todo o projeto. Com o Immortal Empires, ele vira praticamente o maior sandbox de estratégia já feito: todas as facções dos três jogos juntas em um mapa colossal, onde você pode recriar a sua própria versão da história do mundo Warhammer.

Resumo final: Total War: WARHAMMER III é a mistura perfeita de grandiosidade, caos e vício. É tão profundo que você precisa de tutorial até para entender o tutorial. Mas quando tudo clica — quando sua facção cresce, sua diplomacia funciona (ou explode) e sua batalha vira uma ópera de destruição em larga escala — não existe sensação igual.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — 5/5, porque não há nada mais satisfatório do que ver 20 mil soldados e monstros se engalfinhando em alta definição enquanto você grita “POR SIGMAR!”.

Después de tanto tiempo dedicado recomiendo este juego para todos los amantes de la estrategia y fantasía.
Es cierto que el juego no salió de la mejor manera pero parece que últimamente están haciendo más caso a la comunidad y siguen metiendo cosas para mejorar sobre todo la campaña.

全战的优势是大战场排兵布阵，战场之外是一个简陋且封闭的大地图，要玩战场，就得被迫去玩这个大地图。简陋的经济系统、拥有相同建筑槽的城市、只有三两颗棋子的调动能力、为剧本服务的固定的开局布置、四面漏风的领地。与其说是全面战争，不如说是用战争来全面遮羞。
- 这个大地图基本上就是大地图桌游中最无趣的那种一类，规则多玩法少，而且和你一起玩这款桌游的还是 AI，你和他们的博弈仅限于作为一个单一数值的外交条和隐变量，这个隐变量是为了恶心玩家而不是为了让 AI 自己取得胜利。例如说敌人实力实力不佳的军队会和玩家玩躲猫猫，只打守城战，只打明显有利的局面。就这样一套系统，过每一回合要像文明中一样经历漫长等待。
- 领地四面漏风，缺少自然的关隘就算了，为什么要限制玩家将一座普通的城市发展为人为的要塞？为什么镇守一座城池的兵力一定要取决于当地发展度？要防守一座城池要么需要调动一个昂贵集团军，要么就只能靠城池自带的杂兵？总体上，玩家没有任何改变利用和扭转局势的能力，始终是在局势的胁迫之下、不断通过征服更多的城池来面对如何防守城池的问题。
- 既然要模仿桌游，那为什么还要让游戏中的英雄、执政官、科技、建筑的数值始终是百分比级别？而不是像文明那样有质变？这是用数值设计来系统设计的遮丑：把一个科技掰成十个，然后它们分别依赖其他种类的科技。大体上，这些科技无关紧要，但是又不得不点，因为不点亏回合。这类设计强迫玩家“长远规划”，在一开始就定好十个回合的玩法。
作为唯一优势的大战场也是一部比一部差。
- 操控感差。指挥军队和挥舞海绵一样，没有重量、没有威胁度、不听使唤。有时甚至不如挥舞海绵直观，一旦把一支部队丢向敌人的部队，就把它们交给了复杂又不透明的计算过程，例如战锤3在弓箭射击上屡屡出bug。
- 单位的特色排不上用场。明明有特色的兵种但是游戏却试图将这些特色限制在寥寥几种定位上：一个特色兵种只是具有特色的骑兵、本质上是骑兵，而不是在特定情况下能够发挥骑兵的作用。许多单位的特性都是针对玩家的，在玩家手里就只是一个骑兵，而在 AI 手里就是打玩家经济毁灭者。反而是兵种较少的三国更加能发挥特色。
- 军队管理非常痛苦。某只部队在招募时就定形了，精锐在招募时就是精锐，需要金钱和科技而不需要在战场上磨练，而战场中部队的升级也只是增加等级，而杂兵不能转变为其他兵种。因为将领的数量非常有限，所以只能军队管理的上限就是较为万金油的满编队伍。
- 争夺城池非常痛苦。对于攻城与守城，战略的空间很少，亲手攻打相所较花费的情感总是不划算的。作为攻城者，攻城手段需要围城中建造，但是战场外的不断加码的经济竞争基本上不假定你有这样做时间，慢悠悠的围城基本上是 AI 的专属。作为守城方，首先不能自己组织自己的守军，只能利用建筑附带的兵种。其次，守城方不能根据进攻方的部署调整自己的部署，就仿佛更好的视野不是城墙的优势，导致往往直接放弃外城集中防守内部据点来应对多路进攻。
