Total War: Warhammer III to zwieńczenie epickiej trylogii studia Creative Assembly, które w pełni realizuje wizję połączenia klasycznej formuły strategii z bogactwem uniwersum Warhammera Fantasy. Tytuł ten zasługuje na pozytywną ocenę zarówno ze względu na skalę i głębię rozgrywki, jak i konsekwencję, z jaką twórcy rozwijali serię przez lata.

Kampania i narracja

Kampania fabularna oferuje monumentalne doświadczenie, łącząc wielowątkową opowieść o walce z bogami Chaosu z klasycznym zarządzaniem imperium. Scenariusz „Ostatecznej Bitwy” i różnorodne ścieżki narracyjne każdej frakcji sprawiają, że rozgrywka nie tylko ma wymiar strategiczny, ale również narracyjny. Dodatkowo, wprowadzenie kampanii Immortal Empires (łączącej wszystkie trzy części cyklu) sprawia, że gra osiąga bezprecedensową skalę i głębię.

Mechaniki rozgrywki

System zarządzania imperium, dyplomacja, ekonomia oraz rozbudowa armii pozostają filarami serii. Nowością są m.in. bardziej złożone mechanizmy dotyczące legendarnych bohaterów, unikatowych mechanik frakcyjnych (np. rytuały Kislevu czy balansowanie energii w armiach Demonów Chaosu), a także zmodyfikowany system bitew oblężniczych, który wreszcie stał się pełnoprawnym elementem strategii.

Bitwy i AI

Bitwy w czasie rzeczywistym zachwycają różnorodnością jednostek i spektakularnymi starciami. Gra oferuje pełen wachlarz frakcji – od klasycznych ludzkich armii (Kislev, Kataj), przez demoniczne hordy, aż po egzotyczne rasy – co przekłada się na unikalne style walki. Sztuczna inteligencja potrafi sprawić graczowi wyzwanie, zwłaszcza na wyższych poziomach trudności, choć bywa nierówna w oblężeniach.

Warstwa audiowizualna

Oprawa graficzna stoi na bardzo wysokim poziomie. Szczegółowe modele jednostek, imponujące efekty czarów oraz rozbudowane mapy kampanii budują epicki klimat. Muzyka i udźwiękowienie zasługują na szczególne uznanie – monumentalne kompozycje i charakterystyczne głosy narratorów dodają całości odpowiedniego ciężaru.

Aspekt techniczny

Premiera obfitowała w problemy optymalizacyjne, jednak kolejne aktualizacje znacząco poprawiły stabilność i wydajność gry. Dziś tytuł działa płynnie na szerokiej gamie konfiguracji sprzętowych, a twórcy aktywnie wspierają społeczność, dostarczając poprawki i nowe treści.

Społeczność i modding

Overall i really like this game, my favourite game in the rts/grand strategy genre. Playing as various Chaos factions in particular is pretty fun. I could get into it very easily despite not having played Warhammer 1 and 2, just starting with the prologue "The Lost God" explained a lot to get me started with the fun Immortal Empires campaigns. There is a lot to learn with regards to mechanics for each faction, but with a little patience, you can understand enough for it to get really fun :)

on the cons side: some factions like Daniel the Daemon Princes faction are not really fully fleshed out and are very weak in the early to mid-game. Also the game can get really pricy with the many DLCs to add Legendary Lords for every faction. My suggestion there would be to try the free base game Lords and Factions first and then if you like a particular faction already, then you can buy the DLCs for it, if you want. You do not really need to unlock every faction, cuz not every faction playstyle will be to your liking. Some factions are more aggressive, more focused on pure conquest war economy; other more defensive, either focused on economy settlement management, or diplomacy, or trade. Some factions require a lot of micro in manual combat, others do not need much micromanagement during combat - so get a feel for what you like and when you find factions that can deliver that, that is when the game will get most satisfying :)

I've been playing Total war games since Medieval 2, but this (and WH2) have been my introduction to Warhammer. 

Personally I find this combination to be a massive success. You have all of the classic game play from the old games, with the addition of massive monsters, monstrous units, flying units, and magic! Factions Feel unique and offer a large variety of play styles. Magic units have access to multiple spell books each with their own unique feel. each faction has multiple legendary lords with their own feel on top of the faction... i could keep going. you get the point. 

The only major Con to the game is that you need WH1, WH2, & WH3 to experience the full sandbox campaign with all factions. I suggest picking up races you are interested in over time when they go on sale. The main games provide the most content if you want bang for your buck. on the other hand, i love that the content has all been carried forward into the next games. These games are truly massive. 

Oh and you can do 8 person multiplayer campaigns! way more fun than i expected. 

There is so much content to bite into in these games, i have a feeling that after 20 years my go to total war game has been replaced (so long medieval 2).

Before I start, I do want to address the Chaos Mammoth in the room and acknowledge that I am aware that the Total War Warhammer series of games, especially 3, are designed to be more arcade-like. They kind of have to be with how much of a game changer magic is to the Total War formula. Trying to go for something with a sense of realism like they had in Rome 2 or Medieval 2 is a bit of a lost cause.

That all said however, I find garrisons to be one of the more strangely tedious elements of the Warhammer games. Minor settlement garrisons will rarely win against any invading army. The only occasion I can think of was when I was playing the Greenskins, and a vampire army consisting of mostly zombies attacked a minor settlement. Due to having one unit of Black Orcs, I was able to kill the low-level lord, and the whole army crumbled. Otherwise, even armies of 7-8 units can overwhelm most minor settlement garrisons.

I will concede that minor settlement garrisons can be useful when it comes to wearing down an invading army. AI armies rarely stop and heal up, choosing instead to press-on, which can give you a more favourable match up with your actual army. However, my real issue with settlement garrisons is how tedious they can be for you the player. Obviously I don't want to just be able to waltz into settlements and occupy them, that would be boring. But as it stands, most settlement battles are best left to the auto-battler, so functionally its the same just with a few more button presses.

This is part of my greater desire for CA to reduce the reliance on the auto-battler considerably, but I don't want to then force players to have to manually fights loads of easy settlement battles, so I propose doing away with free settlement garrisons. By this I mean, when you upgrade the walls, you wouldn't get a free pile of troops as well. You can still recruit units to a settlement, and over time they would gain experience, but you'd need to think strategically about where you drawn your lines. Which settlements will you hold?

I'll admit, this would be tricky to achieve in the game as it currently stands. With how fast your borders change in the average Immortal Empires game, needing to move around your garrisons to hold the frontline would be frustrating. I also fear that the AI would be at risk of not intelligently guarding its borders, leading to the player having an easy job of conquest, which is precisely the opposite outcome I want.

A change that would really help this system work would be a return to the Rome 2/Medieval 2 system of Cities/Castles and Towns. You have the provincial capital in the form of a city or castle where all your military buildings are housed, then you have towns around it that provide you with economic benefits but don't have any defensive structures. This easily could be implemented in Warhammer with its minor and major settlements. You could choose to occupy an economically important minor settlement to bait out the main army defending the major settlement. Taking the major settlements means your also occupy the whole province automatically. Control of a province only occurs once peace has been negotiated, and the controlling faction cedes control to you. This would mean you can only control whole provinces, which would in turn lead to less disgusting border gore! This also means that wars can be more interesting than you going until the other side is wiped out. While you occupy territory, public order will be constantly ticking down leading to rebellion, so you can just take over a provincial capital and move on, you need to maintain a military presence.

This got way longer than I expected, so I'll wrap up! I'm aware my proposed changes will be unpopular. Many play Total War: Warhammer precisely because there's less strategy and long term planning required, but I've always believed that when implemented correctly, requiring the player to think tactically and long term can be equally engaging. I also recognise the fact that if I want this style of gameplay, why don't I play one of the many Total War games that offer it? Well because I like Warhammer 3 and the insane units it has, and I want more opportunity to have interesting battles with wild combinations of opposing units, but needing to auto-resolve my way through so many boring settlement battles really drags things out, and doesn't make for an interesting narrative.

But also, Warhammer has so many interesting factions, and they all could interact with this proposed system in unique ways. Order-aligned factions do the tradition thing of occupying the provincial capital and suing for peace to have control of the province ceded to them. Chaos-aligned factions just burn down minor settlements rather than occupy them, and taking a provincial capital means the whole province automatically flips to them, but the reverse would be true when any faction was at war with a Chaos faction. You could go even further granular, like Bretonnian factions need minor settlements for their peasant economy, so occupying them really hurts, but on the flip side, each provincial capital has a Breton Lord assigned to it with a retinue of knights, so you can crush their economy, provided you can stand up to the knights. Greenskins can be a sort of inversion, where the minor settlements are their military hubs, and the provincial capitals are where they pile up their shiny things.

As it stands, the overworld of the Warhammer games is sort of set-dressing. It doesn't offer enough points of interaction. You don't ever think about specialising provinces, you just build the same buildings everywhere and any unique buildings if they come up. I want to build up my central province into my main money making centre, and I have to fight tooth and nail to defend it because its paying for my armies, and the surrounding provinces are the bulwark. You know, gameplay and all that.

2025 Review | TLDR : It will give you your money's worth of entertainment
Having played over 300h of this game, I have to recommend it, but I'll just point out Love -> Hate things about this game so you can make you own decision about it. There is much more to be said, but this is just a short review.

Love: The map is big, factions are a plenty and randomness can happen in every playthrough. The lords feel powerful. The factions feel different. Putting together armies and commanding them on the battlefields feels right.
Like: Leveling and gearing your lords gives it a slight RPG taste. The map is pretty and has some diverse zones. Some settlements have legendary building chains which give the world more flavor.
Dislike: There isn't much in terms of lore in the game - locations, lords, factions, items, faction relations, etc. are barely dipped in the rich lore from the WH universe. Item management can easily become a hassle. 
Hate: You quickly arrive at a lack of diversity in making decisions - for army composition, for leveling lords, for settlement development, etc. There is a lack of diplomacy and intrigue. The non-legendary lords feel very blank.
(Bonus) Despised: DLCs. I know it's a business model, but still - I'm still melancholic about the good old days when you unlocked factions that are in the game you've installed by playing and completing objectives, not by having to pay to unlock them. It's just not a practice that would sit right with me as a gamer. (And even so, I've bought some of the DLCs, so take that as a proof of me actually enjoying this game)

It's not a TW Shogun or Rome - it's a warhammer game. But for that it's a bit light on the wh lore you get while playing. Still you'll get plenty of hours building armies and killing other armies with them.

Ugh, hate to do this after spending literally hundreds of hours with WAR2, but it's gotta be said: quality over quantity.

The game is a mess as of WAR3.  The campaign/battle balance is all over the place, due in no small part to the fact that CA kept lathering on layers of new mechanics, races, and lords on top of an existing product.  The balance debt created by this has not been well-managed.

Take, for instance, starting out with Boris for Realms of Chaos: you start out in mountainous terrain next to completely Chaos-corrupted lands that inflict attrition penalties (until you spend 21 turns, minimum, researching a way to remove said penalty).  One of your first enemies is a large faction of Chaos Dwarves in said Chaos-corrupted land.

Now, these Dwarves do not suffer attrition penalties in your provinces, but you do in theirs.  All those terrains and rivers you have to navigate around in your province?  They go right through them via the underground.  The end result?  The most powerful enemy faction you face right out of the gate is also one that moves around your own provinces far better than you do.  They also move exponentially better in their own provinces while you suffer attrition casualties.

On top of that, by turn 20?  Y'know, one turn before you can even level the attrition playing field...  They're fielding armies with multiple pieces of artillery.  Oh, and guess what else happens just after turn 20?  That's right: Chaos incursions!


The end result feels like a haphazard, spaghetti mess that left some races in the dust while others (looking at you, Greenskin crapstacks) are horribly overtuned.  Again: quality over quantity, CA.  I get it: you wanna sell DLC.  But, uhh..  Check out the reviews of said DLC.  You're slowly killing your own rep.

[h1]Prélude[/h1]
Nous sommes le 20 septembre de l’an 2525 du Calendrier Impérial. Les rayons du divin tentent de percer les nuages, mais ceux-ci semblent ternis par les murmures du Nord, des échos diaboliques qui tentent d'influencer le petit serf que je suis. Abandonne ton champ pour satisfaire tes vices disent certains échos, tandis que d'autres me promettent connaissances et savoirs qui me permettront de devenir le paysan le plus prospère de mon petit bourg. Cette nuit encore, le vent portait des syllabes impies qu’aucun fidèle ne devrait entendre. J’ai donc ouvert mon ordinateur, mis mes écouteurs, et toutes les voix se sont éteintes, car j'étais trop concentré à jouer à [i]Warhammer Total War 3[/i].

[h1]Le jugement des images[/h1]
Certains répètent que les graphismes de ce jeu sont dépassés, presque archaïques, comme un Pentium 3, une PS1 ou une vieille tortue des Galapagos. Moi je dis qu’ils sont parfaits pour moi, car je peux faire tourner le jeu sur mon vieux coucou de PC, un engin qui a déjà vu passer plus d’un hiver. Quand je regarde les illustrations anciennes de Games Workshop, celles que l’on trouvait dans les vieux codex, j’avais ça en tête. Ce n’est pas de la haute couture technologique, mais c’est solide, efficace et fidèle à l’imagerie que j’attendais. Le moteur est peut-être vieillissant, mais comme une vieille tortue des Galapagos, il est résilient et affiche une résistance au temps avec ses effets et ses animations.

[h1]La complainte des couleurs[/h1]
Ma véritable plainte va ailleurs. Elle vise la direction artistique. Certaines factions sont magnifiquement rendues, mais d’autres me paraissent ratées. Slaanesh surtout. Trop propre, trop lisse, trop sexualisé. L’essence du dieu noir n’est pas que luxure. C’est l’excès en toutes choses, la gourmandise, l’orgueil, la cruauté raffinée, la quête insatiable. Cette richesse a été sacrifiée. J’aurais voulu retrouver l’ancienne esthétique, plus sombre, plus enracinée dans la fantasy traditionnelle. Dans l’absolu, ce n’est pas la faute de CA, mais plutôt de GW qui a voulu rendre Slaanesh, ses démons et adorateurs, des caricatures que se font les gens d’un club d’échangistes de Bangkok.

[h1]Les blessures anciennes[/h1]
Depuis le premier Total War Warhammer, l’équilibrage demeure une plaie. Certaines factions reçoivent des soins constants, d’autres restent dans l’oubli. Le temps passe et la douleur demeure. Toujours pas de porteurs de bannière non plus, alors que cette mécanique existait dans d’autres Total War et donnait un souffle unique aux armées (imaginez jouer à un Rome Total War sans [i]vexillum[/i] qui accompagne les légions).

[h1]Les Royaumes délaissés[/h1]
Nathan de la chaîne Youtube [i]The Great Book of Grudges[/i] a toujours dénigré la campagne des Royaumes du Chaos. Il s’est réjoui quand Creative Assembly a cessé de la mettre à jour. Pour moi c’était une erreur. Oui, les Empires Immortels dominent aujourd’hui, mais cette campagne plus restreinte offrait une intensité différente. Les incursions dans les royaumes des quatre dieux donnaient un souffle particulier. J’en garde une nostalgie amère. C’est, par ailleurs, une grande déception pour moi que les anciennes cartes de Warhammer Total War 1 et 2 ne soient pas disponibles dans le 3, c’est-à-dire que celles-ci ne soient pas jouables avec toutes les mises à jour disponibles jusqu’ici. J’aimerais vraiment retourner sur la carte du premier jeu et jouer l’Empire avec les unités et mécanismes qui se sont ajoutés avec le temps.

[h1]L’émerveillement intact[/h1]
Malgré tout, je ne me lasse jamais. Voir mes petits soldats et mes monstres s’affronter reste un émerveillement. Les combinaisons, les résultats imprévisibles, les campagnes toujours changeantes. Tout cela garde le jeu vivant. J’apprécie aussi le soutien des développeurs, inégal mais constant. Même si tout s’arrêtait demain avec [i]Tides of Torment[/i], je serais heureux malgré tout, car j’ai vécu des histoires inoubliables et de nombreuses autres m’attendraient encore. Le jeu a tellement de contenu qu’il est impossible de ne pas revenir tôt ou tard, comme pour d’autres jeux de ce genre, tels que [i]Crusader Kings[/i].

[h1]Confessions d’un joueur[/h1]
Je ne sais pas pourquoi j’écris ce témoignage. Il ne sera sans doute jamais lu. Mais il fallait que je le fasse. Warhammer Total War est comme une vieille marque de voiture. Certaines années sont moins glorieuses, certains modèles sont ratés, mais on reste fidèle. Parce qu’il y a une âme derrière, et surtout des souvenirs.

[h1]Le dernier chapitre[/h1]
J’ai longtemps suivi Nathan du Great Book of Grudges, puis j’ai cessé. Trop de spéculations hasardeuses, trop de certitudes jamais confirmées (Je rappelle que le gars prétendait que Khuresh et ses factions allaient être disponibles, tôt ou tard, dans le jeu, puisque Games Workshop avait créé des figurines Naga pour Blood Bowl). Aujourd’hui il parle déjà d’un Total War 40k. Pour moi, je clos les Warhammer Total War et, dans une plus grande mesure, les Total War. Ce genre de jeu demande un investissement financier trop lourd pour moi.

Alors je rends grâce. Ce fut une aventure entière. Je l’ai adorée malgré les défauts, malgré les égarements de Creative Assembly, malgré les DLC parfois décevants. Je ferme ce chapitre avec gratitude. Car Warhammer Total War III n’a pas été qu’un jeu. Ce fut une croisade, une fresque et un morceau de vie.

It's not much different from its predecessors and I really like all the different factions that are now available across 3 games (retroactively, if you own warhammer 1 and 2). I love being able to mash different units together in an army and see how they work together.

Sadly there's also ALOT of DLC that block only 1 or 3 Legendary lords. The prices don't really match what you get though IMO. Yes I've bought many of them, and I enjoy the content; But even I have foregone buying some of the recent ones because it's just not quite worth the cost. But if you can get all three base games on sale, I'd recommend it if you're really interested. You get plenty of whole factions to choose from and it's a bargain. It's worth mentioning that nowadays I exclusively play Immortal Empires which uses ALL factions across all three games. If you're only playing the base game, it feels limited to me.

Overall I'd give Total War:Warhammer 3 a 9/10 WITH the other two games atleast. But standalone? Probably a 6/10 honestly- it just feels a bit lacking without havin more options or bein able to fight all the different enemies in Immortal Empires.

For a long time I simply ignored this Warhammer Total War trilogy, due to the prejudice of it being a fantasy game and not another of the incredible historical titles. In the last Steam promotion that they had, I thought why not, and now I can say with certainty that I do recommend this trilogy that culminated with Warhammer III, and I can also say that I regret not having started playing sooner.

The game has a LOT of content (of course, buying the other two previous games), around 24 "factions", and they all play differently (not only the units, but mechanically), which gives you hundreds of hours of gaming easily. It has an introductory campaign and then a story campaign, both very interesting, a little on track but because it is about following a story really, and even that varies depending on the "faction" you choose to play the campaign.

But the best of the game really is the Immortal Empires campaign. It`s a massive map (the biggest of any total war game) that is alot more sandbox and you can play with any of the 24 "factions" and also different Legendary Lords to guide that faction too. I'm starting an Immortal Empires campaign, after having completed the introductory and story campaigns, and for me a strong point of the game is the AI. I'm playing on Hard (both campaign and battles) and with the two options that they added to make the AI ​​even better (on a patch), and I'm sweating over the decision making in the campaign and battles. One negative point is the sieges, but the developers themselves are aware of the problems and have even made a beta testing changes, I'm looking forward to this patch finally.

I definitely recommend this game (as well as purchasing the entire trilogy to unlock everything it has to offer), of course when there's a sale, because for those of us who arrive late there's a lot to get and the price is steep, which was better for those who followed the development of the trilogy as a whole.

And after all that said, and despite knowing that I will play hundreds of hours of this title, I can't wait for a historical title again, Empire II or Medieval III, with all the improvements that this trilogy brought to the game mechanics and AI.

Total War: WARHAMMER III nabízí rozsáhlý a propracovaný strategický zážitek zasazený do světa Warhammeru s unikátními frakcemi, bohatými mechanikami i epickými bitvami. Hra vítězí zejména díky dynamice kampaně, kde se hodní brání proti neustálé agresi zlých sil, a také díky velmi odlišným herním stylům jednotlivých frakcí s jejich originálními schopnostmi a taktikami. Možnost spojit celou trilogii do jedné mega kampaně výrazně prodlužuje zábavu a umožňuje komplexní multiplayerové i singleplayerové zážitky. Kritika zaznívá k menší variabilitě jednotek a pomalejšímu odemykání nových frakcí, stejně tak i k občasné náročnosti na hardware a absenci výraznějších inovací oproti předchozím dílům, ale celkově je WARHAMMER III považován za velmi kvalitní finále série.

Hlavní plusy
Propracovaná kampaň s dynamickou a tvrdou atmosférou, inovativní herní mechaniky frakcí

Velký obsah a možnost propojení s předchozími díly série v mega kampani

Silná atmosféra a realistické pojetí Warhammer světa s originálními postavami a událostmi

Podpora multiplayeru až pro osm hráčů s rozmanitými herními módy

Hlavní mínusy
Nižší variabilita jednotek v porovnání s předchozími díly

Pomalejší odemykání nových frakcí

Vysoké nároky na hardware a občasné problémy s optimalizací

Chybí velké inovace, hra je spíše rozšířením osvědčených vzorců než revolucí

I honestly don't care at all for the Warhammer universe. That said, this is objectively the best Total War game out there. 

★ Pros

-Huge variety of factions and unit types (fantasy setting allows way more diversity than historical TW).
-Immortal Empires campaign = gigantic sandbox, unmatched replayability.
-Amazing visuals, animations, and unit design (monsters, magic, flying units).
-Smoother performance and UI compared to older Warhammer titles.
-Better tutorials and explanations for new players than most past TW games.
-Ongoing updates and patches keep it evolving.

✘ Cons

-Campaign layer is bloated with too many systems and micro.
-AI is often dumb in diplomacy and strategy.
-Bugs and balance issues pop up more often than they should.
-Expensive DLC, not always great value.
-Less grounded strategic depth than the historical titles.
-Steep learning curve, can be a bit overwhelming at first.

Don't get me wrong, you should wait until a sale to buy the game and all the overpriced DLC, but you won't regret it. Just like any major game there are plenty of bugs and balance issues, but you won't be thinking about them when you land a sweet firestorm or comet of cassendorra and several enemy units disappear. 

Campaign Map - 

Pros - Huge, with a TON of unique locations for each faction. Portals and sea lanes that can get you moving around quicker. Each faction has unique mechanics so each play through feels fresh. Some of the more obscure mechanics can really undo any burnout you might feel - horde factions or 'secret factions' like the changer especially.  Diplomacy can occasionally prevent the whole Order vs Chaos alliances that form by the mid game. 

Cons - Agent actions are worthless, it's almost never beneficial to have agents in the field, keep them in your armies, their effects on the map are trash. I wish they would drop a buff that at least 5x their effects so you have to make a hard choice as to having them in an army or on the map. AI is pretty dumb and is compensated with cheats. Annoying but I get it, AI is hard to make. Unit recruitment mechanics are not great, buildings often serve one purpose and you have limited build slots.  Building cities up takes a veeeeery long time, so most of the time you have won the game by the time you can recruit top tier units. I would prefer a mechanic that is similar to Tomb Kings for every faction where you can recruit at least 1 tier 5 unit in every army, at the start and then you increase that capacity throughout the game. I also don't like that units dont affect the army on the map. I preferred things like in M2 where siege equipment reduced your movement range. This game could have so many things that make your armies more dynamic on the campaign map - artillery = minus movement range, cav = plus range and line of sight, flying units = plus line of sight, reduced attrition, with unique units having unique effects.

Battle Map -

Pros - magic and heros are brilliant. They aren't so amazing that without them you cannot win, but they introduce a dynamic where they are usually the most valuable assets you have so long as you have the right army to support them. The scale of the battles is ungodly sometimes. It can really give you a sense of satisfaction when you obliterate several enemy stacks with just your one army, coming out of it with a battered but victorious force. 

Cons - AI can be exploited. I don't mind the AI being bad in one place OR the other as it usually gets cheats. So an AI that gets money/ growth cheats on the campaign map will have higher tier armies than you and more of them. So I don't mind so much if they don't get cheats in the battlemap as it often leads to some huge fights that feel really hard and against you but are still possible to win.

I have been part of the Total War franchise since it's first inception with the very first Shogun: Total War. For many years it had been a precious game that I gladly put many hours into it. It was always a very welcome distraction from life if I needed a diversion, and a really enjoyable experience.

With the advent of Total War: Warhammer III and the synchronous multiplayer campaign, available for up to 8 people, I was overcome with bliss, since many a friend was made with previous multiplayer campaigns, and I wanted to bring them all together for grand multiplayer campaign.

But there were - and are - also bad times. With much grief I remember the Medieval 2 Collectors Edition, many failed patches and broken promises in several instances of different games within the franchise.

The most recent and on of the most harrowing experience has to be the broken patch 6.3.X, which rendered the AI of several important factions inoperable. This is especially bad, since I wanted to share my Total War experience with some new people, which were eager to try out this fantastic game, just to get their gaming experience wrecked because the AI in their respective starting region went kaputt and they had an abysmal first impression because of it.

I have played this game, together with its predecessor Warhammer II, more than the next 25 games in my steam library combined. Once I start a new campaign, the next week I will spend all my free time playing, logging 40/50 hours until I'm finished with that campaign and have to start speaking to friends and cleaning my house again. It's safe to say I love this game very much.

Now, does it have its downsides? It does. DLC is pricey and while you don't need all of them, it is expensive at the start, since some of them are almost necessary to be able to enjoy certain races. Also, as I'm writing this there is a whole race whose AI has not been functioning for multiple weeks, without a clear solution nearby. So, it is costly, it will take a lot of your time away and Creative Assembly is just not always doing what could be reasonably expected of them.

However, and this is the part where I will share my love for this game, the replayability of this game is huge. If you like other, historical Total War games and are open to a fantasy setting, let me tell you: it is amazing. Each race (and with all games and DLC's there are over 20, maybe 30) is a completely new experience to play. Some rely on firepower, others on magic, or monsters, or being very fast. Did I already mention there is a steampunk version of early modern Germany? There's dragons ruling China! Even some factions within these races offer a complete new experience from the others in the same race. 

I could honestly go on. Having magic as a tool for destruction, having lords that singlehandedly can destroy armies if you know what to do, conquering far away lands to build buildings to make you even more powerful. Every time I have played this, I wished I could play forever. Buy this game only if you have time to spare, and some money to spend. 

Practically: don't think you'll have to buy all DLC at once (or at all even). Youtuber Legend of Total War has a video from a while ago with DLC's and how important they are for your experience/good they are overall (search for 'DLC tier list'). It will help you analyse what you may want to start with, if you plan on buying DLC. I started with Warhammer II and slowly bought all earlier DLC (mostly on sale) once I wanted to play certain factions/races. That way you can see if its worth the investment for you.

From huge monsters, to rocket artillery, to monster powered artillery, Warhammer 3 really has it all. If you like Total War, this is probably one of the franchise's best entries.

Is Creative Assembly a good studio? Depends a bit on what you value, but I think most of us would say no. Over the last few years, corp greed has led to prioritizing new DLC content over fixing game breaking issues. Short of a full community riot, CA is very selective, slow, and quite opaque about how the feedback from the community is handled. CA has a nasty habit of gaslighting its community, reframing the narrative (so that it looks like its listening, but it actually deletes feedback it doesn't like), employing toxic PR staff, and straight up threatening to kill their games if we don't shut up and buy it.
I personally don't understand CA's problem. I don't think they actively try to antagonize the community, but it seems like that's their unique special gift nonetheless.

While it's a game that's had some great moments and is the culmination of a game trilogy I've enjoyed a lot, the state of the game right now and in many ways for the last few years has been deeply disappointing. At the moment, there's a recruitment bug that just about prevents 2 factions from making any new units, completely neutering them on the campaign map; the devs have finally acknowledged it, but dont have a clear timeline for fixing it, and have made the issue worse over the last two attempts to fix it.

More than just that though, the general campaign AI has been extremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for atleast a year or two now. Outside of the more glaring bug listed above, many factions in your game will reach a point as early as the turns 30-60s where their brains turn off, they clump all of their armies by one of their cities, and they proceed to do nothing unless you directly interact with them. This combined with the fact that new dlc lords, faction reworks, and general gameplay changes have made the game easier for years now, you really can't enjoy a challenging experience beyond the first 20-30 turns if you're experienced with the genre.

It's fine for any strategy or 4x game to reach a point of no return where you're too strong to be stopped due to the cascading effects of becoming stronger as you begin to steamroll, but the fact that the game practically starts off that way now, and there's been no meaningful effort to address the second issue listed is why i don't bother playing this anymore. I have a few thousand hours across the series, have had great times with it, and genuinely have no interest in trying the many factions/lords I've never played before, because I know the general campaign experience is going to be worse than it was 7-8 years ago when I played the 2nd game. As someone that's held off on playing a lot of those lords and factions in anticipation of the changes and improvements that the 3rd entry was supposed to bring, it's been pretty disheartening to see the series like this with no clear path towards improving in the 3 and half years since it's been out.

There have been other changes that have genuinely been better than the previous games, including allied recruitment, some aspects of diplomacy, and certain faction reworks, but I don't have any interest in experiencing them when the overall shell of the campaign is so watered down. Considering AI mods don't fully address the army clumping issue, and the overall campaign layer has been streamlined from the very start of the trilogy compared to previous Total War entries, I wouldn't recommend this game to new players at this point. Considering it's upwards of $400 to unlock everything across the trilogy, and more recent dlcs have been more expensive for less quality, I'd steer clear for the forseeable future.

Long Version:

I've loved the Total War games for years. I have hundreds of hours between Rome II, Attila, and WH3. Driving huge armies across the countryside, capturing territory and every few turns zooming out to see just how far I've come is immensely satisfying to me. Battles are also narratively enjoyable, be it grand armies clashing on the field of battle, leaving it littered with untold corpses, or a small garrison desperately defending a city from a tide of foes. Total War gives me this feeling every time.

Total War Warhammer 3 is by far the deepest of the Total War games I've played. The inclusion of magic, different races, monsters and more give an incredibly varied gameplay experience. Even outside of battle, each faction has their own mechanics, making every campaign feel (pretty) unique. You can raise hordes of the dead with the Vampire Counts, unite all of humanity under an Imperial banner, or subtly infiltrate and vassalize factions with the power of the God of Seduction.

Unfortunately, just buying the game isn't enough. To get the full experience, you will need to shill out a huge chunk of cash. Some factions are DLC only. Some mechanics are DLC only. In certain cases, (i.e. lizardmen), you need to buy 3 different DLC's in order to get access to their full roster. That level of minutiae for what are essentially microtransations for actual mechanics is psychotic. To gain access to all features, factions, and units, you need to shill out HUNDREDS of dollars (if the stuff is full price). I currently only own Warhammer 1-3 (because yes, buying the previous games is part of unlocking content), and I FEEL the difference. For most factions, I am blocked from regiments of reknown, and every faction has units I don't have access to. But the AI factions DO have access to these units many of which are VERY powerful, so not buying DLC actively makes your game worse.

Along side that, real support for this game is shoddy at best. Sure, the dev team will come out with new content every few months (which you WILL have to pay for), but the dev team is historically resistant to fixing game shattering bugs. Currently, the Lizardmen and Tomb Kings AI on the campaign map refuse to do anything, allowing them to just get rolled over by and nearby AI factions. This has severe knock-on effects for many campaigns. Say you're playing Morathi, and doing fairly well. You've consolidate the territory above Lustria, taking out the dwarven and Kislevite factions that impede on your space. Just when you're ready to take the fight to Ulthuan and finally settle a centuries long grudge with the elves, Skulltaker comes hurtling out of Lustria, WAY stronger than he's supposed to be because the entirety of the continent just rolled over and let him obliterate them.

This wouldn't be a problem if there was consistent support and communication from the development team about this kind of thing. But the devs basically REFUSE to acknowledge these sorts of issues unless a big youtuber goes viral talking abou the issue. This issue with the Lizardmen has been around for months, and was recently only made WORSE in a new update, with radio silence from the devs until a youtuber went viral talking about it. And this has happened before, with some factions being broken for the better part of a year with no communication.

All this to say, is that there is a lot of fun to be had with this game. But you won't have the full experience without putting in a lotta cash, and you can't trust the devs to not break your favorite faction and leave it to rot.

Fighting does not depend on units physical mass and hit defence ratio as in older total war games but rather on animations and hitpoint system which leads often to fights that depends on HP poll rather than tactics, so even if you flank the enemy apart from morale hit there is no advantage as soldiers in the oposing units will duel each other rather than function as a usefull formation of a unit. -If you’re new, hold off on buying until CA shows consistent commitment to fixing core problems.
-If you already own it and agree with me, let CA know you're not happy with the state of the game.
-As a community, we need to pressure CA (as we successfully did back in 2023 with the DLCs controversy). Otherwise, they may simply wait until frustration dies down without real action.

It saddens me to write this review but I've been recently motivated to write it and who knows, maybe CA will actually take some action, I can only hope. I will change this to a positive review if I see some consistent positive change. On to the actual review.

The core of the game is amazing. It's the type of game I dreamed of playing when I was a kid and it's incredible that this is pretty much the only one of its kind. You have a plethora of all kinds of fantasy races to choose from (though this is somewhat problematic, more on that below) and try to build an empire with.

The "overworld" map (or campaign map) is a turn-based affair where you recruit armies, conquer provinces, engage in diplomacy and attack/defend against enemy armies. Each race has their own unique mechanics they can use to help achieve this goal. The sheer amount of different campaigns (even campaigns within the same faction can differ quite a lot from one another) is incredible, making the replay value near-infinite.

The battles themselves are real-time and quite different compared to other traiditional RTS games in the way units on the battlefield behave: they are slow to respond to orders, they might even fail to complete an order if they are engaged in melee with another unit (or get intercepted); unit size, mass, speed, terrain and other statistics are all a factor so tactical thinking is required.

Armies are led by lords, with each campaign being led by a legendary lord (all of which are taken straight from the Warhammer lore), which can get quite powerful as they level up and gain access to more skills.

All of this is great and makes for great fun, so if I like the game so much, why can I not recommend it?

Well, it basically comes down to two issues as I see them: the DLC model and the fact that CA doesn't seem to work hard enough fixing critical bugs.

The DLC issue is basically this: if you just buy this (the third entry) base game with no DLC, the only factions you'll have complete access to (I think, I can't really check to confirm) are Slaanesh and Legion of Chaos, neither of which have had any DLC released for them yet, and I think Be'Lakor's campaign (I think you have access to all Warriors of Chaos units but only Be'Lakor as legendary lord). For everything else (including the iconic Empire), you need to own DLC. The issue is that some of that DLC is the entire base game, let me explain in detail.

Take the Empire for example. In order to play Karl Franz's campaign (you know, the wielder of the titular warhammer), you need to own the first game in the series. It serves as an Empire DLC pack for the third game essentially. Problem is, there are three more DLCs for the Empire, and on top of that the base game itself still costs $60 or your regional equivalent. Why does this matter? Well, I can live without a legendary lord's campaign, but all of these DLC packs contain units that then become available to the entire faction, without which some factions feel crippled (just try playing base Skaven, half of their roster is locked behind DLC). A lot of these DLCs I don't even buy for the legendary lords' campaigns but just to get access to the units.

Now, to be fair here, this game's legacy stretches back almost an entire decade, of course it's going to have a huge backlog of DLCs. While this is true, and certainly has brought a lot of new life to the game, the business model makes the game incredibly inaccessible to new players. I don't need to imagine what it feels like to start up a campaign and realize that half of my roster locked behind expensive DLC. And again, to be fair, CA has revised that model a little bit to make it slightly more accessible by splitting up the DLC pack, making you able to only buy the lord pack that you are interested in. Great... why haven't they extended the same feature to all previous DLC though? We are still forced to buy Lizardmen content if we are just interested in Skaven, Dark Elf content if we are just interested in High Elf etc.

I won't belabor the second point too much. The game has bugs, a lot of them. Some of them critical to the point they break some campaigns entirely and take months to fix, things that should honestly be a hotfix. Instead, patches are mostly big content updates and are pushed out alongside new DLC packs. So if your favourite faction suddenly doesn't work, well, I guess wait for the next DLC and hope it gets fixed by then.

Both of these points used to be worse but due to community backlash, CA has extended a sort of olive branch and make some changes for the better. I like some of these changes: bug fixes seem a little more common now (though still not common enough, especially for the critical issues), the DLC business model has been changed to allow us to buy the packs piecemeal, and some races from the previous titles have been updated. Good stuff, but in order for me to actually recommend this game, I'd like to see at least some of the following changes:
[list]
[*] Make the game more accessible to new players by making some sort of new player welcome bundle, include some iconic DLCs as part of this pack to lessen the strain on the wallet that this game's sheer backlog of content exerts
[*] Retroactively split up previous games' DLC packs so that players can buy only the stuff they are interested in
[*] Lower the price for TWW 1 and 2 to that of an equivalent DLC pack, that is what they essentially are at this point (yes, I know this would be unfair to all the people who already bought the games, maybe give them some kind of free content to compensate)
[*] Make more of an effort to squash game-breaking bugs, especially ones introduced by new content updates.
[*] Keep up the updating effort for the old content (looking mostly towards Bretonnia and Norsca)
[/list]

That's it from me. In essence, I love this game, it's unique in what it does and has a near-infinite replay value. I'm basically captive audience since I bought in early and own most of the content related to it, but good luck if you're a new player and you're interested. Also, better start praying to Sigmar that the new DLC doesn't break your favourite faction. Cheers!

 Pros

[Cons]

That said, don't buy this game. Since its release, the developers have allowed numerous bugs to persist, some from day 1 and some put in years later. Some of these bugs are annoying but benign (units doing weird spirals and breaking out of formation when being directed to move, single entities running around other single entities and never actually attacking, as they have been ordered to), some of them are outright beneficial to the player if they want to take advantage (Kairos' infinite Winds of Magic, several diplomacy-based bugs, etc) and others are gamebreakingly bad. 

Right now, Lizardmen and Tomb Kings are busted. Their major lords will take maybe a couple settlements. Conquer their first province. Then they just sit there. Endlessly waiting for the End Times to be upon them. Frequently they'll be overrun and wiped out by the first faction that encounters them. Oxyotl doesn't get detected by Kairos, so instead Kairos goes north and takes out Kroq'gar and Tiktak'to as they passively and nervously watch their clocks hoping the Great Plan comes to fruition before turn 20 when they get taken out. 

This is a game where a giant mammoth covered in spear-flinging northmen can charge a defensive line of zombies while fire rains from above. It's a game where a dwarven gun-line can be tested against the might of some ferociously hungry ogres as Ride of the Valkyries plays in your head. 

Ever want to see a bunch of meth addicted rats fire machine guns at a dragon? 

I wish I could say this was the game to do those things in, but for now I recommend skipping the title entirely. Sega won't let CA make this game into the incredible work of art it could be, and you as a player deserve better than what can be offered right now.

Total War: Warhammer III is a phenomenal conclusion to Creative Assembly’s fantasy trilogy. It takes everything great about the previous games and turns it up to eleven — massive battles, deep strategy, and an incredible variety of factions that all feel unique.

The Immortal Empires campaign is the true crown jewel: a gigantic sandbox that unites all races and regions from the series into one epic map. Every campaign feels fresh, and the mix of diplomacy, conquest, and chaos corruption keeps you constantly adapting your strategy.

Visually, the game is stunning. From the icy wastes of Kislev to the daemonic realms of Chaos, every battlefield bursts with detail and atmosphere. The soundtrack and voice acting add to the immersion, giving every faction its own identity and flair.

Performance and balance have improved a lot since launch, and the constant updates show how much care the developers still put into the game. Whether you’re a long-time Total War fan or just love fantasy worlds, Warhammer III offers endless hours of fun and tactical depth.

Simply put: Total War: Warhammer III is the ultimate fantasy strategy experience — epic, challenging, and endlessly replayable.

I've held off writing a review on this game for a long time.  There was no question that it felt disappointing and strangely empty when it was first released.  But a lot of work has gone into it and it's quietly become much closer now to the game which I hoped it would be.  The huge map has filled in, to the point where it now feels almost crowded.
There are some bugs and there is a lot of DLC to buy, if you want to experience the full extent of the variety possible.
But all that DLC I bought for WH1, WH2 - all work here as well.
Realms of Chaos campaign is underwhelming but IE means you don't have to ever consider playing it, so I don't give it a second thought.  I'd have no issue if that just became abandonware and any future development of factions didn't bother integrating into that if it made development of new factions quicker and simpler.

I've been playing a number of the older historical TW games recently, which I always loved.  But I keep catching myself thinking of the crazy things I could do against the odds in TW WH3, with the magic and monsters - developing characters in ways that meaningfully impact your power rather than a little +5% here and there.  High level units are not just basic ones with better stats, they offer whole new opportunities for mischief on the battlefield.

Mostly though, it's the variety of the different factions - technology, magic, faction mechanics, economy drivers etc.  Brettonia is not just a re-skin of The Empire, but with more horses.  Kislev isn't just another generic human faction but with added bears.  The mechanics on the strategy map offer choice and interest.  The developers are not squashing the fun of players who build broken armies quite as much in the name of balance.

There's still a few bugs and issues, but there's been a move to much higher quality DLC recently, more engagement from the developers, and I've got a sense that the game isn't just being dropped.

WH2 in its end state was such a well developed and fun game, that when WH3 was released without hitting that same standard, it caused a huge amount of bitterness.  But years in now, it would be wrong not to reappraise just how far this game as come.  Who knows?  Maybe I'll go back and play WH2 again like I have with some of the other historical TWs and realise there's a lot which WH3 has done that I prefer over WH2 now, and lose a little of that nostalgia.

Smutny koniec tak wielkiego i dotychczas wspaniałego projektu jakim była próba przeniesienia Warhammera Fantasy na grę z serii Total War. Nie ma sensu opisywać tutaj samej gierki, bo jeśli widzicie tę recenzję, to widzicie też setki innych recenzji, które tego tematu się podejmują, a najpewniej i tak dobrze wiecie z jakim tytułem macie do czynienia. Natomiast to co chciałbym tu zrecenzować to jak w ramach trzeciej części pociągnięto rozwój tego projektu i do jakiego miejsca na ten moment to doprowadziło. 

Na początek, pierwsze dwa tytuły to były absolutne bangery. Owszem miały też swoje wady, bugi, pricing i ilość DLC też potrafiły powalić, ale nie było to nic wyraźnie wpływającego na ostateczną jakość gry, a samego nawału płatnych rozszerzeń można nawet jakoś bronić ze względu na ilość contentu jakie dodawały. jedno DLC wprowadzające nową frakcję dodawało do Warhammera tyle treści pod względem mechanik, jednostek itd. ile zawierały w sobie w całości dawne, historyczne Total Wary. Imperium, Krasnoludy, Zwierzoludzie różnią się od siebie tak drastycznie stylem gry, contentem itd. że wręcz nie ma to porównania do takiego Empire Total War, gdzie Rzeczpospolita od Prus różniła się tylko kolorkiem na mundurach i może dwoma unikalnymi jednostkami na krzyż.

Problem gwałtownie jednak nadszedł wraz z premierą trzeciego Warhammera, który od dnia pierwszego wykazywał się o wiele gorszymi technikaliami niż poprzedniczki w analogicznych dla nich momentach. Bugi, glitche, naprawdę skopana optymalizacja. Jeśli dobrze pamiętam to część ludzi chyba nawet nie była w stanie odpalić tej gry dopóki nie wyszła jakaś łatka. Dokonano też pewnych, kontrowersyjnych zmian w balansie i ogólnie w grze. Najbardziej rzucającą się w oczy było "ukreskówkowienie" stylu graficznego na mapie kampanii. Realistyczny, dark fantasy styl planszy strategicznej znany z poprzednich części został przekuty w coś czemu według mnie najbliżej jest do stylu graficznego z Cywilizacji VI - prostsza, pastelowa paleta barw, mniej realistyczne, prostsze modele itp. Dlaczego to zrobiono? Czy pozwala to na jakąś lepszą optymalizację i tak już olbrzymiej mapy? Może, nie wiem. Za to wiem, że wygląda to dziwnie, zwłaszcza jeśli weźmiemy pod uwagę, że wszystko inne, w tym bitwy są dalej utrzymane w starym stylu.

Bylibyśmy szczęśliwcami, gdyby jednak problemy z nowym Warhammerem ograniczyły się tylko do powyższych kwestii. Ale niestety ktoś na górze w CA lub Sedze zadecydował o tym, że już nie warto dalej bawić się w rozwój tego projektu, tylko wycisnąć z niego co się tylko da przy jak najmniejszym koszcie i pójść dalej. Po premierze obcięto zasoby ekipie odpowiedzialnej za rozwój Warhammera i przeniesiono go do mniejszego i mniej doświadczonego studia w Sofii. Zmodyfikowano też politykę DLC (na gorsze, a co). Tak jak wcześniej mieliśmy 2 rodzaje DLC, mniejsze wprowadzające po 2 legendarnych lordów z ich własnymi frakcjami, nowymi jednostkami itd. w obrębie będącej już w grze rasy oraz większe wprowadzające całkowicie nową rasę z 4 legendarnymi lordami i ich frakcjami, tak teraz rozbito mniejsze DLC na osobne dla każdego legendarnego lorda, oczywiście ceny już nie rozbito, więc de facto koszt treści wcześniej sprzedawanej jako to mniejsze DLC teraz wzrósł dwu lub trzykrotnie, a twórcy jeszcze bezczelnie piszczą, że to jest oszczędniejsze, bo możesz sobie wybrać content jakim konkretnie jesteś zainteresowany bez kupowania go od razu ze zbędną dla ciebie zawartością. Z kolei przy dużym DLC podniosła się cena, ale za to spadła jakość i ilość zawartości, gdyż w ostatnim dużym DLC dodającym do gry Krasnoludy Chaosu nie mamy już 4 lordów tylko 3. Spadła też ilość darmowego contentu wydawanego przy premierach DLC i dużych akutalizacjach - w jedynce dostaliśmy za darmo całą rasę (Bretonia), w dwójce kilku legendarnych lordów, tutaj od premiery w 2022 wleciał jeden lord z grywalną frakcją i parę pomniejszych pierdół, które równie dobrze mogłyby być dodane do gry jako część jakiejś aktualizacji. Dodawany content też coraz bardziej odstaje jakościowo, negatywnie wpływa na balans rozgrywki i jest niedorobiony. Przykład? Nowa frakcja krasnali z jednego z ostatnich DLC została wstawiona w miejsce istniejącej wcześniej, generycznej frakcji AI. Ktoś w CA podmienił startowe terytorium tej frakcji na nową, ale już zapomniał o wywaleniu jej ze skryptów. Więc gra zachowuje się tak jakby tamta również dalej istniała i może np. doprowadzić do buntu tej frakcji na naszym startowym terytorium itp. mimo że jej oficjalnie w grze już nie ma.

Jakby tego było mało skrajnie wydłużył się czas pomiędzy aktualizacjami, podobnie jak przy DLC spadła ich jakość przez co doszło do tak absurdalnej sytuacji, że czekamy przez grube miesiące na zwykłą aktualizację, która po drodze zostaje jeszcze opóźniona, a na końcu okazuje się, że na każde dwie naprawione rzeczy psuje trzecią i to nie byle jaką, np. teraz popsuli AI części frakcji, które od ostatniego patcha AFKują przez całą grę, ale spokojnie, zostanie to naprawione w aktualizacji 7.0 za kilka miesięcy. Wisienką na torcie są community managerowie i inni pijarowcy studia, którzy nie radzą sobie z tym i ze "spoko gości" morfują coraz częściej w korposzczurków podirytowanych tym, że gracze (i ich klienci) śmią coś śmieć zamiast grzecznie wydawać kasę na kolejny bubel.

I żeby nie było, aktualny stan Warhammera nie wynika tylko z chciwości firmy i zbyt małych zasobów przeznaczanych na rozwój. Sami devowie odpowiedzialni za grę też ewidentnie sobie nie radzą, nie czują tego co chcą gracze i poruszają się trochę jak dzieci we mgle. Aktualnie w becie znajduje się rework oblężeń, z którego w pierwszej iteracji usunięto całkowicie z gry drabiny oblężnicze (coś absurdalnego) i przywrócono je w nowej formie po "feedbacku" (czyt. community ich opieprzyło za tę głupotę). A zrobili tak wstępnie najprawdopodobniej dlatego, że łatwiej im było wywalić z gry istniejący content zamiast go modyfikować by do niej lepiej pasował. I takich rzeczy jest mnóstwo. W jedynce obecny był system, który podmieniał skiny miast na mapie kampanii by pasował wizualnie do rasy, która kontroluje teren. Z czasem nikomu nie chciało się go aktualizować, więc wyleciał i społeczności sprzedano kit, że się nie da. Jakiś czas później wyszedł mod zrobiony przez jedną osobę, która tę drobną rzecz przywraca w całości. Podobnie modderzy musieli załatwić problem tymczasowych fortyfikacji, które gracz może stawiać na mapie, gdy broni się podczas oblężenia, a wyglądały tak samo niezależnie od frakcji i kompletnie nie pasowały do niczego - ras, map na których rozgrywały się bitwy itd. Gracze prosili o to od samego początku i gdyby sami sobie tego nie ogarnęli to nie byłoby tego dalej. Podobnie jest też z Southlandsami, frakcją, o którą nawet w formie płatnego DLC gracze błagają jeszcze od czasów jedynki. Z jakiegoś powodu twórcy nie chcą tego zrobić jednocześnie tłumacząc się, że to wynika z ich praw do marki i współpracy z oryginalnym właścicielem, tyle że w międzyczasie zdążyli oni stworzyć praktycznie od zera, dwie nowe frakcje Kataj i Wybrzeże Wampirów oraz zreworkować kompletnie trzecią - Kislev. Za to dzięki wyciekom wiemy co nas jeszcze czeka zanim Warhammer 3 zostanie porzucony ostatecznie, a w tym DLC dotyczące End Times, czyli wydarzenia znienawidzonego przez większość fanów Warhammera Fantasy i zarazem sporą część graczy i potencjalnych klientów oraz kilku legendarnych lordów w tym jeden bazowany na Wukongu, bo wiadomo chińska małpa z mieczem jest ostatnio popularna w gierkowie, więc trzeba ją skapitalizować też i tutaj. First of all, if a player uses any of the unique mechanics of their faction, they are effectively cheating because the AI is not even programmed to use or take advantage of these mechanics in the first place. It might be because the CA, the company responsible for this game, decided it's too costly to program the AI properly to use said mechanics and the benefits would have been too small or they realised these mechanics would have been too annoying to deal with for the player. In any case, this just gives the player an illusion that they are "winning" or playing well, when in fact, the AI is simply hampered from the beginning as a game design. Very disingenuous approach.

Las mejores campañas que he jugado han sido gracias a los mods. Algunos solo añaden mejoras visuales opcionales, pero otros —con cambios mínimos— transforman por completo la experiencia: mejores guarniciones, climas dinámicos, íconos de edificios que evolucionan, o interfaces personalizadas para cada facción. Además, la inteligencia artificial sigue siendo el punto más débil. Hoy en día, facciones como los Reyes Funerarios o los Hombres Lagarto están prácticamente rotas: su IA no reacciona, no expande, no representa un desafío. La única manera de hacer el juego realmente difícil es mediante ajustes artificiales, como aumentar las estadísticas de las unidades enemigas o acelerar su reclutamiento.

En resumen, Warhammer III es un juego increíble, pero incompleto. Su comunidad modder lo mantiene vivo, y eso dice mucho: el amor de los jugadores suple las carencias de sus desarrolladores.

I can't recommend this game to new players at this time. 
 
Firstly, the DLC methodology for the series is a nightmare for new players. 

If you want to play the full game, with access to all units and playable factions, you must buy all the DLC from TWWH1 and TWWH2. 

As of writing this, during the Steam Fall sale, the DLC come to a total of 172.56 USD. This is with most of the TWWH1 and TWWH2 DLC at 50% off, and all the TWWH3 DLC at 25% off. That's an absurd paywall to overcome. 

Of course, you could argue that you can just buy the base game, get the free DLCs, and play with those, and if you like the game enough purchase the DLC piecemeal as you play. This approach, however, has it's own problems, namely that many factions will be missing large chunks of their unit roster. 

Secondly, this game is one of the buggiest that I've seen get Mostly Positive reviews. Creative Assembly has a habit of not only introducing new game breaking bugs with every patch, but also a habit of being unable to fix said bugs for months. There have been many occasions where bugs that were introduced and fixed in TWWH1 or TWWH2 have been re-introduced into TWWH3, and then left for weeks. There is currently a bug with many entire races where the AI will essentially not play the game as expected, basically just sitting in their province and doing nothing. This has been present for nearly a month at this point, with no fix.

Thirdly, the AI of the game has somehow gotten worse and worse over time. The AI behaves in an incredibly frustrating way on the campaign map, with anti-player bias so extreme that they will travel 1/4 of the way across the world, ignore all other enemies and objectives, just to assault the player with all of their armies. When the enemy AI is on the defensive, it will avoid all armies that it believes it cannot beat, often letting the player take key settlements, while using it's army to only attack and destroy or occupy random meaningless settlements that the player possesses. On the battle field itself, the AI can struggle immensely, often doing ridiculous things like sending non-ranged ground based units chasing after flying units. They can be easily manipulated into terrible positions that the player can then abuse. The worst part is that because of the anti-player bias explained above, and the overall cheats/buffs that the AI gets, the player often has to resort to this type of cheese to win battles, due to nearly always being incredibly outnumbered. 

Lastly, power creep has been a real issue for the game, and looks to continue to be so. Some older factions (Bretonnia, for example) have been left far behind in the dust. New factions come with absurdly overtuned mechanics and units on release. Also, what would have arguably been the "flagship" faction for TWWH3, The Demons of Chaos faction, is an absolute joke of a faction, with a meme of a Legendary Lord. 

All in all, I can't recommend this game, and I'm not hopeful looking forward at the new Tides of Torment DLC, nor the rumored Total War Warhammer 40K game that is on the far horizon.

 But at some stage before this game even released Creative Assembly took a bad left turn and they have been taking such turns ever since. 

The Souls race campaign, which was designed for people who did not have the previous games should never have been developed. Immortal Empires should have been free to all players from day one. Whilst I believe they eventually did this after much pressure from the community CA ignored all advice from early access users on this and spent tons of time producing poor content that almost nobody plays now and yet is eating up room on all of our computers. It also took time away from other areas of the game, at a critical time in the games life cycle, that they could have made better 

They managed to take the worst aspect of Warhammer 2, the Sieges, and make this worse with the AI incapable of  knowing what to do almost at any stage whilst defending. 

The underlying engine for the game is in serious need of change, with the base code being 15 years old or more now 

Most of the DLC for this game are more known for memes regarding the bad business practices and mistakes CA made at the time, than for any quality of the DLC itself.

The current bug for the Lizardmen/Tomb Kings has been ongoing for almost as long now, initial reports of this was months ago. How they are not taking this seriously is beyond me. 

Finally, it feels like they are already starting the process of killing off this series, when it still had potential. At its glory this series (in warhammer 2) were getting 3 strong DLCs per year, all with lots of content, a 3rd of the price of one DLC now. I think we have only had 1 DLC so far this year which I have barely played out of apathy and I am not even confident the next DLC will come out in 2025.

The Dark Elves, Lizardmen, Norsca and other factions are in need of a full rework. 

I will also not be surprised if we do not get a proper end times send off (I am already imagining CA will handle this like they handled the end of 3 Kingdoms) 

So not only do many of us think that this game is not in a great place now, it has been in several terrible places since launch and I have no confidence it will be in a good place when the final DLC drops.

For a time this series was amazing despite its faults, but CA has ripped all enjoyment out of me and for that reason, I simply cannot in good faith, recommend this game unless the company behind it, gets its act together

Great concept with a lot of potential, and the parts of the game that are working as intended are phenomenally well done.
Sadly all of this is overshadowed by the machinery of greed, driven by a shortsighted, selfish, and hostile company, that abuses it's near monopoly of power in this genre. Creative Assembly has a history of publishing unfinished products (regardless if it's standalone titles, DLCs or patches), downplaying and outright ridiculing player concerns or feedback, making empty promises, and abandoning their own products as soon as the next cash cow appears on the horizon.
I cannot give a full, extensive list of shortcomings and betrayal of consumer trust, because that would need more time than I am willing to invest in this review, and would most certainly exceed the character limit. But just to name a few examples: they ignored a bug that disabled factions mechanics and the ability to recruit core units for a major faction for over 8 months; they have several engine bugs that can softlock siege battles that have been in the game since release; they have 7 major factions, some of them paid DLC factions, that have their campaign AI lobotomized for months now, and the last 3 patches not only did nothing to fix them, but made it worse to the point where they just stay idle and do nothing most of the time.
I cannot recommend investing money in this game or it's DLCs, nor any game developed by Creative Assembly.

CA's support for their flagship titles - in particular bug fixes - has a long, LONG record of being appalling, and their attitude to their community has been poor. Until they change their attitude and demonstrate long-term commitment to bugfixing as well as a respectful and positive rather than grudging attitude towards the people that keep the lights on at their studio - i.e. their customers - I cannot recommend this or any future game that they publish. There are plenty of other companies that are fully capable of achieving this - one particular example being Paradox with their Age of Wonders-series. It is not a tall order, it is fully achievable. We are not asking too much of CA - just the bare minimum a company must achieve to have long-term success. Make a good product, maintain it well, treat your customers well. Right now, they're inconsistent in the first, and consistently poor in points 2 and 3.

$494.19. That is how much a new player would have to spend to unlock 100% of the content for this game. As of writing, almost everything is on sale, which brings the price down to ONLY $190.81. And what does this hypothetical new player get for forking over this much cash? 

They get a game that they could, in theory, spend a lot of time in. A game with a vast amount of factions, each with their own unique leaders, units, and mechanics, all set in a massive, ever-changing world. No two games will ever be the same, even while playing the same faction.

What they may begin to notice, however, is how many of these "unique" mechanics are recycled from other factions. That some leaders are downright unplayable, and that the A.I. for some races is completely nonfunctional. When it is functional, they may also notice how much the A.I. cheats in outrageous fashion.

Personally, I thought the pros outweighed the cons, for a while. Creative Assembly made gradual progress on improving the game and touching up areas that desperately needed some love. But with every new patch came new bugs that were not fixed, and for the longest time I didn't care too much, because they did not seem significant. Yet CA continues to release DLC, driving the price ever upward.

When it comes to maintaining the overall health of a game, including identifying and fixing bugs, reworking old mechanics, optimization, etc., the expectations for quality and diligence should scale along with the price. If this was the passion project of a little indie studio for $20, the current lack of diligence could be forgiven. But this is Creative Assembly and SEGA asking for almost $500 for 100% access. We should be demanding perfection.

It would be easy to say that the reason for the perpetual existence of bugs in this game is the result of it's scope outstripping the capabilities of the game's developers. The continual release of DLC, however, proves to me that they do not care, and only seek to squeeze as much money out of this game as possible. 

I have already spent my money, so I will continue to play the game. But I can not, in good conscience, recommend this game to new players, unless you are the type that has an absurd amount of disposable income. But at that point, I'd imagine you would have better things to spend your money on anyway.

First off I would like to start this review by saying that the highs of this game are very...VERY good.  The problem is all the rest...

1.Main point of contention, the price tag.  Granted there is a LOT of work going into this game and getting everything functional so to a point its to be expected.  But to access ALL of the content/gameplay you are going to coughing up a solid chunk of your paycheck (if you have a high paying job) if not several.  It goes on sale off and on but the most recent DLC's are still going to be fairly pricey and even if you just focus on one or two factions it can add up.  If you're like me and you don't have a lot of spare time to dump on this game, or you get bored and take breaks frequently then you're not going to get your money's worth and should probably pick a different game.  I might have a lot of hours in this game but that's because I've been playing it since nearly the beginning, and to give an idea of how the pricing has changed the majority of what I've spent on this game has very likely been towards the end which is partially what's burning me out on it.  What I spend vs. what I get just hasn't been worth it especially compared to other games.

2.Speaking of factions this is the next issue, imbalance.  There are some factions that have been given absolutely AMAZING treatment, but there are also others that get shafted consistently and are virtually forgotten.  While I hesitate to call it an "ironic resemblance" you can compare this to the tabletop this videogame is based off of where the high demand factions get glazed and the more niche ones often get left in the mud for years at a time.  This is not a game where you can expect to gain the same enjoyment from every faction.  Some, especially whichever DLC faction they're trying to sell at the time, are going to be utterly busted to the point of being broken in a giant perpetual game of powercreep that will likely only end when this game finally ends.  Even within the factions internal imbalance can become a clear problem.  Certain lords and subfactions of the major faction will be obviously better choices than others, with some lords in particular having the most braindead easy start in comparison to another one which is hardmode but in a way that's just utterly frustrating more than anything.  The cheats that the AI gets don't help with this.  They are hardwired to beeline it for the player even if they're getting steamrolled by another AI.  They will literally prioritize your death over their own survival.  This gets particularly annoying especially when you're not at war with anyone and trying to focus on your own issues.  The game is practically guaranteed to pick one AI that you have slightly lowish or neutral relations with to suddenly declare war on you and crank out as many armies as they can (which can be alot since they get cheats) to bumrush through your territory like crazy.  Again, their actions are not designed to make sense for their faction either thematically or logically...they are programmed to make your life difficult in the laziest manner possible.  They are not particularly clever or intelligent either.  They will generally spam whichever units their settlements can produce and do the functional equivalent of an A-move in your direction.  If you're ready for them and know how to deal with them this is a trivial annoyance.  If you're dealing with another problem then it can vary between sucking all the momentum out of your progress and forcing you into complete survival mode, vs. crippling/ending your campaign and forcing you to either savescum or start again.  For a game about war, the most common joy for the average player will be when the onslaught finally ends rather than the actual fighting part (which is frustrating and repetitive).  The final issue with imbalance is just that...especially on harder difficulties...there is a "right" way to play and a "wrong" way to play.  Melee infantry is typically useless with some exceptions, missile factions are strong to busted but require attentive micro/macro, and the most optimal strategy by far is to either load up your armies with heroes and monsters, slap in something that can heal them, and A-move towards your enemies while having points in the blue tree to help you ambush and lightning strike which can completely trivialize everything.  There are traits for your lords and heroes that are utterly useless to point of making you question why you would even have them in the game.  This applies to units as well, some are just things you should never recruit unless you want to frustrate yourself struggling to make them work.  As I said earlier this is a big game with a lot of moving parts so to some degree it's understandable, but it is also an extremely constant issue.  Once you get good enough at this game you will find the optimal way to play, spend the first 20-50ish turns setting yourself up for success, and then if you know what you're doing you will be absolutely unstoppable and no amount of late game crisis's can do more than put a speedbump in your way.  Basically...once you learn it the game gets old real fast and can lose a lot of its magic especially if you're only interested in one or two factions (and again if you want variety be prepared to empty a decent chunk of your bank account).

3.Lastly and by far the most egregious problem is the company itself Creative Assembly.  Now I get it, we all know that major gaming companies can be greedy and stuck up even on the best of days.  CA isn't even the worst, but we also know how low the bar has gotten so that's not saying much.  During one particular DLC it got so bad that they threatened to pull the plug on the game entirely if people didn't cough up that sweet sweet preorder cash.  In the end the community clapped back hard enough to make them see reality but it's a continuous sisyphean struggle to get them to change their mind.  This is the primary source of the game's issues (the ones I complained about before), their arrogance and disconnect from the fandom which has very consistent and reasonable complaints for the game (siege battles being a number one complaint, AI bias being another)  that will often get ignored for YEARS so they can focus on other issues.  Any bug that helps the player will get patched instantly, anything that hurts the player stays.  As usual the rumor mill points to this being less the fault of the developers themselves and more so middle management being their typical gaslighting, disconnected, "My only concern is justifying my paycheck to my immediate bosses" selves.  There's also the problem that this game is old, they are moving onto other games, and how much they continue to support this one is largely determined by how much cash they think they can squeeze out of it.  To put it bluntly, they are slow to fix problems, quick to dismiss, divorced from reality, have a long LONG record of being this way to their fans (so they're not getting any better), and really only act when fans ON MASS force them to react.  The entire point of this review is not only to warn newer players what they're getting into, but also to try to hold this company accountable for the various bugs and problems.  People who work for the company and desperately want this game to succeed have even said that mixed to negative reviews are the only things that will affect their boss' behavior.  The reason I'm bringing these issues up is because like I said, the HIGH's of this game are utterly amazing and I desperately want it to not only succeed, but be a solid stepping stone for more games in the total war franchise.  I have paid a LOT of money for this game and will gladly pay more if I can be sure that I'm getting my money's worth.  I want this game, this franchise, and even this company to succeed and will happily change my review if they change their behavior.  Until then however, I cannot recommend this game.  Save your money.
