Jumping on the bandwagon to give a big thumbs down to my favorite game franchise. Creative Assembly rightfully deserves the negative criticism that is flooding them right now. Game 1 was a pretty decent run, and then Game 2 had a rough start with the code branching fiasco (which happened again), but by the end of game 2, it was in an excellent state.

Game 3 has been a PR and development nightmare. 
The release was crap. Between game 1 and 2 they had the issue where their development branches diverged from each other. This caused issues that they had to basically resolve by rewriting the code into a living branch, and they promised that they would do better so it wouldn't happen again. It is clear that on release, Game 3 did not include a large number of recently added QoL updates that were put into Game 2. So they lied. 

Realms of Chaos: A good concept, but nobody really asked for it, and it was just something to tide people over until Immortal Empires was released so people could play with all the factions. The resources would probably have better been used for releasing with Immortal Empires itself. What is probably saddest though, is that they spent all the resources creating the campaign and the individual chaos realms, but they couldn't be bothered to add those to the Immortal Empires map so you could have a similar experience with other races. Sure, it might not have been as polished as the initial races, but game 3 didn't come polished. It needed to be repaired after release.

Siege Rework: I don't think the siege rework was very good. New maps that aren't just walls are pretty nice, yeah, but turning the siege defense into a tower defense game was a bad move. Sieges in the current state of the game are still pretty bad. Walls are very difficult to hold due to siege towers and ass-ladders. What is supposed to be a very serious defensive tool is a meme that most people ignore. It's better to hold the city choke points than to stay on the walls where you'll get waylaid. Hopefully the new siege rework when it comes will improve things with the removal of ass ladders. 

Shadows of Change: They moved to increase the price of lord pack DLC by a significant margin. The original Grim & Grave DLC was around $9 for 2 lords, some new units, and their mechanics. With the new DLC system of 3 lords, each lord pack costs $9, more than double the cost for a single lord, albeit there is a discount if you buy the whole bundle for a 3-lord DLC together. Shadows of Change was not worth the cost, it is probably the lowest quality DLC that released for WH3. It's pretty sad considering the Chaos Dwarf DLC was one of the best with a great race, great mechanics, and all accepted even though the price was so high.

DLC Schedule: 2025 was supposed to be the year of Total War. As of yet, we have had 0 DLC releases this year. The last DLC was December of 2024. There have been some QoL updates, but it seems that at this point the current engine has since lived past its usefulness. DLC comes out and causes game-breaking bugs, I don't play WH3 as much as I used to, but it is somewhat disappointing that the schedule of DLC releases has been so few and far between to getting more content for races that need it and for other game 1 and 2 factions to receive more and even end times DLC. It's clear that they don't have many people working on the game anymore, and it shows with the pacing and quality of content. Creative Assembly seems to have already moved on from Warhammer 3. 

Hyenas: Nobody wanted this and they blew 100 million dollars on it, yet they're still making terrible choices and refuse to properly support their one solid stream of revenue that they have left: Warhammer 3. Three Kingdoms was a massive success in China, but they axed it and betrayed the Chinese audience, so there goes that money. None of the latest historical games have seemed to gain much notoriety or popularity on account of fantasy provides more cool battles and mechanics as opposed to human people army guys. I'm not anti-historical, I just think after Total War Warhammer, there's nothing left in historical games to keep my interest for more than a while. 

Bugs Bugs Bugs: The game is beyond the limit that their very old and decrepit engine can handle. Warscape Engine came out in 2009 with Empire Total War. We're at 16 years with the engine, and every time they patch the game, they manage to create a new game-breaking bug. Cavalry being unable to hit anything, Armor-Piercing Damage turned off, AI becoming braindead and unresponsive, it's very clear that the game is on hospice. Was it ambitious of them to try and shoe everything into Warscape? Yes? Does it work? Kinda. Are there problems? Absolutely. 

Although I have written this negative review, the Warhammer Total War series remains one of my favorite games of all time. I love Total War and I want the games to be good and successful. It's just becoming clear that Creative Assembly just doesn't make the decisions that are best for the franchise. With how badly they have stewarded Warhammer 3, it has eroded my faith in the company that even if they were to announce something awesome such as Total War Warhammer 40k, or Lord of the Rings, I just can't bring myself to wholly support it. There have been too many lies, too many broken promises, and too much disappointment.

Price of Entry: Total War Warhammer is an expensive game, I'm not going to sugarcoat it. I have pre-ordered almost everything since game 1, mind you here and there I waited for a sale. I have also tried to onboard multiple people into the series from scratch, and let me tell you, it is an ordeal shopping to get into the game. What games do I need? What DLC? Sure, Games 1 and 2 are easily half off if you wait for a sale, but that's still $60 on top of the game 3 price tag. I can't completely criticize CA for the price point though. Until game 3 they did a mostly good job on the game and it was usually in a good state. They put a lot of content into DLC which I can't in good faith say they should just give away for free. DLC came with free content, balance and bug fix updates, and a DLC release was usually a cause for celebration whether you paid or not, especially considering you can still fight new races and units with what you have. I think what CA should probably do is rebrand their old DLC into race packs that are cheaper and easier to digest than the old games and content. If I only want to play the Empire to give the game a try and have all the Empire content for the best experience, I have to buy Warhammer 1, Grim and Grave, Hunter and Beast, and Elspeth. At current prices  (No Sale) that comes out to be $148 including Game 3's price. This just isn't sustainable for someone who wants to try out the game. CA has made plenty of money off the older content, and should consider a system to ease the burden on new players who want to try a specific race out. It shouldn't be an $88 price tag to play one race and ignore the rest. I paid in for all the content updates and bug fixes, but not everyone has that money or was here for it. 

Sincerely, a long-time Total War fan.

As a long time fan of the Total War games and a devout follower of Warhammer, I can say that this game is the culmination of both series coming together to create a near perfect Total War experience. I would disregard the negative reviews, personally, because I believe the game to still be immensely addicting and fun for any fan of Warhammer, Total War, or 4X strategy games in general. 

The combat is unmatched by other RTS titles, but that can be said of nearly any Total War game. I am in the camp of WH3 having the most polished, extensive, and rich battle dynamics of any of the games. In my opinion, it took the best aspects of Shogun 2, Rome, and WH2, then combined them to create an immersive spectacle with so much depth and nuance. However, one thing I do miss is Naval combat from Rome. It would be very thematic to play as a Vampire Coast pirate and raid the waterways. That being said, it makes up for the lack of Naval battles with fantastic siege scenarios and a massive roster of units that can be brought in for every army. It's almost overwhelming the amount of different, fully fleshed out units you will find. Tactics are key, and besides some artillery setups, is very reliant on quick thinking. If you prefer a more casual RTS battle, you can still pause and make orders without the stress.

The campaign itself is where this game really shines. The same template from other TW games applies here, where you will begin a campaign with your favorite faction, and then suddenly 6 hours have passed and you are on turn 50. If you enjoy getting engrossed in rapid expansionism, you can do that. If you would prefer to sit back and defensively dominate foes with alliances and intrigue, you can also do that. I believe the only lacking aspect of the campaign, at least Immortal Empires, is not having multiple paths to victory. You are almost exclusively limited to the factions victory conditions you are playing, but those are varied for each faction. Not much, but they do have thematic differences.

Finally, the level of detail put into this game is unreal. Every unit feels alive and is animated beautifully. The world, models, and battle animations are unreal. Truly, the animators and artists outdid themselves. I really find myself sometimes getting lost in watching units march or battle. If you are a fan of Warhammer, you will especially love the attention to detail for each unit, as it takes heavy inspiration from the Age of Sigmar and Old World lore to portray them. Every faction and leader feels distinct and has a place in the world Immortal Empire builds.

Overall, this game captures my childhood memories of playing Shogun 2, and adds in the deep lore of Warhammer to make a truly unrivaled experience in the RTS space. 20k players mid week even in the midst of a review bombing tell the story better than I ever could. Worth the buy for any strategy fan, as well as the DLC.

I hope a toggle option to block Confederation for all factions can be added to the game settings. As it stands, massive confederations inevitably form in the mid-to-late game, swallowing all minor and sub-factions and leaving only a handful of overpowered major factions standing. This results in overly repetitive, monotonous gameplay loops.
All percentage-based income bonuses from buildings should be displayed explicitly in building tooltips. For example, the Elven Embassy grants +5% Tariff Income and +10% Port Income—players should not be forced to manually calculate the raw gold value these modifiers yield themselves.
Tariff revenue fluctuates constantly based on active Trade Agreements, cancelled trade pacts, and long-term trade partner income multipliers. It is unreasonable to require players to recalculate the exact gold gain from that 5% tariff modifier every few turns.
Enemy faction armies on the campaign map are currently able to march unimpeded alongside my armies and raid undefended backline settlements. Please implement a mechanic that either blocks enemy armies from moving through zones adjacent to friendly forces, or triggers forced Battles when enemies attempt to pass nearby player armies.
On countless occasions, I have surrounded hostile AI armies with multiple stacks on the campaign map, only for the AI to simply march past my entire army group and sack lightly defended settlements in my rear lines.
Total War: Warhammer 2 featured unique narrative intros, exclusive voice acting, and dialogue exchanges between each faction’s Legendary Lords at campaign launch. Warhammer 3 has removed all of these faction-specific story voiceovers entirely, replacing every faction’s opening narration with generic monologues from a single elder figure. All distinct faction lore and unique character dialogue has been stripped out.
While the Warhammer Total War trilogy boasts superior visuals and visual effects compared to Total War: Rome II, its campaign depth and gameplay mechanics are in many ways inferior to Rome II.
Rome II introduced engaging, strategically layered mechanics such as population tier requirements for unit recruitment and upgradable unit armor and weaponry. Dynamic campaign map weather systems and interactive wildlife animations that brought the world to life have all been removed from the Warhammer titles.
Unit recruitment has become far too simplistic and lacks strategic weight entirely. There are no population tier restrictions or secondary resource costs—players can recruit unlimited units indefinitely as long as they have gold. This strips the core strategic planning identity of the Total War series.
Confederation stands as one of the most detrimental mechanics in the franchise. Same-race factions can instantly confederate, granting the combined party full control over dozens of settlements and multiple army stacks in one action. This drastically diminishes the rewarding, gradual progression loop of expanding an empire step-by-step.
AI factions abuse confederation to snowball into overwhelming superpowers with massive armies in short order. Players are forced to rush confederation themselves or fall hopelessly behind in power balance.
Gameplay grows repetitive and stale after a moderate number of turns. Additionally, the game is bloated with excessive paid downloadable content: most factions require separate purchases, every distinct Legendary Lord is locked behind individual DLC buys, and even blood gore visual effects are sold as a separate paid add-on.
Population tier 3 and above accumulates far too slowly. High-tier landmark buildings demand prohibitively large population pools to construct and upgrade, leaving players with nothing meaningful to do in the late game aside from endlessly hitting End Turn to wait for population growth ticks.
The economy balance is equally flawed: either army upkeep costs spiral out of control to create persistent per-turn gold deficits, or income far outpaces all possible spending, leaving players hoarding massive useless gold stockpiles with no viable outlets to invest resources.
The most critical issue is the glacial growth rate of Tier 3+ population, paired with lengthy recruitment times for elite high-tier units and limited army recruitment slots. Players waste dozens of turns waiting for population to fill, units to finish training, and buildings to complete construction. These waiting phases drag down the entire campaign pace and make late-game play a tedious, repetitive slog of skipping turns.
Many factions are built around naval playstyles and can field Fleets, yet naval battles were never implemented in the trilogy. There are no ship-to-ship combat sequences, nor boarding battles between marines aboard vessels—even Rome II fully functional naval combat, a feature absent entirely from Warhammer 3.
Certain paid DLC races suffer from deeply uninspired gameplay loops, such as the Wood Elves. They are confined to defending their native forests, and can only build temporary Outposts with severely limited construction space when capturing foreign settlements.
Outposts cannot be upgraded, offer almost no economic bonuses, and feature minimal building slots. This restricts Wood Elf players from engaging in proper continental conquest and empire-building, locking them into repetitive forest defense gameplay despite being a paid DLC race.
The wide library of paid DLC factions and purchasable Legendary Lords suffer from severe mechanical homogenization. Players pay extra for new content yet receive very few unique gameplay twists to differentiate each roster.
Most Legendary Lords share overlapping core mechanics and thematic identities, leading to repetitive gameplay after multiple playthroughs. Meanwhile, factions with more unique design concepts often end up lacking engaging core loops—Wood Elves once again serve as a prime example, barred from large-scale siege conquest and confined to perpetual forest preservation.
Auto-resolve battles conclude instantaneously when two armies clash, which breaks immersion and realism. Authentic large-scale military engagements cannot be resolved in a split second with no intermediate combat duration.
When multiple army stacks are locked in a joint engagement, triggering Auto-Resolve instantly ends all fighting without any sustained combat window. This eliminates strategic opportunities for players to maneuver reinforcement stacks to aid allied forces mid-conflict on the campaign map.
Instant auto-resolve erodes the game’s strategic depth and removes the tactical planning satisfaction built around coordinating supporting armies during prolonged battles.
While the Warhammer Total War trilogy incorporates rich high-fantasy lore and a vast roster of distinct races, overly powerful Heroes, Lords, Spellcasters, and single-model units have eroded the coordinated multi-unit army tactics that defined historical Total War titles.
Hero units possess an overwhelming toolkit of devastating spells, stacked global stat buffs, and powerful unique magic items. A single Hero can easily duel entire army stacks while sustaining minimal health loss over prolonged combat.
A single high-power spell cast by a Lord or Mage can wipe massive swathes of enemy units and inflict catastrophic casualties. Legendary Lords are functionally immortal: upon defeat, they only enter temporary Wounded status and return to battle after a few turns, retaining all their equipment, permanent stat upgrades, and ability buffs.
Legendary Lords unlock escalating stat bonuses, stronger spells, and unique Legendary Items as they level up. Late-game max-level Legendary Lords can single-handedly decimate dozens of full infantry units unassisted.
This shifts the core battlefield dynamic from coordinated army maneuvering to a Hero/Lord-centric "power fantasy" system, transforming the game into a character progression grind rather than a grand strategy wargame.

Assaulted from one side by self-entitled players who want everything for nothing, and from the other by corporate managers who want to sell nothing for everything, the developers of Total War: Warhammer have somehow, against the odds, made an amazing game.

As a battlefield rank&file RTS game, nothing else on the market even comes CLOSE.  Those that try, resemble Total War's first efforts 25 years ago.  The graphics in this game are beautiful.  The battles (the key part of the game) are exciting and impacted by your tactical choices, as you give orders to each unit in real time.  The commands are easy to perform, governed mostly by mouse clicks to issue orders, and keyboard and mouse-movement to change the camera angles.

In keeping with the best previous Total War series (Rome and Medieval 2), Warhammer enjoys the MOST IMPORTANT feature such a game can have: multiple factions with different unit rosters.  This keeps the game feeling fresh, giving you a myriad of different factions to play as.  If you own all three Warhammer titles, and the race pack DLCs, you have 24 factions to choose from, and within nearly all of those factions, you have multiple Legendary Lords you can pick as your starting general, with their own unique skill trees, mechanics and/or starting locations.  The choice between Legendary Lords further adds to the feel that each option plays differently.  

For example, if you choose to play as the Chaos Dwarfs, you must then decide if you want to play as Astrogoth, a melee/spellcaster who buffs his heavy cavalry option, the bull centaurs; Drazoath, a spellcaster who gets a powerful flying monster as a mount, and buffs K'Dai molten lava daemon units, or Zhatan, a melee specialist with a different type of powerful flying monster mount, who gets an extra trade convoy and faction-wide cheaper artillery.  All three have different starting locations, with different initial enemies.  Scale that up across the factions, where every faction is very different from one another, with almost no shared units across factions, and you get the most important thing for a sandbox strategy game: REPLAYABILTY.  You'll play for hundreds, maybe thousands of hours, and still keep coming back for more!

New mechanics to Warhammer, absent from previous Total War titles, are flying units and magic spells.  In addition, the skill trees for leaders are vastly expanded upon and improved, as are the artillery piece choices.  If you're familiar with the tabletop game, you'll be ecstatic with how Total War brings them to life!  And if you're not familiar with the tabletop, or are even new to fantasy settings in general, the additional tactical options and challenges that flying units and magic bring to the battle should please rather than frustrate all but the most casual of gamers.  The developers have really paid attention to the look and feel of the Warhammer World, adopting its lore (mostly) accurately.  The game feels like it was brought to life by people who love Warhammer, and people who love Warhammer should love this game!

So why the negative reviews from so many?  Well, there's a three major reasons for that, but they stem from the corporate board rooms that pump money into the development of such games.  Understandably, the suits are not fans; they are looking for profit out of their investment.  But that has led to a number of decisions which have proven deeply unpopular among the player-base.   First, across the Total War series as a whole, there's a long history of releasing barely playable games on release, games that had fundamental problems, and several of those games were swiftly abandoned (see Rome 2, Empire, Three Kingdoms, Britannia, Troy and Pharaoh).  Sega, the overarching owner of CA, is also known for pulling titles from other developers, or pushing them into decisions that ruin the released game (Hyenas, Dawn of War 3).  But a protest vote in the form a negative review on THIS game is unfair.  Those other titles deserve to be review-bombed, Warhammer does not.

Secondly, there HAVE been issues with bugs within this game.  A lot of such issues.  None of them have been truly game-BREAKING, but a lot have made particular races or play-styles unworkable until they were patched out.  In a game this size, which now combines three base games, and numerous DLCs, it's hardly surprising that sometimes the developers break something.  But it should be remembered that they broke it while trying to offer us more content, and more content is almost always a good thing, to be encouraged from developers!  The CA PR machine, regrettably corporate in attitude, has historically heaped gaff upon gaff in their statements concerning this, ranging from throwing their toys out of the pram over negative forum posts, to trying to pass off problems as minor enough to not warrant any great attention to fixing.  In large part, the most recent negative reviews were a response to CA suggesting they would not fix a deeply unpopular bug any time soon.   That bug HAS now been fixed, but it probably would not have been for months, if ever, if CA's hand hadn't been forced by the negative reviews.  CA should reflect on that.  Game-theory it out.  Peel the onion, or whatever other wankernomic corporate-speak they use.  Or maybe listen to their blasted development team.  Revolutionary, I know.  No, not the suit you put in charge of them, go talk to the bearded weirdo who sits in front of the screen writing the damn code!  He's the ONLY ONE carrying this project for you.

Thirdly, there have been concerns about the value of particular content-pieces.  Some I sympathise with, some less so.  The single-player "narrative" campaign modes for Warhammer 2 and 3 became increasingly unpopular, leading to CA rushing out the sandbox single-player campaign modes.  Most players prefer the latter, myself included.  But CA shouldn't be lambasted for TRYING to give us an alternative set of objectives/mechanics to make the game interesting.  And, in it's current state, players can just play the sandbox, so there's really no reason to hold this against CA at all.  DLCs, on the other hand. have been extremely variable in terms of content delivered, and CA has tried to maximise the price on these, to the extent that a DLC might cost the same price as a brand new game from some other developers.  Some of the problem here is corporate greed, but some is player-tantrums.  The last new race-pack was for the Chaos Dwarfs.  It was great.  Almost universally loved.  But some bloody fans had to just moan and moan and moan about the DLC price.  They could have waited til it was on sale, of course, like reasonable players do if they think content is too pricey for them otherwise, but instead they left negative reviews, and cried about it so long and so hard that CA were probably left thinking it wasn't worth the work to make another new faction.  In between the tone-deaf PR announcements from CA, they have actually said essentially as much - "stop crying or we stop releasing".  That's not a healthy reaction, but neither is sabotaging the profitability of your most beloved game ensuring you don't get any more decent content.  Since the Chaos Dwarf release, we've had new legendary lords and units, with faction overhauls, but no new factions.  To be fair, the main factions are out already, but for those so very keen on seeing Khuresh/Ind/Monkey King/Fish People (!...I bet you like fish sticks), you probably won't now, and you can blame the players for that, not CA.

Future plans for the game include a Slaanesh faction new lord and rework, as well as the same for High Elves.  Two MAJOR legendary lords remain not-yet-in-game: Nagash and Thanquol.  I'm quite certain those are planned as part of the last update for this game.  

With all of the above said, this is a cracking game.  I wouldn't wait for it to be on sale, but it IS on sale often.  Grab a copy either way and get stuck in!

I want to begin this review by adding: the reviews on this game can be misleading as to the actual quality of the game. This is because the player base (mostly justifiably) outrages whenever a DLC leads to some kind of imbalance or bug.

In my opinion there is only one real negative to this game, that being the usual total war game issue. There are a bajillion different expansions and add-ons as the game not only has its own DLC but also can pull content from the first and second games and their respective DLC. To be fair, you can pick up the majority of this content for pennies when on sale however that does not detract from the egregious amount of content. This however is my only real negative about the game.

The positives:

1. The sheer amount of content and replayability this game has, even at its base, is absolutely mind blowing. Each campaign seriously feels like it's very own game. 

2. Immortal Empires, this is a truly insane game mode. It combines the war maps from all 3 games and drops you in a 300 faction wide slugfest. Truly an incredible game mode to play. Trying to achieve global domination with some mates is great.

3. The game is beautiful, none of that low poly RTS nonsense here. The models are beautifully rendered as are the maps and structures. If you are a Warhammer fan IRL you will be blown away by the clear amount of love that went into making these models.

4. The Total War Battle System, to this day it is easily one of my favourite RTS combat systems. Create your own massive formations and micromanage each bit. Watch out the pitched battles, I sometimes find myself zooming in just watching the battles take place.

5. The Lords, the Legendary Lords (Your main character) are phenomenal for all factions. They have great voice acting and really nail their in universe personality.

6. Unit variety is phenomenal.

7. Faction specific rules are great.

I cannot give this game enough praise, on sale you can pick it up for about a tenner (Ten Great British Pounds for my non brits) and the amount of content you get is phenomenal. (Considering that £10 in this economy hardly gets you lunch).

Meiner Ansicht nach sind viele der negativen Rezensionen deutlich überzogen. Natürlich ist es ärgerlich, wenn bekannte Fehler nicht behoben werden, da gibt es nichts schönzureden.
Aber mal ehrlich. Worüber reden wir hier eigentlich? Gerade beim Thema Preispolitik lohnt sich ein genauerer Blick, bevor man urteilt.


Man darf die Entwicklung von Total War: Warhammer nicht isoliert an den DLC-Preisen messen, sondern muss das ganze ökonomische und zeitliche Umfeld mitdenken.


Früher: kleinerer Umfang → günstiger Preis.

Jetzt: entweder größerer Umfang und höhere Preise oder gleichartiger Umfang bei höherem Preis.


Kleinere DLCs: z. B. nur ein neuer Anführer, ein paar neue Einheiten, meist für eine bestehende Fraktion. 

Größere DLCs: neue Fraktion oder Mini-Kampagne + Einheiten + ggf. eigene Mechaniken.
Der Preis war relativ niedriger – z. B. die ~17,49 € für große DLCs beim ersten Teil. 


Was passiert jetzt bzw. neuere Modelle?

Der Umfang bleibt je nach DLC unterschiedlich, aber wir sehen. Bei manchen neuen DLCs wird mehr verlangt, entweder durch mehr Inhalt oder durch höhere Preise bei ähnlichem Inhalt.

Beispiel: „Shadows of Change“ kostet ~ 25 € und beinhaltet drei neue Legendäre Lords (eine für jede von drei Fraktionen) + neue Einheiten für diese Fraktionen. 

Gleichzeitig das neue „Modell“ bei Thrones of Decay: anstatt einen großen Block, kann man einzelne Teil-Packs kaufen 8,99 € oder ein Bundle für 24.99 €. Damit soll Flexibilität geschaffen werden, damit man nur kauft, was man will. 


Zeitrahmen & Entwicklungsdauer

Warhammer I kam 2016.

Warhammer II folgte 2017.

Warhammer III erschien 2022.
Das sind also inzwischen über 9 Jahre kontinuierlicher Entwicklung innerhalb eines Universums.

Creative Assembly hat das Projekt also fast ein Jahrzehnt gepflegt – mit vielen kostenlosen Updates, Überarbeitungen älterer Fraktionen, neuen Spielsystemen, Balancing, Performance-Patches usw.
Das ist viel länger, als die meisten anderen Studios ein einzelnes Spiel betreuen.


Personalkosten (vor allem in Großbritannien, wo CA sitzt) sind in den letzten Jahren stark gestiegen.
Energie- und Serverkosten ebenso.
Auch Lizenzgebühren an Games Workshop dürften mit jeder Verlängerung oder Erweiterung angepasst worden sein.
Dazu kommt: der Markt hat sich verändert. Früher war der PC-Release der Kern, heute muss man QA, Lokalisierung, Test-Automatisierung usw. viel breiter aufstellen – das kostet.

Wenn man also 2025 einen DLC für 24,99 € verkauft, ist das inflationsbereinigt gar nicht mehr so weit entfernt von einem 17,49 €-DLC aus 2016. Nur fühlt es sich eben anders an, weil der Preis optisch höher ist.

Inhaltliche Kontinuität
Viele der großen Free Updates (z. B. Überarbeitungen alter Fraktionen, „Immortal Empires“, neue Mechaniken, Quality-of-Life-Verbesserungen) kamen kostenlos.
Das ist Entwicklungszeit, die in einem anderen Modell längst in Form kleiner DLCs verkauft worden wäre.

Wenn man das mitrechnet, dann verteilen sich die tatsächlichen Gesamtkosten pro Spieler über viele Jahre und Stunden Spielzeit.
Gerade wer die Serie seit Teil 1 begleitet, bekommt für das investierte Geld unterm Strich ein riesiges, fortlaufend gewachsenes Strategiesystem.

At nearly 1,000 hours, over 2,000 across all 3 titles, buying the DLCs (unfortunately at this point) and loving both the franchises involved in this game, I can't recommend it until the MAJOR creases get ironed out. 
Don't get me wrong, I want to love and have loved this game, but much like a campfire, sometimes you need some distance to avoid getting burned.

Big and small bugs that are not only still rampant but are coming up to a decade old are still present in some form or another. 
Understandably fixing a game that has existed over three titles and running on a now outdated engine isn't an easy task. 
I would assume that CA would have the manpower and money at this stage to at last fix something as simple as ranged units being completely schizophrenic when it comes to firing.
The over world AI bug is at least been reportedly worked on but many small issues still plague the game, ironically Skaven suffering a lot from them.

Для тех кто в танке , Паверкрип это намеренное усиление нового контента , что бы старый был не актуален, тем самым стимулируя игрока к  его покупке. Так например новый лорд, Собиратель черепов , имеет такие колоссальные статы и бафы для своей армии,  на высокой сложности,   что два стека топовых юнитов фракций из первой или второй вахи проиграют в сухую армии из среднеуровневых юнитов , и может быть если повезет с картой , где будет мост или горы с узким проходом , вы сможете заспамить стрелами и заклинаниями , и тогда хотя бы будет Пиррова победа , а половину армии вы потеряете в любом случае. For full transparency, I have played Total War games at least since Shogun 2, and went back to play Rome I (best Total War) and Medieval 2 afterwards: They are cornerstones of my taste in games; which makes reviewing this game that much harder.

Total Warhammer 3 is an uneven offering, with many glaring errors, lackluster mechanics and outright atrocious player freedom. For every neat thing in the game, two to three basic failures pop up. It gets to a point, where you wonder how a studio with so many years of notes from prior games to learn from could keep falling over themselves.

I originally intended to include the Realm of Chaos campaign into the review, but realized quickly in doing so that the main appeal of the game is Immortal Empires, so I will be focusing on that.

Key points:

The voice acting, map stylization from the lore and general presentation is outstanding. It is frankly one of the best realizations of the Fantasy setting I have ever seen, brimming with life and character. From the small things, such as flavored tech and character traits, to the grand stylings of the factions and their visual details. Looking at the factions, their units and the game itself is a visual feast. The sound must also be mentioned. Though there are shortcomings, especially from old content that is legacy from TWW1, the sound design broadly brings the warhammer setting to life, especially with its use of audio cues that makes busy battles easier to parse. There is also a world of magical items, which add a level of flavor that would have been entirely acceptable to see the studio cheap out on, but they did not, and deserve props for their inclusion.

What I cannot be so glowing on is everything else.

The map looks like ass. Instead of an easily parsible map, or an ability to simplify the terrain and give commands, TWW insists upon itself; you will look at its spanning, pointless eyesores and baubles when you just want to move a unit from one mountain range to the next, it's a genuine eyesore to keep track of units on the map.

Then again, you won't be keeping track of many units at a time, becaue Total Warhammer insists on using Rome 2 as its skeleton, meaning you only get to have units run around with generals, who will emerge from nowhere, with no family trees to speak of; which works for some factions, but for human and elven factions, is absolutely ridiculous. It heavily deincentivizes building smaller units and moving them around the map, because anything short of a full stack of units is going to be chowed down by a 20-stack ai unit and its 4 companion stacks coming out of the mist (looking at you, Vampire Counts).

Despite the studios' "best efforts" to bring legacy factions into the newer games with revised mechanics and improved gameplay experiences, they still come up painfully short. The Empire, the face of the series, has a pathetic tech "tree", which rivals Bretonnia for brief but painfully bad. Comparing these to newer factions is genuinely an effort in futility.

And these tech trees are shared amongst factions, which makes for an even worse experience. To alleviate this, each lord has a faction mechanic, which are supposed to individualize them, and in that matter, some of them are excellent: Balthasar Gelt is a fan favorite for a reason, and his colleges mechanic is a lot of fun; but then you have him go to the Empire, and you end up having to fight Nuln and Reikland to unit the EMPIRE, because Gelt doesn't get the mechanic that allows him to interact with the Prestige system; or Bordeleuax, a faction who starts flanked by the newer (see: better) faction Skulltaker with no rites to help his expansion, forcing a turtle playstyle to build up the numbers to auto resolve him to death.

On that note, auto resolve is thoroughly confused. It has never been great, but it is frankly baffling how it's supposed to take things into account, with factions such as Beastmen and Slaanesh always getting the short end of the stick, yet in battles, they rip units to shreds. It gets to the point, where in particularly annoying sessions, I have resorted to stacking trash armies to stack the auto resolve in my favor; a strategy which is near unbeatable, with the exception of the likes of the Skaven and Beastmen, who can ambush you with attacks (and ambushes are extremely fair and balanced, with units running away the moment the enemy makes contact :D) 

Battles are not that much better, with thoroughly confusing statistics like Anti-large, which counts against cavalry, but doesn't actually do well against cavalry, unless it has armour piercing, because armour is the king of stats in the game; especially in Auto-Resolve (hello Dwarves; hate you). Though it is a visual feast to see Imperial gunners rain hell on an enemy, it is thoroughly annoying to play, because the AI will do utterly foolish moves, like archers attempting to go past the defensive line to get closer to an enemy well within range (With bows, mind), or archers turning 30 degrees to the right to hit a unit on the right side of their vision cones; you can't even see the accuracy of units, with some units supposedly having poor accuracy, but nailing an opposing, accurate artillery battery with pinpoint precision. This, coupled with the ATTROCIOUS MORALE SYSTEM, which devolves into running your general in circles to keep your troops in the fight, or having your troops surround your fleeing general, it makes for an extremely unintuitive experience, and makes TWW one of the worst battle experiences in the series.

Most obvious shortcoming in battles however, is the utter lack of decent music. I have tried to find good tracks for this game; it is beyond my grasp on how you can go from Rome, Medieval and Shogun 2 to TWW, where no track stands out to me. The trailer music is more memorable, and it's not even in the game.

The game is, to be quite honest, massive, and there is a bunch of stuff I could mention, such as the map just ending in an ugly, glaringly empty world, or how the game is thoroughly unstable, requiring an SSD to even run at any acceptable rate, but any actual issues, mechanically, visually or gameplay wise, is usually (And sadly) forgiven by the fanbase at large, because no one else delivers the same style of games. The core issue at large, is that even this mediocre experience is consistently knee-capped by Creative Assembly, and their inept QA, stubborn HR, and INFLEXIBLE core team, who think themselves above us mere peasants, who dare play their darlings without their consent (talking about the game is a privilege, not a right).

For more than a decade, they have been doing the routine "we messed up; we're sorry, here's some mediocre content (you need to pay for) to make up for it". It took a youtuber calling them out (and a month's wait time) to resolve basic issues, like the AI sitting on their ass around their castles, not doing anything, whilst some AI's, such as the ogres, Beastmen, Lizardmen and Tomb Kings just decided to stop working. All the while, they want to charge INSANE prices for the same tech tree you burned through before, but this time, the reskinned hero with a different mount and one (1) unique line of powers can do something the other ones in their faction can do, but slightly better! Truly, what would we do without these ground breaking visionaries.

Even with such obvious antagonism, it would be forgivable, if the studio wasn't riding high off their own farts, whilst bullying anyone that steps out of line, to the point of studio whistleblowers having to come out to speak up on how bad the internal state of the studio is, how they actively reuse assets to sell back to the community to keep up their one (1) source of consistent income. They are so reliant on this game's DLC, they (according to rumors) cancelled internal game projects over the failure of Shadows of Change DLC.

TL;DR: Game's mediocre and the studio is cringe. Don't recommend.

Greetings!  Today, we’ll be looking at Total War Warhammer 3; what may be the last of the series that everyone seems to love and hate.  The previous title felt more like an expansion so I was concerned that this one would be more of the same.  Were my concerns well founded?  Let’s Discuss!

Stop Picking Up Strange Swords:  What…is this?  A real campaign!  My heart be still.  Finally we get a ‘real’ campaign with story and development and everything!  The first campaign is more of a tutorial but is still enjoyable to play.  Even the non-tutorial campaign is so much more of a campaign then the previous games and its one that I will even enjoy playing again with other factions.  All of this would have been amazing in the original and saved me many hours of researching how the game plays to actually play the game.

Upgrades! Yes Yes:  Okay, on to rest of the game.  The game is still TWW and most of what is added here is refinement and expansion on previous content as well as a revamp in the menus and UI.  I’ve no idea what was added after release or came stock so I can only really review the current state but I must say I’m very happy with the additions.  The tutorials are significantly better, showing little videos and explaining mechanics in smaller chunks to actually let you play the game.  A lot of quality of life upgrades too; such as inventory management actually being a thing now instead of a pile of items.  Skills are better explained and the units they affect are pictured as well.  Mounts and Immortality are now free, which is a nice upgrade as well.  And finally Siege battles now actually feel like of fun, though can still be a bit of a chore.

Tzeentch always has a Plan:  The biggest issue, from my understanding is an issue with certain factions not playing correctly at higher difficulties currently but I’m a filthy normal player so can’t really comment on that.  I do wish that all the factions had tutorials like the new ones though; I had never played the Lizardmen and learning their special mechanics would have been easier with a tutorial like what the Chaos Dwarfs got.  Same thing with a lot of the ‘raiding’ or ‘travelling’ factions, which I’ve never played either.  I did encounter something I’ve never encountered in any of the previous games…Crashes.  Most of them seemed to be around the long battles of the 4 gods in the campaign or picking up or abandoning artillery units.

I doubt anyone will read this, if you like the TWW series you’ve already got this and if you aren’t sure you’ll probably grab the first of the series.  Either way, if you do read this; the game is amazing but wait for a sale, it’s generally on a pretty deep discount.  Enjoy!

This game is probably my favorite strategy game since the old Command & Conquer games. There's an absurd amount of content, even without buying any DLCs (which you should only buy on sale since they go on heavy sale several times a year - same goes for the base game). If you own the first or second game (and/or their DLCs), you can play all those factions in this game and they don't feel just shoehorned in at all. Every campaign feels different, even if you play the same faction twice. There are lots of great difficulty settings and a very active mod community. Lots of stuff to do on every turn and it feels very rewarding to learn how the world and intricate politics of the different factions work, and to leverage game systems to your advantage. Your faction leader, race/faction mechanics, start position, political standing, and most of all your actions every turn have a huge impact on how the campaign will play out, and there are 200+ factions on the map that also impact everything. The map is also huge (if you are playing on Immortal Empires, which you should be as soon as you've learned the game basics), you could be 100 turns deep and just about to conquer your entire continent, meanwhile on the other side of the map, some faction you haven't even encountered has gotten even bigger than you. 

Sound design and music is good, graphics are good, UI is mostly good but not perfect. Achievements are pretty fun to go for with the exception of the trials of Tzeentch ones, those are such a slog (but at least not that hard). 

The game is also great to play with a friend, you can play any campaign alongside a friend who is playing another campaign in the same world. You could be on other sides of the world, fighting back to back, or going against each other, and it makes politics even more interesting because your allies and enemies probably won't line up with your friend's.  

The game runs well, but load times are really bad if you use a hard drive or an old SSD, so save yourself a lot of time and use a new-ish SSD if you have that option. There are some bugs, but I would be shocked if there were no bugs in a game where this much stuff happens every turn. The game-breaking bugs do get patched out by the devs usually pretty quickly, which unfortunately happens instead of them developing new content. CA's PR team is horrendous and Sega has a skeleton crew working on the game for some reason (seems really weird since this is CA's biggest source of revenue) so meaningful content updates come out less and less frequently, and often with delays. I'm sure this is the main reason this game is getting review-bombed right now, which is pretty valid, but I wanted to put my review here because even though the current trajectory of the game's future looks pretty bad, the game as it is is great, no if ands or buts. I too am unhappy with the bad PR and lack of work going into content updates, but I have almost 1000 hours between this game and Warhammer 2, and could easily milk out a few hundred more with just what is currently available, and that's without addressing mods, of which there are many that add quite a lot of high-quality content.

If you like Warhammer, I feel pretty confident in saying this game is richer in lore than any other Warhammer game, and it interested me enough to get me into the tabletop game and other video games. The lore is very interesting and the world always feels coherent. Most campaigns end up feeling like you're roleplaying a character or telling a story of your own making within the rich world of Warhammer fantasy. 

Overall, this game is just really good and provides a bevy of highly varied experiences. If you like complex strategy games and feeling like you're building a fantasy empire, you'll love this game. I hope CA gets its stuff together and gets more people working on the game's updates, but I doubt that will happen, but even though that makes me sad I'm still glad the game exists and is as fun as it is.

**This is a widespread Proton-specific issue in Total War: Warhammer 3 multiplayer: the Linux client's game "freezes" (often audio continues, screen stuck) precisely when the host (on Windows) finishes loading and hits "Ready"—it's a VRAM misallocation or sync failure during asset transition post-load.**

Happens due to Proton's Windows emulation struggling with the game's DX12/VRAM handling in MP load sync—native Linux avoids it but breaks cross-play.

### Quick Fixes for Linux Friend (Apply in Order—90% Success Rate)
1. **Cap In-Game Video Memory (Top Fix for Load Freezes)**
Edit the Proton config:
`~/.steam/steam/steamapps/compatdata/1142710/pfx/drive_c/users/steamuser/AppData/Roaming/The Creative Assembly/Warhammer3/scripts/preferences.script.txt`
- Find `gfx_video_memory=0` (0 = unlimited).
- Change to your VRAM in MB x1.07 (e.g., 8GB=8589934592; 12GB=12884901888). Use calculator: VRAM GB * 1073741824.
- Save, set read-only (`chmod 444`), relaunch. Forces proper allocation—no more post-load freeze.

2. **Switch to Latest Proton-GE (Better MP Stability Than Experimental)**
- Install ProtonUp-Qt (Flatpak: `flatpak install net.davidotek.pupil` or AppImage).
- Download/install GE-Proton10-12 or 10-10 (NVIDIA-friendly).
- Steam > TWW3 Properties > Compatibility > Force GE-Proton10-12.
- Launch options: `PROTON_ENABLE_WAYLAND=1 gamemoderun %command%` (fixes NVIDIA/Wayland stutters/freezes).
- Verify files after.

3. **Lower Graphics for Load Sync**
- In-game: **Texture/Unit Detail: Low/Medium**; Shadows/AA: Low/Off; VSync: Off; FPS Cap: 60 (RivaTuner or in-game).
- Tree Quality: Medium (High+ tanks Proton perf).
- Both sides: Disable mods; match DLCs exactly.

4. **Linux-Specific Tweaks**
| Issue | Launch Option Addition |
|-------|------------------------|
| **NVIDIA Freezes** | `PROTON_NO_FSYNC=1 __GL_SHADER_DISK_CACHE=1 __GL_SHADER_DISK_CACHE_PATH=/tmp %command%` |
| **AMD/Stutter** | `PROTON_USE_WINED3D=1 %command%` (fallback) |
| **RAM/Desync** | Ensure 32GB+; `gamemoderun` always. |

5. **Test & Logs**
- Host a Custom Battle (small armies); join via Steam Friends.
- If freezes: Check Linux logs (`~/.steam/steam/logs/`); Proton logs (`protontricks 1142710 winecfg` for debug). Share GPU/distro/Proton version.
- Windows side: Run as Admin; cap FPS 60; verify files.

**Both verify Steam overlays off (Steam > Settings > In-Game > Uncheck); disable antivirus.** This combo (esp. VRAM cap + GE) gets MP running smooth—users report zero freezes post-fix. If persists, ProtonDB reports confirm GE-10 series crushes it.

This is a game that I have enjoyed playing for the over 2,000 hours I've put into it.  Its been my way of being able to enjoy the world of Warhammer Fantasy on my own time, something that I cannot do with the table top version of the game.  So for that, I am grateful to Creative Assembly for providing that outlet.  

Having said that, I cannot recommend this game to anyone because it does not seem, to me, that CA has been doing a very good job of ensuring the stability of their game.  Which is a damn shame, because I have friends who have asked if they should get it so we can play together, and I've had to tell them no, due to the concern of how often I (and they) may crash.  Ever since the end of 2024, I've run into issues with my game suddenly locking up, then crashing whenever I'm moving around the campaign map, typically after turn 50+.  My understanding is that this is an issue happening across the board to a number of people, regardless of age of computer or the GPU.  And that it has been an issue that CA mentioned all of once some time early on, and I've read the patch notes for each patch that's been released since then, hoping to see that it has been addressed.  As of the posting of this review, I have not seen anything.

Now, because I can be stubborn as a mule, I've continued playing off an on this year, dealing with the regular crashes since I want to enjoy the game, but I have gone to some, honestly, silly 'rituals' to try to reduce how often I crash.  Things like zooming all the way out on the campaign map before trying to move it around to different parts of the world, never using the button that takes you to your next army that hasn't moved and just moving as slow around the map as I can.  But when you load up the game and get into your campaign, only to either move the campaign map just a little, and have that game crash, and this be your experience for the next couple of load ups, it gets incredibly frustrating that I can't play the game I've put the amount of money into that I have.  I have done the 'verify files' thing, and even fully uninstalled and reinstalled the game and nothing has worked.

So to state once again, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to any of my friends at this time.  I can, and will, remove this negative review should that instability be addressed and fixed.

Tengo más de 1000 horas de juego y puedo decir que este es uno de mis títulos favoritos. Eso no quita que tenga problemas, como el balance entre facciones y la inteligencia artificial en campaña. Sin embargo, aun con esos detalles, pienso que se puede disfrutar bastante; tiene muchos aspectos que podrían mejorar, pero también muchos aciertos.

Uno de sus puntos fuertes es la gran variedad que ofrece a la hora de jugar y el mundo de fantasía en el que está inspirado, que a veces resulta divertido y otras, asqueroso (en el buen sentido). Por eso creo que vale la pena jugarlo, aunque no es necesario comprar todos los DLC: solo los que realmente te interesen o llamen tu atención. Además, aunque para muchos los mods son algo esencial, para mí solo suman, no restan puntos a un juego. Después de todo, ¿por qué comprarías algo pensando en que se arreglará con un mod? Esa es mi opinión. Dicho esto, creo que este juego es perfectamente disfrutable sin mods y, aun así, le puedes dedicar fácilmente muchas horas, aunque eso no quita que tambien le meto mods a mi juego, no valoro eso porque pienso que eso es aparte.

En cuanto al modo multijugador, rara vez lo utilizo; solo he probado las batallas, no las campañas. Es un punto medio negativo, porque pienso que todavía necesita más trabajo en ese aspecto. Aun así, para mí la saga Total War siempre ha sido más de un solo jugador que de multijugador. Y lo digo con base, ya que he jugado desde Shogun 2, Rome II, Attila, Medieval, Troy y Three Kingdoms. Por eso considero que el punto fuerte de la saga siempre ha sido la campaña.

Aunque todavía requiere mejoras, especialmente en el modo multijugador de campañas, pienso que los Warhammer son juegos muy divertidos y que vale la pena darles una oportunidad. No son imposibles, pero aprender a jugar bien lleva tiempo: no tanto como para no saber por dónde empezar, pero sí lo suficiente para representar un reto. Yo, por ejemplo, tardé unas 200 horas en dominarlo en la máxima dificultad. xD

- Some factions' unit rosters are extremely limited without DLCs.

Ich war lange skeptisch gegenüber dem Wechsel zu Fantasy obwohl ich Warhammer mag und Dark Omen ein absoluter Klassiker für mich ist. Dennoch war ich argwöhnisch, ob CA das Schlachtengefühl aus Rome oder Medieval 2 hier herüber retten kann. Nun, das kann es nicht, aber es gibt ihm ein eigenes Ding. Hier geht es definitiv mehr um Spektakel. Wer in früheren Titeln mit donnernden Kavallerieattacken die Schlachten entschieden hat, der wird hier enttäuscht werden. Konventionelle Truppen sind vorhanden, aber Monster und Zauberer entscheiden mehr. Mächtige Fernkampfeigenschaften sind hier viel wichtiger, auch wenn gegenüber Warhammer 2 einiges entschärft wurde und Nahkampf wieder wichtiger wurde. Was dieses Spiel von den historischen Titeln absetzt sind die unterschiedlichen Mechaniken der einzlenen Fraktionen. Spiel man histoisch nun mal Fraktionen die alle Menschen sind und in der Historie mal Elefanten hatten oder Kataphraktreiter und bis in die Moderne dann alle Schießpulvereinheiten kämpfen hier Trolle, Riesen, Drachen usw.
Es ist eine andere Welt als die historischen Titel. Dessen muss man sich bewusst sein. Würde ich im 100er Wertungssystem arbeiten, dann wären es im Bereich 85 - 89%. Für einen 90er Titel ist es manachmal zu buggy und die Entwickler brauchen zu viel Zeit um diese auszubessern.

作為初次接觸《全軍破敵：戰鎚》系列的新玩家，本作帶給我無窮的樂趣，短短一星期就玩了八十小時，已經很少有策略遊戲能夠讓人玩一玩就忘記時間，常常一個下午直接玩到隔天早上。不看場外因素的話，遊戲本身沒有太大問題，確實是一款偉大的作品，個人可以給到 9 分，會選擇給出負評，主要原因是 Creative Assembly 工作室的公關態度和高價到不合理的 DLC 商法。

《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》（Total War: Warhammer 3）是 SEGA 旗下工作室 Creative Assembly 打造，主打 4X 策略與大戰場指揮玩法的策略遊戲。本作結合回合制大戰略地圖與即時戰略（RTS）戰鬥，完美融入中古戰鎚的豐富世界觀背景，自 2016 年《全軍破敵：戰鎚1》發售以來，便吸引了大量遊戲玩家，也成功讓早已完結的中古戰鎚世界觀再次被重視。

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3603471516

對於許多初次接觸《全軍破敵》系列的玩家來說，《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》不像以往主打歷史題材的系列作品，因此在遊戲上手難度上相對容易，比起城鎮經營、內政與兵牌編隊，對新手玩家最重要的是選擇想要長期鑽研遊玩的種族與領主，就像是在《世紀帝國》選擇文明一樣，不同種族與領主派系會帶來截然不同的玩法。

如果是初次接觸遊戲的玩家也不用擔心，《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》用一場宏大的劇情戰役作為新手教學關卡，從最基本的戰鬥到佔領城鎮，再到如何培養領主、招募軍隊、神器任務等玩法都有很詳細的介紹，能夠快速讓新人上手。完成序章後，玩家就能選擇「不朽帝國」（Immortal Empires）模式進行史詩級別大戰役，不朽帝國模式也是本作佔用時數最多的主要玩法。

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3607242138

「不朽帝國」模式是最大亮點，將三代所有地圖與超過兩百種不同派系合併成一張巨型大陸。你可能打了超過一百回合才征服大陸，卻發現地圖另一端的北方有更強大的混沌勢力悄然崛起，突然對你宣戰打得你措手不及。《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》從派系領主、種族機制、起始位置，再次每回合行動都會深刻影響戰局，讓每場戰役都像在編織自己的史詩故事。其實深入探索也沒有那麼難，只要記住三大步驟：升級建築，發展科技和經濟，培養軍隊推平一切。

前面有提到，《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》核心魅力在於其「4X 策略 + 即時戰略」雙重設計，玩家要在地圖上探索、擴張、開發與殲滅敵人。進入遭遇戰後會轉為考驗操作的 RTS 玩法。跟市面上其他策略遊戲類似，遊戲內的兵牌（作戰單位）都有基礎數值，兵種間也有相生相剋設置，領主和英雄甚至可以學習法術與被動技能。有鑑於一名領主最多只能指揮由 20 面兵牌組成的編隊，因此要如何選擇兵牌來對抗敵人部隊是一大學問。

可能會有玩家擔心，在這種通關一局完整戰役可能要花上 20 ~ 30 小時以上的遊戲，如果每一場遭遇戰都要手動操作的話，那麼可能會先累死自己。關於這點不用擔心，當你領主與旗下單位強大到一定程度，對上相對弱小的敵人可以透過「自動解決」（Auto Resolve）系統，選擇自動戰鬥瞬間消滅敵人。不過這也造就了一些問題，那就是當玩家「破局」（達成短期勝利後），如果沒有裝任何模組讓 AI 變得更加強大的話，後期遊戲玩法就是帶著滿編大部隊到處自動戰鬥，最終統一整個中古戰鎚世界。

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3605443656

說到《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》最大爭議，那就離不開付費 DLC 內容的售價與 CA 低下的更新產能，產能方面暫且不提，聽說 CA 都將人手安排在研發《戰鎚40K》版本的《全軍破敵》上了（未證實的非官方消息）。雖說本體基礎玩法就能讓玩家享受上百小時遊戲可玩內容，無需額外 DLC 購買也能暢玩多種派系。然而，先前提到的「不朽帝國」模式作為遊戲最主要玩法，要解鎖所有可玩派系與領主，仍需擁有《全軍破敵：戰鎚1》、《全軍破敵：戰鎚2》、以及原價接近一萬台幣的 DLC 組合包，遊玩門檻是真的高到誇張。

最後提醒想要入手《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》的新手玩家，遊戲內有大量需要等待與讀取的部分，為了遊戲能夠流暢運行，強烈建議將此遊戲安裝在 SSD 固態硬碟，這樣才能夠大幅減少遊戲載入時間。另外也推薦在正式進入遊戲前，可以前往 Steam 工作坊安裝玩家社群自製的修復 Bug 模組，這樣可以讓你獲得更棒的遊戲體驗。遊戲本身品質不錯，可惜 CA 修 Bug 修不明白，傲慢的營運態度跟超級昂貴 DLC 售價都成為本作負評的主要來源，單看遊戲的話，《全軍破敵：戰鎚3》確實是款非玩不可的策略遊戲神作。

I am a long-time fan of Creative Assembly's games.  I've played everything they've produced, including the excellent Alien: Isolation, and the fun, but little remembered, Spartan: Total Warrior. Total War has always been their bread and butter. From Edo Japan, through medieval Europe, classical Rome, the age of empires, to warring states China, and the Bronze-Age Mediterranean, their games have brought past-worlds to life.  Arguably, however, their greatest success has been not in the realm of the historical, but the fantastical.

I should state from the off that I don't generally write reviews for Steam games, but I recently happened onto the store page for Total War: Warhammer III and was surprised to see that the review score still sits at 'mixed'. Admittedly, TWW3 has had a been down a bit of a rocky road but, to my mind at least, it's currently in a pretty good state. With all its factions, units, systems and features it probably has more moving parts than any other strategy game in history and does an excellent job in managing them. Moreover, it is clear to me that the developers have a deep love and knowledge of their subject matter. 

I have enjoyed this game enough to have put 160 hours (the equivalent of almost a full continuous week of my life)  into playing it. Hence my surprise, upon reading some recent reviews, that many of the negative reviewers have put significantly more time into the game than I have. Why, in the name heaven, would you put so much time on a product that you wouldn't recommend? I suspect the answer lies in the fact that there are a number of vocal and influential YouTube creators whose sole reason for existence seems to be based on generating negative buzz around this game. Personally, this persistent negativity has led me to unsubscribe from their respective channels.

A maximalist strategy epic that, at its best, fuses the camp Warhammer vibes with real-time battles into explosive, brutal spectacle. This is the capital-G Greatness of scope and scale that only decades of accumulated AAA experience can build up to: Thousands of units sparring with synchronised animations, artillery blowing entire armies up, and monsters and magic causing mayhem in a way no other game not only can't reach, but doesn't even try to accomplish. A prior investment in Warhammer lore is unnecessary to admire the sheer ridiculousness of the ambition on display in these mega-fights.

However, the 4X campaign mode is dry chasm of interest and challenge, siege maps are awful with effectively broken AI, and bugs are so plentiful that I'd think it were in early access were it not for all of Creative Assembly's post-Shogun 2 games suffering from the same, mounting technical issues for over a decade. Everything outside of the open terrain battles is basically only serviceable for giving the fights context and variety - even if the art and audio teams have excelled again in bestowing every pixel with oodles of flavour.

Let's be real, though: It's hard to turn one's nose up at a game this absurdly ambitious, even if the campaign mode is a dull slog and the battles are functionally broken in anything other than a flat plain 1v1. This is a game stuffed with flavour and personality, most visibly in its intricate battle units, where everything from giant automatons to knee-height gremlins are overflowing with copious detail in their textures and animations. And, after a stressful day, sometimes you just want to smash these extraordinarily crafted toy soldiers into each other. When a giant Mesoamerican dinosaur charges into battle and snacks on an Early Modern handgunner, I challenge even the most self-serious adults among us to not smile and simply sit back and let childish joy wash over you. This is a huge, silly, pie-in-the-sky mess of a game where strategy is optional but bombast is guaranteed.

This has been my primary game played since it launched, yet I am writing to express my built up frustration with how CA has managed the game while advocating for ways to improve. 
My primary frustration is the lack of consistent communication. CA seems to follow a pattern of promising communication, followed by months of barely sharing their plans, only changing their course once the player and content creator community backlash becomes loud enough to force them to speak with us. It has been several years of this immature, lazy pattern. The recent episode from fall of 2025 when CA responded to backlash by fixing the AI of two factions that had ceased to work (and were the straw that broke the dam of anger) is a good example of this. While CA responded to this episode by working on the game and communicating with us, that is only an action fixing an issue that they created. 
What we need is for CA to act consistently as if they are paying attention to the game and to what their player base thinks about the game. There are many quality of life improvements that could be made. Many small changes (such as making High Elf heroes available at one tier earlier) like those suggested and explained well by content creators on youtube would do wonders for replayability. 
DLC like Tides of Torment seems to have focused on a mix of new units and new lords with unique mechanics. That's great! However, I think I speak for many, many players when I say that CA should not neglect other Legendary Lords as they currently do. For example, it's been explained by the Total War playthrough on youtube that Tyrion and Teclis both have had useful changes to their campaigns to make them more interesting. While there are plenty of things that could still be done to improve each (like victory conditions and terrain compatibility for each), neglecting Alith Anar, Alarielle, Imrik and Eltharion is a massive missed opportunity since this is likely the only time High Elves will be looked at again (and first time since Eltharion's DLC years ago). An important part of any DLC is race updates (to all lords). 
Please pay attention to quality of life improvements that make gameplay more fun. For instance, unit variety in the early game and greater challenge in the mid-late game. For too long it has seemed apparent that CA does not pay attention to how the game feels to play. Please don't be afraid to explain why things are happening. Please earn back our trust by working on this and by communicating more effectively.

I didn’t buy Total War: Warhammer 3 to beta-test Creative Assembly’s save-corrupting slot machine disguised as a game.

I lost 20 MANUAL SAVES.
TWENTY.
This wasn’t my mistake. I checked them throughout the campaign. Everything was there. Until suddenly… it wasn’t.

After a battle loss, I went to reload — and the game looked me dead in the eyes and said:
“Manual saves? Never heard of them.”

Quick save survived.
Some prehistoric save from 20 turns ago survived.
Everything else? Digitally incinerated.

I even clicked “Show All Saves” like a clown hoping the game would magically reveal them.
Nothing.
Zero.
A void.
The game straight-up Thanos-snapped my progress.

Cloud sync? Disabled long before this.
Recuva scan? Found one sad, half-rotten save from 10 turns back.
Which means the game is actively discarding legitimate saves behind the scenes because — and let’s be real — modern AAA titles treat basic functionality like an optional DLC.

Now let’s talk about AAA corporations.

These companies charge full price for half-working products, then act shocked Pikachu when players are pissed.

They push out games with:

broken systems,

corrupted saves,

performance issues,

design oversights,

and a glorious unwavering faith that players will “just wait for patches.”

You know what patching means today?
“Pay us now, maybe it’ll work in six months, who knows lol.”

Games launch in TRAINWRECK states but hey — the trailers looked shiny, right?
Publishers squeeze devs, devs squeeze deadlines, and players get squeezed the hardest — right in the wallet and in the sanity.

And the worst part?
They hide the biggest problems behind the refund timer.
Bugs don’t show up in the first hour — they strike at hour 3, hour 10, hour 50.
Right after you lose the right to get your money back.

If any other industry pulled this ♥♥♥♥, regulators would shut them down.
Imagine buying a car that randomly deletes your engine after 100 km and the manufacturer says:
“Sorry bro, you already drove it more than 2 hours, no refund.”

Gaming?
Totally fine.
Totally normal.
Totally acceptable — apparently.

The sad truth

We players have been conditioned to accept garbage.
We swallow patches, day-1 hotfixes, deleted saves, memory leaks, crashes, stutters, broken AI, and unfinished content because the industry has convinced us that “this is just how it is now.”

No.
This is not normal.
This is not acceptable.
This is not “live service.”
It’s corporate negligence masked as development philosophy.

Final Verdict

Warhammer 3 is a fantastic game buried alive under the incompetence, greed, and sloppy standards of today’s AAA machine.

As someone who has logged a combined 3,300+ hours across Warhammer II & III, not counting the time I spent sailing the high seas until I could afford the game, I cannot recommend this game to anyone. As of writing this and to my current knowledge, two entire factions, not just two lords, but two entire factions are completely broken where they will do absolutely nothing. Lizardmen and Tomb Kings do not survive past turn 20 in every game I've tried to play so far. They don't even attempt to capture a second settlement or recruit units to play defensive. They literally do nothing and then just die. You may think "Oh well, I don't really care about Tomb Kings or Lizardmen, who cares if they get wiped out? These are the only factions I know of off the top of my head but I do seem to recall others posting about certain Lords, or other factions, specifically Beastmen IIRC, being just as equally broken as Tomb Kings and Lizardmen. The Great: The amount of raw content and time you can spend in this game is amazing. I've been a long to 4x game and a long time RTS player and the union of the two of them here makes for a very exciting time.

The Less Good: I'm not aware of the all the drama around CA. Weird DLC schedules, treating their best content producers very oddly, not finishing that South bit of Cathay. None of this really bothers me, but this community is quite vocal when something is less than excellent.

The Bad: The learning curve here is atrocious. The AI acts in a bewildering fashion on both the Campaign map and in the battles. The game is *expensive* as well, there are so many DLC's. Don't get this unless it's on sale.

Total War: Warhammer III is the grand finale fans were waiting for. Creative Assembly has taken everything that made the series great and dialed it up to eleven.  

- Immortal Empires gives you the biggest, most replayable campaign map in strategy gaming.  
- Faction variety is off the charts — whether you’re commanding the disciplined armies of Cathay or unleashing the daemons of Chaos, every playthrough feels fresh.  
- Diplomacy and alliances finally matter, letting you build lasting empires instead of temporary pacts.  
- Battles are cinematic, chaotic, and endlessly fun — the perfect blend of spectacle and strategy.  

Verdict: This isn’t just another Total War game. It’s a sprawling, endlessly replayable masterpiece that cements Warhammer III as the crown jewel of the trilogy.

TW WH3 is where I took a deeper dive and it is entertaining for a while. Many lords don't have unique faction mechanics that could make it enticing to play them. Quite some that do have unique mechanics have mechanics that don't really offer you meaningful decisions/choices. Instead you get presented with illusionary choices that are very transparently not meaningful (e.g. Tamurkhan, where you basically have a quite set order in which to get heroes and getting them all is always better than unlocking their abilities.) After you understand how some mechanisms and combat works, it quickly becomes samey unless follow self imposed restrictions. If not, and I am not good at self imposed restrictions, basically every campaign turns into: "how do I get a bunch of heroes with 1-2 casters" and then steamroll most armies. The AI usually just recruits mixed armies with lots of infantry etc. so even if there are units that would work well against a few heroes, they will get army lossed. 
The other issue is that major approach issues of the studio start to show. There is an evident lack of QA and testing of new features and patches. Some bugs make it into the game that make you wonder whether anyone on the side of the study tried the new patch beyond 10-15 turns. The lizardman AI etc. issue is just the latest example. There are lots of bugs in the game that are known for a long long period where for some of them it is unclear why they are not addressed. 
Examples include the random loss of movement (changing e.g. from encamp stance to another stance may mean you can't change back into encamp stance), odd recalculation of HP if mounts change, pathing issues (on the campaign map and battlefield), the gate bug (where sometimes entities trying to break down the gate end up inside the walls and get attacked by everyone or can't attack the gate) etc. and you have not so rarely just crashes of the game (which tend to happen when the game is loading the campaign map after a battle, so you may have to redo a long manual battle again).
The auto resolve is having a very hard time properly assessing the strength of armies. At the same time auto resolve means that an army generally gets completely annihilated, where as with manual battles there will be left overs you have to chase. So sometimes you are incentives to build an army that is strong in AR but not strong in manual combat, to avoid having to spend extra movement to chase leftovers of armies. This was super evident in the Oxyotl campaign where your chameleon skinks will generally destroy all other armies due to stealth and range, and you can always take out anything that would be problematic first with oxyotl first. (Oxyotl + ranger's quiver basically beats every army with enough patience).
Sieges are a mess as basically a 1 dwarf runesmith army can win any siege. Otherwise, caster will do the trick. While defending the walls and towers are in many cases useless. So what should be a highlight becomes a tedious slog and an army that would win handedly in the field for whatever reason doesn't sally out and gets slaughtered. The AI is an issue but not sure how easy it is to fix it.

The game is fun. It has a lot of variety between the playstyles for each faction and in many cases I feel it truly nails the essence of what the faction is. The battles are classic total war, and fans of that will know why it is enjoyable to play both large battles and small skirmishes alike. Not to mention how cinematic it can be with the right camera movements. There is something distinctly satisfying about watching your empire slowly expand its borders, or inversely watch the world burn down.

Bugs do happen. It's an older engine and anyone who's dabbled in coding knows you fix one thing and it breaks five other things. The price tag is also daunting, and I have no defense for that. It's intimidating as a new player to see the cumulative price tag for the game plus all DLCs and not be frightened away.

Overall though, don't let the negative reviews make you feel as though it's all as horrible as it seems. There will always be the next world-ending situation that spells the end of the franchise. Inversely don't allow the glowing reviews to sugar coat things, as there have been bugs over time that are truly game breaking and the model is, unfortunately, greedy.

It comes down to personal preference. What you are willing to overlook. Some will hate the game, seeing a bug or sub-par DLC and tearing their hair out in fury. Others will ignore all the negatives in favor of blind support e.g. CoD. I am looking at it cumulatively. Over the years, have I found myself enjoying the game more or hating the game more? In my case, I've been having fun far more times than I've been frustrated, so overall I say the game gets my stamp.

TW Warhammer 3 é um dos jogos mais divertidos da série. As facções são bem diferentes entre si, as campanhas sempre oferecem algo novo e o jogo vive recebendo conteúdos, atualizações e melhorias que mantêm a experiência fresca por bastante tempo. Para quem curte batalhas épicas e profundidade estratégica, é difícil achar algo tão bom.

O maior problema do jogo é o preço. Warhammer III é caro, e as DLCs são ainda mais. O pior é que muitas delas adicionam apenas um senhor lendário com alguma mecânica nova, o que faz parecer um custo muito alto para conteúdo relativamente pequeno (ainda mais se você ganhar em R$). Além disso, para ter a experiência realmente completa (especialmente no modo Immortal Empires), você precisa ter DLCs dos jogos anteriores, que já têm quase uma década, mas continuam custando caro demais. Não são obrigatórias, mas depois de jogar algumas campanhas você começa a enjoar de usar sempre os mesmos personagens, e aí praticamente vira “necessário” comprar mais conteúdo e isso pesa no bolso. Por outro lado, existe um ponto "positivo" importante: diferente de franquias como The Sims, onde cada novo jogo faz você comprar tudo novamente, as DLCs da série Total War: Warhammer costumam ser reaproveitadas no próximo título. Ou seja, é bem provável que, quando um eventual Warhammer 4 for lançado, todo o conteúdo adquirido nos Warhammer 1, 2 e 3 continue valendo. Isso torna o investimento pesado algo único, e não algo que se repete a cada novo jogo da série, já que da para curtir bastante somente com as DLCs dos títulos anteriores (nesse caso as DLCs dos títulos 1 e 2).

No fim das contas, o jogo é excelente e extremamente divertido, mas o modelo de monetização realmente pesa e pode afastar algumas pessoas, já que não é qualquer um que terá mais de R$ 1.000,00 disponíveis para gastar só em DLCs. Se puder pegar o jogo e suas DLCs em promoção, a experiência se torna muito mais justa (recomendo inclusive esperar alguns meses antes de comprar as DLCs novas, porque elas costumam ir baixando de preço. Até lá, dá para curtir bastante as DLCs mais antigas).

Even though I haven’t played the first two Warhammer titles, my experience with other Total War games made the transition into Total War: Warhammer III surprisingly smooth. The biggest difference, of course, is the shift from historical settings to a fully fantastical universe. Instead of grounded realism, the game immerses you in a world filled with magic, demons, and larger-than-life factions, which instantly makes the overall experience feel more dynamic and unpredictable.

What truly stands out is the Warhammer universe itself. It’s an incredibly rich and captivating setting, and Warhammer III embraces that depth more confidently than any previous Total War game I’ve played. The Chaos realms, in particular, offer a unique tone and style that you don’t get in historical entries. The Chaos factions feel like they belong to a completely different genre, and that’s part of what makes them so exciting. Khorne and Tzeentch especially caught my attention—each having such distinct personalities, aesthetics, and playstyles that they feel like fully realized creations on their own.

On the mechanical side, Total War: Warhammer III stays true to the core formula of the series while expanding it with systems that fit the Warhammer setting. The campaign map feels more dynamic thanks to faction-specific mechanics, randomized rifts, and unique progression paths that push you into constant decision-making. Battles are fast-paced and visually intense, especially when commanding massive daemonic units or powerful legendary lords. Each faction plays dramatically differently—whether it’s Khorne’s aggressive melee-focused armies or Tzeentch’s magic-driven, manipulation-heavy style—which gives the game a level of replay value far beyond traditional historical Total War titles.

Overall, Total War: Warhammer III blends the strategic depth of the series with a universe that’s bold, imaginative, and constantly surprising. Even without playing the earlier entries, it’s easy to appreciate how much care went into bringing this world to life. For someone who already enjoys Total War but wants a fresher, more fantastical experience, this game is absolutely worth diving into.
