Total War Warhammer 1 dışında ne 2'yi ne de 3'ü oynamadım. İlk oyunu sevmiştim aslında ama çok da bilmediğim Warhammer dünyası çok da ilgilimi çekmiyordu. Bu oyunu oynadıktan sonra fikrim yine de değişmedi. Fantezi evrenleri arasında gördüğüm en sıkıcılarından biri Warhammer Old World. Tasarımlar vs çok ilgimi çekmiyor. Ama yine de bu sıkıcı evren bu oyunun en iyi Total War oyunu olduğu gerçeğini değiştirmiyor. Profilimdeki Total War saatlerini aldanmayın, Her Total War oyununu en az 100 saat oynamışımdır. Attila, Rome 2 ve Shogun 2 gibi daha efsane oyunlara 500'den fazla. Empire'ı ise en az 1000 saate yakın oynamışımdır. Hiç biri Warhammer 3 Immortal Empires'ın yanına yaklaşamaz. Diğer her oyun bir kapalı kutu gibi iken Warhammer 3 (Aynı zamanda Warhammer 1 ve 2'de buna dahil. Güncelleme ile Immortal Empires'ı o oyunlardan da açabilirsiniz) gerçekten tam anlamıylar bir dünya. Immortal Empires 3 Warhammer oyunun maplerini alıp birleştirip tek bir dünya yapıyor. Haritada ne ararsanız var. Immortal Empires Expanded modu ile haritayı daha da büyütebilirsiniz. Kıtalar arası görsel ve iklim değişikleri direkt belli oluyor. Harita gerçekten çok büyüyor. Oynanışım bir yerinde Teclis ile Caelith Boğazı'na (Ya da kapısı, doğrusunu tam bilmiyorum) 5-6 tur arası sürdü. Gerçekten uzun bir yolculuk ve uzak diyarlara gittiğim hissiyatını verdi. Tek güzel yanı harita değil. Her ırkın aynı zamanda her ırk içindeki bazı ulusların farklı oynanış mekanikleri olması. Her ırk zaten çok farklı ama aynı ırktan farklı ulusların bu kadar farklı olmasını beklemiyordum. Oynanış inanılmaz çeşitleniyor. Tek sorun DLC'ler. Örneğin siz DLC olmayan bir ulusla oynayacaksanız sonrasında sizle aynı ırktan olan bir ulusun farklı asker, lord, kahraman birimleri olduğunu görüyorsunuz. Oynadığınız Lord veya ulus ne tercih ediyorsanız, DLC'lere muhtaç kalıyor. İçeriğin yarısı oyunlarda diğer yarısı DLC'lerde. Sırf Yüce Elflerle ilgili DLC'lere tam 15 dolar verdim. Tek bir ırkı tam anlamıyla denemek için bile ciddi bir miktar para vermeniz gerekiyor. Teknoloji ağaçları ise ilgi çekici. Bretonya uluslarında teknoloji açarak diğer uluslarla birleşebiliyoruz. Aynı HOI4'de odak ağacı gibi. Empire'da benzer birleşme olayları vardı İspanya ve BK için ama bunu görevler aracılığı ile yapıyorduk. Bu oyunda daha çok kullanılan bir yerde olması çok daha hoş olmuş. Irklara özgü farklı birimler olması da oldukça hoş. Yİne örnek olarak Yüce Elf'lerden gideceğim. Yüce Elf'lerin kendine özgü Nam (Tam Türkçelerini bilmiyorum bu terimlerin, oyunu modlu oynadığım için İngilizce oynuyorum), Bilgi Tomarları, Ejder Gemisi Malzemeleri, Anka Kral Seviyesi gibi tamamen kendine özgü birimleri, kaynakları var. Oyunda 20 tane falan ırk olduğunu düşününce üzerinde ne kadar uğraşıldığı belli olan bir oyun Warhammer 3. Eğer fantezi ve Strateji seviyorsanız kesinlikle oynayın (Immotal Empires veya Mod ile indirilen Immortal Empires Expanded dışında diğer haritaya çok bakmayın). Alternatifi nadir olan bir oyun.

Total War: Warhammer 3 é daqueles jogos que não pedem licença para ocupar espaço na sua vida, ele simplesmente chega, abre um mapa gigantesco, joga dezenas de facções em conflito eterno e diz “agora se vira”. E o melhor é que virar-se nesse caos organizado é exatamente onde mora a diversão. O jogo consegue unir como nenhum outro a estratégia de longo prazo, típica da série Total War, com batalhas absurdamente espetaculares, nas quais exércitos colossais se chocam enquanto magia, monstros e heróis transformam o campo de batalha em um verdadeiro show de destruição. A sensação de escala é constante, desde o mapa da campanha, que parece não ter fim, até os confrontos em tempo real, nos quais cada decisão tática pode significar glória eterna ou uma derrota humilhante que rende boas histórias depois.

O grande trunfo de Total War: Warhammer 3 está no conteúdo praticamente inesgotável. Cada facção não é apenas uma variação estética, mas um jogo dentro do jogo, com mecânicas próprias, estilos de campanha distintos e formas únicas de travar guerra. Isso faz com que iniciar uma nova campanha nunca pareça repetição, mas sim uma nova história, com novos desafios, novas estratégias e novas formas criativas de errar. É aquele clássico “só mais um turno”, que facilmente se transforma em horas a fio, enquanto você administra impérios, planeja guerras em várias frentes e tenta apagar incêndios que surgem onde menos se espera.

A experiência se torna ainda mais impressionante graças à comunidade de mods, que praticamente transforma o jogo em uma plataforma infinita de possibilidades. Mods como o SFO e o Radious são exemplos claros disso. O SFO aprofunda o aspecto estratégico, tornando economia, progressão e identidade das facções ainda mais marcantes, quase como uma versão mais densa e desafiadora do jogo base. 

Já o Radious amplia a variedade de unidades, ajusta o ritmo das batalhas e oferece uma sensação constante de novidade, deixando cada campanha mais dinâmica e personalizada. Somam-se a esses inúmeros outros mods, desde ajustes de qualidade de vida até reformulações completas de sistemas, garantindo que sempre exista algo novo para experimentar, mesmo depois de centenas de horas de jogo.

Se existe uma crítica mais contundente, ela fica concentrada no preço das DLCs. Embora adicionem conteúdo de qualidade e expandam ainda mais esse universo gigantesco, o valor total do pacote completo ultrapassa facilmente os 1200 reais, o que acaba sendo um obstáculo significativo para muitos jogadores. 

É um investimento alto, especialmente para quem quer vivenciar a experiência completa, com todas as facções, campanhas e possibilidades que o jogo oferece. Ainda assim, mesmo com essa ressalva importante, Total War: Warhammer 3 se consolida como a melhor experiência Total War do mercado para muitos jogadores, um jogo de escala verdadeiramente colossal, capaz de oferecer milhares de horas de conteúdo, histórias emergentes e diversão estratégica quase infinita.

As someone who has never played a Total War game before, or any turn based strategy more complex than "kill everything", this is a really fun game! I love how differently each faction plays (or at least usually), and I especially love the real time battles. Monetisation is a huge issue and I despise the way they done it, but hey! I'm getting the DLC for free through their website so I don't fully care. 

The worst part has to be Denuvo, it's on all 3 of the games, and it practically ensures that EVERYTHING you purchase is not yours. £200+ spent on DLC? Too bad! If the servers go down, there goes your DLC and everything you bought and paid for. This seems to be an issue with Total War Warhammer 2 rather than 3.

And how could I not mention the DLC? The entire game is locked behind Total War: Warhammer, Total War: Warhammer 2, and then ALL of the DLC from all 3 of these games. The pricing is absurd. I would not want any of my friends to get into this out of respect for them, unless they could get DLC for free. The most complete factions are ones that are effectively standalone, like the vampire coast, wood elves, chaos dwarves, tomb kings, and beastmen. Buying their DLC would get you all or most of their units immediately, nothing would be locked behind several different DLC. And factions like dwarves, high elves, chaos factions, etc, feel severely incomplete if you don't have the DLC. Some of their buildings give you NOTHING without it, just acting as a tier with slightly better stats above the previous. Please spend your money wisely.

The probably most efficient way of getting more factions for relatively cheap would be getting the 3 games in a bundle for cheap, as you get all the factions included in those games, and they also have free DLC. Total War: Warhammer has free DLC of the French, with some lords for other factions, and Total War: Warhammer 2 has free DLC of individual lords. The Creative Assembly dashboard also would get you some free heroes and regiment of renown units. And then the workshop for modded units and modded factions.

The easier thing to save your money, would be to not get this game at all.

As someone who avoided this series for nearly a decade because of its intimidating DLC, Total War: Warhammer III--specifically Immortal Empires--should be viewed less as a traditional video game and more as a virtual tabletop experience. Just as you aren’t expected to buy every Warhammer miniature, you don’t need to own every DLC to enjoy the game.

The only real “requirement,” if you want the full Immortal Empires experience, is owning the first and second games to unlock all base content. Considering I picked up all three games for around $30, that’s an excellent deal. That said, if you only want to play Warhammer III’s standalone campaign and factions, the base game is completely sufficient.

Immortal Empires is a massive open-world campaign where over 200 factions compete across a world that loosely resembles Earth. It’s the definitive Total War: Warhammer experience, offering an incredible variety of campaigns, many of which feel radically different from one another. You can easily spend over 100 hours on a single faction, and I strongly recommend doing exactly that. The learning curve is brutal. You will lose often and rely heavily on auto-resolve just to survive, but once the systems finally click, the game can feel almost trivial at times.

I describe Immortal Empires as a virtual tabletop because learning it becomes a hobby in itself. The sheer depth and interconnected systems practically force you into becoming a hardcore player, even if you never planned to. There’s a genuine sense of discovery as you slowly piece together how everything works.

That said, the game isn’t without problems. Culturally, Warhammer occupies an uncomfortable space. Its Earth-adjacent setting carries troubling implications—regions resembling Africa or the Americas are often depicted as chaos-worshipping or “savage,” while the most conventionally heroic factions resemble white European or East Asian societies. It’s an issue the setting never fully resolves, though the fact that Chaos is effectively designed to win without player intervention complicates the idea of clear “good guys.”

Another major issue is how difficulty is handled. The game separates campaign difficulty from battle difficulty. Campaign difficulty affects economy, upkeep, and AI aggression, while battle difficulty determines combat bonuses and AI behavior—including auto-resolve outcomes. This creates a major trap for new players: on Easy or Normal battle difficulty, the auto-resolve may predict a decisive victory, but manually fighting the battle results in a loss—no matter how well you play. This isn’t because you’re doing something wrong, but because your army lacks the hidden bonuses auto-resolve assumes at lower difficulties.

Auto-resolve isn’t meant to measure battle difficulty; it’s an accessibility tool designed to help players progress without mastering real-time tactics. A far better indicator is the Balance of Power bar, which appears when hovering over an enemy army and shows relative strength directly.

For a more consistent experience, I strongly recommend setting battle difficulty to Hard while keeping campaign difficulty on Easy or Normal. This produces auto-resolve results that more closely match what you can realistically achieve in manual battles, while also giving room to win "unwinnable battles".

My two cents on the Warhammer III campaigns that i played and changes compared to Warhammer II:

Bretonnia
Great Cavalry, good magic, useful missile units, utterly useless infantry. Build your armies accordingly or suffer.
The only change compared to Warhammer II at the time of this recension is, that the neighboring Barrow Legion is much more aggressive now and has to be dealt with early.

Dwarves
Strong but expensive unit roster with sturdy line infantry and a lot of missile damage dealer options. Rune Magic has more of a supportive character.
Changes to the grudge system are fun, but economy and garrisons got nerfed compared to Warhammer II. The grudge system forces a more offensive played campaign, which the economy can barely support now.

Empire
Very strong artillery, strong magic, good cavalry, useful missile units, but Infantry is more of a liabiliy in mid to late game.
Reikland:
Changes to the Electoral Machinations are an improvement and has game changing potential, but the elector states get wiped out so fast now, that it makes no impact at all (in most campaigns).
Golden Order:
Starting position and changes to the order mechanics makes for interesting opportunities. If you want a wizard blizzard to wipe out the competition, here it is.

High Elves
Strong magic, strong bowmen and hybrid infantry, good flying units, useful cavalry and infantry, only one mediocre artillery piece.
If you are looking for a more relaxed pace, Eataine (Tyrion) is the go-to-campaign.
New patrons system which is nice, but has not much impact on the overall campaign.
The champions mechanic on the other hand has the potential of a game changer if used correctly.

Skaven
Strong missile units and 'special forces', good magic, useful 'cavalry' and monsters, weak infantry to throw at the enemy for biding time.
No changes compared to Warhammer II at the time of this recension.

Vampire counts
Very Strong magic, useful cavalry and monsters, very few missile choices, mediocre infantry to throw at the enemy for biding time, no artillery at all.
No changes compared to Warhammer II at the time of this recension.

In all honesty, I planned on writing a positive review, however I could not bring myself to recommend this game. I want to preface this by saying that I love this game, I cannot stop coming back to it. However, there are some major issues at the very core of this game that stop me from recommending it to a new player. 
 
Starting with what works: 
- If you are a fan of Warhammer fantasy or Warhammer in general this game can be amazing. Creative Assembly has done more work than Games Workshop in keeping this setting alive and interesting for people who never got to be involved with original WAF before the setting was sunsetted. 
- I am not an expert (nor competent) in PC specs so please take this with a grain of salt; but the game runs incredibly well on my pre built PC. I rarely run into performance issues with this game 
- The AI is (usually) a fun challenge to play against. 

What doesn't work: 
- The main issue with this game is shortly after purchasing, you will come to find that calling Warhammer 3 a full game is misleading. What you are buying functions more like a large DLC pack for Warhammer 1&2, and without those games, you are severely limited in the amount of content you are able to play with. This problem alone is why I cannot recommend this game in good conscious.
- The prevalence of DLC in this game is also an issue. Even if you were to only play the base game, the core factions you get are still incomplete with many of the most consistent and most powerful late game units being locked behind some other DLC's paywall.
- The pricing structure is another major issue. The full game costs $59.99 with each subsequent faction costing in the ballpark of $8.99. Adding onto that you can expect to buy Warhammer 1&2 for between 40 and 60 USD. This is where the problem of this game being a bloated DLC pack by itself becomes apparent. Even after you buy this game at the full AAA studio price, you will be expected to shell out a large sum of money to get more and more content. 
TL;DR
All in all, I do really love this game, however the pricing structure asks the player to buy an incomplete experience for $59.99, and it is not worth your money in my opinion.

I'm more than disappointed in the outcome of this franchise, but before anything we should go over what the game does right because for all the wrongs there's a lot of good. Unit models are excellently crafted and are absolutely exuding with life and energy. They cover both Old World and Age of Sigmar content with both covering a surprisingly large amount of their respective areas. Combat plays out well, sticking with the magic system present in the table top games (so 6 available spells note this excludes character unique spells in most cases) allowing for deep interactive gameplay. Micromanaging cavalry, lords heroes and so proves to be a rewarding learning curve especially me, an entirely new player to not only Total War games but at any challenging rts experience (something tells me Pikmin doesn't count). Which leads me into the negatives, as I just stated I'm new to this kind of game so then I ask why must it take a new player over 200 hours before they start to feel as though they're making any progress? Seriously how poor of a user interface can you have, I'm so sick of games having a big mess you just have to figure out so many games do it that I've become exhausted on this trope. Now there are actually a lot of reasons why this game is rather tricky to learn and it's because it doesn't want to tell you anything. Ordinarily if there was a more sandbox orientated mode which wasn't hidden behind a tab I expect little players to click on reading as just "battle", myself had only clicked to see what it would do and continued fiddling around with it for the purposes of a review. What player is going to click on something as broad as battle willingly when it reads more like the tutorial campaign mode and not something along the lines of freeplay. These things sound small and nitpicky but this is psychology at play here, maybe new players might stumble onto it but the screen selection is incredibly daunting and overwhelming to new players that they could easily mistakenly see it and decide to come back on e they understand the game more and not vice versa. Realistically players won't get a concrete way of testing what specific things do (on a side note that really shouldn't be the point of this game anyway having these themes of adventure and discovery outside of campaigns which are mainly used to roleplay anyway, it's just a strange choice if intentional) so my way of learning often came from stumbling around Youtube videos. When I plan to review content I just like to see what other people think so I tend to watch challenge videos, rarely actual reviews and the like to get a feel for the game. Thanks to Legend of Total War because my information on a lot of deeper mechanics came from him. Such as bonus vs large works and charge bonus, they add too melee attack, excluding that there's also a lot of poor ai choices at large no matter where you look. In battle you can bait all the enemy ammunition or easily put them in "aggro" by casting fodder spells and on the campaign map you can sell settlements for a few thousand of gold consistently, granted is helpful as a player but why do they pay this much for low tier settlements in regions they don't control. There are also funny interactions the most recent for me was when I was at war with a faction (the usual) but there was another factions army barrelling at them at a much higher strength rank. Instead of defending their last settlement they attack me who was just chilling there to raid they attack me, admittedly I lost but I couldn't help but cackle at a totally brain dead player as when my turn came they were wiped from the game. I feel the need for this next part to reiterate how amazing it is the developers managed to fit all this content into Warhammer 3 and have it somehow  run. Doing a 180 here this game runs poorly and has always run poorly (from my knowledge this is the case for most Total War games) so then how have they not found a way to optimise the ai, even on my computer (for specs I'm running an AMD Ryzen 7, 5080 Ti and 16gb ram) turns take up to minutes and I can easily recall a time where my pc was weaker and was taking on average 3 times that. Sometimes the ui just breaks entirely and you can no longer see outlines on the battlefield but specifically the battlefield and nothing else even though ui increases are across the entire game. On top of that when putting the ui scaling back to normal after it breaks it still doesn't reset, only closing the game does that. So my guess is the ui is passively killing itself? How, how do you have some of these issues genuinely? Some of you might be asking that right now as me so moving aside from the bugs (There are more famous ones like diplomacy making the game chug along too but I'll spare you more of that), in my personal opinion, it's because Creative Assembly is completely money hungry. Don't think I forgot when you were charging people for Immortal Empires aka the only campaign anyone plays behind a £40 paywall (tied to the first instalment of the trilogy). Scummy business practices all around, they charge for gore in a Warhammer game of all things, hundreds of pound of dlc not only locking legendary lords but units and you still have to buy the previous instalments for certain factions. Maybe instead of adding more content to a barely functional game why not deepen this puddle because god is it shallow. There is little difference between legendary lords within each faction (at least the ones that aren't dlc) making versatility and replay value limited. It doesn't help that when choosing them you don't want to pick anyone because the cover art re-emphasises this by making them look so vapid when their actual models do them so much more justice (seriously fire all the ui guys at this point). We could of gotten a personalised experience for each faction leader, specialised units fit around the bonuses given by the leader for the tailor made units, with campaign effects that lent themselves to the faction but in their own way. Even if all the man power was re-directed I do believe that all the content at this point would be too much to manage so in an ironic twist of fate the games greatness achievement was its' ultimate weakness.

Tl;dr: The need to implement Immortal Empires has left the game's core unchanged since 2016, making this like more of an overpriced expansion than a sequel. Other Total War games in the interim have been making meaningful strides moving systems forward, especially non-combat systems, making this game's lack of core improvements even more noticeable. The new factions are also Chaos heavy, with very little inspiration and unique ideas compared to Total Warhammer 2's core factions. However, it's a great "expansion" if you pick it up for $30, and an absolute win for Chaos fans. I am not a Chaos fan. 

    - This series has been heavily held back by the need to implement Immortal Empires into every entry. I know the mode is beloved, but it required them to essentially make the same game 3 times. Every entry is more like a big then a new Total War game. 
     - The price is a major point of contention in these games. I won't talk about DLC, as this is a review for the core game. However, a core game has never felt more "DLC" before. It is, essentially, a "Chaos Expansion" for Total Warhammer 2, with every new addition other then Grand Cathay and Kislev being Chaos. None of the new factions do anything new enough to feel worthy of a sequel, and none of the systems in the core game have been improved. This is the same game with some new, extremely uninspired factions. 
   - Total War games outside of Warhammer have made strides over the years with core systems, most notably non-combat systems. Three Kingdoms vastly improved Diplomacy and Alliance systems, allowing for a more nuanced and exciting game then just "Steamroll the map".  It's hard to go back to that gameplay style and systems from 2011 (Shogun 2), after experiencing Total War finally taking a step forward with non-combat systems. This won't be a big deal to players that just want the classic Total War experience with more factions, but the Warhammer series' greatest strength of faction uniqueness and variety is lacking here.
   - Finally, you have to own the other two games to play the corresponding factions in Immortal Empires. This might seem like a "No duh" thing to mention, but it keeps me from being able to recommend this game from a "Complete experience" perspective. 
   -   Get this on a sale for $30 or less if you want a cool Chaos Expansion for the same game you've been playing since 2016.

I've read several reviews before getting this, after getting this, and occasionally throughout the 700 hours I have played since the beginning of November. A common trend is that a lot of the negative reviews are about how the developers market their DLCs. Let me summarize this quicky, to get it out of the way.

[h2]Base Game Races and Factions:[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Kislev[/b] - 3 of 4 Factions
[*][b]Grand Cathay[/b] - 2 of 3 Factions
[*][b]Daemons of Chaos[/b] - 1 of 1 Factions
[*][b]Khorne[/b] - 2 of 3 Factions
[*][b]Nurgle[/b] - 2 of 3 Factions
[*][b]Slaanesh[/b] - 2 of 3 Factions
[*][b]Tzeentch[/b] - 1 of 2 Factions
[*][b]Warriors of Chaos[/b] - 1 of 8 Factions
[*][b]Bretonnia[/b] - 4 of 4 Factions (included if you own any of the three games, including WARHAMMER III)
[/list]

[h2]Races and Factions [b][u][i]without[/i][/u][/b] any DLC:[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Beastmen[/b] - 4 Factions between 2 DLC
[*][b]The Empire[/b] - 5 Factions between 3 DLC and WARHAMMER I
[*][b]High Elves[/b] - 7 Factions between 3 DLC and WARHAMMER II
[*][b]Lizardmen[/b] - 7 Factions between 3 DLC and WARHAMMER II
[*][b]Ogre Kingdoms[/b] - 3 Factions between 2 DLC
[*][b]Tomb Kings[/b] - 4 Factions between 1 DLC
[*][b]Vampire Counts[/b] - 5 Factions between 1 DLC and WARHAMMER I
[*][b]Dark Elves[/b] - 6 Factions between 2 DLC and WARHAMMER II
[*][b]Norsca[/b] - 3 Factions between 2 DLC
[*][b]Skaven[/b] - 6 Factions between 3 DLC and WARHAMMER II
[*][b]Chaos Dwarves[/b] - 3 Factions between 1 DLC
[*][b]Dwarves[/b] - 6 Factions between 2 DLC and WARHAMMER I
[*][b]Greenskins[/b] - 6 Factions between 3 DLC and WARHAMMER I
[*][b]Vampire Coast[/b] - 4 Factions between 1 DLC
[*][b]Wood Elves[/b] - 4 Factions between 2 DLC
[/list]

[h2]Race Rosters and how DLC affects them:[/h2]
Using The Empire's Roster as an example ([url=https://prnt.sc/YeYG1g2ox-Ew]visual[/url]), they only have access to two Missile Units; a Crossbowmen and a Handgunner. With all of the DLC for The Empire, you get ten new Missile Units, five of which are Regiments of Renown.

Just because you have the Race unlocked, [b][u]does not[/u][/b] mean you get access to the entire Race's roster of units. In the above example, owning Markus Wulfhart grants two new units and their RoR counterparts. Elspeth von Draken grants two new units and one RoR counterpart. Volkmar the Grim adds one new unit and two RoR. This is just for Missile Units.

According to the Internet, if you don't own WARHAMMER I or II and you purchase a Race introduced in it, you get access to the entire Base Roster. For example, if you purchase Elspeth von Draken but don't own WARHAMMER I, you'll only have access to her as a playable Faction, [i]BUT,[/i] you'll have access to all of The Empire's base units, and any units included within the DLC.

[h2]WARHAMMER I, II, III and Immortal Empires[/h2]
If you own any of the previous games and their DLCs, they [i]WILL[/i] carry over to this game. If you look at the DLC section, the DLC is actually the DLC from all three games, so if you own anything then it will tell you.

[h2]My Thoughts..[/h2]
I don't approve them breaking everything down.. Having to own all three games and all of the Factions of a specific Race to utilize the entire Roster.. It sucks. I won't deny it. I'm aware you don't [i]HAVE[/i] to buy anything.. but you're sort of coarsed into it when you're playing a Faction and see the AI using units you don't have access to.. Like when I played Grand Cathay and confederated one of the Major Factions. I wasn't aware of it at the time, so when I saw a bunch of weird, new units in my newly acquired armies.. I realized I didn't have everything.

I own roughly half of the DLCs now, and bought WARHAMMER II to complete my collection. I bought Markus Wulfhart for $5.99CAD exclusively to use the new Mortar Wagons with Elspeth's mechanics.. She can give Mortars Stalk and Snipe, and her Engineer Heroes can give War Wagons Vanguard Deployment.. That's literally all I bought it for. I'll never play Markus, or the Lizardmen Faction that came with it.

While I don't approve of the practice, I am enjoying the content I recieve.

As for the bugs, glitches, and everything else wrong with the game? I've only crashed once in all of my 700 hours. I use mods. I've experienced the AI cluster and not attack settlements here and there but it doesn't seem as bad as people make it out to be. I haven't noticed problems with Missile Units not firing.. I've been having a lot of fun with this game.

My biggest gripe with the game is ladders. If a [i]SINGLE[/i] ladder exists, everyone and their mother wants to use that as opposed to the wide open gates or breaches in a wall. It's easier to never use ladders or the siege towers, because they prioritize them and it can be agonizing. :P

Yes, I recommend this. I put 700 hours into this across several campaigns between Grand Cathay, The Empire, and Wood Elves. I've had a few moderate campaigns between Skaven and High Elves. All within three months. I haven't even gotten to the overhaul mods that add new campaigns and factions..

Looking back on my purchase two weeks ago, this game has more than won me over.

Starting up the game, I soon realized that you don't get a lot of guidance "of the bat" as to where you should begin your journey, or what the game is all about.

But following a prompt to begin the first campaign/prologue called "The Lost God" (functioning as a sort of "tutorial" or introduction into the game) I entered what I felt was a somewhat underwhelmingly silent, empty map, with outdated graphics in low resolution.

This immediately made me rather skeptical to the game.

There was no fireworks, or flashing game mechanics trying to immediately hook me in as I am used to in most other games, but I pressed on for what felt like an hour of reading and soon realized 3 hours had gone by.

Now having passed 90 hours of gameplay in roughly 2 weeks, It's safe to say my addiction to this game has grown profoundly.
90 hours in, I still get the sense that I've just barely touched the surface of what this game has to offer in terms of playability.
The fact that the developers are able to balance over 90 factions, across ~24 different races, many with quite different playstyles and mechanics is astonishing to me.

This game is massive, and at the same time the game mechanics are dynamic enough that most people shape their games to what they like as they go along and grow as a player.

I can play a campaign with the intent to follow and build a believable story, trying to stay true to my characters and faction playstyle, creating allies or destroying foes as they would. (Honorable or holy factions despising undeads and chaotic factions etc.)

Or go a complete opposite route, demolishing everything I come across on the path to world domination, or even giving conquered territory to some other faction, building them up as a partner in the path of world domination.

- I could focus on creating massive armies, fighting awesome battles with guns/arrows/boulders/fireballs/bombs flying across the battlefield.
Or I could skip the real time combat all together, letting the fights be like a throw of dice, focusing on building my empire, or perhaps raiding someone else's empire, bound to no land at all.

Personally, I go back and forth between these as I go along, slowing down animations to slow motion watching bodies or monsters fly from a boulder I threw, or just throw the dice on a battle, depending on what the game throws at me, or maybe just my mood at that time.

If I compare the cost of this game to any other subscription based online MMORPGs like world of warcraft, I honestly don't see the difference in cost, other than people not being used to a strategy game having such insane amounts of complex content, all balanced together in the way Creative Assembly does with Total War: Warhammer 3.

After 90 hours of barely touching the surface of this game, I can wholeheartedly recommend at least trying out the base game for a few hours if you like strategy games with just a little more depth than the standard "close/ranged/air/tank-mechanic with 10 different unit types spread across 5 types"-type of RTS.

[h1] Warhammer und Total War? und das zum dritten mal! [/h1]

Ich bin mit Warhammer schon sehr lang vertraut, auch wenn es primär die Version im 41. Millennium ist. Total War war für mich etwas neues, das ich vorher nur von Erzählungen und YouTube Videos kannte. (Auch wenn ich bereits den zweiten Teil angespielt habe, bin ich nie hinter das Konzept gestiegen, wenn ich ehrlich bin.)

[b]Was kann ich also zu Total War: WARHAMMER III sagen?[/b]
Ich empfand das Tutorial, welches als Prolog verpackt die Geschichte von einem Kislever Prinzen verfolgt, als sehr gelungener Weg neuen Spielern wie mir, das Spielprinzip nahe zu bringen! Die Geschichte war interessant, Grim Dark und Fantasy gefüllt!
Habe ich durch den Prolog alle Mechaniken verstanden, definitiv: Nein. Ich denke das ist auch gar nicht das Ziel. Negativ hervorheben kann man jedoch den Textdump, der vom Tutorial vollzogen wird...
Abgesehen vom Prolog hab ich bisher zwei (weniger erfolgreiche) Kampagnen gespielt, die bis zu meinem Kläglichen ende (zunächst an Dunkelelfen und dann an zu vielen Gruftlords) Spaß gemacht haben!

[h1] Weitere Pros [/h1]
- Unfassbar viele detaillierte Einheiten und Völker mit interessanter Lore
- Komplexe abwechslungsreiche Echtzeitkämpfe (Terrain hat starken Einfluss, Belagerungen usw.)
- Interessante Lore (Viele verschiedene Rassen, die zugleich Einfach genug gestrickt und ausreichend tiefgehend sind)
- viele verschiedene Möglichkeiten, die selbe Rasse zu spielen (verschiedene Lords, Items, RNG usw.)
- viele DLCs die das Spielerlebnis erweitern (+ dafür, das die alten DLCs auch hier wirksam sind!!!!!)

[h1] Cons [/h1]
- extrem Komplexes Spiel, viele Werte die sich gegenseitig beeinflussen, teilweise schwer Nachvollziehbar
- Medium befriedigendes Tutorial im optionalen Prolog (Wenn ihr wie ich neu in Total War seid, spielt unbedingt den Prolog, sonst wisst ihr gar nicht wie das Spiel geht!!!)
- viele DLCs die zwar das Spielerlebnis erweitern, aber die Kosten für das Spiel in die höhe Treiben!

[h1] Konklusion [/h1]
[b]Total War: WARHAMMER III ist ein gelungenes Strategiespiel mit Interessanten Rassen in einer fantasievollen Welt, das scheinbar unendlichen Wiederspielwert hat.[/b] Ich finde den Vollpreis daher gerechtfertigt! Es kann schwer sein in das Spiel einzusteigen, deshalb bekommt es von mir
[b]8.5 von 10 Punkten[/b].

Stop Treating Us Like Cash Cows: A Modder’s Perspective
I desperately want to love this game. I want to love the Total War series. But with every passing year and every lazy release, Creative Assembly (CA) makes it impossible. I’ve reached my breaking point with the sheer incompetence and the "money-first, players-never" attitude that has infected this studio.

The "Impossible" Fixes Let’s look back at the infamous Skullmuncha issue. CA flat-out told the community it was "impossible" to fix. I fixed it in five minutes before I even finished my morning coffee. I turned it into a mod, and suddenly, like magic, CA "remembered" how to fix it themselves. This proves they don't even try, let alone care.

The Texture Disaster The textures for races ported from older games are a complete eyesore—over-saturated and still covered in those damn red dots. Yes, CA, THEY ARE STILL THERE. I spent the last year manually fixing these textures by hand. I reached out and offered them to CA for ZERO compensation. I wanted to give them away for free just to make the game better. Their excuse? "It would increase the file size too much." Absolute nonsense. I rebuilt the data packs myself and the size difference was negligible. They assumed I used lazy AI upscaling; they didn't realize I did the hard work in Photoshop, combining diffuse and specular maps and remaking material maps from scratch because the originals (especially for Vampire Counts and Chaos) look like garbage.

A Legacy of Abandonment Since Shogun 2, this series has been a revolving door of broken releases. Support is dropped while game-breaking bugs—bugs the community has screamed about for years—remain untouched. It is utterly pathetic that every single title requires a "Community Bug Fix" mod just to be playable. CA treats us like walking wallets, pumping out a million overpriced DLCs while the core game is rotting. We aren't dairy cows to be milked; we are the fans that built your company.

My Message to CA Stop focusing on the next $20 Lord Pack and start fixing your damn game. Your "too hard to fix" excuses don't work when modders are doing your job for free in their spare time. You brought this reputation on yourselves.

Final Thought I asked a CA developer how many staff members it takes to change a lightbulb. He told me it was "technically impossible" due to engine limitations, but they’d be happy to sell me a "Daylight DLC" for $15.99 next Tuesday.

Total War: Warhammer III est, en soi, un très bon jeu. Le contenu est riche, l’univers est excellent, et le jeu devient réellement plaisant lorsqu’on y joue entre amis. Les campagnes en multijoueur ( entre amis ) apportent une vraie dimension stratégique et conviviale, et sur ce point, le jeu fait clairement le travail.

Cependant, sur la durée, surtout dans des parties longues en multijoueur, l’expérience devient de plus en plus compliquée et frustrante. Les interruptions constantes pauses automatiques lorsqu’un joueur se fait attaquer, lorsqu’un ami lance un combat, etc cassent complètement le rythme. Plus la partie avance, plus ces arrêts deviennent fréquents, et cela pénalise fortement les autres joueurs qui n’ont rien à faire pendant ce temps-là.

Autre point très frustrant : la politique de contenu payant. Le manque de personnages est flagrant.
Tu veux jouer un autre seigneur ? Paye.
Tu veux jouer plusieurs personnages d’une même faction ? Paye plusieurs fois.

Je ne critique pas le principe de payer pour du contenu supplémentaire c’est normal mais quand on achète quelque chose, la moindre des choses serait d’obtenir la faction complète avec ses personnages, et non de devoir repasser à la caisse à répétition pour jouer pleinement ce qui devrait aller ensemble.

Malgré ces défauts importants, le jeu reste agréable, plaisant à jouer et possède un énorme potentiel, surtout pour les amateurs de stratégie et de l’univers Warhammer. Mais ces choix de conception et de monétisation finissent par nuire à l’expérience sur le long terme, en particulier en multijoueur.

El último que realmente me atrapó fue Shogun 2. Desde ahí, esta etapa más fantástica de la saga nunca terminó de cerrar conmigo. Las unidades, el tono, el enfoque… me pasa exactamente lo mismo que con el Warhammer II: entiendo el atractivo, pero no conecto.

Warhammer III se siente un poco más amigable para jugadores nuevos, eso es verdad. La gestión es más llevadera, más accesible, menos áspera que en entregas anteriores. Pero todo eso se cae cuando vuelve a aparecer el gran problema:
si querés probar más unidades, más facciones, más variedad… tenés que pasar por caja.

Y eso, personalmente, me la baja muchísimo. Sentís que el juego está fragmentado a propósito, diseñado para venderte pedazos de experiencia en lugar de ofrecerte una base completa.

⸻

✅ Puntos positivos:

• Más accesible para jugadores nuevos.
• Gestión más amena y menos engorrosa.
• Muchísimo contenido… si pagás por él.
• Técnicamente sólido.

❌ Puntos negativos:

• Exceso de DLC pagos para disfrutar el juego “completo”.
• Las unidades fantásticas no terminan de convencer (al menos para mí).
• Se siente pensado más como plataforma de venta que como juego cerrado.
• No tiene el encanto estratégico de clásicos como Shogun 2.

⸻

🎯 Conclusión:

Total War: Warhammer III no es un mal juego, pero desde mi punto de vista tenés que ser fan de Warhammer para disfrutarlo de verdad. Como Total War puro, me sigue pareciendo inferior a otros títulos de la saga. Tiene mejoras, sí, pero arrastra decisiones de diseño que le juegan en contra.

🔸 PUNTUACIÓN FINAL: 6/10

📝 REVIEW IN ENGLISH

🔶 Sometimes rediscovering a game in your library says more than buying a new one.

⸻

Total War: Warhammer III caught me by surprise — mostly because I didn’t even remember owning it. So I decided to give it a fair shot.

And just like I said in my Warhammer II review: it’s not a bad game. Not at all. But it’s also not a Total War that truly clicks with me.

The last one that really hooked me was Shogun 2. Since then, this fantasy-heavy direction never fully worked for me. The units, the tone, the overall feel — it’s the same issue I had with Warhammer II. I understand why people love it, but I don’t connect with it.

Warhammer III is definitely more new-player friendly. The management is smoother, more accessible, and less punishing. But all of that loses weight when the core issue shows up again:
if you want more units, more factions, more variety — you have to pay.

That design choice really kills my enthusiasm. The game feels deliberately fragmented, built as a DLC platform rather than a complete experience.

⸻

✅ Pros:

• More accessible for new players.
• Smoother and more approachable management.
• Tons of content… if you pay for it.
• Technically solid.

❌ Cons:

• Excessive paid DLC to experience the “full” game.
• Fantasy units don’t resonate with everyone.
• Feels more like a product ecosystem than a standalone game.
• Lacks the strategic soul of classics like Shogun 2.

⸻

🎯 Conclusion:

Total War: Warhammer III isn’t bad, but you really need to be a Warhammer fan to fully enjoy it. As a Total War experience, it still falls short compared to other entries in the franchise.

🔸 FINAL SCORE: 6/10

[h1]🎮 Reseña de Total War: WARHAMMER III[/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Total War: WARHAMMER III es la receta clásica de “una campaña por turnos para sentirte un genio” + “batallas en tiempo real para demostrar que en realidad eras un improvisado”. Manejas imperios, economía, diplomacia y expansión en gran estrategia, y cuando llega la hora del golpe… te vas al campo de batalla a microgestionar monstruos, infantería y magia como si tu teclado fuera un altar de sacrificios.

La primera impresión es clara: esto no es “estrategia bonita”, es estrategia con esteroides y un lore que te grita en la cara. Es espectacular, sí… pero también es el tipo de juego que te hace decir “solo una batalla más” y de pronto ya amaneció y tu vida social fue absorbida por el Caos. Acción y Estrategia en el mismo paquete: una mano en el mapa, la otra en el pánico.

[h2]El Reino del Orden… y el Caos de tus Decisiones[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ 🧠 Campaña de gran estrategia adictiva: turnos que se van como agua y decisiones que sí importan.  
✅ ⚔️ Batallas tácticas en tiempo real enormes: cuando funciona, es cine bélico-fantástico.  
✅ 🎭 Mucha variedad de facciones/estilos de juego: no juegas “lo mismo con otro color”, aquí cambian reglas y ritmo.  
✅ 🤝 Multijugador y cooperativo: para arruinar amistades en JcJ o fingir coordinación en coop.  
✅ ☁️ Comodidades modernas: Steam Cloud, guardar en cualquier momento y dificultad ajustable (gracias por dejarme ser orgulloso… o prudente).

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ 🤖 IA irregular: a veces brillante, a veces con decisiones que parecen escritas por un goblin con sueño.  
❌ 🧩 Curva de aprendizaje pesada: te lanza sistemas como si fueran confeti… pero de metal.  
❌ 🖥️ Rendimiento exigente en batallas grandes: cuando hay demasiada magia y unidades, tu PC también invoca demonios.  
❌ 🎯 Balance/disparidad entre estilos: algunas estrategias se sienten “correctas”, otras “castigo divino”.  
❌ 🧼 Mucho que gestionar: si odias la administración, aquí vas a sufrir como noble sin impuestos.

[h2]Conclusión (Excelente)[/h2]
Total War: WARHAMMER III es un monstruo de estrategia: gigantesco, vistoso y lo suficientemente complejo como para hacerte sentir un comandante brillante… hasta que una mala batalla te recuerda que eras mortal. Si buscas Acción y Estrategia con escala, variedad y batallas que parecen apocalipsis controlado, aquí hay banquete.

¿Perfecto? No. La IA puede tener lapsos, el rendimiento puede ponerse quisquilloso y la administración puede sentirse como hacer contabilidad en el fin del mundo. Pero con 33346 jugadores activos y 96690 recomendaciones, está claro que la comunidad no está aquí por casualidad: está aquí porque el juego engancha, incluso cuando te hace sufrir.

I got this game when they released it to people who already had Warhammer II and/or I on Christmas last year. I'm not surprised by all the "mixed" reviews, the game is garbage and the support for it is even worse by being non-existent. The game is over beyond the first tutorial battle because after that, at least on a Macbook Pro M2, it quits responding altogether and all menus are inaccessible. There's no way out but to quit and then what? I loved Warhammer II and always wanted a sequel but having read all the reviews over the past few years about Warhammer III I just didn't want to spend my money on trash. Now that I have it for free, it's still trash.

Soooooo I quit alcohol and sort of got really deep down into WH3 for 2 months. The TLDR for you people not wanting to read my whole review: This game fills a void that no other game can, it combines both world domination and RTS. For me as a LOTR fan this comes closes to also filling my void for a fantasy world domination game with interesting RTS combat It also contains so many factions even though you yourself do not own them, they exist in the world and you can fight them. But be ready for awful AI, many bugs and the game recommending ♥♥♥♥ campaigns for you. Lastly of course all the DLC, even though I got into this game late WH2, is really expensive (if you buy everything). If dlc ever is a question their are videos about it on YouTube, what dlc is worth it or not (my fave is the one with Ikit Claw).

So I want to begin with the base game and the base game experience (today everyone has access to the Immortal Empires by just owning any of the earlier games or DLC, which is really great, but I want to start where I started on release). This might sound insane, dumb, or just weird, but the last achievements I completed where all achievements related to Realms of Chaos. Realms of Chaos is the main campaign in the game, leading you on a goose chase for 4 demon souls to then have a big fight to then complete the campaign. In a sense it is fun for some people to have a goal when they play a game, it was refreshing when doing this as my last playthrough, but it has issues. So in Realms of Chaos every 15-30 turns Portals spread all over the map and this is your chance (and opponents chance) to chase 1 soul of your choosing by letting your main lord enter a portal. So far so good. You can of course attack other lord's trying to enter the same realm as you. But here the weakness starts showing which for a new player might be something that they never know or notice. When you enter the portal, the portal stays, which is terrible, first of all it covers the area it is in with corruption and after some turns release armies. This means you need to have armies defending your homeland, but you also have other enemies and you need to expand at the same time to even have a chance against your opponents. You as the player suffer from something the AI do not, supply lines. Supply lines pretty much means that for every army you recruit all your armies and the troops in them become more expensive by a certain %. We can discuss why it is good or bad, but in my mind, supply lines is a stupid system which makes you focus on growing few but big armies with cost efficient troops, it makes your campaigns much less flexible, it is less of an issue in Immortal Empires though, because of not having a race for collecting souls and also having armies constantly appearing in portals. Lastly we have to name anti-player bias, which makes these portals and other factions really annoying. A faction can be at war with you and another faction, but still ignore the other faction, sometimes running through other enemy factions regions just to reach you. My only thought why they keep this in the game is because they somehow are scared that people will get to little combat. You can mod this to make the game better, but I know there are many purists out there, so I really hope they make the AI different in later games. The AI should focus on expanding and actually attacking threats to their supremacy, not only the player. So after all these issues with the portals themselves, we also have the realms themselves, they are not fun. The longer your character is in each realm, the more debuffs (for some weird reason). It actually feels like the realms was made for your annoyance. Many of the issues you have, the AI usually completely avoid, so most of the punishment is usually for the player. If you can accept the annoyance, actually like this in your games (some people do), then the Realm of chaos is for you. There are also other victory conditions that do not need you to collect the souls, but I really recommend doing these other victory conditions in Immortal Empires instead both for less stress and also since you have much more freedom.

So let us talk about Immortal Empires. Immortal Empires is your paint the map mode, where if you do not hunt specific victory conditions, it can be really fun. For me 100% the game I had to face all the issues with the victory conditions, which seem really bad, since they are not really balanced for WH3 and not really on the same level for all factions (I am looking at you wood elves). Atleast completing End Game scenarios counted as actually completing a long game victory (in terms of achievement). End Game scenarios are basically scenarios that happen after a certain amount of turns (if on) that spawns multiple armies (the strength and type of the armies are decided in the campaign options screen before campaign start). The armies are mainly your enemy, but they also become the enemy of other nearby factions. I can talk about every faction and their issues, but I won't. I will leave a general note according to issues with factions: Many factions have not been touched in a long time and are not balanced for WH3 (looking at you Brettonia). Many factions also have very few landmarks (unique buildings with unique effects). As a last part connected to specifically campaigns in Immortal Empires, I wish similar factions to your own was stronger, since many factions have mechanics to confederate lord's of the same races and they just die off long before that happens.

Next part diplomacy, diplomacy in Warhammer is really simple. You trade, you make non-aggression pacts, defensive alliances or military alliances. Some factions focus more on making vassals (kinda like making a faction your slave, forcing them to join your wars). In WH3 they also added the ability for giving and taking settlements. This system is flawed both ways tbh, if this system would be better it would also help the victory conditions for some factions requiring you to own certain places. They added some weird artificial wall that makes it almost impossible to buy a settlement from another faction, you usually have to swap settlements instead and the value they put on their own settlements vs you own is really insane. Most of the time it is impossible to buy some settlements, however much money you would offer. They also added a reliability value for you the player and no one else, meaning that the AI can act however they want without consequences, but if you declare war to close to a non-aggression pacts ending or you do not want to join a completely unnecessary war you allied created, suddenly all factions will see you as the most evil person ever, declare war on you, end trade agreements and so on. My wish for the future is a more interesting diplomacy system where the AI and you actually can make interesting agreements. For example why is peace seen as something negative, yes you made peace with a faction that is probably the enemy of your friends as well, but understanding war is understanding nuance. Peace might be needed when there are too many fronts and your friends should be understanding or not react in a childish manner. They should really rework how other factions react to vassals, they should not see you negatively for vassalizing an enemy, they should be happy and vassals should not hate each other.

So factions I guess? I will keep it really short on this point. This game has many factions and I cannot explain all of them. Generally the newer the factions, the more interesting, but with more updates, more and more factions become viable. I will also give the game a plus here, they have added free factions throughout all games which are actually really good in some cases. I will not even try to talk about balance, this game is really not balanced, but I wish some factions had better economy, sometimes I also wish for alternative starts. 85 hours.

85 hours that included a 10 hour tutorial and one single High Elf campaign using Tyrion.

That's just one (1) leader. ONE of HUNDREDS across DOZENS of factions. Now those 1000s of hours of playtime from most fans makes a lot more sense: it's not just for the love of the game, that's simply how long an Immortal Empire can take. 

While I'm sure that sounds way, WAY too long for most veterans, this was my first time ever playing this genre, and what an uphill battle it was (positive). Hours of off-game time doing research and watching videos, plus many more hours of restarting saves, making horrendous mistakes, and completely misunderstanding my army until the last 20-30 hours when it all clicked. 

It was grueling. It was never easy, It was satisfying in a way I haven't felt in a long time. 

That's not to say it was a flawless experience: load times are abysmal and should be an embarrassment of Creative Assembly. The inability to undo a move is a pain, and oftentimes you're not totally sure how you Lord will take a path. Army sizes can't be adjusted mid-game, meaning if you chose the Low setting due to your computer specs but later benchmarked a higher possibility, you're stuck with tiny squads that make battles feel less epic after looking up a few more videos. 

And that's still not everything. Autoresolve is often crap, monetization is a HUGE hurdle if you haven't been a fan since day one, siege battles are boring at best, and this game is way more demanding than it has any right to be--it looks good, but not THAT good. 

But despite all of these flaws, there's something so special about this experience. You're never in a position to snowball your way through the entire map, and danger can strike at any time. Alliances can rise and fall, your best-laid plans can be stonewalled after two turns, battles can turn from a predicted victory to absolute victory, money can go as easy as it comes... it's insane just how eventful and addictive the experience can be. Long evenings could turn into late nights on a weekday if I wasn't careful. 

I have so much more to see and experience, and I'm so excited. I hope CA and Sega can stop being such ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to their community and get their asses back on track for 40k and beyond, but what I have now is going to tide me over for the entireity of 2026 and beyond.

Ich spiele meistens das Imperium. Weil Artillerie.
Während andere auf Monster, Magie oder fliegende Albträume setzen, glaube ich an etwas Höheres: Artillerie in allen Formen. Nichts ist befriedigender, als zuzusehen, wie Artillerie das Chaos ordnet.

Meine natürlichen Feinde?
Waldelfen. Diese verfluchten, baumumarmenden Gänseblümchen Schnüffler aus Laub und Pfeilen. Du marschierst ordentlich, Linien stehen, Artillerie bereit und plötzlich spricht der Wald. Pfeile aus dem Nichts, Einheiten verschwinden, Moral zerbricht, und du fragst dich, seit wann Bäume taktische Entscheidungen treffen. Meine Antwort darauf ist Forstwirtschaft mit Schwarzpulver. Jeder Wald ist potenziell feindlich, jede Baumlinie ein Hinterhalt. Wenn der Wald zurückschießt, wird er gerodet und niedergebrannt. Vollständig. Systematisch. Mit Kanonen.

Und dann sind da die Skaven.
Diese verdammten Ratten haben Massenvernichtungswaffen. Vor allem Ikit Claw dieser kleine, miese alte Hurensohn auf zwei Beinen. Erst kommt die halbe Armee per Tunnel direkt in deine Backline und zerlegt Artillerie und Fernkampf. Und wenn du denkst, schlimmer wird’s nicht, fällt dir plötzlich auf, dass gerade eine zweite Sonne in deinen Truppen aufgegangen ist. Skaven sind eine Fraktion, in der Leben weniger wert sind als die Munition, die man verschießt. Sie schießen auf dich, sie schießen auf den Gegner, und oft genug schießen sie einfach auf sich selbst. Und jedes Mal denke ich mir: Das dürfte eigentlich nicht funktionieren tut es aber. Leider.

Warhammer III lebt von Eskalation: absurde Fraktionen, übertriebene Schlachten, Momente zwischen „genial“ und „warum existiert das“. Und genau darin liegt der Reiz. Wenn meine Linien halte, fühlt sich selbst der Weltuntergang kontrollierbar an… zu beginn… dann nicht mehr… Linien? Welche Linien? Am ende rennt alles einfach nur noch gegeneinander.

Empfehlung?
Ja. Für Trolle, Artillerie-Fetischisten und alle, die glauben, dass Ordnung manchmal aus Schwarzpulver besteht.

While this game was never as polished or well thought out as Total War Hammer 2 which managed to continually improve throughout its life cycle and finished on high note. TWH3 did start out in a place with a lot of potential with Creative Assembly's talk of upcoming plans making it sound as though even if the game had a slow start it was building to be a great ending of the series. Sadly most of what Creative Assembly said ended up never appearing and while they did make marked improvements that lead to me hopping the game would reach a stable place so at least we could have a solid foundation for mod support. Creative Assembly seems to have made the decision that the game isn't worth the support need to get it to a solid place because after second major update to fix issues they seemed to decide that instead of doing the work required to finish off the remaining major issues it would be better to focus on minor fixes. Which wouldn't be terrible were it not for the fact that even when addressing theses minor issues they don't seem to want to have the developers invest the time to properly test the fixes before pushing them. So we get a stream of mini fixes that then result in multiple other bugs all while dam near game breaking bugs for some factions sit around for months at a time while they basically put out small fixes to some of the problems created by the last hot fix. I have also found that the DLC's have reached a point where they are so poorly tested before they are sold that they are often releasing with massive bugs as well. Which is crazy because how is their not enough qa testing for a product that is going to be sold for them to realize that units added with the dlc don't work. Like I could understand not realizing that the dlc may change an older unit in an unexpected manner ,but anything added in the dlc should work from day one and instead we get buggy units/campaigns that are then fixed weeks to months after you have already paid for the product. 

Personally as it stand I would suggest that anyone looking to get into Total War: Warhammer purchase 2 because at least that way you are getting a solid game with good mod support. Unlike 3 which seems to become more unreliable with every hotfix, patch, or dlc. It really is so disappointing because I really enjoy the factions and the mods for this game ,but as time has gone on the game seems to have more and more technical issues that bring down the whole experience. To the point that i have had to stop playing whole factions because of how the bugs have affected game play. As someone who loves fantasy and Total War the Warhammer series was like a dream come true and it is really sad to see how Creative Assembly took all of the improvements we saw from 1 to the end of TWW 2 and instead of deciding to build on them to make an amazing end of the series they decided to turn the final game into a cash grab the was seemingly was never given the development resources it needed to become a good product let alone an improvement over the other games in the series.

This is definitly the way to go if you know you like the Total War series/game play. If you are unsure then TWW3 is the culmination of the balance tweaks and changes of the series and is the best place to start. Still buy it on sale.

As for as the game itself - half the time its turn-based empire managment and the other half is real time battles which are thrilling once you get the swing of fighting.
Do you need to like the Warhammer Fantasty asthetic to enjoy the game? No, but if you dislike the asthetic, characters etc then don't try don't buy. For me as a Warhammer fan, it enhances the gameplay, see models come to life living and breathing with wonderful animations and details in the world.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
TW:W3 is a turn-based Total War game set in the Warhammer Fantasy tabletop universe, without historical realism for magic, monsters, and machines. It features a narrative Story Mode and a sandbox called Immortal Empires, which has the largest map in the entire series (and most people play this version). While the base game offers plenty of content, you'll eventually need DLCs to access the full variety and deeper and “cool” mechanics. Unlike other historical TW games, I think TW:W3 is quite beginner-friendly with a simple building system focused on growth, order, and corruption. Combat follows a rock-paper-scissors logic across different unit tiers, and you just need to manage climates to avoid debuffs. When you are playing ultimate sandbox mode, your goal is simple: conquer or raze everything in your path.
[h2] Graphics [/h2]
Honestly, the graphics are decent, but the atmosphere is mostly dark. If you try to turn up the brightness, you have to deal with the blinding whites on snow maps; they definitely failed to find a good balance there. Another thing is that you literally need a DLC just to get proper blood effects. Other than those issues, the graphics are good and watching the units on the battlefield feels really satisfying.
[h2] Audio [/h2]
Unlike other TW games, I actually really like the sound design in this one. Since it's not just humans, the voices of different factions add a lot of variety to the game. You can easily tell who's "evil and cruel" just by their voices. The battlefield sounds are also great; as unit variety increases, you hear a wider range of noises. The screams, shouts, monster roars, and cannon blasts really get you hyped up during the fight.
[h2] Story [/h2]
Honestly, I recommend taking a look at the "Warhammer Fantasy" lore outside the game because that’s what everything is built on. In TW:W3, you're just playing as a faction leader within this universe, but the background lore is absolutely massive. The game’s story mode focuses on the search for Ursun, Kislev's lost god, but I'll leave it at that for now. As for the sandbox mode, there isn't any set story to follow.
[h2] Difficulty [/h2]
First off, the game's difficulty changes a lot depending on which faction you play. Some start out easy and chill, while others get attacked from all sides and just struggle to survive. But generally speaking, the campaign AI is terrible. As someone who plays on Very Hard (I skip Legendary because of its annoying restrictions), nobody can stand in my way once I reach a certain power level. No one even bothers to form alliances against me to make things challenging. On top of that, the AI is trash at calculating power levels and just feeds its armies to me for no reason. It never protects its cities properly; it tries to recruit armies in border settlements, and by the time I attack, they get wiped out before they can even finish. Their entire territory just ends up defenseless. In my opinion, the worst and most frustrating part of the game is how stupid the AI is, and to hide this, they just give it cheat-like bonus buffs. Even with those, it’s still pretty incompetent.

Let me just tell you how stupid its math is. I don't really truly understand it, so I may be wrong, feel free to correct me:

When the hitbox of the weapon of your unit meets with the hurtbox of an enemy it starts the calculations. There are limits to how many units can be damaged by one attack, so often units that fly away from a powerful attack in fact take no damage at all. 

First, the Melee Attack is calculated against the Melee Defence. If they are the same, your unit has only 35% chance to do damage. I changes by +/- 1% for every 1 point of a difference, min. 8%, max. 90%. 

If the attack passes through that check, the damage is calculated. The unit does as many damage to the enemy's HP, as its Weapon Strenght value. However, the Damage value is reduced by Armour. Armour reduces a random value ranging between half its value and its value, but the Armour value is capped at 200. Some of the damage may be armour-piercing, meaning that certain damage value is not affected by enemy's Armour at all. This gives you the Unmodified Damage. 

The Unmodified Damage can then be modified by various percentage changes, depending on unit's traits. A weapon can deal either physical or magical damage - if so its damage is modified by an appropriate Weakness or Resistance, capped at 90%. If the weapon is Flaming, you also calculate to that enemy's Fire Resistance or Weakness. Bear in mind that certain races easily stack a lot of Fire and Magic Resistance. 

Now riddle me this: if you are playing as the Grand Cathay fighting both the Chaos Warriors and Skavens, is it better for the average melee damage dealt by your generic general to equip a sword that adds a flat +25 armour-piercing weapon damage, or one that increases its whole Weapon Strength by 10% and makes its attacks both Magical and Flaming?

The answer is: it doesn't matter. You do not need to understand TW math to win. You only need to cheese the AI.

TW:WH3 is one of my most‑played games. My relationship with it has been a mix of admiration for the game and frustration with the company. I’ve followed creators like LegendofTotalWar since WH1, and they helped me appreciate the series more and more (until the end). Many players’ negative reviews feel rooted less in the game itself and more in how the company handled pricing and communication. I respect that stance, and I think the recent price “drop” only happened because the community pushed back.

For new players, the context matters. From a medium‑skill perspective, most bugs aren’t game‑breaking for casual play. Fixes do arrive—sometimes slowly—but the team does address (most) issues. The factions are varied and fun, with different playstyles to explore. Battles are great, though sieges can drag, and I often auto‑resolve them. Resource management is solid, and the magic and item systems have improved. Early‑ to late‑game progression is enjoyable, though once I build an unstoppable army, the campaign can feel formulaic. More diverse endgame scenarios or lore‑driven win conditions would help.

Overall, the game itself is genuinely fun, and I do recommend it. Play the base game, wait for sales, and pick the factions that interest you—you don’t need everything to enjoy the experience. If the company slips back into bad habits, the community has shown it’s willing to hold them accountable. I hope the lesson sticks, and I appreciate the developers who make the game great.

战锤作为全战的巅峰之作，内容量应该是全系列最多的。你问我为什么打差评?
因为全战系列逐渐抛弃了自己的战术，尤其是开了这个头的战锤系列，玩家的流程核心并不是战术操作，而是大部分时间都花费在叠各种buff,叠垃圾兵堆自动分
什么？你说你想要全部手操？全部手操的后果就是不可避免的变成某叠buff单位高出场率，而最高难度下基本变成单体叠叠乐。
你问我为什么一定要叠叠乐，不叠就等着和一堆50级英雄一个技能直接弄死一群兵说吧。战锤3相比2代再次进化，更加强调buff和单体性能，由于大家的英雄和领主都有抽象buff还能上装备，经常一个领主可以单挑好几支部队，配上技能两三个领主基本可以杀光20支一本兵。如果你不这样玩你又会被敌人恶心，毕竟敌人领主也是能放技能的，高难度下车轮战几回一个技能下来起码你也死个小半队兵，你的常规部队死了都没法补充，而单体单位不容易死，也不会出现掉兵模（掉血）等于掉战斗力的情况，领主等等如果有回血技能可以无限车轮战别人

所以战锤3虽然内容很多，但是所有势力都只有前期好玩，到后期就不可避免的滑坡变成这样了，要嘛走手操全单体流，要嘛走自动分垃圾兵平推流，战术是一点没有的，输赢全看技能

After more than 1000 hours in Total War: WARHAMMER III, this is easily one of the most complete and replayable strategy games available on Steam.

The scale is massive. With Immortal Empires, the game becomes a near-endless sandbox where every campaign feels different depending on faction, starting position, and diplomacy. The variety between races is exceptional: each one plays by its own rules, with unique mechanics that genuinely change how you approach both the campaign map and battles. This is not cosmetic variety; it is mechanical depth.

The real-time battles are the best the Total War series has ever offered. Unit animations, spell effects, monsters, flying units, and heroes create battles that are both tactical and spectacular. Balance has improved significantly over time, and the game now feels stable, polished, and well-supported. Performance, AI behavior, and quality-of-life features are in a much better state than at launch.

On top of that, mod support is outstanding and extends the game’s lifespan almost indefinitely. Combined with frequent updates and DLC that meaningfully expand gameplay, this is a title you can keep coming back to for years.

Pros

Enormous replayability (especially Immortal Empires)

Deep and varied faction mechanics

Excellent real-time battles and visuals

Strong modding community

Continuous post-launch support

Cons

Steep learning curve for new players

Full experience requires DLC investment

Verdict:
If you enjoy grand strategy, large-scale battles, and long-term campaigns, Total War: WARHAMMER III is a must-own. After 1000+ hours, it still offers new challenges and reasons to start “one more campaign.” Highly recommended.

Before I get into it, I have spent HOURS doing research on this game and watching countless playthroughs before buying. I wanted to leave this review early in my playtime life of the game so the research i did and initial impressions of the game were both as fresh in my mind as can be.

So this game is interesting to me. I am a HUGE Warhammer fan, both Aos and 40k. I know the lore and play the table top games. But total war was never a game on my radar until recently, and after looking at the mixed reviews, it took me a bit to even purchase the game. For me at least, i wish i hadn't waited. 

There is a lot of lore packed into this game. I have 7 hours in and just barely finished the prologue campaign (Its Kislev, they're ice themed badasses with ice bears, its great). I tell you this because the "small single player campaigns" aren't small. At least not to me. And thats not even considering the main thing this game has going for it, which is Immortal Empires. 

Immortal Empires is where ALL the factions are on one map. It is, for all intents and purposes, the actual main game of Total War Warhammer 3. The campaigns are more akin to faction tutorials with some nice lore. They are a blast, for sure, but Immortal Empires is where the main game play is. Now. Regardless of what DLC you own, all factions are there as enemies and they all kick ass in their own way. Now i say all factions are on one map because you cant play with every faction initially which is where the game gets its mixed reviews from.

The long and the short of it is that the game released with less than stellar acclaim due to bugs and not doing a good enough job telling people how its DLC work. So let me do that real quick. If you own any of the previous warhammer games (1 or 2) or any of the DLC from the previous games, the faction leaders (Called lords) and their unique units from said content are available to you. 

If you find yourself wanting a certain faction, do a quick internet search and buy the dlc that has the faction leader for the faction you want, and thats really it. BUT!!!!!! That only unlocks that faction and lord for Immortal Empires. Which to be clear again, Immortal Empires is really the main game. 

That's pretty much it. Each lord in each faction plays different, each faction, lord and to a greater extent greater faction (Order, Chaos, Ruin) all play in unique and fun ways. The mixed reviews are mostly for confusion over how the DLC worked and initial bugs which for the most part are long since fixed. So if you (like me and many others) are waiting for Total War 40K or Dawn of War 4 to come out and you want to sink your teeth into something pretty damn fun and expansive, this is probably a good fit for you. 

Happy gaming!

Total War: Warhammer III is, at its core, an excellent strategy game.
The scale of Immortal Empires, the faction variety, and the sheer ambition of combining three games into one massive sandbox is genuinely impressive. Battles feel weighty, factions are meaningfully different, and when everything clicks, this is one of the most enjoyable Total War experiences available.

However, the DLC strategy seriously undermines that experience.

This isn’t about being “anti-DLC”. I have no problem with cosmetic DLC, expansions, or optional content done well. Games like Warframe prove that monetisation can exist without damaging the core experience.

The problem here is that core faction identity is segmented and resold.

Armies that exist in the game world from day one are partially or completely locked behind DLC.
If a faction happens to be your favourite, the DLC stops being optional and starts feeling mandatory just to make that army feel complete. You’re not paying for something extra — you’re paying to finish what you already bought.

What makes this worse is that this isn’t just a pricing issue — it’s an experience issue. Progression, mastery, and understanding are fractured when content is sliced up this way. Instead of learning and growing naturally with a faction, you’re presented with gaps that can only be filled by opening your wallet.

Yes, you can technically ignore the DLC.
But doing so means accepting a lesser version of the game, especially if you care about certain armies.

That creates a constant sense of being nickel-and-dimed in a game that otherwise thrives on long-term investment and mastery.

Verdict:
Total War: Warhammer III is a fantastic strategy sandbox that I enjoy playing.
But its DLC model feels exploitative of player attachment and actively detracts from the sense of completeness and progression.

I recommend it with caution — go in with open eyes, buy selectively, and understand that enjoying your favourite faction fully may cost far more than the base game suggests.

Long Review (for people who can read):

- I recently purchased the full game and all of the WH2 content. 

After more than a FULL DAY of playtime in less than two weeks, I can safely say that: 
This game is good. VERY good. 

Realms of Chaos has been my favorite so far, since the turns are much faster as the "bloat factions" basically make no appearance on the map. There seems to be an issue with consistency between runs, however, as playing as Khorne is essentially RP'ing as God during his teenage angst phase - whereas playing Slaanesh feels like taking the role of an anorexic Victorian loom operator. (I love Slaanesh though, the units are cool - the corruption is cool).

Immortal Empires is ok. The biggest map I've ever seen in a Total War game to date in terms of settlement count (though that isn't exactly a positive since it slows the game down WAY too much imo) with a variety of factions that genuinely feel distinct to play.
It's one of the first times I can remember playing a game in this franchise where I'm encouraged NOT to take over the entire map - and instead focus on objectives given to my character (including quest battles, which are SUCH a neat idea - fighting a dragon so I can KEEP said dragon playing as Norsca? *chefs kiss*).

Multiplayer has been a blast as well, I'm not that great at it since I don't have nearly as many hours as other players - but the community has been really nice to me as a newcomer (had an opponent actually correct me on my use of Slaanesh units - then rematch me so I could see how much better it was to use them in a different way, a unique experience I hope to have more of in the future).

Overall, the game plays good, looks good and the music is amazing. The visuals of a Bretonian Cavalry charge into a horde of Nurglings cannot be beat. The feeling of winning a battle the auto resolve says will be a "valiant defeat" - losing only three rats in your swarm - cannot be beat. The music that accompanies it all is just brilliant - to say the least.
