Theoretically great game, awful company. My review is more a review of the developers, not the game itself. Greedy dlc model and barely fixing issues with the game.

DLC greed: Most factions are locked behind dlcs or owning the previous games. And the factions you do get with the base game feel somewhat incomplete. A great example is tzeentch. Without dlc, your only decent infantry are chaos halberdiers, a tier 3 unit (tiers go from 1-5, the higher, the better). Tzeentch basicaly doesn't get a frontline. For that, you need to buy a dlc which gives you chosen swordsmen and halberdiers, both of which are t4 infantry. Without them, tzeentch doesn't have a proper army. I can understand not adding a dozen free factions to the game with updates and instead selling the as dlcs. I don't like, but I can understand it. But making the base game factions incomplete so that you have to buy dlcs to play them properly is too much.

Developers attitude to fixing issues: While by far not the only example, one of the best ones has to be the lizardmen AI bug. I didn't play back then, but from what I've seen in the community forums, the lizardmen AI was bugged for eight months. And the bug was quite severe. The bug was that the AI doesn't play the game. It just sits around and doesn't do anything, making it easy for other factions to pick them apart. That bug went unfixed for eight months. Only after LegendofTotalWar, a youtuber who has now stepped back from the total war genre, made a video about it did the developers finally decide to fix it. And they did fix it, so this isn't specifically about the lizardmen AI bug specifically, it's about the devs attitutude when it comes to addressing issues with the game.
I could go on and on about this, about the gate bug that has apparently been present in total war for eight games. Not just eight months in one game, but eight games as a whole, and never been fixed, or about the issues with units getting stuck on each other, or about ranged units not firing, or units forgetting what orders you gave them. But I don't want to get into it that much, because I've made my point.

Lastly, I want to talk about the campaign AI. This isn't something that's wrong with the game, it's just something I think could use improvements to make the game a lot more interesting. The current problem is that the only really interesting part of the campaign is the early game. Once you survive the initial struggle, the campaign becomes pretty easy. In the early stages of the game, you have very limited resources, which you need to make the most out of in order to survive. You need to  consider where you want to take your armies and what battles you want to pick. As the game goes on, this becomes less and less relevant. The AI is terrible at keeping up with the player in the late game. The main issue I noticed is army positioning. The AI has no idea where to place its armies. I once declared war on an AI while I had eight armies right at its borders. The AI immediately rushed to fight me - with one army. It sent one army against my eight. It kept two and a half armies near one of its settlements. I approached with three armies to fight them - the AI rushed one army against one of mine, lost the one versus one and just kept the two other armies where they were, letting me overwhelm them with my three armies. The AI also had a few other armies, each of which it either did nothing with or sent on solo suicide mission. The AI has no idea how to strategically use its armies. This makes the game too easy in the late game, and changing the difficulty doesn't address that issues. The difficulty just gives the AI more resources and the player fewer, but the AI is still just as dumb as before and can be easily outmaneuvered. Honestly, I think this is the biggest issue the game has. The battles and campaign can be fun, but often, the AI is too stupid to make them feel interesting.

Devs have a bad, greedy dlc policy and don't fix issues in the game. If not for that, I would leave a positive review, even with the issues I have with the campaign AI being too dimwitted to make the game very interesting, because I do think that the game is pretty fun. But with these devs, I just can't give it a positive review.

Total War: Warhammer I was the first game I ever purchased on Steam and as a fan of the fantasy genre, it felt like a miracle. Such large-scale and complex battles unfold with modern fidelity. Fast forward to Warhammer 3, which is on a scale that feels enormous, I feel the community has taken the original magic of the franchise for granted. There is no doubt that Creative Assembly has made some horrendous decisions during the development of the third game, from its abysmal launch to the incredibly inconsistent delivery of DLCs. That being said much of the mistakes that took this franchise down from reaching its full potential comes down to the greedy corporation that runs it and not the passion and hard work of the developers who actually build the game piece by piece. Because of these greedy corporate types who have had catastrophic impacts all over the gaming industry, I often see fans attack the developers when they should be attacking the decision makers not the people who have to follow tighter budgets due to failures of other SEGA projects. 

However as the game is reaching the end of its life and we look towards 40k, I hope fans look back at this trilogy fondly as an attempt from developers to deliver something that has never been done before in terms of scale, detail, unit variety, and visuals. While some things may never get fixed, like boring endgames and practically non-existent diplomacy, we should hold our heads up high as many of the things we complain about now may be resolved and improved upon in the much-anticipated 40K universe. Overall the Total War: Warhammer franchise has been a spectacle to behold. When the DLC drops are meaningful and impactful, it is one of the best gaming experiences in my opinion.

To drop into a fresh campaign with new units, new lord mechanics, a starting position you've never played in, a giant map, and when you look at it from that perspective compared to other games for $80 and the cost of some DLC, the amount of hours you can sink into a game like this is truly worth it. Thank you to C.A. for all you've tried to do and a big ♥♥♥♥ you the brainless leaders of SEGA who stopped this game from reaching the full breadth of what it could accomplish. But I think fans should appreciate that they did not fall extremely far. And over the years it has without a doubt produced many memorable campaigns, battles, and cinematic trailers.

It's been a few years since Total War: Warhammer III has been out and Immortal Empires was patched in along with quite a few paid DLCs that have come out since then. To this day (at the beginning of 2026), TW:WH is content wise the largest scale strategy game that has ever been made. Ten years in the making, there's currently over 100 mostly unique legendary lords with their own campaign and over two dozen different factions with their unique and distinct unit roster. That is before mods, which can pretty much double that content.

At the point of this review, the main downside I often hear about it the very high price for getting everything. And to this I can genuinely claim: Even at full price without any discounts, it is absolutely worth it if you are willing and able to sink in the thousands of hours necessary to play everything. This won't apply to most players that play a game for less than 100 hours, but those are perfectly fine with just getting the base game and ignoring any and all DLCs or getting only one ortwo they are most interested in. But anyone that is going to play this game for a substantial amount of time will get their moneys worth even if they shell out 500 quid for everything undiscounted. And you don't need to do that, with all the sales all year round the entire content over all three games can be bought for around 200 with a little bit of patience.

There's nothing not to like about this, apart maybe from entitlement and not being able to grasp the amount of work that has gone into developing a game of this scale. The playerbase has been pretty constant for the last 10 years as well, so CA objectively must have done some things quite right.

I have never seen a game with so many fundamentally different factions that isn't sprite based. This franchise isn't like most other games where different factions just get a repaint and that's that. Every faction has unique models, animations, completely different game mechanics and an entire campaign to themselves with quest events, voice acting, cinematics, lore and unique faction lord legendary item quests of up to five per lord, usually on a unique map of their own on top of that.

At this point in time I have spent 400 hours with a single TW:WH3 faction and have played 3 of the total of 100 legendary lords. I've spent more than 20.000 hours in TW:WH2 to play literally everything, so just going by the new content of the third game along, I still have quite a wayto go with the third installment. It does not get boring.

Worth every damn penny thrice over, and I bought everything at almost full price when it released. I hope CA and especially SEGA don't read this, but I also would have paid more than double for everything and still would have been happy.

TL;DR: Really fun strategy game in the Warhammer Fantasy universe! Pricing of content and DLC is weird and expensive, but you only need the DLC for the factions you want to play, and if you own anything from the old games you own it here as well.

-----------

Really fun "just one more turn" game! Looks like it would play like Civilization games, but it plays more like boardgames like Smallworld or Risk with a lot of unique mechanics for each faction. Each faction and each lord feels really unique, to the point where some factions are like entirely different games. Not balanced by any measure, but fun. Whether you like warhammer lore or not, the game is fun, and you can really see that a lot of love has gone into the development.

Oh, and there's real-time strategy battles if that's your cup of tea. Honestly though, I've played hundreds of turns using nothing but auto-resolve. Maybe on harder difficulties it becomes more important to actually learn the battle mechanics, but I'm cruising along on normal difficulty with Skaven on auto-resolve.

The game is a real performance hog, so beware if your hardware is lacking. My computer isn't the newest, and I can hear every fan inside go into overdrive as soon as I boot up the game. I've heard a lot of complaints about crashes and game-breaking bugs, but I'm almost 70 hours into the game and it hasn't crashed once, and the only bugs I've noticed is that it can be a bit finnicky to place armies next to each other on the map.

The pricing for the game isn't the greatest. It's expensive and confusing at best, and predatory and misleading at worst. On the plus side, you don't need every DLC to play the game; just get the factions you're interested in playing as and ignore the rest. You don't need to own the factions for them to show up in the massive Immortal Empires campaign, so only get them if you really think you're going to play them, and if you alreay own the previous games and DLC you automatically own them in this as well.

This is the best 4X game ever made; however, this is a heavily qualified positive review. 

This is an ecstatic and complex game with a lot of issues. I will begin with a basic overview and conclude with the state of the game as it continues to be updated. Summary at the bottom. 

Gameplay:
What you see is what you get for the most part. Awesome Warhammer fantasy models go head to head in RTS (with pause) battles and you complete grand 4x campaigns on a large map. The animations are breathtaking if your PC isn't a potato. The battles are snappy, strategic, and have a lot of depth. Easy to learn, hard to master. 

Graphics:
This game looks great for the most part. It is sometimes poorly optimized and demands good hardware to run well. The graphics are immersive and watching your units commit violence against your enemies provides otherworldly levels of satisfaction.

Story:
The hard coded story and cutscenes are mediocre at best. They function like a chopped of singular warcraft cinematic. The accompanying campaign, The Realm of Chaos, is frustrating and poorly designed. Originally, the game only released with this campaign which upset pretty much everyone. The way you acquire the McGuffins can be somewhat fun depending on which faction you pick the first time or two. The way your faction's individual story unfolds is compelling overall but it severely harmed by the execution. After 6 months of this miserable campaign, players were finally given the Immortal Empires campaign. Much more in line with traditional Total War, the story here is driven entirely by you, the events in your empire, and your imagination. It's utterly brilliant and the experience is truly your own. Story wise, Immortal Empires is fantastic. 

Sound Design:
I'm not an audio guy. This is the least important part of a game to me. Simply, it's average. There isn't a lot of variety and you will for sure hear some repetition. It doesn't help or hurt the game it gets the job done. The musical score is quite good though overall. 

Technical Performance:
Besides being a challenge to run the game well, the game is a jumbled mess of awful spaghetti code. The developers outsourced most of the DLC to overseas companies. This would be fine if the DLC wasn't intertwined with the basic game at every level regardless of if you bought it. There are bugs that have been in the game since launch that haven't been fixed and new ones are added with each DLC they release. Bugs range from minor and niche to highly noticeable. Some factions' specific mechanics have in the past or continue to simply not work, making them unplayable or unintentionally weak and unbalanced. Unlocking them typically costs real money so you have to look up whether they work before purchasing them. 

Multiplayer Live Service:
Servers are available for you to host and play campaigns with your friends. It's extremely fun but the developer doesn't provide any other service besides the servers. The game balancing is pitiful. Premium factions are strictly better than free ones most of the time and obliterate their free competition with next to no effort. You and your friends should play cooperatively or enforce a laundry list of special rules to make the game less absurd. The other multiplayer option is custom games (mostly fighting one off battles against others). Again, all that is provided are servers. The balancing has improved slightly over the years and they occasionally tweak powerful individual units but the vanilla meta lacks diversity. Players are again forced to create rules, formats, and matchmaking communities. You have little to no hope of finding a good match just within the game. 

Total War Philosophy: 
Default AI and singleplayer campaign setup is hard-coded to annoy you instead of creating a balanced experience. I have never played a single second of an unmodded campaign and I never intend to. The new player friendly" factions even on normal difficulty will be apocalyptic for a player who is brand new to the franchise without intense save scumming (which sterilizes your experience). Depending on which faction you choose, certain AI factions will behave differently.  Rather than create AI that behaves like a player and tries to win, instead it is cheesed to create artificial number checks at various stages in the game. For example, if you pick a "good" aligned faction. The "evil faction" who is 4 or 5 empires away from you will not expand beyond a certain hard-coded point. They will reach a certain size and amass as many armies as they can, often bankrupting themselves. Quantity over quality, these will be the dumbest armies you have ever seen, but there is going to be 5 of them. It's turn 60, and you will most likely steamroll them because legendary lords are utterly cracked when leveled up. There's is level 18 because they have been sitting there for 30 turns waiting for you. Utterly stupid. I use an AI mod to make the AI behave like it's trying to actually win the game. It removes some of the hard coded early game events that are somewhat challenging but makes it so I don't come across as many trash-tier armies in the late game. If they had a balance philosophy, it would be to make you mad so you buy more DLC. 

Workshop content:
Bless any of you who create workshop content. Thank you so much from the bottom of my heart. You are doing someone's literal 6 figure job for them. You are a saint and deserve so many blessings. Do you have strong opinions like me and many other nerds who might play this type of game? That's fine a balder nerd coded up a solution to your problem and it works great! Without the workshop content, the game is literally unplayable in my opinion. It's free though so I don't think it's a very tough solution. Tragic it has to be one though.  

The state of the game:
It's pretty pathetic for a 4 year old game, but the game is extremely fun. The developers don't have a lot of trust from the community. They have not delivered on many of the promises they made on social media. There is hope that the game is mostly free of bugs before it goes into life support mode at some point. If not, workshop modders will probably have it fixed in a year or two. 

Pricing scheme:
This long-winded discussion doesn't belong in a game review. Simply put, it's predatory, and you need to put in a lot of hours to get your money's worth. 

Summary:
This game is your dreamy goth gf. She is beautiful and everything you ever wanted but she absolutely has major emotional problems. You have fun together as long as she takes her medication which she sometimes forgets. You can be together but she isn't going to make it easy. You end up paying for most of the things you do together. You go to couples counseling but she insists that you do it on zoom with her friend from another country. Their accent is so thick that you can barely understand them.

Total War: WARHAMMER III is a really strong strategy game when you are actually playing it. The faction variety is huge, battles are cinematic, and the Immortal Empires campaign is basically a giant fantasy sandbox that can eat hundreds of hours of your life if you are into this style of game. When everything is working, it feels like one of the best large scale fantasy strategy games ever made. Recent DLC has been kind of mixed. Some newer content has been received really well, while other packs have gotten pretty split or negative reactions, so it really depends on which ones you are looking at.

The biggest complaints from players usually are not about the core gameplay, they are about everything around it. DLC is expensive, and if you want the full experience you are realistically buying a lot more than just the base game. Some DLCs feel worth it, others feel thin for the price. Bugs have also been a long running frustration. Things like AI randomly doing nothing, siege battles feeling repetitive because of limited map variety, and certain issues sticking around longer than people think they should.

A community made mod called Community Bug Fix Mod is highly encouraged by many players and is updated often. It fixes a lot of smaller issues and quality of life problems that have not been addressed yet, and for many people it noticeably improves the overall experience.

Overall, if you like deep strategy, fantasy settings, and long campaign games, there is a lot here to love. If you hate heavy DLC models or get annoyed by technical issues that take time to get fixed, you might want to wait for sales, patches, or bundles before jumping in. The game itself is great. The surrounding business model and polish level are what divide people.

At the end of the day, this is one of those games where the core experience is excellent, but you have to be okay with some rough edges and extra costs along the way. If that tradeoff does not bother you, you will probably get a ton of enjoyment out of it. If it does, it can wear on you over time.

Is it a good game? – Yes, but not a massive thumbs up.
Should you get it? – It really depends on how familiar you are with Total War games and what you expect to get from it.
Should I wait for a sale to buy it? – Definitely.

[h3] In Details : [/h3]
[hr][/hr]
[i]Disclaimer: A lot of people are upset at Creative Assembly for numerous reasons (myself included), but I will objectively focus on reviewing the game and not the company.
This review will also act as a review of TWW1 and TWW2, since this product is considered the final stage of the series' development (*note on this at the end*).[/i]

I'll start by saying that I am not a Warhammer nerd at all [b]BUT[/b] I am very happy to finally have a Total War game set in a medieval fantasy setting. A lot of gameplay additions not seen before (to my knowledge) have been added in this game that, in my opinion, improve the overall quality of life and feel:

-When an army is in your territory, you can "poke" it to signal the faction to leave. They have 3 turns to comply, after which you can declare war with no penalty.
-Quick Deals in the diplomacy tab. A huge time saver to quickly see which factions are open to diplomacy.
-Rogue armies. They add a bit of flavor and roleplay with neutral armies roaming the map.
-Minor faction potential. A setting that improves minor factions’ AI and decision-making. It creates both more and less movement around the map at the same time, though I am not sure how impactful it truly is.
-Habitats. Some provinces/settlements are not suitable for your faction to occupy. I am 50/50 on this. Roleplay-wise, it’s perfect. In practice, it can be annoying. If it’s mildly unsuitable, you get manageable penalties (control, building cost, construction time, reduced income, etc.). If it’s highly unsuitable, the penalties are massive and simply frustrating. The AI does not seem to care and will occupy them regardless, so even in that regard, it ignores the roleplay aspect. You be the judge.
-The addition of magic spells and special infantry (monsters, constructs, flying units, guns, artillery, heroes, etc.). This is expected from a medieval fantasy setting, but it nonetheless adds another interesting layer to battles.

Now for the map and factions. There are a ton of choices—and by tons, I mean [b]TONS[/b] of factions to choose from. Each faction has multiple lords with different playstyles and bonuses. Honestly, it’s amazing to have so many options for a distinct and customized experience, but sometimes it feels almost overwhelming and difficult to choose (a happy problem, so I shouldn’t really complain).

The map is massive (on the Grand Campaign, a.k.a. Immortal Empires). Depending on where you start, there’s a good chance you won’t see the entire map in a single campaign.

Now this is where the game doesn’t quite deliver for me. Even though there is a massive roster of factions and lords, I don’t feel like there is much nation- or faction-building gameplay. The game heavily focuses on battles and warfare, while settlement/province management is practically nonexistent.

There is no sanitation, no tax slider, and no food system. Public Order has been replaced by Control (which, overall, doesn’t do much and is difficult to influence), and Religion has been replaced by Corruption (which taints the land and provides penalties or bonuses depending on whether you are “good” or “bad”). Buildings either unlock specific units or generate income—that’s essentially it.

While the addition of Quick Deals is great, other factions are generally not very inclined toward diplomacy with you, even if you share similar alignments (“good” or “bad”). Trading has always been an important aspect of Total War games, but in this game, trade provides meager income at best.

Because the game is so massive and involves a lot of AI factions, campaigns often become chaotic and extremely fast-paced. The game’s balance also feels off. Of course, it’s a Total War game, so Doomstacks will always exist, but they seem more common here than in previous entries. Some factions feel significantly stronger than others, which leads to another point: in my campaigns, I’ve noticed that certain factions almost always end up dominating. But again, you be the judge.

On that note, I highly suggest disabling “Endgame Scenarios” in your settings. These events trigger around turn 100 (you can adjust this) and massively boost a random faction from a predetermined list—similar to Attila in Total War: Attila (if you’ve played it). While the idea is interesting, in practice these scenarios feel frustrating. The chosen faction receives 5–6 full-stack armies, declares war on everyone, gains massive replenishment bonuses, and becomes diplomacy-locked.

Bugs: It’s been quite some time since release, and while there are still regular patches, they haven’t fully ironed everything out. The bugs are nowhere near as bad as at launch, but minor issues still appear from time to time.

[i]*Note regarding TWW1 and TWW2*[/i]
I’ll keep it short: In some aspects, TWW1 and/or TWW2 are better; in others, this game is better. If you love the Warhammer universe and strategy games, by all means get them—their respective campaigns are enjoyable. If you simply enjoy Total War games and want a fantasy setting, just get this one.

Total War: Warhammer 1-3 — одна из тех игр, которые незаметно поглощают часы вашей жизни и заставляют вас задаться вопросом, куда делся реальный мир.

Я провёл в игре около 200 часов, играя только в кампанию, в основном в режиме «песочницы», и значительную часть этого времени я провёл в кооперативных кампаниях с другом. Честно говоря, это, пожалуй, лучший способ пройти игру. Координация дипломатии, планирование атак и постепенное завоевание территории вместе с другом доставляют невероятное удовольствие и удивительно расслабляют.

Что касается фракций, да, я виновен в классическом выборе: гномы и высокие эльфы. Они популярны не зря. Каждая фракция действительно отличается от других, а не просто имеет другие характеристики, и изучение их экономики, армий и стилей игры — половина удовольствия.

Тем не менее, эта игра не идет на поводу у игрока. Расширение полноценной армии и империи похоже на жонглирование тарелками во время езды на одноколесном велосипеде. Здесь много движущихся частей. Экономика, дипломатия, синергия юнитов, технологические деревья — и хотя эта глубина впечатляет, она также делает достижения комплиментаристов практически невозможными. Что разрушительно, потому что мой мозг их хочет, лол.

Warhammer лучше всего умеет погружать игрока в мир игры. Как только вы в него погрузились, вы уже не можете выбраться. Часы пролетают незаметно. Сочетание истории, масштаба и долгосрочного планирования втягивает вас и не отпускает.

Я еще даже не приступил к сюжетным кампаниям. Только к песочнице, и она уже кажется огромной. Один только Immortal Empires — это игра, в которой можно жить.

Если вы никогда раньше не играли в Warhammer — да, это много знаний, но если вы уделите ей должное время, вы не пожалеете.

Очень рекомендую, только сначала освободите свое расписание... и, возможно, спрячьте выписки по кредитной карте от своего парня.

You start Warhammer, no tutorial, no explanation at all. And the game has some complex mechanics. It’s impossible to understand what you are supposed to do or how you are supposed to do it. After a few hours of suffering, Warhammer III is finally downloaded and installed. After some time fighting with the ads: “Get this, get that,” you finally start the game. You watch some stupid animations for a while, and hallelujah, this one has a tutorial (the prologue). The prologue itself is not easy. Some battles you will have to repeat many times. Then, after hours and hours of fighting in the prologue, you smash them. You have understood how the game works at this point. Nice, eh? Well, not quite. You start the first campaign, and most of the things you have learned are useless, as the real game has a lot of differences. And if that’s not enough, you are thrown against 300 players… Yes, 300. You have no break. You move: they attack. You breathe in: they attack. You breathe out: they attack. You even blink: they attack. Also, you make your move in 5–15 seconds, then you wait minutes until the other 299 players move. There are battles that you cannot just auto-resolve. You need to actually play them in real time. If I wanted to play an RTS, I would play an RTS. The idea of turn-based strategy games is to be more relaxed, more strategic. Well, this one is neither. It’s not worth playing even for free.

This game is incredible! And this is coming from someone who has never played any other Total War games (I did try Warhammer 1 a while back, but I found it too complicated and hard to access), and who is not a strategy game buff at all. The closest game I have really played before was... Heroes of Might and Magic V and that was almost 20 years ago.

So, why did I bounce off of TW: Warhammer 1, but got so deep into TWW3? It's thanks to the free tutorial campaign (which took me about 4-5h to complete - whole other games sometimes last that long), which explains most of the mechanics of the game in a very clear way, and has an interesting story to boot. After that I was still a bit confused as to what should I actually be doing in a regular campaign to succeed, so I went to YT for guidance and tried out a couple factions before settling on N'Kari and completing The Realms of Chaos campaign with her. And I had a blast! 

I did play Immortal Empires campaigns after that and most of them were very enjoyable. It's amazing how each faction (or even each legendary lord within a faction) felt actually different to play - and it was not only due to a different army roster. Each faction has a prefered style to play, but each legendary lord (or maybe not each, but most of them) has their own mechanics and skills that incentivise playing in a different way. Also their distinct starting positions make each campaign feel very different.

Everyone into the classic Warhammer Fantasy will quickly recognize the familiar names of places, lords and heroes. Wanna reunite the Empire as the Emperor Karl Franz? There you go. Wanna burn the world in a vain attempt to reclaim your master's favour as Skarbrand? Knock yourself out. Wanna invade Ulthuan and raze it to the ground, because you just hate elves? You're going to have a good time, trust me. And if you're not into Warhammer Fantasy yet - this is a great place to start!

Let me start by saying that I'm not into Warhammer or fantasy in general, but as a long-time fan of the historical Total War games, I picked up Warhammer III when it went on sale, simply to scratch an itch.

Despite finding CA's business practices to be quite gross—ie. for no apparent reason I had to purchase a copy of Warhammer II (which was on sale for like 90% off, thankfully) in order to play as Karl Franz in Warhammer III—I have to say that I've been impressed by the depth and really enjoy the factional variety/asymmetry, which continually forces you out of your comfort zone as you have to develop new tactics depending on the composition of the opposing army, ensuring that battles don't become too formulaic too quickly, which has been a consistent drawback of the historical TW games, particularly mid-late game.  Spellcasting, monstrous units and powerful ranged units ensure that you can't simply "testudo" your way to victory using the same exploitative tactics ad infinitum/nauseum.

Although I'm not interested enough in the setting/lore to return to the game for multiple playthroughs, those who enjoy high fantasy will find that Warhammer III offers an insane amount of replayability.

In short, it's a solid game—if you're into TW and high fantasy, you'll absolutely love Warhammer III and get your money's worth, even at full price.  If you're like me and just want a new TW experience but don't particularly enjoy the fantasy setting, wait for a sale, but don't write it off altogether.  If nothing else, there is definitely fun to be had on a strategic/tactical level.

[b]Total War: WARHAMMER III[/b] is the culmination of [i]Creative Assembly[/i]’s grand strategy trilogy set in [i]Games Workshop[/i]’s [i]Warhammer Fantasy[/i] universe. It is simultaneously a refinement of the studio’s long-running Total War formula and an ambitious attempt to deliver a campaign structure with stronger narrative propulsion than its predecessors. The result is a dense, mechanically rich strategy title that excels in asymmetrical faction design, large-scale tactical warfare, and systemic complexity.

On the campaign map, players manage provinces, construct buildings, recruit armies, engage in diplomacy, and expand territorially. In battle, thousands of units clash in real time with full 3D rendering, terrain effects, morale systems, magic, flying units, artillery, and monstrous entities.

The combined mega-campaign, [i]Immortal Empires[/i], merges content from all three [i]WARHAMMER[/i] titles into one massive world map. It is arguably the definitive way to experience the trilogy. This mode transforms the game into a sprawling sandbox where geopolitical narratives emerge organically. For strategy purists, this is the franchise at its most complete.

Battlefield engagements are visually spectacular. Large entities (dragons, greater daemons, elemental bears) create cinematic clashes. Spellcasting remains a defining differentiator versus historical [i]Total War[/i] entries. That said, balance fluctuates between patches. Ranged dominance and single-entity monster meta occasionally skew competitive play.

[b]Total War: WARHAMMER III[/b] represents the most mechanically expansive entry in the [i]Total War[/i] franchise. While its initial narrative-driven campaign can feel restrictive, the Immortal Empires sandbox elevates the experience into one of the most content-rich strategy games available.

For fans of grand strategy, asymmetrical faction design, and large-scale fantasy warfare, it stands as a definitive capstone to the trilogy. Its complexity demands commitment, but few strategy titles offer comparable scale, variety, and emergent storytelling potential.

As for the game itself, while there are elements and aspects both in game and outside of it that could REALLY do with some revision and re-evaluation, one thing remains consistent for this title above all others: 

It is BEAUTIFUL. 

Yes it could also use more optimization and is a big system hog but like, with good reason. I have lost hours (and advantageous strategic positions) just hiding the UI and zooming in and watching the carnage unfold. 

There is a deep satisfaction to the combat and the diversity of engagements that pairs very well with the absolutely gorgeous meticulously crafted world maps of each campaign, along with very sleek and effective UI elements. And there are a lot of excellent audio elements up and down every aspect of the game that really add that immersive oomph. 

If you like grand strategy (or are curious about it) and you have a decent PC, this game is an experience few others can match in spectacle, and is an excellent gateway into the genre where other titles become far more complex and in depth but never quite reach this level of beauty and awe.  

Now, lets take the rest of this review box to talk recommendations for the title and the developers as a whole with the entire total war series, because my reviews always include helpful suggestions that help me set myself apart from just another person going "me like game : ) " or "me no like game : ( " 

[b] TOTAL WAR SUBSCRIPTION [/b]

[b] FACTION UI's [/b] 

Add unique UI themes and sounds for each faction that is distinct from one another enough to warrant it. This will add even more beauty and immersion easily

[b] END TIMES CONSOLIDATION [/b] 

With the start of the end times, it is finally reasonable to start considering packaging the 1st, 2nd and 3rd game and ALL of their DLC's (excluding any end times DLC's of course) Into a permanent all in one collection that sells for like $60.00 normally and goes on sale for 50% off each time one of the new end time DLC's comes out, and make every non-end times DLC $5.00 often going on sale for 50% off as well during each end times release 

This will generate a lot of hype and good will and give excuses for players to get newcomers into the whole ordeal, so they can invest in the end times hype too!  

[b] ADVANCED MODE [/b]

That adds things like:

- Complex settlement management (Logistics, exports / imports, more build projects, local politics and corruption, espionage, trade optimization etc etc)  
- Camp supplies and per faction upkeep of armies that is not just one resource consolidated 
- Removes "immortality" from all characters but those with in lore reasons why they might constantly be a reviving pain in the butt (like demons, or very powerful vampires / tomb kings generally can be)

[h1] Total War: Overpriced and Underdelivered 3 [/h1]

Disclaimer: I bought this game on Epic this past holiday period after trying out the Immortal Empire’s campaign from WH1, decided to get it here to leave a review.

Warhammer 3 is overall a great game, with a large number of factions with unique play styles that leans away from the design philosophy of “make everyone balanced with minor changes” but more to the “make everyone different and give them their own really strong mechanic with unique strengths and weaknesses”. In doing so, they create a game that encourages repeat playthroughs and accommodates a large number of playstyles in doing so. However, there are a number of core issues that cause the game to be very difficult to recommend to new players.

[h2] Expecting players to pay hundreds of dollars of DLC for core game content [/h2]

The game’s monetisation is shockingly bad. Not all content is included in the base game, to be able to play as every faction in WH3 you need to buy WH1 and WH2, as well as several other DLC’s. You will see this when you start a new campaign and see that the better part of 80% of lords/factions have not been unlocked. This is despite much of the content being out for a decade at this point and could have easily been added to the base game, the same way that other titles (such as Age of Empires 2) have done. This means that even with the current sales going on, if you want absolutely everything in full, you need to pay $260 AUD. This is made even worse by the fact that CA deliberately broke up faction rosters across several DLC’s, meaning that even if you did get the faction you want in the game you paid for (e.g Greenskins) you now have to go and pay for other DLC’s to get the full experience for that faction. It’s an absolute scummy financial practice that needs to be called out.

Edit: I went into the game to count how many lords you start off with, with only WH3 purchased. You start off with 9 out of 52 unlocked, for an ownership of 17.3%. Imagine spending $100 just to own only 17% of a game, unreal.

[h2] Bugs and glitches never fixed, multiple reworks needed [/h2]

The main problem with this game is that the high cost of the game is not matched with the same level of quality. There are bugs and glitches that have been ongoing for months (reported by the community on mass) that have not been reported, sieges are clunky and have limited maps -> unfun to play. A lot of animations will also frequently have clipping problems, because they were simply never designed correctly. There are also several factions that are in desperate need of a rework despite being in the game for years, such as Bretonnia and Norsca, that never got the attention that they need because once they were developed they weren’t getting monetized any further. Occasionally, an issue will pop up that will get the player base to review bomb the game and only then will the devs address the issue. However, it won’t be a thorough fix of the game that ensures it and similar issues won’t happen again, but will instead put in the bare minimum of effort to band aid patch the game and wait for the community to calm down, before moving on as usual with no overall structural changes. All in all, if you’re paying such absurdly large amounts of money for a product, there comes an expectation of a certain level of polish with that. That expectation is not even close to being met, these are longstanding issues that have been known for years at a time that have not been fixed.

[h2] CA loves to troll new players [/h2]

Another sign that this game does not put in effort is their lack of attempts to ease new players into WH3. The biggest “noob trap” that they do is that they have Karl Franz as their recommended starting game, because he was the one for WH1. This is a bad idea due to how relatively complex he is for a new player, with a number of easier lords recommended by the community. Another thing that CA can’t even be bothered to do is to give a brief description the pros/cons when picking a lord, e.g this lord has a good infantry focus and is overall easy, this other one is gunpowder focused and is overall hard etc. It is such an easy thing to implement, (Shogun 2 did so over a decade ago), would go such a long way to help new players and yet hasn’t been done.

Overall, whilst the game certainly is fun and offers a huge amount of replay ability and content, due to the high price and huge number of issues, it ultimately isn’t worth getting WH3 or even WH1/2. Instead, you would most likely be better of sticking with some of CA’s historical titles (at the very least they have a lower cost of entry) or even going to different games/genres all together (can strongly recommend Age of Mythology, even if it is RTS compared to WH3’s turn based and real time tactics).

This is written from the position of a Total War noob. Never played a single one of the games in the series till a few days ago.

TL,DR: Said in the most insulting way possible to me; "Git gud, noob!"
In regards to the entire Total War series, the Player has to be COMMITTED to learning the game. Not new player friendly - in any way, shape or form. I recommend watching as many beginner help videos on Youtube as you can, you are gonna need a lot of info to play well. These games do not respect your time. If you have a job, this game is now your hobby.

PROS: Epic visuals, wargaming at its finest. Tactical controls and clickies are satisfying to use, and offer a great deal of depth for strategies. Themed settings give the feel of their IP's very well, if you ever wanted to be in the ancient world, a napoleonic battlefield or in high fantasy- these games deliver! 

CONS: These are hard games, because they teach you practically nothing straight up...and nothing is as intuitive as it seems.

You must learn to like losing, figure out what went wrong, and steadily improve that way. Basic trial and error, for hours. You are not even taught the shortcuts you need to make both simple and complex maneuvers possible. You will have a high chance to lose every battle you take a hand in with no experience of how the battle system works - knowing the states of unit readiness, order of engagement, even basic maneuverability does not work intuitively. Warhammer is especially egregious, the addition of magical effects essentially requires you to know what EVERY unit and faction can do to have a decent chance at victory.

You will be overwhelmed by tooltips, which in turn have their own tooltips. They will explain almost nothing.

Simple sandbox diplomacy and city building round out the experience; you are here to fight a strategic battlefield wargame, that's most of your skill time. The development of your cities is actually quite consequential, but again you do not actually know what you will need until you are far too invested to change course. Diplomacy can matter, but it relates to a great deal of hard power tactics against the AI...if you have a strong army, they tend to be agreeable - precisely when it wouldn't matter.

Finally, in campaign mode, save before every battle. The computer has a habit of just summoning flanking cavalry or monstrous units whenever. You could say," Oh, well that should be expected - its a dramatic moment of challenge!". It's not. It's a cheap shot meant to hobble beginners, to prevent you from committing all your forces to attack like the borders of the map meant something. I suppose it could be a demonstration of learning to play conservatively, practicing self-discipline because of what might happen on the ever changing battlefield...but its not. You can't do that, the story can. It's just another metric that you have to learn by reloading.

Ok, judging by the previous paragraphs you might think I don't like the game. I do. I like it a lot.

But that's because I'm a Warhammer nerd and a masochist. If you weren't already a sweaty gamer, used to unfair odds and thriving in them, willing to devote time and effort to learning something new - you might feel the Total War series is a bad purchase. It can be very fun, but only if you are willing to fail. That takes time, time that a lot of people don't have. And I feel a lot of tryhard games lately don't have that on the box. There is a genuine sense of accomplishment when you finally get it, but you could have been doing at least a dozen things that actually matter. If you weren't already a fan.

I treat my feelings on this series like I would treat trying to teach Magic: the Gathering to a newbie. I've been playing since Alpha, the rules are mostly known to me already. But they are arcane (no pun intended) to a complete novice, and the states of play may take months of games to get down properly, not to mention the individual rulings. You have to WANT IT to get good. And have a boatload of money for decent cards.

Will this game make you a Warhammer nerd? Sure! The models, world and voice acting make it come to life, the sound design and the music make you feel like you are there! The dark world draws us in and makes you want to learn MORE...about the story. Which is gated behind that battle you are gonna have to fight.

Better buckle up an git gud, noob...its a rough ride from here to Chaos Gate.

Ich finde die Welt und das Setting von Total War: Warhammer grundsätzlich sehr gelungen. Die Atmosphäre, Fraktionen und das gesamte Warhammer-Universum sind spannend umgesetzt und bieten viel Potenzial für ein tiefgehendes Strategiespiel.

Leider habe ich jedoch den Eindruck, dass sich seit längerer Zeit keine wirkliche Mühe gemacht wird, das grundlegende KI-System zu verbessern. Dadurch fehlt dem Spiel ein wichtiger Teil der strategischen Tiefe. Die KI scheint über nahezu unbegrenzte Ressourcen zu verfügen und kann Verluste sehr schnell ausgleichen, was strategische Entscheidungen stark entwertet.

Zum Beispiel ist es kaum möglich, einen Gegner bewusst zu schwächen oder sich vorübergehend zurückzuziehen, um sich einem anderen Konflikt zuzuwenden. Selbst nach schweren Verlusten baut die KI ihre Armeen in kürzester Zeit wieder auf, ohne dass dies nachvollziehbar oder strategisch begründet wirkt. Das vermittelt den Eindruck, dass die KI eher durch Vorteile „schummelt“, statt durch intelligente Entscheidungen zu überzeugen.

Insgesamt führt das zu einer eher oberflächlichen Spielerfahrung, da strategische Planung und langfristige Entscheidungen weniger Bedeutung haben. Dadurch habe ich persönlich den Spaß am Spiel leider verloren, obwohl die Grundlage und das Setting sehr vielversprechend sind.

Total War: WARHAMMER III is a massive, ambitious strategy title that I’ve spent an incredible amount of time with — even if I still think Total War: WARHAMMER II edges it out for me personally.

I’ll admit upfront: I’m biased. The Dark Elves are my favorite faction, and Warhammer II is where they really shined for me. That attachment definitely shapes how I view the third entry. There’s something about the pacing, faction balance, and overall flow of Warhammer II that felt just right in my memory.

That said, Warhammer III is far from a downgrade. The scale is enormous, the faction diversity is impressive, and the Immortal Empires campaign is a genuinely ambitious undertaking. I still sank a significant amount of time into it, which speaks to how strong the core formula remains. The battles are cinematic, the faction mechanics are flavorful, and the sandbox potential is still there.

Where it started to lose me slightly was the familiarity of the gameplay loop. After hundreds of hours across the trilogy, the recruit–expand–battle–snowball cycle began to feel repetitive. That’s less a criticism of Warhammer III specifically and more a reflection of how much time I’ve already invested in the series as a whole. I had a lot of fun — a considerable amount — before that sense of fatigue set in.

As for the DLC situation, I understand why the community is conflicted. There’s a lot of additional content, and the pricing model has sparked debate. Personally, I see it as part of the broader challenge modern developers face: how to sustain long-term support and player retention without compromising trust or the integrity of the source material. It’s a difficult balance. While not perfect, I think the overall value of the trilogy and its ongoing expansion can justify the model for players who truly love the setting.

In the end, even if I slightly prefer Warhammer II, Warhammer III is still an impressive, content-rich strategy game. If you enjoy grand strategy, large-scale fantasy warfare, and the Warhammer universe, there’s a lot here to appreciate.

It may not have fully recaptured the magic I felt with my favorite faction in the previous entry — but I still got a tremendous amount of enjoyment out of it. And that’s worth recommending.

If you’re wondering whether you should play this game, here are two things you need to know first:

There is a learning curve.

You will probably restart at least one campaign after realizing you had no idea what you were doing.

Even with experience in previous Total War games, this one can feel overwhelming at the start. There are a lot of systems layered on top of each other, and the game does not exactly hold your hand. But once the mechanics start to click, it becomes seriously rewarding. What feels chaotic at first slowly turns into strategy, and that is when the fun really kicks in.

If you are jumping into Total War: Warhammer III for the first time, I recommend starting with Grand Cathay. They are straightforward, balanced, and play in a way that feels familiar if you have touched any traditional Total War faction before. The game will suggest The Empire, but unless you enjoy being constantly harassed by Vampire Counts, ambushed by Skaven, and bullied by Chaos, you might want to save that experience for later.

It also helps to watch a few videos about the Warhammer Fantasy lore. Understanding the world makes everything feel more immersive, and it explains why everyone seems so dramatically intense all the time.

Overall, the game is absolutely worth the patience. The beginning might test you, but once it clicks, it is hard to put down.

Good luck, and try not to set your own capital on fire.

I cannot recommend this game.

It has a lot of factions, a lot of different units, a lot of variety in general.
I won't even go on actual details, as I only need to talk about 2 major points.

1) The game is overly expensive even on sales as in order to have all factions / generals you need to buy Total War : Warhammer 1, 2 and 3, as well as their DLC's or you'll end up with a fractionned game.
Personally, I absolutely HATE to have a game that isn't complete. And to make Total War Warhammer complete, you'll need to throw A LOT of money out the window, even at 50% or more on sales. It's absurd.

2) The AI. The main reason to play total war games are the different campaigns on which you battle against various AI factions on large campaign maps. In Total War : Warhammer 3, the AI has only 2 objectives : run away from your armies and attack your weakest settlements.

I've played various Total War games, some having better AI than others. But this game's campaign AI is the absolute worst and makes the game 200% NOT FUN to play. What happens is that AI's will declare war on you for no reason at all, travel the entire map to attack you despite having severely higher priorities in their direct vicinity, and only and ever assault your weakest settlements. If you try to get your armies clsoer to theirs, the AI will always run away from you, even if they have superior numbers and troops. They'll always, EVERY-SINGLE-TURN, be 1 pixel out of reach of your armies, and keep sacking, razing or taking your weakest settlements, in completely pointless manoeuvres. 
And what did I find out? You can simply take their entire territory without any resistance since their armies will just attack your most useless settlements without ever approaching your troops. So basically, fighting another faction can be summed up by : ignore their armies, take all of their settlements, then send a few armies chasing their to the very border of the campaign map while a few others retake what their stole from you, stabilize, repeat ad nauseam. 

In short, this is a Total War game in which there is NO WAR. Only chasing petty children who just discovered the concept of trolling and believing it'll make them look like beings of superior intelligence and unreadable motives in a pathetic attempt to look mysterious and cool. 


In short, Total War : Warhammer 3 is all about wasting a hell lot of money to get annoyed by useless kids on a vast but ultimately empty campaign map.

Either mod the crap out of the game or avoid it at a cost that'll always be far inferior to what you might have paid for.

I honestly have nothing to criticize about this game at this point, except perhaps Creative Assembly’s DLC pricing strategy. Some of the additional races and Lords can feel overpriced, especially if you do not already own the previous titles or are not buying during a significant sale. At times, it can border on feeling pay-to-win.

That said, everything else is outstanding. The gameplay – both on the world campaign map and in the real-time battles – is incredibly engaging. The sheer number of races and Lords to choose from, the scale of the Immortal Empires campaign, and the endless replayability in both solo and co-op make this a massive time sink in the best possible way.

If you enjoy the Warhammer universe, this is an easy recommendation. Buy it on sale, find a like-minded friend, and you can easily get hundreds of hours of genuinely great fun out of it.

I recommend using community sites such as wikis for lore and history; Warhammer Fantasy has such an enormous variety with so much depth that being educated on the factions and characters adds even more to the experience of playing.

If you are completely new to RTS or grand strategy games, this isn't a good buy for you to go into without an understanding of how the game works, or the rules (you will have an extremely difficult time learning to play it). However, if you are willing to put in the time and effort, then you will have a great time with this game.

How the many unique races each feel completely different from each other is what I love about the game. Each faction has different mechanics, different ways to play the game, and a different style of doing so; which is what keeps the game from becoming stale.

There are a couple of minor issues that would be nice to see developed and fixed. But they don't take anything away from this being one of my all-time favorite Strategy Games.

Overall score: 10/10.

[h1]Excessive Abstraction[/h1]

A broad sentiment that this game evokes in me is that it feels... two-dimensional, like one big abstraction? The roster boasts hundreds of ostensible unique units. However, this so-called "unit variety" - a term the community loves - mostly boils down to this or that unit having two more or less melee attack or whatever other minuscule difference. They all have the same attack speed. Why aren't there units that, for example, attack very fast but with weak attacks, the most basic facilitator of variety since the dawn of video games? Everything in this game is on the same exact 4-5-second metronome, whether a dual-bladed assassin or a massive dinosaur.

The result is a massive roster that looks diverse in terms of 3D models but feels incredibly homogeneous mechanically. It feels like a deception, but it sure as hell seems to sell copies nevertheless.

The game promises spectacle, and it does deliver that, but only on the surface. Once you zoom in, given you're perceptive enough, you will invariably notice that the 3D engine in Total War, especially today, is essentially a fancy dress costume on a spreadsheet. The combat resolution is almost entirely stat-based tick calculations that doesn't utilize the 3D or physics engine in any way. Unit A has X attack value, fires it off at Y interval, hits Unit B's Z armor value, and so on. Boom, that's your "battle." The 3D models are basically just animated Excel rows.

Every battle just becomes this awkward demonstration of polygon blobs shuffling and grinding/sliding against each, occasionally remembering they're supposed to be fighting. There's an alarming lack of intensity and effort.

Regarding gameplay on the campaign map, Warhammer 3 lacks a proper settlement and economy planning components, making the campaign gameplay feel somewhat shallow. In previous, historical titles, you had more or less all buildings affecting other buildings somehow. This made you think in terms of synergies. In Warhammer, you have the individual money building for money, public order building for public order, etc, and that is it. There's more or less nothing to learn about the empire building aspect.

I would broadly describe the game as promising more depth than what's actually there. It offers lots of variables that in practice blend together due to a lack of mechanical distance. The parameter space is claustrophobic. It has a wow-factor for the uninitiated, but bit by bit the pretty paint crumbles and the game is revealed for what it is: a plain and repetitive wall. This is exacerbated by the watered-down campaign map gameplay.

Fun can definitely be had, but I can't help but feel a sense of betrayal after everything is said and done. It's not a bad game, but it's not great either. If I could, I would give it a mixed rating. I am, however, giving it a negative one because I see it as a regression compared to certain past titles in the franchise.

Fun game to play. I've played Warhammer 2 and 3 exclusively co-op, never done a single player campaign. It can be buggy at times (use the community bug fix mod), and the DLC can be expensive, but it is still an incredibly fun game that I don't believe warrants 'mixed reviews'.

If you're on the fence about the game pricing wise, and its DLC, they've pretty regularly had 75% or more off sales for things in the past. Just wait for a sale.

As far as the bugs, most are negligible with the community bug fix mod. It's not great that a mod is required for this, but it's available, Theoretically I'm even playing a buggier version of the game since I doubt they actually put a lot of QA into the co-op experience, and even then it's still barely noticeable when it happens. An example of this was me playing Aislinn and my friend playing Ostankya, and at a certain point later in the campaign (we believe after I confederated someone) he just flat out lost the ability to trade settlements in diplomacy. The button just entirely disappeared and never came back. Silly, but not a deal breaker.

If I had to give a numerical rating to this game, rather than just a binary yes or no, I'd say easily a 7/10 overall, 9/10 if it was less buggy, 4/10 for its pricing scheme.

The game gets a lot of hate (deserved) because of the greedy DLC strategy (who tf sells gore and blood as DLC for a war game).

But the game itself is incredibly fun. There’s a lot of depth, and every lord/faction offers a unique gameplay experience. I already knew a bit about Warhammer Fantasy before playing, but this is the game that really got me hooked. I might even like it more than 40K, to be honest.

The game also fully supports modding, so you can easily tweak the experience to whatever makes the game the most fun for you.

also, it has that same “one more turn” effect as Civ, so don’t forget to sleep.

There's no other strategy game out there that can compare with the sheer amount of variety that the Total War: Warhammer series brings to the table. So many factions. So many units. So many strategies.

And so many dollars to buy them all.

This is a phenomenal game, but it's also one of the most expensive, with massive amounts of content being locked behind DLC. And it's not like you can just ignore the DLC either - when you play the Immortal Empires mode, you will run into factions or units that you haven't bought yet. Expect the character select screen to have dozens upon dozens of characters that look cool and sound fun to play, only to notice that they are locked behind yet another DLC. Keep in mind, you are not signing up for just one game here. Immortal Empires (the main game mode that everyone plays) also utilizes the previous two games and their DLCs as well, so you are looking at buying three full price games and multiple DLCs for each if you want the whole experience.

With that said, when this game gets going, it is truly a masterpiece. Gorgeous visuals, solid framerate, and even a great soundtrack during your massive battles. But, to get to that point, expect to drop hundreds of dollars to collect all the armies and heroes you want. I recommend buying the first two games during a steam sale when you can get them for ten bucks or so. If you can snipe a few DLCs on sale, you can save a lot and enjoy the game that much more.

But hey, if you're a Warhammer fan, you're already used to getting robbed by Games Workshop anyway, so this should be right up your alley.

EDIT - I made this review years ago and it needs to be updated now that the game includes Immortal Empires for free. A much better value than it was before, although you can still expect to pay for numerous DLCs if you want the complete experience.

120.7 hours of Total War: WARHAMMER III and it's the trilogy's crowning glory, a massive leap forward from WH2 that turned my "one more campaign" into non-stop chaos! I dont have as many hours as WH2 yet, but the improvements and added changes make this a glorious addition. 

This takes WH2's foundation and supercharges it: say goodbye to minor settlement cheese with fully revamped sieges—towers crumble, walls breach dynamically, and every assault feels like a huge siege war! Diplomacy's smarter with stances and quick deals, Lightning Strike got a glow-up, and the UI/battles are buttery smooth. But the real MVP? Immortal Empires, a mega-map fusing all three games for infinite sandbox domination. Add in bear-patrolling Kislev ice queens, harmony-balancing Cathay gunpowder dragons, and god-specific Chaos Daemons (Khorne rage, Nurgle rot, Slaanesh seduction, Tzeentch tricks) these races outshine WH2's roster with bonkers mechanics!

I'm addicted to the daemon princes ripping armies apart, armored bears mauling orcs, spell barrages melting foes battles are a next-level spectacle! IE lets me mix lords like never before; I've lost days to Cathay world-domination runs. Mods and DLC just multiply the replayability.

one of the most ambitious strategy games I’ve ever played. It combines grand strategy, real-time battles, and the massive Warhammer Fantasy universe into a single experience. At its best, the game feels like commanding armies in a living fantasy world.

One of the biggest strengths of the game is the variety of factions and playstyles. Each race feels unique, from daemon armies that rely on corruption and chaos to disciplined human empires and monstrous hordes. The amount of content becomes enormous, especially with the Immortal Empires campaign where almost every faction from the trilogy can appear on one giant map. Battles are visually spectacular, with huge monsters, magic, artillery, and thousands of units clashing at once.

Another thing I enjoy is the Warhammer lore integration. Legendary Lords feel powerful and distinct, and the world has a lot of personality. The art design, voice acting, and music help bring the setting to life.

However, the game is far from perfect. Performance and optimization can be inconsistent, even on fairly strong PCs. Large battles and late-game campaigns sometimes suffer from slowdowns or long turn times. The AI can also be frustrating, occasionally making strange strategic decisions or behaving unpredictably in battles.

The DLC model is another mixed aspect. On one hand, it adds a huge amount of content over time. On the other hand, the full experience can become very expensive if you want every faction and expansion from all three games.

Overall, Total War: Warhammer III is an incredible strategy sandbox with massive scale and replayability, but it requires patience with its technical issues and a willingness to invest in the larger trilogy ecosystem.

Score: 8/10 – A fantastic strategy game for Warhammer fans and Total War players, but not without its flaws.

Total War: Warhammer III – Ehrlicher Ersteindruck nach dem Prolog

Ich habe keine große Erfahrung mit der Total-War-Reihe. Ein bisschen habe ich früher Empire gespielt, aber die Strategiespiele, mit denen ich mich wirklich auskenne, sind eher Heroes of Might and Magic, Age of Wonders und Civilization. Deshalb bin ich an Total War vor allem mit dem Blick eines klassischen Strategiefans herangegangen, der Planung, Übersicht und nachvollziehbare Mechaniken erwartet.

Grafisch und inszenatorisch finde ich das Spiel ehrlich gesagt nicht überragend. Natürlich wirken große Armeen beeindruckend, aber die Darstellung ist stark vereinfacht, damit die vielen Einheiten überhaupt dargestellt werden können. Das ist nicht unbedingt schlecht, aber spektakulär fand ich es nicht. In Spielen wie Dawn of War hat es mir deutlich mehr Spaß gemacht, einfach in Schlachten hineinzuzoomen und sie zu beobachten. Selbst das alte Empire wirkte für mich übersichtlicher. In Warhammer III wird das Gefecht sehr schnell chaotisch – ich musste ständig pausieren, um Befehle zu geben, und habe trotzdem oft komplett die Übersicht verloren.

Wichtig: Meine gesamte Erfahrung basiert nur auf dem Prolog. Ich kann also nicht beurteilen, ob das eigentliche Spiel später besser wird. Leider hat mich dieser Einstieg so stark frustriert, dass ich wahrscheinlich gar nicht erst bis dorthin komme. Wenn man schon beim Tutorial das Gefühl bekommt „ich schaffe nicht einmal das Tutorial“, hinterlässt das keinen guten Eindruck.

Ein konkretes Beispiel ist die Mission „Angriff auf den Messingaltar“. Man bereitet seine Armee vor, stellt sie logisch auf und denkt, man hat die Situation im Griff – und dann spawnen plötzlich massive Verstärkungen mitten hinter den eigenen Linien. Nicht vom Kartenrand, nicht nachvollziehbar, sondern direkt im Rücken der eigenen Truppen. Das fühlt sich weniger nach Strategie an und mehr nach „Du musst einmal verlieren, um das Script zu kennen“.

Auch die Informationsdarstellung ist teilweise verwirrend. Ein Beispiel: Ein Held gibt einen Bonus von +5 % Einkommen, mit dem Zusatz „reduziert im feindlichen Gebiet“. Aber um wie viel reduziert? Auf 4 %? 1 %? Null? Oder reduziert es hier die gegnerischen Einnahmen? Solche Angaben fehlen einfach. Für ein Strategiespiel, bei dem Entscheidungen auf Zahlen und Effekten basieren, sind solche unklaren Beschreibungen ziemlich frustrierend.

Ein weiterer Punkt sind die Level-Ups der Helden. Sie passieren gefühlt ständig und fühlen sich gleichzeitig erstaunlich belanglos an. Die meisten Boni wirken sehr klein und abstrakt: ein paar Prozent mehr Rüstung, etwas schnellere Feuerrate für Bogenschützen oder ein bisschen mehr Munition. Nichts davon löst dieses typische „Yes! Mein Held ist jetzt wirklich stärker geworden“-Gefühl aus, das man aus anderen Strategiespielen kennt.

Auch das Gameplay auf der Kampagnenkarte wirkt im Prolog sehr belanglos. Der Ausbau der Provinzen besteht meist nur aus der Wahl zwischen zwei sehr ähnlichen Gebäuden, die immer nach einer Runde fertig sind. In der nächsten Runde klickt man dann wieder das nächste Gebäude in jeder Siedlung an. Oft ist es nur die Entscheidung zwischen „mehr Einkommen“ oder „mehr Wachstum“. Gerade im Tutorial fühlt sich das seltsam irrelevant an, weil klar ist, dass diese Entscheidungen für den weiteren Verlauf kaum Bedeutung haben.

Das gleiche gilt für viele Heldenaktionen auf der Karte wie Attentate oder Sabotage. Sie kosten Ressourcen, haben aber gefühlt kaum spürbaren Einfluss auf das Spielgeschehen. Dadurch entsteht der Eindruck, dass man viel klickt, ohne wirklich strategische Entscheidungen zu treffen.

Es gibt natürlich auch positive Punkte. Die Kampagnenkarte ist übersichtlich gestaltet und die Benutzeroberfläche ist grundsätzlich gut lesbar. Wirklich herausragend fand ich die Präsentation allerdings nicht. Die großen, spektakulären Schlachten, die man aus dem Marketing kennt, konnte ich persönlich kaum genießen, weil ich ständig pausieren musste, um überhaupt noch Befehle geben zu können.

Mein Fazit nach dem Prolog:
Das Spiel hat ein interessantes Setting und eine klare Benutzeroberfläche, aber der Einstieg hat mich eher frustriert als motiviert. Wenn das Tutorial schon so viele Fragen offenlässt und stark geskriptete Situationen erzeugt, nimmt mir das die Lust, mich weiter hineinzuarbeiten.

I’m going to be writing this review as someone who started the Total War: Warhammer series and the RTS genre as a whole with this game. This is the first time I’ve played a game like this, but I am not unfamiliar with these types of CRPG games, so if I seem clueless on a few things then sorry in advance.

I wanted to pick up this series because I really love the Warhammer IP, my first game in said universe being Vermintide 2. I bought this game at a major discount, and after doing the absurdly long tutorial/prologue, I had high hopes. But then that excitement turned into dread the moment I took a quick glance at the insurmountable amount of microtransactions in the game.

The vast majority of the Factions in this game are locked behind DLC, but even worse is that if you want to own every Faction in the game you also have to buy the previous two entries AND all of their DLCs as well.

WHAT?

Was this game secretly influenced by Activision??

This is essentially a $60+ game with hundreds of dollars of DLC that you’re missing out on. This causes MAJOR problems to the gameplay, and I’ll get into that.

Not all Factions in this game are equal, there are a handful of Factions that are just flat out better than others, and that’s where the game goes into straight up Pay 2 Win territory, whether you’re playing PvP or the Campaign mode. Even base game Factions have a handful of their units locked behind DLC as well which is the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard of.

There are also other pretty huge problems with the difficulty scaling, balance, and optimization of this game.

The Battles in this game are insanely clunky and or not working right.

Sometimes I tell my melee units to attack a specific group of enemies, they run in but then they just stand there while they let the enemies cut them down. Sometimes they also chase enemies running away but don’t attack them even though they have the agility to finish the job.

Ranged units sometimes just don’t shoot and just stand there while I’m trying to micro manage other units in the fight. Sometimes they just don’t fire at will even though they have ammo and the terrain is suitable enough. This is very bad if you’re playing an all Ranged Faction, as your units will just stand there like braindead lemmings which can cost you big battles.

After finishing the Prologue, I decided to jump into Campaign mode so that I could conquer the map all on my own using everything that I had learned.

But then that initial confidence turned into pure unadulterated frustration as I would get repeatedly smacked around by opposing Lords who are over 10 or 15 levels higher than me and not being able to do anything about it, forcing me to admit defeat and end my entire run multiple times.

Basically, I found out that the AI in this game are dumb as bricks who only ever attack first and ask questions later, and as such, they by default get way more resources than you do, meaning they will always have larger and stronger armies than you, immediately putting you at a disadvantage the entire time as you’re just trying to build up your settlements and unlock better units so that you can actually stand a chance in case someone tries to attack you.

Sometimes a Lord who is 15 levels over me will declare war against me for practically no reason, and no matter what I do I cannot negotiate peace with them, so they’ll just run around the map steamrolling all of my settlements which further cripples by resource farming until I take the settlements back, but then it reaches a point where my units are so under leveled it’s practically impossible. So then they’ll invade my castle, wipe me out immediately, and then the run is just over.

This has happened to me three times in a row on just the Normal difficulty setting. It is absolutely infuriating.

This wouldn’t be so bad if there were actual defenses like walls forcing the enemy to do a siege before they can actually reach and attack the settlements, but because there are none whatsoever, some random group of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ can just sugar plum fairy waltz into town, probably armed with full auto AR-15s, not giving a single ♥♥♥♥.

This basically forces me to stop everything that I’m doing while I’m trying to unlock more settlements, earn more income, upgrade my research trees, level up my Lord, and make allegiances with other Factions, just so I could waste multiple turns running across the map and deal with it. And while I’m wasting time, all the other enemy Factions are getting stronger, getting ready to launch an invasion against me, and not before they kill all my other allies until I’m the only one left.

And I simply don’t have the resources to have big armies on standby at every single settlement in case of an attack. Losing even one settlement can be devastating to my overall growth and survival throughout the run.

Also, this game is very unoptimized even though I’m on a mid to high tier PC. Why is this game 120GB when I don’t even have any of the DLCs??

I’m also forced to have this game installed on my SSD even though the Steam page says it’s not required, otherwise the game will either take 3-5 minutes to load, or it will crash during the loading screen even though the game isn’t even that graphically impressive and I am well above the recommended specs. 

Also, when you end your turn the game’s frame rate takes an absolute nose dive when you use the fast forward button to speed up the turns of everyone else because it takes so long, and this causes the frame rate to go as low as 5 or 10 and the stuttering is non-stop, it honestly makes me feel like my game is melting down.

If the studio was going to ask everyone to pay for all of these DLCs, then you would think that they would use that money to polish the game and actually make it more fun to play, but this is the opposite of that, it’s one of the most egregious examples of prioritizing monetization over the player experience.

I would not recommend you to pick this game up, especially if you’re new to this type of game. There are many other better alternatives from what I’ve heard.

Jeśli ktoś zastanawia się, czy Warhammer 3 to strategia godna polecenia, to odpowiedź brzmi: oczywiście… pod warunkiem, że lubisz patrzeć, jak Twoja armia stoi w miejscu, podczas gdy przeciwnik robi dokładnie to samo, tylko szybciej i z większym przekonaniem.

Kampania zapowiada epicką walkę o losy świata, ale w praktyce przypomina maraton chodzenia od portalu do portalu, żeby znowu walczyć w tej samej mapie, tylko z innym kolorem przeciwnika. Klimat mrocznego fantasy? Jest.. Problem w tym, że po kilkunastu turach zaczynasz się zastanawiać, czy Chaos nie próbuje przypadkiem zniszczyć świata z czystej nudy.

Bitwy są widowiskowe, przynajmniej przez pierwsze pięć minut. Potem okazuje się, że połowa Twoich jednostek stoi, druga połowa biega w kółko, a jedna dzielna jednostka kawalerii goni pojedynczego goblina przez pół mapy. Sztuczna inteligencja potrafi jednocześnie być genialna i kompletnie bezmyślna, co jest imponujące.

Nie można też zapomnieć o legendarnych momentach optymalizacji, kiedy komputer nagle zaczyna symulować działanie elektrowni węglowej, tylko po to, żeby pokazać Ci 20 demonów bijących się z 20 ludźmi w 15 klatkach na sekundę.

A przy okazji drobna rada techniczna: lepiej nie klikać „kontynuuj kampanię” przy uruchamianiu gry. Istnieje spora szansa, że gra w tym momencie postanowi zakończyć swoje życie razem ze Steamem, Twoją tapetą i prawdopodobnie połową procesów systemowych. Efekt jest taki, że po chwili budzisz się z czarnym pulpitem i zastanawiasz się, czy to jeszcze Windows, czy już nowy tryb Chaosu.

Лучшая и самая масштабная игра Creative Assembly на данный момент, просто любовь с первого взгляда ❤️, хотя до TWW3 играл только в историческую линейку и был не очень знаком с лором Вахи. За 300 часов я, кажется, изучил максимум 30% контента — и интерес только растет.
Очень порадовал кооператив на 8 человек. После других частей, в том числе исторических, где в кампанию можно было играть только вдвоем, это ощущается как огромный шаг вперед.
Огромная карта, куча фракций и отличная реиграбельность. Причем разные фракции играются настолько по-разному, что иногда создается ощущение, будто играешь в другую игру. Моды — отдельный плюс: они реально закрывают слабые места и добавляют больше разнообразия (и расширяют саму карту).
Да, базовая игра дает примерно 10% доступного контента фракций. Но покупка DLC здесь не раздражает: почти все куплены по скидке, а желание попробовать новые фракции и механики только подогревает интерес. Единственный минус — часть отрядов привязана к DLC с лордами, и игра не всегда прямо говорит об этом. Новичку бывает сложно понять, почему некоторые юниты недоступны.  

+ Атмосферное и масштабное фэнтези
+ Довольно хороший баланс фракций, при их обилии
+ Большое количество отличных модов
+ Реиграбельность 
+ Кооп на 8 человек

- Синхронизация модов в коопе удобнее через сторонний лаунчер
