Слухайте сюды, пацаны! Наш вождь щас вам обзор накатает. Лайк киньте, не западло, а то вечером сидим, скучно аж зубы скрипят. Ага?

Как вождь начинал

Вождь удачливый был — купил Вархаммер третий. Сначала вождь глупый был, нихера не шарил: «Да как так-то?» — думал вождь. Но вождь — он упёртый. Сел в ваху, пиво рядышком, и сидел, сидел... И умный становился, понял? Ух!

Про карту, от которой челюсть отвалилась

Когда вождь на глобальную карту глянул — челюсть аж отвалилась, пацаны! Там такая красотища, прям как в настоящем походе: горы, леса, крепостища, все эти земли, где можно WAAAGH! устроить. Вождь рот открыл и забыл закрыть, пока грот не подбежал и не приставил обратно. Продуманная кампания — это тебе не грязь жрать. Вождь одобряет.

Через пять десятков часов

Через дохрена часов (по-вашему — через 50) вождь уже на новые рассы посматривать начал. И тут вождь понял, что попал, пацаны. Начал вождь дополнения покупать. И это оказалось просто денежным пылесосом, понял? Потому что вождю ВСЁ нравилось. И эти рассы, и те рассы, и даже эти гнилые людишки вдруг вкусными стали, когда за них доплатил. Вождь тырит монетки из копилки гномов, несёт их в магазин, а оттуда — шшшшш! — деньги улетают, а вместо них новые боссы, новые отряды, новые карты. Вождь довольный, но кошелёк плачет горькими слезами.

Так что осторожнее, пацаны. Ваха — она как гриб: попробуешь раз — и уже всё, ты в рабстве у проклятого денежного пылесоса, и тебе это нравится, ага!

Короче

Обзор вождь дописал, пиво кончилось. Итог: ваха годная, карта красивая, дополнения тянут все деньги, но оно того стоит. А теперь вождь пошёл гномов лупить. Лайк ставьте, да позырьте — вождь глянет, может, ещё накатает. WAAAGH!

FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF SOMEONE WHO HAS NO WARHAMMER OR TOTAL WAR BACKGROUND

This game is truly awesome. There is an incredible amount of depth- as of right now there are 105 different factions and 24 different races to play as that all feel different. The reason for this level of depth is that this game has been having content added to it since 2016, because the vast majority of content from the previous two games has been rolled into it. Even if you don't own all of the DLC, you still get to play against the races and lords you don't own, which adds variety. If price is an issue, you can buy as you go and wait for Steam sales to bring the prices down. At 415 hours into this game, I still have not gotten close to playing as all of them.

The game itself is turn-based until two or more armies overlap on the campaign map, which triggers a real-time strategy battle. This allows you to take your time to focus on the strategic decisions building up your empire without being rushed and focus only on combat during combat, unlike other real time strategy games. Both the strategic turn-based gameplay and the real time battle gameplay are awesome. While there is a lot to learn, the easiest difficulty is, well, easy, so the learning curve is not too punishing. There is also an introductory campaign that does a great job teaching the basics.

I had no experience with Warhammer before this, but it is incredibly easy and exciting to get into the different races and factions- from undead pirates, to elves, to dinosaurs with space lasers, to Vikings riding mammoths, to demons, etc. there are a ton of fun options to choose from. The entire world in the Immortal Empires mode is huge- it has about 300 factions, which keeps the game fresh. This game is a must for anyone who loves fantasy, real time strategy, and turn-based strategy games. You don't need to have any connection to Warhammer or the other Total War games to have a blast with it.

Literally 10% of a game.  Don't Buy unless heavily discounted.

I paid for a full game.  Here's what I get out of the box:
- 9 out of 24 factions are playable
- Approximately 10% of the total leaders are playable.
- I can buy the rest of the game for MORE THAN $300!

This is not a real game.  It is an addendum to a previous game.  I am genuinely flabbergasted why so many other reviewers are giving TW a free pass on this.  I paid for 100% of a game and only get 1/10 of the game!


Here are some more issues that other reviewers have overlooked:

By far the worst balancing I have encountered in the 10+ total war games I've played:

  -  Just about any lord with a regeneration ability and aoe attack can easily solo entire armies.  Why should I even bother training armies?
  -  Some of the monstrous units are mediocre, but many/most DRASTICALLY outperform regular-size units relative to their cost - even killing many regular units with the anti-large trait.
  -  The speed of some of these units is wild.  Ogres and obese rats run faster than horses.  SERIOUSLY?
  -  Some factions have dozens of redundant units.  Others don't have a proper spear unit.
  -  Regular cavalry is insanely weak relative to monstrous units.  Spear and halberd units have charge reflection even when they're facing the wrong direction.  How exactly does that work?   Why bother training cavalry when the enemy is immune?
  -  Any regular-size offensive unit without armor piercing or magical damage might as well just not show up. 
  -  Walls are entirely irrelevant.  Armies don't have to lay siege and build siege equipment.  No, the units simply remove entire ladders from their buttholes, and put them up on the wall.  There are two reasons why this doesn't work in real life:  
1) Most buttholes aren't that big.   
2)  THE GUYS ON THE WALL CAN SIMPLY PUSH THE LADDERS OFF THE WALL!!!
Seriously, this incredibly idiotic aspect completely breaks the balancing of TW strategy.  Any army can just walk in and take your walled settlement with butthole ladders!

Horrific ranged unit mechanics: 

   - They can't friendly fire, but instead just STOP SHOOTING whenever their target gets close to a friendly unit.  Why on earth would I want them not to fire on a half dead friendly unit when there's a 100-foot-tall dude rampaging through my front lines???   Why can't they just shoot the top half of the 100-foot-tall guy??
   - The super narrow front-facing range thing means they constantly do that annoying thing where they refuse to turn their bodies, instead taking 10 seconds to rotate the entire unit, only to realize that the enemy you told them to fire at has now moved, so they must rotate their entire unit again (and again).  This problem exists in multiple TW games, to be fair.

Worst reliance on NPC cheating mechanics I have encountered in 15 years of playing Total War:

   - After killing a faction's ONLY TWO REMAINING armies (you can check this from the diplomacy screen - 100:0 strength), I should have free reign to conquer them.  Instead, next turn they routinely spawn A FULL ARMY with MAX TIER UNITS (only 15 turns in!) that can generally solo my 2-army wrecking ball.  THEY DON'T EVEN HAVE THE NECESSARY MILITARY BUILDINGS TO TRAIN THESE UNITS!!!  This makes for extremely unsatisfying gameplay.
   - Funny how NPC factions can easily support 3-5 armies with ZERO ECONOMIC BUILDINGS while I have 10 level 2 or 3 economic buildings and can almost support two armies.  FUN.
  -  The NPC AI was genuinely much smarter many years ago.  It peaked in Rome 2, imo.  How is it that the NPC AI has gotten so much worse when we're living in the age of AI? This is incredibly lazy!

Positive aspects:
 - Better allied army coordination than previous tw games.
 - Far more diversity in playstyle than I am used to in total war games.
   -  TOO BAD THAT DIVERSITY IS LOCKED BEHIND A $300 PAY WALL!!!

If this wasn't abundantly clear by now:

HEY TOTAL WAR:  GIVE ME A FULL GAME OR PLEASE KINDLY REFUND MY MONEY!

Edit:  after trying all the factions I am able to play, I have cobbled together enough play time that I feel obliged to begrudgingly change my official recommendation from "Don't Buy" to "Only Buy at a Steep Discount"

Après presque 300 heures, j’ai toujours l’impression d’avoir quelque chose à faire, à tester ou à mettre en place, alors même que je maîtrise le jeu.

Le roster est immense, avec énormément de factions, d’unités et de styles de jeu différents.
Chaque nouvelle partie donne envie d’essayer autre chose, ce qui offre une rejouabilité impressionnante sans que l’ennui s’installe.

La carte de campagne est vaste, vivante, colorée et bien animée. 
Entre la gestion, la diplomatie, le développement de son territoire et la guerre, on a réellement l’impression de contrôler l’avenir de sa faction.
Et lorsque les armées se rencontrent, participer à des batailles en temps réel réunissant 40, voire 80 unités, reste toujours impressionnant.
( Soit des armées de 5000 à 10.000 soldats en tout genre) - (puis @@@, c'est STYLED à regarder).

Le principal défaut reste l’équilibrage. (et DLC payant)
Certaines factions paraissent plus délaissées que d’autres, soit parce que leur campagne est moins intéressante, soit parce que leur armée manque d’options réellement déterminantes sur le long terme. 
Heureusement, il y en a suffisamment pour tous les goûts et toutes les couleurs.

Je continue d’y jouer parce que j’ai toujours la sensation d’affiner mon apprentissage selon la faction choisie. 
Certaines sont plus amusantes que d’autres, mais l’ensemble ressemble presque à un immense bac à sable où des dizaines de peuples se développent, s’allient et se font la guerre. (C'est très cool de pouvoir faire de la géopolitique)

Je continue d’y jouer. 
C’est sans doute le meilleur argument que je puisse donner.
Je Recommande !

Total War: Warhammer III is what happens when a grand strategy game decides that diplomacy, economics, and politics are important—but giant demons punching dragons is also important.

The scale is incredible. Whether you are commanding immortal daemons, ancient dragons, undead legions, industrial war machines, or hordes of rat-men with questionable engineering standards, every faction feels distinct and encourages a different playstyle.

Campaigns combine empire management, diplomacy, city development, and massive real-time battles. Watching carefully organized armies clash across the battlefield never gets old, especially when legendary lords and monstrous units start turning entire engagements upside down.

The Immortal Empires campaign is one of the game's biggest strengths, offering a gigantic sandbox filled with dozens of factions, endless rivalries, and enough content to keep strategy fans occupied for hundreds of hours.

Turn times, DLC costs, and the complexity of certain systems may overwhelm new players. Some campaigns also require a significant time investment before your plans fully come together.

They fixed everything bad about TW: Warhammer™ II ©  in TW: Warhammer™ III © . 

Although the visual content in the game is 95% the result of the two previous iterations, all but a handful of the factions have been turned into premium commodities to be unlocked through an off game grind. This is called a 'job'. That unique progression mechanic equates to roughly one and a half hours at the job grind giving you the ability to unlock one faction of your choosing to play as or against. This is nuanced by complicating factors which you'll have fun navigating. For example, the Bretonnian© faction, despite having 'FREE' written on it, is locked until you figure out how to activate it as DLC. The added learning curve of managing your purchases and 'free' content is steep but satisfying, and unlocking factions feels weightier than before, especially when there's no Steam sale event and your car needs repairs.

Speaking of the visual content, units in this game typically bear resemblance to the premium cosmetic items and pets unlocked as digital store purchases in the likes of successful games, like World of Warcraft or Path of Exile. There's lots of gooey looking colours, such as horses with bright orange magma feet. Coupled with unit abilities that cause appearances to glow and sparkle, the result is a premium aesthetic, with the highest-level units evoking that 'I'm Level 70, have a toiletsock and am seriously invested in this' vibe which resonates with me as a DLC completionist.

All in all I give TW: Warhammer™ III © a total of five Warhammer™'s out of five for revolutionising the wheel. DLC and base content from the previous games was creatively repackaged. This may be a £50 game (reduced to £7.50 as of writing) but there are 100s of pounds of repurposed legacy content embedded in it for a non-negotiable fee. 

Just Buy It.

Okay, look... I'm not a genre veteran, nor an ardent fan. But still, I've gotten a pretty good handle on the game; I can see both its problems and its strengths. But since this is a review, I'll mostly talk about the bad parts. First, what immediately catches my eye is the terrible balance between factions and units. When one faction fades into insignificance over another... That's probably not right. For example, take Tamurkhan, an incredibly powerful lord; he can single-handedly take on an army! He has a more or less comfortable starting position and access to good units. And compared to him, Epidemius in the Nurgle faction... He's a good lord, but he's simply not fun to play. Malus, who's terribly close, is the epitome of a bad start. And there are plenty more examples to go on. Secondly, the AI... The AI ​​in this game is incredibly dumb. The whole difficulty lies in the buffs for him. How can that be interesting?! When the AI ​​already has a rare item on turn 5, and the player has brown pants and 5000 in their pocket... It seems like a really bad hack, simply to hide the AI's stupidity in battles and overall behavior. Thirdly: disgusting diplomacy. Diplomacy in a nutshell is something like this: first a treaty with a faction, then the next turn it can break it for no reason... Or just suddenly declare war! And of course, the AI ​​will ignore everyone around it and go specifically for the player... There's no flexibility in diplomacy; the Thracians have a strong dislike for each other, for example, the Empire hates chaos, etc. But perhaps in a strategy game with a huge map, a more flexible and merciful displomacy could have been implemented, right?... And fourthly: terribly long updates. Waiting for a third year for siege changes!? For CA, this is the norm. DLC at some really unreasonable prices? For CA, this is the base. And there are actually many more problems, but these are the main ones for me personally. Should I buy it or not? I'd say no... Unless you consider the mods. The community in this game is incredibly creative, with something for almost every taste! I literally rebuilt the game using mods. And overall, if it weren't for mods, this game would have quickly died...

Eu terminei minha primeira campanha e levei umas 80 horas para isso. Consegui cumprir todos os meus objetivos, alcançar a vitória da campanha e ainda enfrentei a crise que apareceu no meu território. Ainda tinha bastante coisa para fazer, mas decidi que já era suficiente. Eu já tinha feito tudo o que queria naquela campanha.

E isso tudo jogando com apenas um personagem de uma única facção. Eu jogaria novamente sem nenhum problema com outra facção e outro personagem, porque isso muda completamente a experiência.

Eu joguei por 80 horas, expandi igual maluco e, mesmo assim, acho que descobri no máximo 1/5 do mundo. Talvez tenha conhecido menos, algo como 1/10 das facções existentes, e mesmo dessas eu enfrentei uma parcela ainda menor. Esse jogo é simplesmente gigante.

Se você está com receio por causa da quantidade de DLCs, não precisa se preocupar tanto. O conteúdo das DLCs está presente no jogo, você só não pode jogar com aqueles personagens e facções sem comprá-las. Eles continuam existindo no mundo e você pode encontrar esse conteúdo durante a campanha.

Se você tiver interesse em alguma DLC, é só pegar as que realmente gostar. E, sinceramente, cada DLC pode facilmente adicionar dezenas ou até centenas de horas de conteúdo dependendo de como você joga. É um jogo que dá para passar tranquilamente de 1.000 horas.

Eu provavelmente não vou chegar nem perto disso, porque não sou mais moleque com tempo para jogar 24/7, além de gostar de jogar vários jogos diferentes em vez de ficar preso em um só. Mas ainda assim, Total War: Warhammer 3 é um jogo gigantesco e, principalmente, muito divertido.

Com certeza vou rejogar quando tiver outra oportunidade. Na próxima, quero jogar com os Anões.

Também achei o jogo muito bem otimizado. Dos Total War que já joguei, acho que foi o que apresentou o melhor desempenho para mim. Só tive um travamento durante uma batalha, em um cerco de 40x40. Foi algo bem rápido e aconteceu justamente no momento mais intenso do combate, com muitos projéteis, unidades e magias acontecendo ao mesmo tempo.

Fora isso, tive batalhas até mais intensas e não tive travamentos ou quedas de FPS relevantes. Então considero esse problema algo bem pontual e fora da curva.

Acho que é isso. Recomendo demais o jogo.

The Review

Total War: WARHAMMER III is a massive strategy game that brings the Warhammer fantasy universe to life on an incredible scale. It combines deep turn-based empire management with huge real-time battles, creating an experience that can easily keep you playing for hundreds of hours.

One of the biggest strengths is the enormous amount of content. There are a huge number of factions and legendary lords to choose from, and each one offers a different playstyle. Managing your economy, expanding your territory, researching technologies, negotiating with other factions, and building powerful armies gives the campaign a tremendous amount of depth.

The battles are still the highlight. Watching massive armies collide is incredibly satisfying, and there is a lot of strategy involved in positioning units, using magic, managing heroes, and taking advantage of different unit strengths and weaknesses. The variety of factions makes the battles feel fresh, since every army fights differently.

The Immortal Empires campaign is also a huge selling point. Having such a massive combined map with so many factions creates an enormous sandbox with almost endless replayability. No two campaigns have to play out the same way.

However, the game has a steep learning curve, and the sheer number of mechanics can be overwhelming for new players. Campaigns can also become extremely long, and managing a huge empire can sometimes feel more like work than fun. There are also moments where the AI and certain mechanics can be frustrating.

Overall, Total War: WARHAMMER III is an incredible strategy game and one of the best ways to experience the Warhammer universe. Its massive battles, incredible faction variety, deep campaign mechanics, and huge replayability make it easy to lose hundreds of hours in.

Rating: 10/10

Tras más de 200 horas de juego, puedo decir sin temor a equivocarme que Total War: Warhammer 3 es una auténtica obra maestra y la cúspide de la estrategia moderna. Si te apasiona este género o el universo de fantasía oscura, este juego es el Olimpo definitivo, combina lo mejor de las dos entregas anteriores.

Lo que Creative Assembly ha logrado aquí es descomunal, empezando por la variedad de facciones. No estamos hablando de simples cambios de color o estadísticas; cada raza se juega como un videojuego completamente diferente. Desde las brutales cargas y la gestión de la fe de Kislev, la majestuosidad celestial y la armonía de Catai, hasta las retorcidas, únicas y asquerosas mecánicas de campaña de cada uno de los Dioses del Caos. La personalidad que desborda cada facción dentro de su propia raza hace que la rejugabilidad sea, literalmente, infinita. Cada vez que inicias una campaña con un Señor Legendario distinto, tienes que reaprender a jugar.

Visualmente y a nivel de ambientación, la variedad de escenarios es una delicia. Estás batallando en páramos desolados corruptos por la magia del caos, defendiendo murallas colosales en las fronteras de imperios orientales, o emboscando enemigos en bosques densos y oscuros. Cada rincón del mapa se siente vivo y peligroso.

Pero el verdadero clímax del juego está en sus batallas. Cada enfrentamiento es brutal, caótico y completamente distinto al anterior. El choque de infantería pesada, el rugido de los monstruos gigantescos devorando líneas enemigas, los hechizos masivos que cambian el rumbo de la guerra en un segundo y los asedios rediseñados... la espectacularidad táctica y visual te deja con la boca abierta incluso después de cientos de batallas. No hay dos enfrentamientos iguales; el terreno, la composición del ejército enemigo y la magia te obligan a adaptarte constantemente.

Es un pozo de horas infinito. Tiene sus detalles, como todo juego de esta escala, pero la ambición, el mimo al lore y la escala monumental de este título lo convierten en una joya imprescindible. Compra obligada. 

Mi Puntuación Personal dentro del Genero: 8/10. Solo le resto puntos porque literalmente tiene demasiados DLCs, lo valen, porque cada Facción es casi que un juego nuevo, pero es que son DEMSIADOS y para tener todo el 100% del Juego necesitas pagar mucho!!

На очень высокой сложности, люди после потери армии уже на следующий ход восстанавливали стек из 20 т3-т4 туш, при том, что у меня, даже не восстановились все войска с прокачанным героем и наукой. На этом для меня минусы заканчиваются.

7. Магия. Магия.

I told myself I would play one quick campaign. That was a hundred hours ago.

This is the grand finale of the trilogy and, once combined into Immortal Empires, it is the biggest strategy sandbox I have ever sunk a worrying number of hours into. You pick a Legendary Lord, you get a map roughly the size of a small planet, and then you set about ruining everyone's afternoon with an army of demons, rat-men, or undead pirates.

The campaign is a glorious tug of war between the turn-based map, where you scheme and expand and quietly go bankrupt, and the real-time battles, where all that careful planning meets ten thousand screaming enemies and immediately becomes improvisation. When a battle line holds against impossible odds, it is magnificent. When your general panics and legs it, taking the entire army's morale with him, that is your own fault for not guarding the flank.

The factions offer plenty of variety. Not every one reinvents the wheel, and a few play fairly conventionally, but the standout races introduce genuinely unique mechanics that make starting a fresh campaign feel like buying a new game.

Worth mentioning the mods, too. The workshop is enormous and adds a huge amount of value, from quality-of-life fixes to overhauls that keep old campaigns feeling new. If the base game ever gets stale, the community has almost certainly already patched the boredom out.

Now the one real gripe. This is an expensive hobby. The base game is only the start, and the full experience is locked behind a genuinely eye-watering pile of DLC. Individual lord packs and race packs add up fast, and buying it all at once would make your wallet leg it faster than a routed general. My advice is to wait for the sales, pick up the packs for the factions you actually care about, and build your collection gradually rather than in one painful lump.

Would recommend to anyone who likes their strategy enormous, their lore ridiculous, and their evenings gone.

Wir bekommen hier ein Spiel in dem nicht einmal 50% der Fraktionen zur Verfügung stehen! 

Jede Fraktion hat ihre Kommandanten und diese müssen erworben werden ansonsten sind die Fraktionen komplett gesperrt.
Das besste ist: Die wollen, dass wir neben den unzähligen DLCs (die alle nur Kommandanten und / oder Fraktionen beinhalten) noch den ersten und zweiten Teil kaufen um die Kommandanten und damit die Fraktionen erst freikaufen zu können. 

Das übertrifft jegliche Dreistigkeit in der DLC-Politik. Das zeigt sich auch sehr and den Rezensionen zu den einzelnen DLCs. Die Bewertungen fallen durch die Bank weg immer nur ''Ausgeglichen'' aus. 
Das liegt wohl dran, dass die Fraktionen doch nicht eine solch riesige Vielfallt bieten um den völlig übertriebenen Preis von bis zu 20 Euro für einen neuen Kommandanten zu rechtfertigen. 

Es wäre eine Sache gewesen wenn alle Völker / Fraktionen in diesem Vollpreisspiel zur Verfügung gestanden wären und wir nur einzelne Pakete welche neue Kommandanten beinhalten kaufen hätten können. 
Natürlich nicht für die lächerlichen Preise welche uns hier angeboten werden.
Hier sehen wir ein richtig gutes Beispiel dafür wie die Entwickler einfach nur Geld aus dem Konsumenten pressen wollen.

Kauft den 1. und 2. Teil + die DLCs vom 3. Teil und wenn ihr gerade dabei seid euer Geld zum Fenster raus zu werfen kauft doch gleich noch die DLCs von den ersten beiden Teilen. 

Im Sommersale hat dieses Spiel immerhin keine 10 Euro gekostet (-85%).
Somit ist es gerade noch in Ordnung wenn man bedenkt, dass man die andere Hälfte der Fraktionen + den Vorgänger kaufen müsste um es als Vollwertiges Spiel zu betrachten. 

Wenn ihr Total Warhammer III aber als komplettes Spiel spielen wollt macht besser mindestens nochmals 300 Euro zusätzlich locker.

Ich habe die vorherigen Total War Spiele wirklich sehr gerne gespielt und das Warhammer-Universum war immer eine tolle Idee, aber in Total War Warhammer III ist die Kampange einfach nicht spielbar. 
Ich habe bereits durch andere Titel massig Erfahrung gesammelt aber hier stoße ich echt auf meine Toleranzgrenze. Ich schildere folgendes Szenario: mittlerer Schwierigkeitsgrad bis ca. Runde 35.
Seraphon - Gor Rok schnelle Expansion, um die Skaven von der Südflanke wegzubekommen. Allianzen geschmiedet mit den südlicheren Seraphon und den Seefahrenden Hochelfen. Militärbündnis. 
Soweit so gut, Level 15 bei beiden Helden, Khorne Dämonen erklären mir den Krieg. Ich versuche mich für den Kampf vorzubereiten. 

Schädelsammler auf Stufe 25 greift direkt Itza die Hauptstadt mit einer weiteren vollen Armee, beide Armeen mehr oder minder komplett Elite. Der Kampf in der Stadt nicht machbar, trotz massiver Verzögerungsgefechte. Soweit so gut, Itza verloren, Hauptstreitmacht war auf dem Weg, werde angegriffen von der Armee des Schädelsammlers (1 Armee). Gor Rok Taktik geht auf, ich schaffe es die komplette Elite Armee mit massiven Verlusten zu schlagen und töte den Schädelsammler. Hoffe ein paar Runden ruhe zu haben. Falsch gedacht. Eine neue Armee samt Schädelsammler jetzt auf Stufe 31 greift mich original eine Runde nach dem ich ihn besiegt habe erneut an, meine Armee natürlich nach einer Runde so gut wie nicht erholt. zweites Gefecht natürlich verloren. 

Jetzt frag ich mich SEGA, wie schlecht kann man eine KI programmieren, dass man absolut keine Chance hat, sich irgendwie dieser völlig unverhältnismäßigen Flut an Gegner zu erwehren??? 
Es ist so frustrierend, die Zeit die man darein investiert um in der Kampagne irgendwas zu erreichen, auch mit schneller Expansion und dann wird man von allen Seiten mit KI Gegner zugeworfen, die dann auch noch, wenn man sie irgendwie besiegt, sofort neu generiert werden und man den ganzen Blödsinn nochmal machen muss? Wenn das euer Ernst ist, dann ist die schlechte Bewertung mehr als gerechtfertigt. Wer pures Meta Gekaufe und Positionieren möchte bitte, aber das hat nicht mehr mit einem Echtzeittaktik Spiel zu tun, wie es die Titel vorher geschafft haben. 
Ich bin als langjähriger Fan mehr als enttäuscht und kann nur hoffen, dass ihr Warhammer 40k Total War nicht auch völlig an die Wand fahrt. Wenn es so werden sollte wie der Unrat hier, dann schaue ich mir das max. zwei Stunden an und werde sofort eine Rückerstattung beantragen. 
In diesem Sinne, überarbeitet eure KI! Wenige Sekunden nach dem man eine Flut an Elitegegnern besiegt, steht die gleiche Armee eine Runde später erneut vor den Toren. 

Edit: Bevor ich es vergesse, ich empfinde es als eine absolute Frechheit, dass man für alle Spielinhalte mehr oder minder drei Mal diesen Titel erwirbt, um alle Inhalte zu haben. Wenn das die Zukunft der Spieleindustrie ist, dann werde ich mich wohl mit alten Titeln die man mit allem drum und dran erworben hat, begnügen. Es ist irgendwann wirklich mal genug.

This is my first grand strategy game (although I do enjoy 4X like Civilization and RTS like Company of Heroes). I think it's awesome! 

This game is really less the third part of a trilogy, and more like the second expansion to the first game. The DLCs of each all add onto each other and if you want a decent amount of choice, you're going to want to buy (at minimum) all three games and possibly invest in some DLC too. However, all of the factions will appear in your games regardless of whether you own them or not-- and definitely do research on whether you actually will enjoy a faction rather than just blindly purchasing so you can save your money.  

Now with ALL of that said, CA are still pumping out updates, and the gameplay despite being rather hard to get into, is very addicting. 

The gameplay loop is basically turn-based on a massive map sort of similar to a 4X game where you construct cities and build out your civilization, but combat which occurs when you have two Lords face each other down, you use their accompanying army to win on a huge sprawling map similar to an RTS. The blend is really fun if you come from both kinds of strategy games.

In the Immortal Empires mode basically you pick a faction and they have their own specific campaign, including a defined map start and unique win conditions to said faction. There is something for everybody, whether you like the classic humans, elves and dwarves, or something different like gothic vampires, Mesoamerican-inspired Lizard people, Chaos daemons et cetera. Warhammer Fantasy in general is a really cool rabbit hole to dive into.

I went into Total War: Warhammer expecting to enjoy it because I have played the Total War series for many years. I love the historical games, especially being able to command armies, manage a campaign, and watch battles unfold up close.

There are definitely things that Warhammer does well. The battles are impressive, the unit variety is huge, and I can see why many people enjoy the fantasy setting. However, it just wasn't for me.

The biggest issue is the setting. I understand that the fantasy world is the main appeal for many players, but I personally found it too focused on fantasy gods, demons, and religious-style factions. I prefer historical settings where the focus is on real armies, cultures, and conflicts rather than a world built around fantasy religions and powerful gods.

Another issue I have is the amount of extra content that requires additional purchases. After buying the game, I don't like feeling like some of the factions and experiences I want to try are locked behind more DLC. I understand that developers need to support games over time, but from a player's perspective it can feel disappointing to buy a full-price game and then discover many interesting factions require more spending.

I also don't enjoy the multiplayer experience. Like other Total War games, there is noticeable input delay where your units don't always respond instantly to commands. It makes battles feel less smooth and takes away from the experience.

Overall, I can understand why people love Total War: Warhammer, and it has a lot of depth and variety. But for me, the fantasy setting, DLC approach, and multiplayer delays make it difficult to enjoy. I prefer the historical Total War games where the battles and campaigns feel more grounded.

Alright...the good, the bad, and the ugly:

The good: 
By far the most fun grand campaign in any of the TW games, or at least the ones I've played. Each faction has mechanics that *typically* make them feel unique and grounded in the lore and realm. Whether you're playing as Karl Franz trying desperately to unite your lands while watching your northern cousins get STEAMROLLED by Archon the Everchosen and his loose alliance of misfit skaven, norsca, and daemons. Or when the call of the WAAAAAAGH is just too overwhelming and you must once again call upon the hordes of Grimgor Ironhide. And who doesn't love sending waves of skeletons into enemy lines as the Von Carsteins cast devastating spells? But say you have a favorite playstyle? Well *luckily* for you, there's literally hundreds of dollars worth of DLC to sort through and find legendary lords that fit how you want to play. The AI on the campaign map, when it's working properly, tends to play how you would expect a game titled TOTAL WAR to play. There will be war, and lots of it. 

The bad:
Despite the fact that there are several factions that are naval leaning, there is no naval combat. This is by far, my biggest complaint. Why would you label ANYTHING as naval combat when "naval combat" is ALWAYS played out on a land battle map? When did naval combat become irrelevant? I may be in the minority for the community, I truly don't know. But I think it is absolutely ridiculous that other, older titles were able to deliver naval combat but this one can't. I honestly think it comes down to laziness on the developers end. I don't think they can be bothered to figure out how to combine magic and naval combat. Unfortunately the laziness of Creative Assembly will be another huge one for the "bad" category. Do they update a lot? Sure. Do they listen to their fans? Only after getting review bombed. And to top it all off there is SO MUCH MONEY that you have to spend to unlock all the legendary lords that you have to shop deals and do it over a huge amount of time if you have, you know a normal life with bills to pay. And their lack of care for their customers and their greed has definitely cause major problems amongst players in the past and I truly doubt we've seen the last of that. 

The ugly:
The lore of the Warhammer world is problematic. However, this is Steam so that's all I'll say here on that specific topic. What I will say is that this game, like many others in the TW franchise, suffer from late game Waritis [TM]. Scroll through YT and you'll find the same sentiment over and over, we love this game and want to play it, but the end game SUCKS so much that you have to create your own goals and criteria for a campaign after a while. Things like ranged only armies, one city campaigns, and low tier only are some of my personal favorites. However, I truly believe this could be solved if there was a more in depth diplomacy system in the base game itself. For starters, I think the simple change of allowing the player to confederate any faction with a high enough relational score would be huge. Imagine growing the Dwarven Kingdom so large and powerful that your long standing ally finally bends the knee to your power and now Thorgrim Grudgebearer sits on the throne of the Empire of Man. Is it "lore accurate"? NO! Of course not, but isn't the point of this game to be able to tell the story that we want to tell on that specific playthrough? Because I'll tell you that it's also not "lore accurate" for Elspeth Von Draken to sit on the throne but I've conquered the entire Old World with her more times than with Karl. My point is, the accuracy to the lore should and does only matter up to the point in which the player presses that "begin campaign" button.

TL;DR
Good- Unique grand campaigns for different factions, WAR
Bad- No naval combat, greedy company that doesn't listen
Ugly- Problematic lore + lack of in depth diplomacy between different races = boring late game

[h1]Лучший тотал вар[/h1]

Каждая фракция с уникальными механиками. За каждую фракцию побегать в песочницу есть интерес. 

Не помню игру, в которой я мог поставить 296 модов и отыграть 160 ходов без критических лагов, вылетов и т.п. При чем битвы я играю. Не зря же я миллион юнитов новых надобавлял каждой фракции. Полный угар. Что самое интересное, Ai-шка даже базовая нанимает юнитов с модов. Но естественно некоторые моды могут быть несовместимы. Хотя вот вам мой пример. Если что я не особо че то выбирал или вдумывался. Я буквально налайкал 300 модов +, поставил их на игру, даже моды со старых версий, и у меня все работает. Учитывайте еще, что играю в компанию бессмертных империй, а это карта 3 вархамеров вместе. Выходит бионикл из тысячи деталей. 

Из-за столь огромной карты и большого количества минорных фракций создается ощущение тотальной глобальной войны. На высоких сложностях большой брат в лице сильных мейн фракций во всех частях карты будет постоянно качаться.  

В игре есть полноценный лейт гейм. К концу игры собирается 3-6 локальных лидеров на разных частях карты. Также советую обязательно включать галочки сюжетов конца игры. Это создает полную суету, глобальный кризис.

Не слушайте любителей исторических тотал варов. Чтоб скинуть напалм на орду орков и получить с этого кайф не нужно вычитывать тысячи страниц лора вахи. 

Закрасить карту на высоких сложностях это реально челендж, ну или хотя бы выиграть компанию. 

А с такими скидками на Тактиконе, ну кто урвал тот урвал. Я за фулл прайс брал для себя и не пожалел, пока только за темных эльфов и кислев 1/4 карты закрасил и был не самой мощной фракцией на карте. Это если еще накинуть моды на улучшение AI, ну короче есть что поделать, как пофаниться.

Да, по существу в игре одна главная проблема. Отсутствие отката на более старые версии это прям ужасно, учитывая все эти внезапные баг фиксы и прочее. На игру тонна отличных модов, но многие из них уже не работают на более новых версиях. Думаю это намеренная политика разраба. Даже так комьюнити мододелов продолжает поддерживать многие топовые моды за что ребятам бесконечный респект.

TLDR: Game is amazing and infinitely replayable and has a large modding community but can be glitchy for some and everything costs money to unlock.

This is one of my favorite games and while i dont have thousands of games i have more than a large amount of people so this is really saying something. The entire game is locked behind dlcs and owning the previous games. To fully buy the game at full price as of me writing this review is over $700 CAD and will rise. On sale this drops to less than half of that. Even at full price, its cheaper than a single actual Warhammer tabletop army and the game has HUGE amounts more content and replayability than it. The good news is you dont have to buy everything at once, a lot of stuff you dont even have to buy at all because chances are you wont want to play every single one of the dlc lords. I have played almost 100 hours now and have BARELY played any of the lords because of how much time it takes to complete a single campaign and how many there are, i dont even own every dlc yet. If you enjoy the core gameplay loop of diplomacy with 300 nations, managing your economy, and battles with thousands to tens of thousands of units, you can easily get thousands of hours of gameplay out of this. Every single faction is unique, you can play as rats who throw slaves and rats with miniguns onto the battlefield and drop nukes on everyone, humans with more guns per battle than all of the USA combined, short humans who pilot flying canons, really angry green guys who can yell really loudly and double their armies for no extra cost, demons who hate everyone and can recruit entire armies in an instant, and like 50 more. Every campaign is completely unique and often takes well over a full day of continuous gameplay to beat on normal difficulty. Theres tons of unique end time events which are pretty much challenges which in the late game buff certain enemy factions a ton. The game never gets too repetitive and is rarely too easy to enjoy (excluding playing the changeling that guy physically cant lose and has the most boring campaign of all time). The game also has a large modding community which has tons of qol and retextures but also entire new factions, new legendary lords, faction overhauls, new units, and more. If you ever somehow play everything the game has you can download mods which adds tons more. You can also just do challenge runs limiting yourself to make completely new experiences. Sure the game can at times be a bit buggy but i have almost never experienced any problematic glitches. The ai can sometimes cheat with their economy but its not a big deal. The only major issue with the game is that almost no new or past content is free. The game is still great but expect to pay quite a bit to fully unlock the content.

Ich hätte nie gedacht, dass ich jemals eine negative Rezension über Total War: Warhammer III schreiben würde. Mit über 2.250 Spielstunden sollte jedem klar sein, dass ich dieses Spiel liebe. Es ist eines meiner absoluten Lieblingsspiele und meiner Meinung nach eines der besten Strategiespiele, die je entwickelt wurden. Gerade deshalb tut es mir unglaublich weh, diese Bewertung zu schreiben. Ich spiele das Spiel zu rund 90 % im Multiplayer, meistens mit drei bis vier Freunden. Und genau hier liegt das Problem. Seit über zwei Jahren kämpfen wir mit regelmäßigen Abstürzen. Anfangs waren wir überzeugt, dass unsere Mods schuld sind. Also haben wir nach und nach alle entfernt und spielen seit etwa einem Jahr ausschließlich Vanilla, also komplett ohne Mods.

Und wisst ihr was?

Es hat absolut nichts geändert.

Das Spiel stürzt weiterhin regelmäßig ab. Kampagnen werden unterbrochen, Spieler fliegen raus, alle müssen neu verbinden oder den Spielstand neu laden. Und das passiert nicht einmal selten, sondern so regelmäßig, dass man sich innerlich schon darauf einstellt, wann der nächste Absturz kommt, nicht ob.

Bevor jetzt wieder jemand schreibt: "Dann liegt es wohl an euren PCs."

Nein.

Unsere Rechner sind alle erst zwei bis drei Jahre alt und liegen deutlich über den empfohlenen Systemanforderungen. Das Problem besteht bei mehreren Personen, auf unterschiedlichen Systemen und sogar komplett ohne Mods. Irgendwann muss man einfach akzeptieren, dass das Problem nicht bei den Spielern liegt.

Und genau das macht mich so wütend.

Denn unter all diesen technischen Problemen steckt eines der besten Strategiespiele, die ich jemals gespielt habe. Die Fraktionen sind einzigartig, die Schlachten machen unglaublich viel Spaß und die Immortal Empires Kampagne ist ein Traum für jeden Warhammer Fan. Aber was bringt mir das alles, wenn der Multiplayer seit Jahren in einem Zustand ist, in dem man ständig Angst haben muss, dass die nächste Kampagne wieder durch einen Absturz unterbrochen wird?

Ich würde dieses Spiel jedem empfehlen.

Wenn er Singleplayer spielt.

Sobald aber jemand sagt: "Ich möchte das hauptsächlich mit meinen Freunden spielen", kann ich inzwischen nur noch antworten:

Lass es.

Und glaubt mir: Niemand schreibt diesen Satz ungerner als ich.

Nach über 2.250 Stunden hat selbst meine Geduld irgendwann ein Ende gefunden. Es fühlt sich an, als würde man eine langjährige Beziehung beenden. Man liebt den anderen Menschen immer noch, erinnert sich an all die schönen Momente und möchte eigentlich nicht loslassen. Aber irgendwann muss man sich eingestehen, dass es so nicht weitergehen kann. Genau so fühlt sich Total War: Warhammer III für mich heute an. Ich hoffe von Herzen, dass Creative Assembly den Multiplayer endlich ernst nimmt und diese Probleme nachhaltig behebt. Denn dieses Spiel hätte es verdient. Bis dahin kann ich den Multiplayer jedoch nicht mehr empfehlen. Und das ist vermutlich die traurigste Rezension, die ich jemals geschrieben habe.

Ein Traum für Fantasy- und Herr-der-Ringe-Fans

Total War: Warhammer III ist für mich eines der motivierendsten Strategiespiele überhaupt. Der größte Pluspunkt ist die unglaubliche Vielfalt. Es gibt unzählige Fraktionen mit völlig unterschiedlichen Einheiten und Spielweisen. Ob Menschen, Zwerge, Hochelfen, Dunkelelfen, Orks, Vampire oder Chaos – jede Fraktion fühlt sich einzigartig an und erfordert eine andere Strategie.

Besonders gelungen ist das Schere-Stein-Papier-Prinzip der Einheiten. Man gewinnt nicht einfach mit der größten Armee, sondern muss seine Truppen clever zusammenstellen und taktisch einsetzen. Dadurch entstehen immer wieder spannende Schlachten, in denen man mit der richtigen Taktik auch stärkere Gegner besiegen kann.

Das absolute Highlight ist für mich jedoch die Immortal Empires-Kampagne. Die riesige Weltkarte mit nahezu allen Fraktionen des Warhammer-Universums sorgt dafür, dass man hunderte Stunden investieren kann. Jede Kampagne verläuft anders, sodass der Wiederspielwert enorm hoch ist.

TL;DR: Total War: Warhammer III is one of the best strategy games as a newcomer to Total War I've ever played and an incredible finale to the trilogy. The sheer variety of factions, excellent visuals, and almost endless replayability have kept me coming back for hundreds of hours, and I still haven't experienced everything the game has to offer. It isn't perfect; the mountain of DLC, annoying Skaven spam, and lack of more cinematic campaigns are definite downsides, but the core gameplay is outstanding. If you're a fan of strategy games or Warhammer Fantasy, this is an easy recommendation. Just be prepared to spend a bit more if you want the complete experience.

Total War: Warhammer III is the third and final (perhaps?) game in the epic trilogy Creative Assembly has crafted with Games Workshop. I've been playing these games since nearly the beginning, starting with the first game in 2017 (I got it from that Humble Monthly nearly nine years ago).
This is an absolutely vast game. I've played the trilogy for over 300 hours across all my playthroughs, and I haven't even played half the factions yet. This was also my first Total War game, so I can't really judge whether the balance is out of whack or what does and doesn't work. People far more experienced than me, who have put thousands of hours into the series, have done a much better job covering those aspects, so I won't really go into them. All I can do is tell you whether I recommend it, provide my own take, and offer whatever meager criticisms I can.

So, a quick rundown. Total War is a long-running series of real-time strategy games with light-to-moderate grand strategy elements in which you play as a lord, noble, general, king, or similar ruler across whatever historical period the game is set in (Shogun focuses on Sengoku-era Japan, Empire on the 18th century, Rome during the Y2K Crisis... etc.). You grow your realm, conquer your rivals, and then inevitably get ganked by the cheating AI.

Total War: Warhammer is unique because it's the first game in the series based on a fantasy universe. Speaking of Warhammer, I suppose a brief overview is in order. It's basically an amalgamation of everything some British dudes in the '80s thought was the coolest ♥♥♥♥ imaginable. Ancient and medieval history from countless cultures mixed with WWI, Napoleonic warfare, Aztecs, and a whole host of other influences, alongside The Lord of the Rings, Elric of Melniboné, Conan, and much more. Basically, it can be as high fantasy as World of Warcraft (which is quite a sore spot for Games Workshop, but let me not digress) or as grounded as a 19th-century American Civil War battle if you want. I could go through all the factions, but we'd be here for a good hour. At its core, it's an excuse to make your expensive tabletop models fight. I should at least describe the factions that debuted in this game, though.

Warhammer III has a focus on "newcomers" to the Warhammer world. First is Kislev, a human-focused "Not Russia" (yes, I'm oversimplifying, but we're short on time) faction that didn't have a proper army roster until now. Guns, artillery, bears, horses, bears, ice magic... and bears.

Next up is Grand Cathay, essentially Not China. I haven't played as them yet (or even fought them in battle, funnily enough). Did I mention how huge this game is?

The four Chaos God factions have also been added to the series. Chaos has technically been represented since the first game in 2016, but they were quite lacking (really lacking) missing much of their flavor and identity, largely being represented by Chaos Undivided (and yes, explaining that properly would take forever). Now each of the four Chaos Gods has its own army. Khorne focuses on heavy infantry that excel in melee combat (fitting). Tzeentch is a spellcasting powerhouse. Nurgle emphasizes durability and poisonous units (while also being delightfully disgusting). Slaanesh is incredibly fast and focuses on devastating charges.

The Ogre Kingdoms were also a long-awaited race. They're essentially Not Mongols with a focus on monstrous heavy infantry. They were free for players who preordered the game or bought it at launch (which excludes me!).

So, with that very "concise" overview out of the way, let's get into what works and what doesn't, at least for me.

The game looks fantastic. Creative Assembly really did Warhammer justice and did an excellent job making every army feel visually distinct. On top of that, everything is incredibly detailed to a degree you wouldn't expect for a game of this scale. The Chaos Daemons, which were long awaited, are wonderfully varied and beautifully animated. You can only imagine how long it must have taken to animate the Nurglings or the Slaaneshi Pleasureseekers.

You'd think that a game capable of putting thousands of units on screen would struggle to run. While my PC is admittedly quite powerful at the time of writing (RTX 5070 Ti, 64GB DDR5, Ryzen 7 9800X3D), the game only really hitches a little during the late game on the campaign map. I honestly don't remember the actual battles ever lagging.

It's also just really fun to play. Even though I've been playing these games for almost ten years, I'm pretty sure I'll still be playing them ten years from now. There's definitely a learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, it's really not that bad. Just stay far away from online until you've completed at least a few campaigns.

Criticisms? Well, it's plain to see that there's an avalanche of DLC. I own a good chunk of it, but I haven't picked up much of the Warhammer III DLC yet. Each game contains four core races (with the first game also including the free Bretonnia race), while the rest comes through DLC. Thankfully, it all goes on sale pretty frequently.

The good thing is that you can still fight against DLC factions even if you don't own them, and Creative Assembly has added a lot of quality-of-life updates and free content over the years, which makes the whole package a bit easier to swallow. Of course, if you want absolutely everything, you'll probably be paying somewhere in the neighborhood of $200, even during sales, and it doesn't look like they're done releasing DLC yet.

One thing I find incredibly tedious is the Skaven spam. If you're playing in the Old World, it feels like the mid-game inevitably turns into a giant game of whack-a-mole. I think there should be a better way to make the Vermintide less obnoxious.

I've almost exclusively played Immortal Empires (the sandbox mode) and haven't touched the main campaigns. The sandbox can become a bit samey after a while, but it's mostly intended for roleplaying anyway. It would be great to see campaigns based on major lore events like the War of the Beard or the Age of Three Emperors. It's strange that, almost ten years into the trilogy, we still don't have something more cinematic along those lines.

I also don't really care for siege battles, so I haven't fought many of them. The few I have played felt overwhelming and a bit tedious because of how enormous the maps are. Since I don't have much experience with them, though, don't put too much weight on my opinion there.
And then there's the Blood DLC. I've already bought it, but paying to uncensor a game is just nonsense. Thankfully, you only have to buy it once for the trilogy, but it's still a silly practice.

Overall, this is nothing short of a masterpiece that can easily provide hundreds, if not thousands of hours of gameplay. Just be prepared to open your wallet if every race catches your interest.

[h2] Еще 1 ход и спать... [/h2]

[h3] Нет лучше выбора для любителей жанра стратегий и фэнтези сеттинга. [/h3]

В Total War я начал играть с Rome II, в основном ради режима сражения. Это было как глоток свежего воздуха. Как только позволило железо, решил опробовать новую игру серии и ни разу не пожалел. (Хотя в этом обзоре буду делать фокус на минусах) Сейчас я прошел пролог и отыграл первую кампанию за китайцев на ср/ср сложности, делюсь впечатлениями.

[b]ПЛЮСЫ:[/b]

[b]+Сеттинг[/b]
Я не хейтер исторички, мне понравился второй Рим, да и третью Медь буду ждать, но субъективно, чуть интереснее проходить кампанию именно в выдуманном мире без исторических рамок. К тому же фэнтези открывает кучу возможностей для подобного жанра игры. Ниже подробнее о каких возможностях речь.

[b]+Визуал[/b]
Римляне и египтяне конечно отличаются внешне, однако все же не на уровне дворфов и крысолюдей. Каждая раса, фракция, лорд, отряд выглядят уникально, ярко, атмосферно.

[b]+Контент[/b]
Да, в игре куча рас (больше 20) и еще больше фракций, это потенциально бешеная реиграбельность на сотни часов, если не больше.

[b]+Сражения[/b]
Главная фишка всей серии TW — масштабные сражения. В вахе у фракций еще больше отличий по боевым механикам, опять же благодаря сеттингу. В исторических частях такого не найдешь. Д0лбаные крысочеловеки будут брать тебя числом, зомбаков не обратить в бегство, огромные чудища пугают селян с копьями, ну а аое-спеллы - это больно.


[b]МИНУСЫ:[/b]

[b]-Платный контент[/b]
Тут каждый про это написал, вы итак все поняли, с одной TW:WH3 в библиотеке вам доступны только 9 из 24 рас, а значит примерно только треть контента. Если вы, как и я, не хотите играть на нечисти всякой, то к вашему вниманию 3 норм фракции: китайцы, русские и французы. За немцев, дворфов и эльфов придется доплатить. Я не оспариваю право разрабов фармить голду на своем детище, их право, без базара, но по фулл-прайсу это вам влетит в копеечку. Так что, господа, ждите скидок. Ну или...

[b]-Просчет конца хода[/b]
Это очень долго, реально, даже на неплохом железе. Я конечно все понимаю, гигантская карта, больше 200 фракций изначально, только если добавить математики: в среднем 20-30 сек на просчет в кампании на 100-120 ходов = грубо говоря 1 час времени афк ждешь действий ИИ.

[b]-Нудный лейт-гейм[/b]
Не зря говорят, что после первых 100 ходов кампания становится невыносимой. Может не для всех так, но когда у тебя 30+ поселений, 6-7 армий, 10-15 лордов/героев, плюс уникальные механики фракций, управлять этой махиной становится охренительно скучно. Я считаю, разрабам надо внедрить какую-нибудь систему автоматизации рутины в поздней игре, она как бы частично есть, но этого недостаточно.

[b]-Сложный лейт-гейм[/b]
Снова про лейту. Казалось бы вот, ты укомплектовал все армии, выровнял экономику и готов идти на победу в долгой кампании, как какая-то мра3ь нашлет чуму на 20 из 30 твоих городов, все армии с лордами будут постепенно разваливаться и это будет длиться 15 ходов, а потом еще ходов 10 ты будешь восстанавливать силы. В игре кучу механик-кризисов конца игры, чтобы вам не стало "скучно", ну или чтобы у вас сгорела жепа.


[h3]Подводя итог, обозначаем: игра — топ. Стоит своих денег. Затягивает сильно, 40 часов за 2 недели, поэтому аккуратнее со временем. Иногда лучше просто сохраниться и выйти из игры вовремя.[/h3]

Et nous arrivons au troisième opus avec ce Total War : Warhammer III qui propose, dans la lignée de son prédécesseur, plus de factions, plus de campagnes... plus de tout ! Toujours développé par Creative Assembly et sorti en 2022, il est vrai que je me suis mis à cet opus avec un peu - sinon pas mal - de retrait, d'appréhension... sachant que la seule raison d'existence de ce titre était une sorte de refonte graphique avec un simple ajout de quelques factions et seigneurs de guerre ; et il semblerait que nous soyons tous contents de payer les différents mais pas si différents épisodes toujours aussi chers, quand bien même cette vision se discute. Mais j'ai fini par l'acquérir et me suis innocemment engagé dans de nouvelles conquêtes qui, en premier lieu, m'ont laissées un goût bien amer en bouche...

Effectivement, rien ne change concernant la recette. Ce qui était déjà le cas pour le deuxième me direz-vous ! Exact. Mais le précédent opus avait au moins su susciter mon engagement grâce à des apports que j'ai trouvé intéressant, là où le troisième m'a accueilli assez froidement, sans forcément le vouloir certes mais le mal était déjà fait...

Pour l'histoire, nous avons le droit à de nouveaux scénarios en lien avec les nouveaux événements mondiaux qui secouent les différents peuples du Vieux Monde. Ces derniers sont toujours aussi prenant et se laissent découvrir avec joie. Nous avons également une campagne tournant autour de la faction de Kislev, qui reste sympathique malgré quelques clichés inhérents à l'univers de Warhammer, ce qui m'a paradoxalement un peu ennuyé tant on s'attend aux différents revirements que nous fait vivre cette campagne solo. Notons également le retour des batailles de scénario qui ont le mérite de nous faire creuser les méninges et soulignons également que les nouveautés de cette section m'ont également pas mal ennuyé pour une raison que je détaillerais dans les prochains paragraphes. Mais voilà, en soi, nous n'avons guère de changement à proprement parler concernant l'histoire : on reste dans des intrigues martiales plutôt bien réfléchies, et c'est quelque part tout ce que l'on attend d'un Total War, d'autant plus estampillé Warhammer.
Donc, en bref, c'est toujours un plaisir de se lancer dans une campagne ou d'entamer un nouveau scénario nerveux.

Là où cela se gâte, de manière strictement personnelle, c'est avec les nouvelles factions. Nous accueillons dans ce troisième jeu les factions du Chaos : Nurgle, Slaanesh, Khorne et Tzeentch, ainsi que le Grand Cathay, les Démons du Chaos, les Nains du Chaos, les Royaumes Ogres et Kislev. Et tout comme avait pu l'être les factions inédites du deuxième jeu, j'ai débuté mon aventure au moment où les factions du Chaos étaient surpuissantes ! Et étant borné - notamment grâce, ou à cause du précédent opus - à jouer la Bretonnie ou l'Empire, mes factions de cœur, je me suis fait arracher en boucle comme pas possible, au point de me décourager et de me faire abandonner le jeu pendant quelques mois. Et je vais sûrement être en désaccord avec une grande partie des joueurs mais... je ne tiens pas plus que ça à élaborer tous les quatre matins de nouvelles stratégies pour espérer sortir vainqueur d'une campagne. Encore une fois, il s'agit du même jeu ! Le même que celui que nous avons vu paraître en 2017, en plus beau et plus complet certes, avec un 3 à la place du 2, mais il n'en demeure pas moins le même ! Je n'ai pas passé 500 heures de jeu à peaufiner une stratégie militaire et économique pour qu'on vienne me dire durant le premier quart d'heure de jeu sur ce nouvel opus : "Oublie tout ce que tu as appris !"
Alors certes, je comprends que l'on souhaite ajouter du fil à retordre aux joueurs vétérans, les pousser dans leurs derniers retranchements... mais j'ai juste eu l'impression d'être puni purement et gratuitement en me privant de stratégies qui fonctionnaient à merveille dans les opus précédents.
Humeur de petit Calimero à part, les nouvelles factions sont assez inégales dans la facilité à les prendre en main, où certaines mécaniques restent assez complexes en comparaison avec la relative simplicité des mécaniques des toutes premières factions. Mais dans l'ensemble, on comprend assez rapidement ce qu'il faut faire pour se constituer une armée digne du Vieux Monde, même si, encore une fois, les armées du Chaos sont - malgré les mises à jour - affreusement pénibles à affronter, que ce soit en campagne, ou lors des Épreuves du Chaos, de fameuses batailles de scénario en mode sans fin où l'on combat les armées de différents Dieux du Chaos.

Pour l'aspect RTS de ce RTS, on va retomber dans le déjà dit puisqu'à partir de ce paragraphe, on ne va plus avoir énormément de nouveauté. On demeure donc sur le schéma classique que l'on connaît bien depuis les débuts et qui est toujours adéquat dans ce troisième opus.

Du côté des graphismes, nous restons sur un visuel issu du deuxième jeu, ce qui ne veut pas dire que nous sommes face à un opus moche : la qualité visuelle est toujours au rendez-vous, pour notre plus grand plaisir.

Pour les combats, nous sommes sur la même critique faite pour les deux premiers jeux.

Tout comme pour la bande son qui reste fort sympathique.

Tout comme pour les lieux ainsi que les décors qui n'ont que peu bougé depuis le deuxième jeu, si on exclut évidemment les régions orientales, à tonalité asiatique pour l'architecture des bâtiments, qui font leur apparition ici.

Total War : Warhammer III est un très bon jeu et un excellent RTS. Le problème, et il est, une fois n'est pas coutume, strictement personnel, c'est que ce troisième opus m'a beaucoup moins emballé que ses prédécesseurs pour les raisons mentionnées au cours de ma critique mais également à cause du système économique derrière où on doit dépenser près de 60 euros à chaque fois uniquement pour quelques factions supplémentaires et une nouvelle région. Mais je ne suis pas naïf : je suis bien conscient que j'ai pu, par le passé, traiter de manière plus élogieuse de jeux utilisant un procédé identique. Mais la difficulté extraordinaire de mes premiers essais couplé à ce système que je juge inutile et à la longue emmerdante m'a fait comme l'effet d'une douche froide. Mais encore une fois, cela n'impute en rien la qualité et le loisir procuré par ce nouveau titre : c'est toujours aussi plaisant de combattre des armées gigantesques, d'embusquer, d’assiéger, de mener des charges... tandis que petit à petit se profile à l'horizon la Fin des Temps...

I've been a fan of both strategy games and Warhammer for close to two decades now (yes, I'm showing my age!). Watching the Total War: Warhammer series evolve from the original game to where Total War: Warhammer III stands today has been incredible.

Creative Assembly has created something genuinely unique. Every race feels distinct, not only in appearance and lore but also in how they play. Each faction has its own mechanics, strengths, and challenges, yet the overall design is intuitive enough that once you've learned the fundamentals, transitioning between races feels natural. Every campaign teaches you something new, and with each playthrough you become a better strategist.

While I personally spend most of my time enjoying the grand strategy side of the campaign rather than fighting every battle manually, I still jump into key engagements—and that's where the game truly shines. The balance between turn-based empire management and large-scale real-time battles is excellent, making both aspects feel equally rewarding.

For anyone who enjoys strategy games, Warhammer, or ideally both, Total War: Warhammer III is one of the finest strategy experiences available. It's a game series thats (TWWH1,2,3) I've happily invested hundreds of hours into, and I still find myself eager to start "just one more campaign."

Do not buy Total War: WARHAMMER III.

In my opinion, this game uses a very anti-consumer business model. Even after buying the base game, you don't get access to a large portion of its content. If you want to play many of the factions or Legendary Lords, you're expected to buy additional DLC.

The result is that you pay for a full-priced game but still find a huge amount of content locked behind extra purchases. You can't simply choose any faction and start playing without being asked to spend even more money.

It feels more like the monetization of a free-to-play online game than a premium title that you've already paid for. I believe this should be made much clearer before people buy the game.

If you're expecting to buy a complete game with access to all of its main factions, you may be very disappointed.

I've played nearly every TW game and have over 1k hours in TW WHII. At the current state of the game, here's what I'd want you to know before picking it up. I'll keep it to my top 3 likes and dislikes to make this easier to digest. 

Positives: 
1. Endless options and ways to approach the game. If you like "map conquering" this is THE game for you. There are so many different factions, unit types, magic types, etc... you won't get bored. 
2. Visually the game is pleasing. It's not this modern day everything must reflect light as if it's just been polished junk, it just looks good. Unit models, terrain, effects, etc... convey what they need to without going overboard even on medium settings. If you're a die-hard graphics lover, it might not be as fancy as you want, but if you just want the immersion, you'll be fine. 
3. COOP - The game's coop options are solid. You can gift one another units in battle to let your friend(s) control them. This can make micro-heavy factions more accessible and relaxing to play. You can also recruit units from your allies which is a great way to fill out weaknesses your roster may inherently have. Example: Lizardman frontline with High Elf archers supporting them is both fun and effective. 
BONUS PS: This has a tutorial campaign which actually teaches you how to play and does a fairly good job at it. Previous TW's just threw you to the wolves and said "figure it out, chump." 

Negatives:
1. If you want the full experience, you'd need all three games and several DLCs. This is a high barrier to entry game for the full package. The games built-in campaign is bleck at best so you'll want to play the big sandbox mode "Immortal Empires." To have full access of this, you'd need all 3 games and DLC. Wait for a sale to pickup any of that. 
2. Support and handling by the developer. TW WH2 was handled well and is STILL the superior game overall. With this one, it was obvious the devs were done with the franchise and wanted to move on. Rushed DLCs, overpriced DCLs, the game on release was poor at best. In its current state, it's better and the devs have come back to it but problems which existed in TW WH2 still have not been resolved. Siege battles got a rework in this game and they found a way to make it so much worse. If it's a siege battle, I almost exclusively autoresolve the battle and apparently so does much of the community. 
3.  Not every faction is built the same. Several factions feel massively outdated and almost depressing to play compared to their contemporaries. Brettonia is such a neat faction if you like cavalry but they feel punishing to the player to play as. Norsca only recently got updated, meanwhile Chaos Dwarfs (a DLC faction) has almost every possible tool and micromechanic to play with. DLC faction Vampire Coast got massively nerfed going into game 3 as ranged damage got a debuff. They are now so unpleasant I rarely play them and they are tied with Lizardmen for my favorite faction.  Mods can make up for these issues, but you should not have to rely on modders to do the developing studio's job. 

Overall, the game to me is a solid 8/10. It's a game you can chill out with for 30 minutes, have a good time, and go on with your day. I would not buy it at full price as it is. Wait for a sale, pick it up, and your patience will be rewarded.

This is the first and only experience i have ever had in the Warhammer universe. I never played Warhammer 1 or 2, I dont know anything about 40k, etc. My RTS experience thus far is Command and Conquer Generals and Age of Empires II DE. Id had my eye on this for awhile, mainly just noticing that it kept popping up more frequently in my youtube shorts feeds, so I must have spent more time watching/rewatching clips from this series a good deal. Finally stumbled across a Zerkovich video, which, paired with a massive sale at the time, lead to me buying the game. I'm around 200 hours (i think.....?) in game and have formulated a pretty stable opinioin.
First, there is a HUGE LEARNING curve to the game. EVERY FACTION has it's own mechanics, and there's never more than 3-4 factions that play the same. Namely, many factions have a form of "second" currency, aside from the same generic primary currency that all factions share. For example, you obtain gold from sacking an enemy, things like that. But many factions have a second currency; depending on what faction you are this currency may be Food, it may be Souls, It may be Favor, it may be Skulls, or Labor, or Slaves. Initially, it's overwhelming becuase you think "crap, now i have to memorize THIS new mechanic" but when you take a step back and instead of reading "Souls" or "Labor", just think of it as "alternative currency". This simple thing (to me) helped to organize my thoughts much easier. Instead of thinking "okay now what do i have to do with this "favor of slaannesh" mechanic" when in truck all I had to think of it was is "oh, its just an alternative currency this faction uses, no different from the skaven with food, chaos dwarves with labor, etc).
 The game recommends playing as specific factions right off the bat, The Empire, High Elves, etc. This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ignore their recommendations. After trying and failing Immortal Empires on easy mode playing as over half a dozen factions, including all the recommended ones, I finally beat my first playthrough as Lizardmen (Grok-Gar) before than moving to one of the undead egyption pharoah factions. That one was easy enough i bumped difficulty up to normal, tried as skaven and got crushed within 30 rounds on about 4 attempts. Finally switched to dwarves and dominated, before branching out from there, and now i am able to MOSTLY consistantly achieve short victory with any faction on normal, and about half i can get to long victory.
Things I like: Ability to not only control overall map expansion, but also control units in individual battles. Tons of interesting units. Tons of unique lords and heros. Massive map.
Things I hate: WAY the hell too many confusing mechanics. I shouldnt have to run ChatGPT on my second screen while playing as a new faction, becuase the game does a terrible job of explaining many of the mechanics and you'll lose many times by trying to figure them out for yourself. I wish they made more factions that played the same as each other. If you have a specific playstyle that you choose (for me, i'm a slow-expansion, defense and economy first, "turtle" playstyle). This basically locks me out of playing 3/4 of the available lords (at least using this playstyle) as many of them can ONLY succeed with aggressive, overwhelming domination of the map. Some factions dont even have the option to build bases, you literally are just a lone Lord, wandering the map with no place to call home, attacking enemies as you see fit and acting as a mobile base yourself. I hate the fact that so many factions are also locked behind the first 2 warhammer games, requiring you to buy those just to play as certain lords. 
Overall though, its an incredibly fun game that I return to frequently. Every few months i get the urge to play it, come back and log 25-50 hours before getting my fill, leaving for a few months, returning again for another 50 hours, rinse/repeat.

Surprising I don't have a review for this one yet. I think it is finally time to write one. Because the game is actually in a pretty good place right now.

For a long time I would not have recommended this game. There are so many good things about it but it's foundation was fundamentally flawed. However it does appear that not only have CA been working on that for some time, but it has actually been a successful endeavor.

My current campaign after the 8.1 AI update is reminding me of all the things I love about this game. The AI is playing it well. Everyone in the top 15 rating has 20+ settlements - some with 30+ and one with 40+. It's turn 90 and I'm not even in the top 5 strength rating on Very Hard campaign. The AI moves with all their armies, calls for support from allies, and does not completely die after the first major encounter.

There's a load of other things to say about the game - the improved UI and quality of life, expanded diplomacy, and the major mechanical overhauls for so many of the races and factions. But I mainly made this review to say that I actually finally think the foundation of the game is growing strong and is in a better place than it has been since they started running into issues way back in 3.0.

Genuinely surprised that I'm having fun again and am looking forward to playing the current and future campaign.

Total War: WARHAMMER III had a rough start, but it has grown into a worthy conclusion to the trilogy.

The biggest strength is the sheer scale of the experience. Immortal Empires brings together the entire Warhammer world, creating one of the most ambitious strategy sandboxes ever made. With dozens of factions, legendary lords, and completely different playstyles, every campaign offers something new to discover.

The new factions are also a great addition. Kislev, Cathay, and the Chaos factions bring unique mechanics and armies that feel distinct from what came before. The battles remain spectacular, with massive armies, monsters, magic, and legendary heroes creating unforgettable moments.

However, the game launched with several issues. The original Realm of Chaos campaign was restrictive and repetitive compared to the sandbox freedom of previous games, while bugs, balance problems, and performance issues hurt the experience. Even today, AI and diplomacy still have room for improvement.

After years of updates, WARHAMMER III has become the game it should have been at release. It may not have had the same impact as the second entry, but it delivers an incredible fantasy strategy experience.

This game made me discover the Warhammer universe, even though I was already familiar with the TW franchise (Empire, Napoleon, Attila, Three Kingdoms), and before getting into what I like in this game, I'd like to tackle the most common comments I see here:

-Yes, the DLCs and the 3 games together are quite expensive, but it's not a single-player play-and-forget 6-hour campaign, it's a game with massive replayability, so take that into account. Every € spent can amount to several hours in-game. Plus, if like me, you buy during sales, you'll get the 3 games plus a lot of DLCs for about €100-150 depending on what you buy, which gives you access to Immortal Empires and its vast map and numerous regions. If you think it's a scam, go buy a few single player campaign-only games, and compare the time spent in-game with the amount you've paid.

-Next, the fact that there are bugs: there are bugs in every game, and honestly, being quite hard-to-please in terms of games, I don't see why people are so picky about this game, having experienced only a few minor bugs, which I could easily circumvent. Besides, the developers are not particularly lazy or venal, they just find themselves trying to fix bugs on a 10+ year-old engine that can create new bugs everytime you fix one. Changing the engine would require to sell a new game to everyone, which is what every AAA company usually does, and this time it would be a scam.

-Regarding AI, yes it has its perks, but have you ever seen intelligent and realistic AI? AI is always going to be something scripted and programmed into the game, with a limited set of behaviors, and knowing that every complex decision-making is very CPU-heavy, you'd run out of FPS to face a competent AI, what's the point of that? The Total War AI has always massively been boosted in terms of economics and recruiment capacity,, but I've seen worse in RTS games, and never better. Some mods (SFO, Radious, etc.) can help make the AI a bit more aggressive, and tweak some game mechanics, but even without this, the gameplay is still very much enjoyable.

As far as I'm concerned, there is so much content, so many game mechanics, so many factions, character abilities, magical powers, types of units and playing styles that it takes a lot of time getting used to, even for a veteran Total War player.

What hit me the most is that I've known about this game saga for 10 years, and I've never really wanted to get into it because I was not familiar with Warhammer and I was not sure the complexity would appeal to me since I was accustomed to "classic" military strategy, but I deeply regret not getting into it earlier, since I really love this game now.

If, like me, you like magic, fantasy, huge epic battles supported by epic music, and strategy of course, then I'd advise you to try this wonderful, very varied game, and enjoy tens, hundreds of even thousands of hours of playtime.

As of version 8.1, the Reikland campaign in the Immortal Empires mode on VH/VH might just be the pinnacle of the "against all odds" strategy gameplay: poor Karl is besieged on all fronts, having to run around and put out progressively more devastating fires while the useless elector counts happily let their provinces get overrun by grotesque monstrosities. 50 hours of tense back-and-forth gameplay later (unless you cheese), you'll have barely secured the historical borders of the Empire just in time for a brutal endgame crisis. I couldn't help loving it. And that's just one Legendary Lord for one faction out of a couple of dozen: TW3 offers quite a megalomaniac world map and quite the menagerie of heroes and villains to play as, each with its own unique challenges and mechanics.

While there are criticisms that can be levelled at Creative Assembly for dubious DLC policies and seemingly unsalvageable siege battle mechanics, and while the game does little to address the genre's single-player nemesis (the end-game slog), Total Warhammer 3's chief strength is the unparallelled diversity of fantasy factions on offer whether you're into the tabletop lore or not. You can pick any poison you like, from terrorist rats to BDSM elves, and have a great time leading them to greatness. Eventually I get bored of sandbox strategy games, and I'll probably get bored of this one too, but I'll always enjoy knowing it exists for me to come back to because it speaks to that restless child I once was, making up non-existent fantasy video games of unreasonable scale in my workbook and knowing they won't ever see the light of day.
