As an old-school Total War purist, I have played absolutely every single game in this franchise. I have spent hundreds of hours locked into Rome 2 using the ultra-hardcore Divide et Impera (DeI) mod, chasing that gritty, realistic, historical tactical perfection. I am a historical purist through and through—in fact, I absolutely hate Three Kingdoms and won’t even touch it.

Because of that, I avoided Warhammer 3 for a long time. I thought it was just a silly, colorful fantasy game that lacked real tactical depth.I was completely, utterly wrong. Warhammer 3 is pure gold.Once you actually dive into the campaign map, the sheer depth of this game slaps you in the face. Playing as Kislev feels incredible. The tactical variety is unmatched compared to historical titles.

 You aren't just clashing generic swordsmen into generic spearmen anymore; you are managing complex, asymmetric battlefields where your human gun-lines and defensive box formations are actively holding the line against massive 20-stack undead vampire armies, flying monsters, and heavily armored Chaos Dwarfs.The campaign mechanics are remarkably deep. 

The way the map dynamically forces you into desperate political scenarios—like turning former rebel factions into vital buffer states to shield your borders while managing complex regional devotion meters just to unlock your army blessings—creates an intense, gritty atmosphere that rivals the best historical campaigns.

If you are a hardcore historical purist who has been snobbishly sitting on Rome 2 or Attila thinking fantasy can't do real strategy, do yourself a favor: swallow your pride, buy this game, and set up your first defensive gun-box. You will not regret it. 10/10.

Total War: WARHAMMER III ist für mich eines dieser Spiele, zu denen ich immer wieder zurückkehre. Selbst nach Hunderten Stunden gibt es noch neue Kampagnen, andere Strategien und Fraktionen, die sich sehr unterschiedlich spielen. Genau diese enorme Abwechslung sorgt dafür, dass das Spiel auch nach langer Zeit nicht langweilig wird.

Meine persönlichen Favoriten sind die Elben. Ihre Spielweise, die starken Einheiten und die besondere Atmosphäre gefallen mir einfach am besten.

Ein weiterer großer Pluspunkt sind die Mods. Sie sind eine echte Bereicherung und erweitern das Spiel teilweise enorm. Neue Einheiten, optische Verbesserungen, zusätzliche Inhalte und viele kleine Anpassungen sorgen dafür, dass man sich das Spielerlebnis sehr gut nach den eigenen Vorstellungen gestalten kann.

Die riesige Kampagnenkarte, die vielen Völker und die gewaltigen Schlachten schaffen eine Spieltiefe, die nur wenige andere Strategiespiele erreichen. Oft startet man mit dem Gedanken, nur noch ein paar Runden zu spielen, und stellt irgendwann fest, dass es längst mitten in der Nacht ist.

Nach 790 Stunden kann ich klar sagen: Total War: WARHAMMER III gehört für mich zu den besten und umfangreichsten Strategiespielen überhaupt. Und obwohl ich schon so viel Zeit darin verbracht habe, fühlt es sich noch lange nicht so an, als wäre ich damit fertig.

Für mich ist Total War: Warhammer III eines meiner absoluten Lieblingsspiele. Über den Multiplayer kann ich allerdings nicht viel sagen, da ich ihn bisher nie ausprobiert habe.

Was die Singleplayer-Kampagnen angeht, bin ich dagegen von fast jeder Fraktion begeistert. Es ist beeindruckend, wie unterschiedlich sie sich spielen. Die Hochelfen mit Tyrion bieten meiner Meinung nach einen perfekten Einstieg für neue Spieler sowie die Orks mit ihrer  WAAGH!-Mechanik oder die verschiedenen Chaos-Fraktionen. Wer hingegen eine echte Herausforderung sucht, findet ebenfalls zahlreiche Kampagnen, die genau das bieten, wie beispielsweise Khalida und Boris seine Kampagne sowie die meisten Bretonen Kampagnen die aber auch allgemein mal ein Update vertragen könnten.

Trotz meiner inzwischen ziemlich schwachen Grafikkarte hatte ich nur sehr selten Abstürze. Außerdem finde ich es klasse, dass sich das Spiel auch auf niedrigen Grafikeinstellungen problemlos spielen lässt, ohne dass der Spielspaß darunter leidet. 

Natürlich gibt es auch Kritikpunkte. Die Belagerungsschlachten gehören für mich definitiv dazu, diese Kritik kann ich absolut nachvollziehen. Da ich allerdings keine anderen Total War-Teile gespielt habe, kann ich nicht beurteilen, wie viel besser solche Schlachten dort umgesetzt wurden. Ich denke aber, dass sie mit weniger Bugs schonmal deutlich mehr Spaß machen könnten. 
Ein weiterer Schwachpunkt sind für mich die Kampagnensiegbedingungen. Soweit ich weiß, sollen diese in zukünftigen Updates überarbeitet werden aber meiner Meinung nach deutlich zu spät.

Bei der Preispolitik sehe ich das Ganze etwas anders als viele andere. Natürlich kann man kritisieren, dass alle DLCs zusammen inzwischen über 420 Euro kosten – das ist ohne Frage eine enorme Summe. Gleichzeitig ist der Wiederspielwert von Total War: Warhammer III für mich aber außergewöhnlich hoch. Wenn heutzutage viele Spiele bereits 90 bis 100 Euro kosten und nach 80 bis 100 Stunden praktisch abgeschlossen sind, dann lässt sich das meiner Meinung nach kaum mit einem Spiel vergleichen, das hunderte oder sogar tausende Stunden abwechslungsreichen Spielspaß bieten kann. Deshalb freue ich mich persönlich über jede neue Ankündigung und jeden zusätzlichen Inhalt.

Ich kann Total War: Warhammer III jedem empfehlen, der sich für die Warhammer-Welt oder Strategiespiele interessiert. Für mich ist mit diesem Spiel ein Kindheitstraum in Erfüllung gegangen: Meine Tabletop-Armeen endlich in riesigen Echtzeitschlachten zu sehen, ist einfach ein großartiges Gefühl.

I'm not a huge Warhammer franchise fanboy, this game is my only actual exposure to the franchise so I think I'm fairly unbiased when I say this is objectively the best Total War game made to date.  I love Shogun 2 and played a bit of Warhammer 1 when it came out but didn't really get into, I kinda decided I was just a historical total war kinda guy and believed the whole "it's just action figures smashing against each other with no strategy" that I've heard so many times and that could not be more wrong. This is the only total war game I've played where the campaign side of things has enough depth to actually be considered grand strategy, I could make an entire review on just the campaign side of things and I have NEVER enjoyed the campaign side of things in any other total war game. This is one of the few games I can easily say has up to 10,000 hours of replayability, the faction and unit variety is incomparable to any other total war game, nothing comes even close, and with that variety there is IMMENSLY more depth to the battles, each faction will be an entirely different puzzle to solve on the battlefield you will constantly have to change your strategies and how you approach things.  You won't even begin to notice the issues with the game until you have thousands of hours at which point it's given you more value than most other games you'll find. I would recommend this game to pretty much anybody who has an interest in this kinda game except I guess hardcore competitive multiplayer kinda players because the game is not as balanced as historical ones and hardcore tacticians will get pissed off getting outplayed on the campaign so badly they cant win on the field anymore. Oh and don't make my mistake by starting on normal just crank it all up to very hard is doesn't make the game that much more difficult and for aggressive factions actually makes the game easier while giving you wayyy more opportunities to learn and improve because there is a LOT to know in this game.

"Total War: Warhammer III," developed by Creative Assembly and published by SEGA, is the ambitious and spectacular conclusion to the trilogy, delivering the most massive and varied fantasy strategy experience ever created. Launching players into the demon-infested Realm of Chaos before expanding into the colossal Immortal Empires sandbox, it brings together the maps, factions, and Legendary Lords from all three games into one epic, chaotic whole.

The sheer scale and variety are the game's most significant achievements. With seven unique base races, up to a staggering 100 Legendary Lords across 23 iconic factions in the combined campaign, and hundreds of units, the gameplay variability is seldom seen in any other title. The cinematic, real-time battles are more breathtaking than ever, and the ability to finally command daemonic forces from all four Ruinous Powers is a massive draw for fans. Furthermore, the monumental Immortal Empires campaign offers an unparalleled sandbox experience, and the community continues to be supported with new content and DLC. However, the game's massive scope comes with frustrations. The Realms of Chaos narrative campaign can feel tedious, and the DLC-heavy model requires a significant financial commitment to unlock the full faction roster, which some players find greedy. Additionally, certain core systems have drawn criticism, particularly the diplomacy which is described as shallow and rudimentary compared to other Total War titles, and unit balance continues to be a point of contention for veteran players.

Pros:

-Incredibly vast and varied factions with unique mechanics, offering immense replayability and a huge world to explore.
-Spectacular, cinematic real-time battles that bring the Warhammer fantasy to life with unprecedented scale.
-The massive Immortal Empires sandbox campaign is a definitive, genre-defining experience that unifies the entire trilogy.

Cons:

-The significant and expensive DLC model locks a large portion of playable races and Legendary Lords behind additional paywalls.
-Shallow diplomacy systems that lack depth and feel underdeveloped compared to other Total War entries.
-Tedious campaign management and some enduring faction balance issues that can impact the overall experience.

Overall, "Total War: Warhammer III" is the definitive fantasy strategy game and a monumental achievement in scope and spectacle. While it is hampered by a hefty DLC cost, some underdeveloped systems, and lingering complexity, the core experience of commanding legendary armies in epic battles across a unified world is unparalleled. For fans and new players willing to dive into its vast, chaotic waters, it offers a rewarding and endlessly replayable campaign. 8.7/10

Honestly, **Total War: WARHAMMER III** is probably the best strategy game I’ve ever played.

Yes, the game is expensive. The DLCs can be pretty expensive too, and getting all the content can cost a lot. But to be fair, that’s the reality with many big strategy games, so WARHAMMER III isn’t really an exception.

What you get in return is a huge amount of content and a lot of different ways to play.

You can’t just pick a faction and play every campaign the same way. Every race has its own economy, mechanics, armies, lore, and playstyle. Something that works great for one faction might be completely useless for another. That’s what makes the game so interesting — you constantly have to learn, adapt, and try something new.

I’ve already played several different factions, and even after dozens of hours, I still feel like there’s a lot I don’t understand yet. Economy, buildings, diplomacy, territory management, armies, heroes, magic, sieges, massive battles — there’s a lot going on, and it all comes together into one huge system.

The fantasy setting is probably my favorite part. Demons, vampires, humans, elves, dwarfs, orcs and many other races make you feel like you’re actually building and commanding your own fantasy empire.

And the battles… they can be absolutely insane. Seeing hundreds of units fighting, monsters charging into the enemy lines, magic going off everywhere and legendary commanders leading their armies gives the game a scale that’s hard to find anywhere else.

The game also gives you **a lot of different ways to develop your faction**, although I wouldn’t say you can literally do whatever you want. Every faction has its own mechanics, limitations and strengths, so you have to play around them. And that’s exactly why different factions can feel like completely different games.

It’s not perfect, of course. There are definitely things that can be frustrating, and the amount of mechanics can feel overwhelming when you first start. It takes some time to understand the economy, buildings, armies, diplomacy and the unique mechanics of each faction.

But once it starts to click, it becomes incredibly fun.

**10/10 from me.**

One of the best strategy games I’ve played, and definitely one of the best choices if you love fantasy.

Every new campaign can feel completely different, especially when you switch to another faction — and that’s what keeps me coming back.

Скажу чесно — Total War: WARHAMMER III для мене стала, мабуть, найкращою стратегією, яку я взагалі пробував.

Так, гра дорога. DLC теж можуть коштувати немало, і якщо захотіти зібрати весь контент, сума виходить дуже відчутна. Але, якщо бути об'єктивним, це реальність багатьох великих стратегій, і WARHAMMER III тут не якась унікальна.

А от що гра реально дає за свої гроші — це неймовірну кількість контенту та можливостей.

Тут недостатньо просто вибрати фракцію й піти завойовувати карту. Кожна раса грається по-своєму, має власну економіку, механіки, армії, лор і стиль ведення війни. Те, що працює за одну фракцію, може бути абсолютно марним за іншу. І саме це змушує постійно пробувати щось нове та вивчати гру.

Я вже встиг пограти за різні фракції й зрозумів, що навіть після десятків годин тут залишається дуже багато того, чого ще не знаєш. Економіка, будівництво, дипломатія, розвиток територій, армії, герої, магія, облоги, великі битви — усе це складається в одну величезну систему.

Особливо мені подобається саме фентезійна складова. Демони, вампіри, люди, ельфи, гноми, орки та безліч інших рас створюють відчуття, ніби ти реально керуєш власною фентезійною імперією.

А ще тут просто неймовірна атмосфера. Коли запускаєш велику битву, бачиш сотні юнітів на полі, магію, монстрів і командирів — відчувається масштаб, якого дуже мало в інших стратегіях.І головне — **у грі є дуже багато різних варіантів розвитку**, але не скажу, що вона дозволяє робити абсолютно все, що захочеш. У кожної фракції є свої механіки, обмеження та особливості, і саме їх потрібно враховувати. Через це за різні фракції гра відчувається зовсім по-різному, і кожну з них фактично потрібно вивчати окремо.

Не скажу, що гра ідеальна. Є моменти, які можуть дратувати, а на початку кількість механік може навіть трохи перевантажувати. Потрібен час, щоб розібратися в економіці, будівництві, арміях, дипломатії та особливостях конкретних фракцій. Але коли поступово починаєш усе це розуміти, гра стає набагато цікавішою.

**Моя оцінка — 10/10.**

Для мене це одна з найкращих стратегій, особливо якщо вам подобається фентезі. Тут величезна кількість фракцій, різні стилі гри та багато можливостей для експериментів.

А головне — **кожна нова кампанія може дати зовсім інший досвід**, особливо якщо вибрати іншу фракцію.

Total War: WARHAMMER III Review (87/100, excellent)

Finished campaigns before the review, in order: Kislev The Lost God prologue, Pirates of Sartosa (2 times), Talsyn (wood elves), Itza (Lizardmen), Knights of Caledor (HE), reworked Eataine (HE), Yvresse (HE), Nagarythe (HE), Khemri (TK), Couronne (Bre), Har Ganeth (DE), World Walkers (Nor)

Campaigns I gave out: The Ice Court (Kislev), Sylvania (Vampires)

Stuff I haven’t done: The Realm of Chaos mode, many many races which are available

TLDR summary: The game is still great and has added a lot of interesting and fun features on top of Warhammer 2 but isn’t really fixing their previous problems. It has become clearer how some factions feel overly powerful while other weaker ones have been left behind in a miserable position. I’m starting to dislike the overall “arcady” feel of WH3 where everything needs to happen as fast as possible, leaving out slower, more in depth slower strategic options. 

Pros 
+Immortal Empires map is huge and offers a lot of interesting decisions
+So many actually different factions to choose from, that often have totally different goals  
+Order tide takes longer time to get going vs WH2, more interesting for both sides 
+Looks really good
+Runs well, crashes were super rare
+Much better battle map variety/quality than in WH2
+Ambushes have been made interesting and less deadly than before
+Factions have usually clear strengths and weaknesses 
+Emphasis on making a lot of strong and different units (some factions can still doomstack)
+Magic one-shotting half an army has been mostly removed
+You can stack more magic reserves now and do more spells 
+Better diplomacy than before
+Trading settlements and recruiting allied units felt interesting (can be abused too)
+Making most battles outside the city walls is a good change
+Attempt was made to improve sieges, but…more from that in cons section
+Buffs given for melee units and cavalry
+AI does decent rushes with their armies if given chance

Cons
-Somewhat expensive game with full price, try to get it from sale (don’t buy DLC before you need it)
-Feels mostly the same than Warhammer2 (take a break from previous game before this or risk burnout)

-Battles are still way too fast, it's not immersive to see one huge elite army get wiped in less than 5 mins against another similar force
-I had a 4 armies battle which lasted only 4 mins after the engagement had begun…
-Units are too explosive and fast moving for realistic micro (this problem gets worse with unit / hero abilities)
-Greenish outlier of units gets lost too easily in the grass etc, why was it changed? It’s especially bad on snow maps 
-it takes too long to get their shot out for certain ranged units (vampire coast problem)
-Ranged units should stay still after attack command even with no line of sight 
-20 unit gap feels too limited for the scale of the game, many factions work better with larger armies
-Horses still get stuck too easily and need to spam commands to move out
-Stale battle music for certain factions (Wood elves, Vampire coast, Norsca)
-Certain factions/units start to feel too strong (literal nukes, dreadquake mortars, waywatchers, hero-spam armies, sisters of avelorn, Malus at early game)
-Late game battles get very repetitive and boring with auto resolve over-valuing slowly moving stat-checkers, it feels bad to play more than 150 turns as it takes long time to wait in between of battles (need for very high end PC)
-having 32 gigas of RAM makes late game waiting times tolerable and is highly recommended 

-Sieges still feel horrible/tedious/not worth it (just auto resolve if possible)
-Best siege strategy is mostly just cheese, not immersive (heroes and mages are too powerful) 
-It’s not uncommon to take out tier 5 city with few heroes and taking literally no casualties
-Siege AI overall seems broken, can’t do anything coherent
-Siege AI is somehow bad at both defending and attacking

-Variety of the campaign often drops in late game (just spam your strongest units) 
-Game often “ends” in mid point and late game is a slow grind to get long camp done
-End game crisis feels bad and boring and your allies are lazy to react (if they react)
-Chaos invasion from the North felt more thematic in Warhammer2 (now it feels like there is no story tied to end game crisis) 

-Certain AI-factions feel overly passive and leave all the action for the player
-Diplomacy still feels brainless, why is the ally refusing to trade some useless land for huge money? (wood elf problem)
-At the same time they overpay from useless settlements you can then confederate later for free (huge oversight) 
-Some factions have aged badly and feel overly nerfed (Sartosa, Kislev, Bretonnia, Norsca)
-Some factions are a bit too good now and have low challenge (Orion somehow prints too much money, Tyrion is totally bonkers with HE rework, any faction that can spam sisters of Avelorn eventually becomes unstoppable)

-City building is still boring and unengaging (pls remove the slot cap) 

Siege improvements:
-Improve pathfinding (make troops prioritize the fastest route through the gate, not the shortest through ladders)
-Remove free ladders (walls should have higher value)
-Give walls better defense/immunity against direct ranged fire (realism)
-Allow defender to stay out of tower range - maps should be bigger overall 
-Make gates unbreakable against most units, monsters should be able to break them
-Allow players to design their own defensive state troops and boost them with money if needed (It’s not realistic that 1 ordinary army can just roll through multiple tier 5 settlements) 
-Give defender roughly 2x more defensive units that are not top tier level (more grandiose feel) OR give less but more powerful elite troops
-Remove defensive towers inside the cities (feel horrible to play against/mobile game feel)
-Make barricades more meaningful (could some of them be unbreakable?)
-Remove live building, breaks immersion (this is not fortnite) 

Battle improvements: 
-Double the durability of most units, especially the weaker ones that don’t do much damage
-Improve morale of weaker units, they break now in less than 1 minute (total joke)
-Especially Bretonnia suffers from this as most melee peasant units are unusable as they run away
-Slow every unit  (why are everyone sprinting like Usain Bolt) 
-Increase army size towards 25
-Allow more flexibility in formations (wider and more spread out formations should be available)
-Force units to retreat after ONE command (there is often no time to give multiple retreat orders) 
-Force units to try to attack their target after one command
-Improve how fast ranged units are able to find viable targets 
-Lower armor pen dmg overall, currently units in heavy armor tend to melt very fast
-In short I’d wish this game would run more like Medieval 2 Total war which had amazing pacing in it’s battles

Came expecting fantasy StarCraft. Got a Civilization × StarCraft hybrid where you're building an empire while eldritch horrors, daemon invasions, rat empires, and dinosaur cavalry all somehow fit the same world. I get the hype now.

1. Performance and technical issues

Frame rate drops and stuttering during large battles.

Long load times for campaigns and battles on some systems.

Occasional crashes and bugs, especially around major updates.

2. AI problems

Underwhelming tactical AI in some battle scenarios (poor unit micro, odd pathing).  I am screaming at my screen as I stare in awe as they are moving in the most unaccepted directions.  Artillery attacking a tower, by walking toward it and getting in range of said tower.

Campaign AI quirks: enemies sometimes make strange strategic choices or fail to use faction strengths effectively.

Siege and pathfinding issues where units get stuck or behave unintuitively.

3. Balance and design of factions

Power creep and balance swings between patches; some races or legendary lords feel overpowered or underpowered at different times.

Asymmetric faction design can lead to steep learning curves and perceived unfairness in multiplayer or campaign matchups.  With new updates, older factions get left behind more and are not really playable unless you cheese or use of doom stacks.  Neither option I find fun personally.  

Unit redundancy: some rosters include units that feel unnecessary or too similar to others.

4. DLC and monetization model

Fragmented experience due to paid DLC, many players feel the base game is incomplete without multiple paid expansions and race packs.

Perception of content gating: key features or fan-favorite factions arriving as paid add-ons rather than in the base release.

Frequent paid cosmetic/content drops that some see as nickel-and-diming.

5. Campaign pacing and UI

Main "story" campaigns are largely abandoned and are not any good in the first place after Immortal Empires release.

Campaign pacing issues: late-game can become a slog for some factions; diplomacy and campaign systems sometimes feel repetitive.

Clunky or opaque UI elements for managing certain mechanics (e.g., agent actions, diplomacy details, or late-game management).

Overly complex mechanics that aren’t always well explained to new players.

Loss of camera control often in campaign overview, with the camera wildly scrolling in between turns, and sometimes not returning to where it was.

6. Mod support and community expectations

Reliance on mods to fix or improve certain features; while the mod scene is strong, some players resent needing mods to get a polished experience.

Inconsistent official support for mod compatibility after updates.

7. Visual and audio complaints (minor but recurring)

Reused assets and animations across units/factions leading to less visual variety than expected.

Audio repetition: some voice lines and music loops can feel repetitive over long campaigns.

None of these complaints are new.  They have been around sometimes for years.

There is enough content in the Immortal empires campaign to keep you busy in between purchases, not to mention the huge number of mods for the game. Again It is best to think of TWW as a platform for this kind of game like a lot of paradox games such as Hearts of Iron 4 or Stellaris verses a series of games in a trilogy. In order to get all of the content you do need to own all 3 games as each installment in the future has the prior installments as playable factions with updated graphics and with some races updated mechanics. Total Warシリーズ中でも最高傑作のひとつ

舞台は「Warhammer Fantasy」というファンタジー世界。
この世界で起こる終末戦争「End Times」の少し前を舞台に、さまざまな勢力から1つを選んで戦っていきます。

世界が徐々に混沌に飲み込まれていく中で、自分の勢力を発展させ、敵対勢力と戦争を繰り広げていくゲームです。

やはりこのゲームの一番の長所は、いつでも味わえる大規模戦闘でしょう。

HOI4で言えば独ソ戦、EU4で言えばオスマン帝国との大規模な戦争のような、普通ならある程度の国力や時間をかけてようやく実現できるような大規模戦闘を、自分の好きなタイミングで手軽に楽しめるのは本当に画期的で楽しいです。

しかも、ただ兵士の数が多いだけではありません。

ファンタジーならではの、現実では絶対にありえない組み合わせの戦いを眺めているだけでも非常に楽しいです。

槍兵が巨大な恐竜に襲われていたり、騎馬突撃を受ける戦車がいたり、コウモリに襲われるヘリコプターがいたり、銃兵に狙撃されるドラゴンがいたり……。

本当にバラエティ豊かで、戦闘を眺めているだけでも楽しめるゲームだと思います。

欠点らしい欠点はあまりありませんが、やはり一番の欠点は価格でしょう。

昔にTotal War: ROMEを遊んでいたこともあり、このシリーズの面白さは分かっていたので迷わず購入できましたが、本体とDLCをすべて揃えようとすると、セール時でもかなりの金額になります。

そのため、購入を迷っている方は、まずセールを待ったり、実況動画などを見たりして、自分に合っているゲームなのか確認してから購入することをおすすめします。

大規模な戦いを遊びたい方、劣勢を覆す戦いの快感を味わいたい方、ファンタジーならではの戦いを楽しみたい方には非常におすすめです。
私自身、気づけばかなりの時間をこのゲームに費やしていました。それでもまだ遊んでいない勢力が大量に残っているので、これからもしばらく楽しめそうです。

最後にこのゲームは世界の歴史やキャラクターの設定を知ってから遊ぶとさらに面白くなります。

キャラクター一人一人に非常に重厚な歴史があり、「このキャラクターとこのキャラクターは実は昔から因縁がある」といった背景を知っていると、ゲーム中の戦争や会話にも違った見方ができるようになります。

興味がある方はぜひゲームを始める前にこの世界の歴史を少し調べてみるのもいいですよ。

And it's not just the purchasing of the DLCs that gets you access to them, a lot of the lords and units in the game require you to also own the other games, or at least the overall faction DLC before you can play them. It just appalls me that a game could be this money-hungry; what other game requires you to own previous games in order to play over half the content? Do not buy unless you are willing to spend at least 50% more than the game's actual price in DLCs and other games.

Total War: Warhammer III es ese maravilloso engendro que ocurre cuando alguien decide meter prácticamente todo el universo de Warhammer en una licuadora, agregar estrategia, demonios, dragones y cantidades industriales de violencia, y luego decir: “Bueno, muchachos, que sea balanceado”.

Spoiler: **no siempre fue balanceado.**

Warhammer III trajo cosas enormes: nuevas facciones, nuevas mecánicas, el mapa combinado Immortal Empires y una escala que directamente es ridícula. Immortal Empires terminó convirtiéndose en el verdadero monstruo de la franquicia: una campaña gigantesca donde podés pasar horas conquistando territorios, haciendo diplomacia y planificando tu imperio… hasta que un vecino decide declarar una guerra porque aparentemente se levantó cruzado.

Las nuevas facciones tienen mecánicas muy copadas y hay una variedad de ejércitos que sigue siendo difícil de igualar. Cada campaña puede sentirse completamente distinta. Una partida podés estar jugando como un señor demoníaco del infierno y a la siguiente como un enano que considera diplomacia internacional prenderle fuego al vecino.

Ahora bien, **Creative Assembly también tuvo sus momentos de “¿pero qué carajo están haciendo?”**

El lanzamiento fue bastante accidentado, con problemas de rendimiento, bugs, balance discutible y decisiones de diseño que hicieron que más de uno mirara el monitor con la expresión de un aristócrata inglés al descubrir que su hijo se casó con una plebeya.

Y después están los DLC.

Señores, yo entiendo que hay que pagar las facturas. Pero llega un momento en que uno mira la tienda y piensa que el Imperio de Karl Franz no necesita conquistar el Viejo Mundo: **necesita conquistar mi tarjeta de crédito.**

A pesar de todo, Warhammer III terminó siendo una bestia.

No necesariamente perfecta. No siempre equilibrada. A veces bastante hinchapelotas. Pero cuando una batalla sale bien, cuando una estrategia funciona y ves a dos ejércitos monstruosos chocando en pantalla, se te olvida todo.

Y ahí está la magia.

**9/10.**

Creative Assembly somehow managed to take two excellent games and birth a third one that feels like it was assembled by a committee of tired interns during a company wide hangover. The campaign starts with the Chaos Realms, which is basically a series of glorified fetch quests wrapped in purple fog and pretentious monologues. You spend hours trudging through the same three environments while the AI does its best impression of a wet paper bag. The race to the center design is so artificial it makes the old race to the vortex look elegant by comparison. Performance is a special kind of joke. Even on high-end hardware the game stutters, freezes, and occasionally just decides to take a nap mid-battle. Loading times are long enough that you could brew coffee, drink it, and still have time left to question your life choices. The AI is somehow both brain-dead and psychic. It will happily suicide entire armies into your walls one turn, then the next turn perfectly snipe your isolated army from across the map with surgical precision. Sieges remain the same boring, multi-hour slog they’ve always been, only now with more pathfinding that makes units walk into walls like drunks at 3 am Immortal Empires finally arrived and… it’s fine? It’s the same map you’ve seen before with more factions bolted on, still plagued by the same jank, still missing basic quality-of-life features that should have been there at launch. Every major update feels less like refinement and more like damage control And let’s not forget the DLC strategy. Release a half-baked game, then charge full price for content that should have been in the base game, rinse, repeat. The community has to do half the balancing work themselves while CA drops another overpriced legendary lord pack Combat still looks spectacular when it works, the soundtrack slaps, and the Warhammer aesthetic is peak. None of that saves the fact that the actual game underneath is a buggy, poorly paced, overpriced mess that somehow feels smaller and less ambitious than its predecessors Buy it on deep sale if you must. Otherwise, go replay Warhammer 2 and pretend this one never happened.

TLDR: modern DLC greed takes the fun out of everything

There are 24 Factions. Of those, only 9 (37% of all factions) are playable when you buy WH3. You're buying a non indie game and you're denied access to more than half of the playable factions. Its a terrible look when open up the Faction selection screen and to be greeted with loads of DLC banners that remind you that your poor ah actually needs to spend more money to get full(-er) experience. So you go to the steamshop and look at what those DLCs would set you back. The DLC basket of TWWH3 is literally "worth" 500 Bucks. At 50% Sale that is still 250 Bucks. 10 Dollar game, you just need to get 250 worth of DLCs. BTW, one of the DLCs only purpose is to add cosmetic blood effects to the ingame troops models. Yes, they made that a product that you can buy with real world money.

Oh wait. Theres a another way to get more factions that doesn't involve those DLCs. Great! You just have to own the first 2 games, TWWH1 and TWWH2. Released in 2016 and 2017 respectively. So now you just buy 2 whole games that you probably aren't interested in playing as you already own the most recent one. They're both still priced at 60 bucks BTW. But its fine because they put in on Sale in the trilogy bundle - they are each almost 200% as expensive as WH3 in the same sale btw.

Finally, you bought the whole trilogy. Can you play all the factions now? Nope. You only unlocked 11 more, 7 are still locked with a DLC banner. So when you own the whole trilogy you're still only granted access to 17 factions (70% of all factions)

If you don't already own the old games and want to play the most recent one (Its a total war game, you're not gonna play TW Rome 1 if the next entry is already available) you are basically being tricked. They are selling you WH1 and WH2 as games but in reality its just like spending 120 Bucks (30 in a 75% sale) for DLCs to get more playable factions. So after spending an additional 300% of the base game I'm still missing 7 factions that are still presented to me with the DLC banner in the faction selection screen.

In the end, we now bought Total War Warhammer 3 for essentially 33% off if we factor in the cost for WH1 and WH2 and still have a basket of absurdly priced DLCs waiting for us and 7 factions missing in the game.

Apparently the developers never heard of the phrase "to lay an ambush" or "to lie in ambush", because they believe an ambush is an attack. Several times now, I have moved my army in a territory / near a settlement for extra defense (they have finished the move and I press "end turn"). The enemy moves his army towards my army and all of the sudden they perform an "ambush attack" on my stationary army. My army is for some reason in marching order (in a line with no defensive positions) and the reinforcements from my other armies in the area (that are in range) is also not coming. Of course the enemy army can receive their reinforcements. I mean, why is my army in march order (positioned in a line) when they are not marching? If the enemy is allowed to perform a sneak attack (with no or delayed reinforcements for me), at least let my army be in defensive positions.
On another occasion, I was attacking the enemy with three armies. I moved two of them in range of the enemy army that I wanted to attack, so they can all attack together. But, when I moved my third army in as the attack move, another enemy army (that was lying [!!!] in ambush) placed way behind the enemy army that I was attacking let to an ambush situation, and all the sudden I was cut of from my other two armies with no reinforcements facing the enemies' 4 armies. How does that work? I mean, at least let my other two armies come as reinforcements (perhaps with an delayed arrival) or let the enemy not have reinforcements either. Or, even better, let it just be an ambush if I actually move my army into the enemy army that is lying (!!!) in ambush.
I never had issues with ambushes in other Total War games and it does not make sense the way it is implemented here. 
There are other issues with Total War: Warhammer 3, but the ambush issue is the one thing that constantly ruins it for me.

-Cavalry nearly useless, just bumps into the enemy line and then gets stuck, impossible to then move it out to reposition

This is my first Total War game, and I’ve never played anything from this genre before. The tutorial was pretty basic, but it did a good job of introducing me to the core mechanics and explaining what the game is about.

I started my first campaign with Cathay, mainly because they have a wide variety of units for different roles. I think this is a great faction for learning the game and understanding how an army works.

One thing I absolutely love about Total War: Warhammer III is how different every faction feels compared to the others. This is something I’m missing in games like Civilization VI. Every faction has completely different campaign mechanics and its own playstyle, which keeps the game interesting and fun. There is just so much to discover, and I love it.

I do have to say that I had to search online quite a few times to understand what certain things or mechanics actually do. I feel like the game could do a better job of explaining some of its deeper mechanics. Something like the Civilopedia from CIV6 would be really helpful here, or maybe I just haven’t found the equivalent yet. Luckily, there’s always the internet.

It didn’t take long for me to buy Warhammer I and II as well, since owning all three games unlocks a huge amount of additional content and factions. At that point, I was already hooked and hungry for more.

Yes, there are a lot of DLCs. But if you “only” buy Warhammer I + II + III, you already get an insane amount of content combined into one game, including access to the vast majority of the factions. The rest of the DLCs will become interesting to me once I’ve played every faction at least once, which could take quite a while.

I also don’t really understand all the negative comments about bugs and crashes. I’ve played for 135 hours so far and haven’t experienced a single crash or any major bug. And if you can get all three base games on sale for around 39€, I think that’s more than fair for the amount of content you get. Especially considering how diverse it is. The factions and campaigns don’t feel repetitive, and there is a huge amount of variety.

Most of the DLCs also seem to add new Lords to factions you can already play, rather than being completely necessary to enjoy the game.

At this point, I honestly think this could be the first game I reach 1000 hours in. I really got hooked on war. :D

Ich habe Warhammer 3 inzwischen zum dritten Mal ausprobiert, erst Vanilla und dann mit Mods, die die für mich viel zu schnellen und chaotischen Schlachten verlangsamen. Trotzdem springt der Funke einfach nicht über.

Ich glaube inzwischen, dass das Problem tiefer liegt: Die Schlachten sehen spektakulär aus, sind aus der Nähe aber erstaunlich nichtssagend. Überall riesige Animationen, Blut, Partikeleffekte, Zauber und irgendwelche Anime-Moves, während gleichzeitig kaum erkennbar ist, wer eigentlich gerade wen trifft oder stirbt. Selbst wenn ein Modell stirbt, wird es nach der Schlacht einfach wieder „verstärkt“. Animation, Schaden und Konsequenz sind dadurch weitgehend voneinander entkoppelt.

In Medieval 2 kann ich dagegen minutenlang einem einzelnen Gefecht zuschauen. Ein Soldat bekommt einen Schlag ab und man denkt tatsächlich: „Oh ♥♥♥♥, geht der durch?“ Wenn er stirbt, ist er weg. Eine Formation wird zurückgedrängt, ein Tor wird gehalten, Bogenschützen verursachen sichtbare Verluste. Das Geschehen ist viel konzentrierter und trotzdem für mich wesentlich taktischer und verständlicher.

Warhammer 3 steckt unglaublich viel Aufwand in die spektakuläre Darstellung seiner Schlachten, aber für mich geht dabei genau das verloren, was Total War-Schlachten interessant macht: eine lesbare Abfolge von Ursache, Wirkung und Konsequenz.

Warhammer 1 hatte für mich noch eine überschaubare Fantasy-Schlacht mit klaren Archetypen. Mit jedem Teil kamen mehr Fraktionen, Sonderregeln und Fähigkeiten hinzu, bis aus der überschaubaren Schlacht für mich ein unlesbares RTS-Clickfest geworden ist. Nach drei Versuchen bleibt bei mir jedenfalls nur: Sieht cool aus, macht mir aber keinen Spaß.

This is one of the most amazing PC games ever made in it's genre. All three TW WH are. 

First it's one weakness: 
WH3 has the weakness that sieges sucks in my opinion, although I'm sure many likes it. They made the sieges more akin to games like the original Dawn of War, but without the fun, and the problem is DoW is a very different game and doesn't mesh very well with Total War. More to the point you have a very limited form of live base-building during the battle and it just doesn't fit this format. For me it's so bad I cannot play the game without modding the sieges away.

However:
Yet even so the game (and all in the series) is absolutely brilliant. One of the awesome parts is that they followed through with their promise of three games, each with a multitude of DLCs, that all contribute their content to any later game in the series. So while each game provided 4-5 factions at start, acquiring all the content provides more than a hundred. Some ppl hate DLCs, that attitude is misplaced here. They aren't cut content, rather content that would never have been made without the DLC structure. Even so the game is still very much playable without a single DLC or older game in the series, getting a full experience. Even tho I love them, for some the DLCs are a big drawback.

The game is severely moddable.

Beyond that there are too many positive elements to this title for me to even know where to start. It's the best Total War game in my opinion. It's the best Warhammer rendition of any kind, including the old board-game. It's even better played after reading the books about the faction or hero you're playing.

Total War: WARHAMMER III to ogromne zwieńczenie trylogii i jedna z najbardziej rozbudowanych strategii fantasy dostępnych na rynku.

Klasyczna formuła Total War nadal działa znakomicie – na mapie kampanii rozwijamy imperium, prowadzimy dyplomację, zarządzamy gospodarką i armiami, a wielkie bitwy rozgrywamy w czasie rzeczywistym.

Największą siłą jest różnorodność frakcji. Kislev, Wielki Kataj czy armie bogów Chaosu różnią się jednostkami, mechanikami kampanii i stylem prowadzenia wojny. Smoki, demony, potwory, artyleria i tysiące żołnierzy potrafią tworzyć naprawdę spektakularne bitwy.

Prawdziwym potworem jest jednak kampania Immortal Empires, która łączy zawartość całej trylogii na gigantycznej mapie. Liczba ras, legendarnych lordów i możliwych kampanii jest absurdalna i spokojnie wystarcza na setki godzin.

Gra miała problemy po premierze, a AI, balans i optymalizacja nadal nie zawsze zachowują się idealnie. Ogromna liczba płatnych DLC również może odstraszać nowych graczy.

Mimo tego obecnie jest to niesamowicie rozbudowany sandbox w świecie Warhammera, w którym każda kolejna kampania może wyglądać zupełnie inaczej.

Dla fanów Total War, wielkich bitew i Warhammera – zdecydowanie polecam.

At this point in time, the game is basically like fast food; 
Looks very good, the first bites are really tasty, but the more you eat the less you want to eat it and afterwards you feel bad about it because you knew from the beginning it wasn t quite what it looked like.

Basic gameplay is still shallow, especially the strategic component;
Building up your empire and creating elaborate strategies is not really possible due to
lots of isolated features that don t interconnect or a general lack of options regarding buildings/taxation/ seasons / population.
You get spammed with buffs and most features are also simple number buffs, even most technologies don t provide game-changer abilities/unlocks etc.


The battles are very fast paced and very character centric ( one-man-armies are a powerful strategy) and a plethora of  buffs make unit roles more like suggestions. 
There are no night battles or battle weather changes still, neither are animated unit formations. 
Battles quickly degenerate in blob-fights, until those are wiped by magic or said powerful characters.

Generally, CA is trying to make every faction unique, but they are limited by their own foundations. 

The game technically has massive replayability value due to the amount of factions x subfactions, but if you are only interested in 1-2 factions, it gets stale very quickly.
Lore accuracy is decent enough though.

The game has lots of potential, sadly, I think, we are only going to see it realized once CA stops active development and modders can fully take over.

If I want to be defensive, hide in my house like the man-child I am, play Cathay and order Uber Eats?

Because **I HAVE RATS WITH NUKES.**

Yes, the DLC list is massive, but they are NOT essential in order to have a good time.

When you look at the store page, it’s understandable to have a minor cortisol spike. There's three mainline games and a decade worth of Lord Packs, seeing "90% of the game's content behind a paywall" turns a lot of people off.

Here is the truth: You don't need to buy the extra content to get hundreds of hours of fun.

1. The base game is already packed

You don’t need 40 DLCs to enjoy the core experience. Simply buying Warhammer 3 unlocks the massive Immortal Empires map alongside a stacked cast of base factions: Grand Cathay, Kislev, all four Chaos Gods (Skarbrand, N'Kari, Ku'gath, Kairos), a fully customizable Daemon Prince, and even Be'lakor representing the Warriors of Chaos. That alone gives you hundreds of hours of content before you even think about opening your wallet again.

2. DLCs are modular, not mandatory

This isn't a pay-to-win live-service game where you get locked out of the fun if you don't buy the latest pass. All the DLC factions, lords, and units still appear on the campaign map as AI opponents for you to fight for free. You only pay if you specifically look at a faction and go: "Yeah, I want to personally control that exact Character." If you don't care about playing a specific Lord or accessing niche unit rosters, you are losing basically nothing other than a few unique mechanics and quirks. 

3. Credit where it's due

Creative Assembly built something truly incredible here. Gathering three massive games worth of map, lore, and mechanics into one seamless sandbox is a major achievement. The scale is staggering, the flavour is unmatched, and at no point during a standard campaign does the game aggressively force you to buy extra stuff. It’s just sitting there on the shelf should you fall in love with the game and eventually want additional flavour.

Verdict:

Buy the base game. Play Miao Ying, Katarin, or Skarbrand. Unify your realm (or burn it down). If you put 100 hours into it and decide you want to play as a mutated rat with radioactive gatling guns or as a crazed ginger scottish OSHA violation, grab that specific DLC on a sale. If not, enjoy one of the best strategy games ever made without spending a single extra penny.

10/10 — Glare at the DLC list, ignore it and withhold judgement then go conquer the world.

As someone approaching the close to 1000 hr mark on the franchise (WH1-3) let me give an honest review.

Firstly lets start with the elephant in the room all the bad reviews point out... Yes, there are a lot of DLCs for the game. Yes, you need to own older versions for some of them. Do you need them to have fun? Absolutely not. You can own every DLC in this game (like I do) and I promise you well still end up spending hours and hours on the same couple of factions you find out you like the most, and still never play the same campaign exactly the same way. Even with just the base game factions. You make your decisions every campaign, the game might have good vs evil or separate chaos corruption based "guidelines" for you to make your campaign easier, but there's nothing saying you cant go against the grain and make enemies of all those factions that would typically deem you friends, or maybe you want to do a campaign with only 1 unit type. The countless hours you can spend replaying the same lord and having a different experience each time is amazing.

Now with that being said, should you pay full price? No, absolutely not. The game goes on sale often, as well as the DLCs. Pick it up at a bargain, id say even 25 dollars is a steal for this game. If you have a faction in mind that you really like the look of and think it will be fun, grab that too. 

How are the DLCs? Well, your always going to have ups and downs when it comes to what a DLC provides, especially if you like to play the game a certain way. Are all the DLCs fantastic? As someone who owns every single one, and has played them all, I can whole heartedly tell you...No. They arent all fantastic. Does that mean they arent fun? No. I have never played a DLC in this entire franchise that I couldnt have fun with. I find myself returning to DLCs that I didnt care for as much as others even after 4, 5, 6 playthroughs. For example, I dont much care for the wood elves faction, some people love them, they arent my favorite. But I have still played each mulitple times. 

So which DLCs do I recommend for new players? (Without buying any of the older games) Anything that looks cool! The hardest faction to play in this game  in my opinion for a new player is going to be the chaos dwarves. They have an economy system that is quite unique and takes a bit of getting used to, however the trade off there is their military battles are usually quite easy. My personal top picks if your just starting out and absolutely must have a DLC instead of just the base game would be  The prophet and the warlock DLC, Bashiva character pack for cathay, The Omens of destruction and Thrones of decay DLCs both of these are fantastic to buy in the whole pack because they are loaded with strong, fun, relatively easy to play lords. 

My recommendation would be to give this game a good honest try. Its loads of fun, has pretty good graphics, and if you really want to have fun, go into a skirmish Vs Ai battle or play with a friend and spectate, and just throw your troops into the enemies, Press K to enter cinematic mode, and watch the battle, see if that doesnt immediately make your experience 100x better. 

Final Notes: If youve made it this far, thank you for reading my book of a review, I usually dont review many games and when i do its short and to the point, but I feel this one deserves a longer one. Plus, have you noticed at the time of most of these negative reviews are after only just a couple hours of playing the game, and then the people who complain still manage to rack up another 20, 30, even 40 more hours? Must be a terrible game.

I got into Total War: Warhammer III quite by chance. Even though I love tactical, turn-based, and strategy games, I was initially very hesitant to try this one. The turning point came when my friends started streaming it for me. They eventually talked me into buying it, and... it completely hooked me. I started enjoying it so much that I decided to hunt down all the achievements (including the notoriously hard ones, like winning a battle with a 10-to-1 disadvantage) and explore almost everything the game has to offer. Here are my thoughts after hundreds of hours of playtime.

The Positives:
First and foremost, I have to praise the visuals. The game features beautiful graphics and a massive, brilliantly designed map, especially in the Immortal Empires mode. I was also pleasantly surprised by how deep and interesting the lore is, considering the Warhammer universe was completely off my radar before.

The biggest draw, however, is the gameplay and replayability. The game offers a massive variety of mechanics, and thanks to the dynamic decisions made by the AI, no two campaigns ever unfold the same way. A huge plus is how distinct the factions are. Playing as Grand Cathay, for example, is a completely different experience from spreading your influence as the Skaven with Clan Eshin or Clan Moulder. Each faction has its own specific mechanics, which keeps the game constantly fresh.

The Negatives:
Unfortunately, the game has its dark sides, the most prominent being the pricing policy. The base game itself is quite expensive, but the real issue is the sheer amount of content locked behind paid DLCs. Sure, you can play without them, but you miss out on a lot of tactical options and legendary lords, which is quite off-putting and taints the overall experience.

Another disappointing aspect is the technical state of the multiplayer. More than once, my friends and I encountered minor bugs or complete game crashes, which can be incredibly frustrating right in the middle of a tense battle.

Conclusion:
If it weren't for the massive amount of expensive paid content, this would be an absolutely stellar game. I definitely don't want to say it's a bad game – on the contrary, it's an exceptionally high-quality strategy title that can keep you glued to your screen for a very long time. It's just a huge shame that so much of its true potential is locked behind extra paywalls.

Overall Rating: 8/10

Total War: Warhammer III has a vast campaign and an incredibly vibrant unit roster. The faction mechanics are generally fun and creative, and learning how to use each faction’s unique mechanics can make campaigns much easier. However, these mechanics are not necessarily what makes you overpowered—you still need to play it like a Total War game: build your economy, develop your settlements, raise more armies, and conquer your enemies.

Unfortunately, the biggest problem with the game is the DLC model.

To be honest, a lot of the fun feels locked behind DLC. Without the DLCs, many factions have only partial unit rosters, which makes the base game feel significantly less complete. The amount of content available behind the paywall can be frustrating, especially when you consider how much of the game's appeal comes from its enormous variety of units.

Personally, I think it would have been much better if the developers focused more on faction DLCs rather than splitting individual units and additional content across numerous DLCs. The game already has an incredible foundation; making the core rosters feel more complete would make the experience much more satisfying.

The second major issue is multiplayer.

The multiplayer ladder is currently buggy, and the matchmaking system feels poorly designed for a competitive game. At the moment, two players enter a lobby and then choose their factions. The problem is that players can leave during the army-building stage without any meaningful consequences. This means that if someone sees a matchup they don't like, they can simply quit and search for another opponent.

I think a better competitive system would be:

Players choose their factions before matchmaking.
They are then matched with an opponent based on those faction choices.
Leaving the lobby after being matched should result in an ELO penalty/loss.
Army building should have a fixed time limit, such as 2 minutes.
Both players should have the same amount of time to build their armies.

Currently, if one player presses ready, the other player gets a limited amount of time to finish their army. That's perfectly reasonable for a custom lobby, but I don't think it's ideal for a competitive ranked environment.

Aside from the DLC/paywall issue and the multiplayer problems, I think this is a fantastic and genuinely fun Total War game.

The game has managed to build a massive player base for a strategy game, which is impressive in itself. The sheer variety of factions, units, campaigns, and mechanics gives it an enormous amount of replayability.

If Creative Assembly continues improving the multiplayer experience and addresses some of the monetization concerns, I think Warhammer III could have an even longer lifespan.

Despite its problems, I still have a lot of fun playing this game. Recommended, but I strongly suggest getting it on sale—especially if you plan on buying the DLCs as well.

Would absolutely invade my neighbor again. I bought Total War: Warhammer III expecting a fantasy strategy game. Instead, I got a comprehensive political education where every faction has apparently discovered a different way to violate international law.

Kislev: Your economy is collapsing, your cities are freezing, and everyone is angry.
Solution? Conscription. You are now running Eastern Europe Simulator.

Cathay: The emperor has centralized everything, controls trade, maintains an enormous bureaucracy, and occasionally turns into a dragon.

Khorne: Diplomacy is for cowards. Their policy consists of: Find country. Kill country. Kill the survivors. Ask why nobody wants diplomatic relations. Somehow still has better economic growth than my country.

Nurgle: You don't conquer territory. You improve public health outcomes negatively. The game should honestly have a warning: “Playing as Nurgle may violate several international conventions.”

Slaanesh: Everything is about excess. Gold? Excess. Food? Excess. War crimes? Excess. This faction somehow made the Geneva Convention feel like a suggestion box.

Tzeentch: Every time I think I understand what is happening, Tzeentch changes the rules. I don't even play the faction anymore. I just assume my government has been overthrown by my own advisor.

Skaven: Fascism? Democracy? Communism? No. Rat Communism. Everyone is equal because everyone is equally disposable. The Skaven have successfully invented a political system where the state owns everything, the workers own nothing, and the leadership owns several million slaves. Karl Marx would uninstall this.

Greenskins: No ideology. No manifesto. No political platform. Just Boiz doing WAAAGH. Honestly, the most honest political movement in the game.

Chaos Dwarfs: Basically, industrial capitalism entering the chat. They looked at slavery, child labor, pollution, weapons manufacturing, and environmental destruction and said: “What if we made this an economic strategy?” And somehow it works.

Vampire Counts: Immigration policy is simple. Everyone comes in. Nobody leaves. The ultimate closed-border policy.

Empire: A technologically advanced bureaucracy held together by paperwork, artillery, religious disputes, and one guy named Karl Franz desperately trying to prevent the entire country from collapsing. So... government simulator.

Dwarfs: They have spent 2,000 years maintaining a spreadsheet of everyone who has ever mildly inconvenienced them. Honestly, terrifying administrative efficiency.

Wood Elves: “Protect nature.” Burns down your settlement because it is located slightly too close to a tree. Environmentalism has never been this aggressive.

This is an excellent game. It teaches economics, diplomacy, logistics, military strategy, religion, political extremism, industrialization, colonialism, environmental policy, and why giving one person absolute power is probably a bad idea.

Warhammer III è una droga. Più ci giochi e più hai voglia di iniziare una nuova campagna, soprattutto perché ogni fazione cambia completamente il modo di giocare. La cosa che mi piace di più è proprio la varietà: eserciti enormi, unità completamente diverse tra loro, eroi, magia e battaglie che possono ribaltarsi in pochi secondi.

Graficamente è davvero bello, soprattutto quando ti ritrovi con centinaia di unità che si scontrano contemporaneamente. E anche se all'inizio può sembrare abbastanza complicato, una volta capiti i meccanismi diventa tutto molto più naturale.

La parte gestionale secondo me è altrettanto importante delle battaglie: devi pensare a economia, territori, alleanze, eserciti e a come espanderti senza ritrovarti circondato da nemici.

Non è sicuramente un gioco per chi cerca una partita veloce, perché una campagna può durare un'enormità di ore. Però è proprio questo il bello: ogni partita può diventare una storia completamente diversa.

Secondo me è uno di quei giochi che o ti prende tantissimo oppure dopo qualche ora lo molli, ma se entri nel suo meccanismo è veramente difficile smettere. Per gli amanti degli strategici e dell'universo Warhammer, è praticamente infinito.

As a long time total war player and fan of the Warhammer universe I was excited when creative assembly launched the Warhammer games and each one is genuinely fantastic but the 3rd takes it to the penultimate level. Stunning visuals, in depth and immersive lore, balanced strategic combat with factions that have independent and differentiated play styles and a monstrous campaign map. This is the kind of game you can get immersed in for hours on end and my girlfriend often makes me sleep on the couch because of it. Even if you’re new to the Warhammer universe I think most would find it genuinely interesting and a campaign experience with high levels of detail. Yes there are numerous paid DLC‘s to purchase to complete the experience which has its frustrations - but worth it in the end (IMO). I do miss some of the more political features from the old total war games (particularly med 2 and Rome 2) which would flesh out the immersion more - but can understand that does not feel entirely relevant to the old world as its chaos/ all out war on apocalyptic scales with little time for politics! There are however plenty of playstyles with factions that have their own unique features which I find makes up for this. Excited for the lords of the end times update and even more excited for total war 40k!

I'd consider myself a Total War veteran - I've been playing since the original Mediaeval days. Yep, the clunky one. And it's been interesting to see the direction that Total War has taken these past two decades, it really has - Warhammer seemed like a no brainer. Each time, I've bought into the idea behind the mythos, and I've given them a good go. Each time, however, I've found that some areas of the game have been oversimplified (since Rome II, everything's been a bit downhill in this respect), others have become overcomplicated. Like, there are SO many different units for Chaos that it can become a bit too much.

Still, however, I see many of the old problems haven't been resolved. AI being able to field multiple armies without their economies crashing being the primary problem. The overall unevenness to battling on the field (like, some armies just feel downright indestructible to play against). And maybe I'm just not that good at the game, even on Normal.

That raises the final problem I have. This is really 'half' a game. The prologue is a bare-bones, on-rails teaser for a faction you still need to purchase as optional DLC. The Immortal Empires campaign has the same problem - half the factions are locked behind paywalls. And that's just about all the game really has to offer.

I think what's happened is, Total War have made things a mile wide, but inches deeper in terms of gameplay. I wonder if they'll be able to strike that balance again with the upcoming 40k universe (it'd be nice to see a mash-up of space and land battles, perhaps smaller sized squad fights). That's another kettle of fish altogether. But if you're thinking of dropping full price on THIS particular bad boy, I feel like you're not going to get much out of the experience if you've already played Warhammer 1 and 2.

Sehnsucht nach den Tagen, als Total War noch übersichtlich war.
Als Schlachten taktisch waren, nicht epileptisch.
Als Kampagnen strukturiert waren, nicht ein gigantischer Fantasy‑Fiebertraum. Ich rede von diesem "Total War Gefühl".
Von diesem Medieval / Shogun 2‑Flow, bei dem du eine Armee bewegt hast und nicht gleichzeitig 17 Menüs, drei Chaosportale, fünf Diplomatie‑Popups und einen Dämonenprinz verwalten musstest.
Damals war Total War noch ein Strategiespiel.
Heute ist es ein „Wie viel kann ich dem Spieler gleichzeitig ins Gesicht werfen?“-Simulator.

Die DLC‑Politik Creative Assemblys Lieblingsdämon, aus dem Bilderbuch.
Seit Rome 2 ist klar: CA liebt DLCs mehr als funktionierende KI.
Und Warhammer 3 ist der Höhepunkt dieser Tradition.
Neue Fraktionen?
Klar, aber bitte 20 Euro.
Neue Einheiten?
Natürlich, aber nur im „Premium Content Pack“.
Ich warte nur darauf, dass sie irgendwann die Pausetaste als DLC verkaufen.

Das Gesamtgefühl es ist, als würde man versuchen, ein brennendes Haus zu löschen, während gleichzeitig ein Orchester spielt, ein Dämon dich anschreit, die Steuererklärung auf dem Tisch liegt und jemand im Hintergrund „Übrigens, das kostet extra!“ ruft.
Das Spiel ist nicht nur überladen, es ist aggressiv überladen.
Ein Angriff auf die Sinne, die Geduld und den Geldbeutel.

Fazit:
Total War: Warhammer 3 ist ein monumentales Chaoswerk, das beweist, dass „mehr“ nicht immer „besser“ ist.
Und während ich mich durch dieses überladene Fantasy‑Inferno kämpfe, denke ich nur:
„Ich will zurück. Zurück zu Shogun. Zurück zu Medieval 2. Zurück zu Total War, bevor es mich aktiv bekämpft hat.“

The "world map/strategic" part is a lobotomised version of "Heroes of Might and Magic" that pretends to be a lobotomised version of "Civilization". The smaller "real-time combat/tactical" part of the game with its physical projectiles reminds me of a lobotomised version of "Myth: Fallen Lords/Soulblighter". So it scratches, if poorly, both HMM and Myth itches that cannot be scratched by many modern games. And that is the best compliment I can give.
The downsides of the game are multiple.
• There is a huge number of factions to play, but don't be mistaken: the gameplay is very "wide", but not even remotely deep. All factions follow the same basic principle, with small faction-unique gimmicks thrown on top. Half of the gimmicks are useless, underdeveloped, obsolete or boring. Be it Repanse's "wasteland water supply" that is either unnecessary or does not work in most deserts; Mother Ostankia's hex crafting that is so poorly implemented interface-wise, it becomes a chore after tenth repetition; or whatever undercooked monstrosity the whole Changelling gameplay is. Etcetera, etcetera, etcetera.
• The AI is bad. Bad politically, strategically and tactically. Like "gives you an obscene amount of gold and enters war against its ally in exchange for a useless settlement" bad. Like "will pay you forever to cyclically trade the same settlements for no reason" bad. Like "will send five armies across the continent and forget why, so they'll just graze around some field, while the capital burns" bad. Like "does not comprehend that to take a city one needs not only defeat the defenders, but also take the city" bad. Like "what is this 'unit cohesion' and 'tactics' things you are even talking about?" bad. Like "sieges are not just broken, but actually depressing to watch" bad. Like "squad got stuck in terrain and will not move again" bad. It is impossible to say that AI is "buggy", "cheesable" or "easily exploitable": bugs in this game are the only way of its operation and are indistinguishable from features.
• The narrative is, well, basically non-existent. Which is bizarre, because Warhammer Fantasy/Old World has rich and deep lore with many interesting stories to tell. The game fails to tell any of them. The missions, campaign goals and victory conditions are grotesquely empty and unsatisfying. Considering that AI is too dumb to even role-play and properly pursue its lore-accurate goals, the narrative each campaign manages to present is as rich as the story mode of original Tetris. And there is no story mode in original Tetris.
• The interface of the game is an abomination. Pages over pages of bloated lists and menus that somehow hide important data in even more submenus. Pop-up windows in the corners of the screen that do not attract players' attention but partially block controls until closed (I repeat: partially, not fully, and with no explanation, so when something stops working, most newbies don't understand why). Pathfinding previews that often fail to properly indicate the path your lords will actually follow, or if they will be able to reach the destination this turn at all. The assets that obscure critical objects and UI elements. The camera that falls in every decorative hole on the map or makes it impossible to click the terrain when placed on a hill. The unit figures that are often too small to distinguish or interact with without severely zooming in. Unit banners that do not have enough variations to distinguish units and are often obscured by everything from UI elements to tree shadows. I competitively played RTS games for decades, but I fundamentally cannot properly micro in this game.
• Performance is meh, but "meh" in this case is unexpectedly high achievement.

So.
Should you play this game?
Yes, as long as you like Warhammer Fantasy, don't take the game too seriously and don't expect much from either gameplay or story. The game basically provides you with a set of great animated figurines and a jumble of mechanics, and leaves the rest of the game to your imagination and the modding community.

Should you buy this game, especially for the full price?
Absolutely not. The game is basically a Chaos Dwarf project: owned by unrepentantly evil and greedy slave-drivers, and developed by their starved, questionably sapient greenskin slaves.

Honestly, Warhammer 2 is the better game. This beats it on scale and map size and number of factions, but Total War: Warhammer 2 is the tigher, objectively better balanced and optimised grand strategy game.

My play time has been limited but I feel like combat has regressed massively between the two games. Not just in terms of the noticeable lag between issuing orders and the unit actually doing anything, but in particular ranged units no longer work because of the awful new line of sight system. What has been a satisfying game mechanic for decades they've now changed, and not for the better.

Siege battles have gone from epic wall battles to tedius settlement building that is fine the first few times but quickly becomes incredibly repetitive. Compared to the old system, this is really horrible.

I can appreciate that they want to keep evolving the formula and trying new things but I don't really see the sense in changing core mechanics of the series when there was nothing wrong with the original systems - I'd rather they improved on the series' weak points: for example the (much improved) diplomacy system, or the shoddy AI. On the former they've actually managed some improvements, on the latter they've overcorrected to what I think may be one of the most ludicrously overaggressive AIs I've seen in any Total War game to date.

I held off on this review because I figured in the time since release they would have optimised and balanced the game to the point where it was as fun as its predecessor. More than 4 years later and while I'm wowed at the dizzying array of paid DLC - there are so many paid DLC factions, to the point where when I start a campaign I feel a bit like I'm playing the demo version of the game - I'm really disappointed by the lack of attention and focus paid to the core of the experience.

I would still recommend this game as they do get a lot right - the sheer scale of it, lore, the flavour and character of the factions, the visuals, the diplomacy system... this is a really professionally made game that stands on the shoulders of many grand campaign games before it. But for me, even now over 4 years after release... I still can't get into this one. For me, the fundamental sticking points have not been addressed at all, which is a huge shame.

This is is a "don't recommend" for me - not because it's a terrible game, because it isn't. Simply based on the fact that TW: Warhammer 2 is by some distance still the better game, and your hard-earned money would be far better spent on that.

At the time of writing this, I'm slightly under 200 hours of play time and I've only played maybe three or four campaigns out to a campaign victory. I haven't even gone deep enough into a campaign yet to trigger the end game crisis.

Which does actually lead me to a small point of criticism; for me, this game shines when you're fighting challenging tactical battles. Howver, after a certain point, the campaign game becomes so large and you're fighting battles on so many fronts that you're just autoresolving most fights because you simply don't have the time to fight them all. Which turns the late game turns into somewhat of a box-ticking experience. Although, like I said, I haven't actually reached the endgame crisis point yet so maybe that will change things? The point remains that getting there requires you to spend a lot of relatively uninteresting turns just mopping things up on the campaign map.

Another point against this game is the horrific amount of DLC. Sure, you get a playable version of the game when you purchase the base game. However, a majority of factions you see on the campaign map aren't playable until you purchase their respective DLCs, with even the DLC packs for the previous installments still pretty much going for full price. The other, and in my opinion bigger, issue with this is that, even in the factions you do get access to from the start, you don't get to recruit all of their units. Sure, add a new lord with a new starting location and new campaign mechanics, but locking certain (pretty basic) units behind DLC paywalls just feels bad.

In the end though, especially if you're willing to spend on the DLC, this game offers an insane amount of replayability and lots of ways to play. I don't think I'll go in on the upcoming WH40K game due to previously mentioned DLC practices, but with this game being nearly complete I would say it gets my recommendation.

2. Single entity unit doomstacking - This is a Total War game. You expect Large armies that fight other armies. However because of some factions abilities and magic that I describe as “Wonder Weapons” (looking at you Imrik) that devastate whole units without much warning or time to get them out before they are nuked. Because of this by mid to late game you are incentivized to recruit single entity units as they tend to have High HP pools and can tank the damage. This is not fun and makes me have to cheese to win however I don't see this changing and in fact expect it to expand in the new 40k title. 

3. Factions left without a chance - If you like the Empire, Elves, Dwarves, Cathey, Rats or some Chaos forces then this section is not a big deal for you. If you are a fan of anything else then you will not have seen new content for multiple years more than likely. I could go on but its similar to other factions. 

I could go on but I’m gonna stop here. The game is good but I have glaring issues that need to be addressed especially before the 40K title drops cause if CA doesn’t knock 40K out of the park then the other strategy titles in 40K will eat CA’s lunch.

I’m genuinely shocked I haven’t reviewed this yet, because Total War: Warhammer 2 and 3 are basically my most played games on Steam by an embarrassing margin.

I’ve got about 2,276 hours in Warhammer 2 and 1,476 in Warhammer 3. Now, yes, some of that will absolutely be me leaving the computer on while I’ve gone to bed or wandered off to do something else. But even if you knocked a third off, it’s still very much “sort your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ life out” levels of playtime.

And the reason is pretty simple: these games are masterpieces.

Yes, Creative Assembly have had their ups and downs. Yes, some DLC has been better than others. There have been dodgy patches, balance issues, pricing arguments, all of that. But zoom out from that for a second and look at what they’ve actually created. For a pretty large, even if still slightly niche, group of people, this is basically the dream game.

You get this huge strategic layer that is genuinely engaging in its own right — expanding, diplomacy, economy, building armies, managing heroes, all the Civilization-style stuff — and then you get the meat and potatoes of actually taking those armies onto the battlefield and fighting these enormous battles yourself.

I played Rome, Medieval and the other Total War games and liked them, but it’s hard for historical games to compete with the sheer mentalness of Warhammer. Giant monsters, dragons, undead, artillery, magic, flying units, ridiculous heroes, completely different races and factions. Half the fun is just discovering what new beasties and units you can get your hands on.

And you start getting genuinely attached to your armies as well. You’ve got heroes and lords who have been with you for dozens of turns, they’ve levelled up, you know exactly what they’re good at, and eventually you’re going into battles thinking, “Right, that guy is going on the right and he’s going to absolutely murder that unit.” There’s a bit of that XCOM thing where these stop feeling like random units and start becoming your characters.

Then there’s the actual tactics.

You can go incredibly deep if you want to. There’s definitely a “get good” element, but I don’t think the barrier is that ridiculous. Watch a few decent videos, read a couple of guides and you’ll understand the basics pretty quickly. But after playing for stupid amounts of time, you realise how much depth there actually is.

One of the most satisfying things for me now is walking into a battle where the odds are massively stacked against me and somehow pulling a win out of my arse. I’m obviously not at the level of the absolute lunatic top YouTubers, but there’s a brilliant feeling when you look at the balance of power, know you’re supposed to lose, and then manage to completely turn it around through positioning, match-ups, flanking, magic and generally knowing exactly what your army can do.

And the variety is ridiculous.

Different races. Different factions within those races. Different legendary lords. Completely different campaign mechanics. Different army compositions. Different starting positions. Different enemies.

It’s basically an evergreen game.

If you don’t have loads of money to constantly buy new games, this is almost a no-brainer because the amount of game you can get out of it is absurd. If someone wiped my memory of Total War: Warhammer and stuck me on a desert island with only a handful of games, this would 100% be one of them.

And then you get to the modding.

Jesus Christ.

The modding scene is enormous. New units, new factions, new legendary lords, new campaign mechanics, AI changes, balance changes, graphics, maps, quality-of-life stuff — you can tweak the game to an almost ridiculous degree and basically make your own version of Total War: Warhammer.

I’ve been playing games for about 35 years now. I’m in my 40s, I own around 500 games on Steam, I’ve played vastly more than that over my life, and I’m not somebody who only plays one genre. RPGs, strategy, shooters, tactics, everything.

And Total War: Warhammer is comfortably in my top three games of all time.

So, yeah.

Highly recommended would be putting it mildly.

With the end times upon us, I felt it's probably time to finally review the game for anyone looking to hop in now.

Overall, it's easily one of (if not the best) strategy game of all time. Sure, there are buggy moments *coughcoughsiege*. It is a bit overpriced to get the entire game... But if you're going to actually play the entire game you will easily get your money's worth. If we go on the high side and say it costs 1000$ for all the dlcs, WH 1,2 and 3, than I paid less than a dollar an hour for one of the best experiences in gaming. My hour count will undoubtably end over 1500 by the time I've exhausted every avenue as well.
Plus, you don't HAVE to get the entire game. There are quite a few character packs that won't interest you, and unlike games like Stellaris you aren't missing out on massive gameplay mechanics if you choose not to do so.

Gameplay wise, it's pretty balanced for how large the scope of the game is. It doesn't have major issues with narrowing tactic choices on higher difficulties (W2 melee being dog for example), magic can be broken but also very counterable. AI anti player bias is tweaked with 9.0 and I've heard positive things, but even without them it's only miserable if you blindly attack everything. New endgame reworks keep the game engaging past short victory, which is an amazing change. And if you end up craving more? massive mod community, some with entire game overhauls and some just great quality of life additions. 

Only real downside in my opinion is you do need a decent PC to run it if you plan on having literally anything else open. 

It's the closest game I've ever had to being a 10, and if you're somehow still on the fence I recommend giving it a go. So, so easy to sink thousands of hours into.
